A new hard dataset, built for validation, helps show where description models still fail.
arxiv-2510-19160:
Paimon Goulart and five co-authors test whether a vision-language model can extract mouse behavior from video to help explain fear expression. Sorting behavior by hand is slow, and few programs classify what a mouse does in its environment accurately with little user input.

Using an open model, the team improves classification with careful prompts, labeled examples shown in context, and frame-level preparation of the video. The model outputs a behavior record over time for each mouse and session, forming a dataset for fear research. Each of the added methods raised accuracy, suggesting a cheap route to richer behavioral data.
arxiv-2510-19260:
Mukul Lokhande and four co-authors introduce Res-DPU, a resource-shared processing-in-memory unit for edge artificial intelligence chips. Computing inside memory attacks the bottleneck of moving data between memory and processor, but earlier digital designs wasted area on bulky cells and transistor-heavy adder trees, limiting scale and efficiency.

Res-DPU shares resources through a compact memory latch and small logic gates, cutting the array's transistor count by more than half against leading designs. A redesigned adder tree trims power further. For small devices that must run neural networks on tight power budgets, such savings decide what is feasible.
arxiv-2510-19560:
Yao Deng and five co-authors tackle a mismatch that holds back object tracking systems combining ordinary and event cameras. Standard cameras capture rich texture but limited speed; event cameras react extremely fast and handle harsh lighting, yet record almost no texture. Because the two sensors image the world so differently, their data are hard to fuse.

Their framework, called HAD, transfers knowledge from the combined system to a compact student network through hierarchical asymmetric distillation. The design explicitly models the spatial and temporal gaps between the two camera types, reducing information loss while keeping the student small and fast. Across experiments, HAD beat leading methods, and ablation tests confirmed each part of the design earns its place.
arxiv-2510-19860:
Ketai Qiu and three co-authors present E-Test, a method that grows a software test suite by mining what actually happened in production. Test suites always miss scenarios, and the executions users really trigger are the best guide to what is missing. E-Test uses large language models to spot production scenarios the current suite does not cover, then generates test cases that exercise them.

The evaluation set held one thousand nine hundred seventy-five scenarios from popular open-source Java projects and a defect benchmark. Existing regression and field testing approaches topped out at low F1 scores, and a plain language model did little better, while E-Test reached a markedly higher score. The authors argue the approach cuts the manual effort of keeping suites current.
arxiv-2510-20360:
Tianyi Zhang, Caihua Wan, and Xiufeng Han give signs that flag a phase shift point in magnetic systems from response curves. A known shift point helps dodge sharp breaks and cuts test cost. Broad ways to flag such points for both calm and driven shifts have been scarce. Their signs rest on how the system reacts to a small probe field.

For a calm shift, the still response spikes at the key field. It also shows the shift rank and its power laws, and noise does not hide it. For a driven shift by spin torque, the still sign fails. There the live response at the spin wave tone spikes. Both signs join in one frame of first-order linear systems.
arxiv-2510-20460:
Christian Hobelsberger and four co-authors rate four ways to gauge doubt in large language model replies. Model replies shift in both doubt and truth, so trust is not a sure thing. The four ways are VCE, MSP, Sample Consistency, and the mixed CoCoA way. Tests run on four question tasks with a top open-source model.

Each gauge tracks a fresh side of model trust, the tests find. So the pick among them is not a free swap. The mixed CoCoA way gives the best trust marks on the whole. It lifts both fit of stated trust and the split of right from wrong replies. The team weighs gains and costs and gives pick rules for real use.
arxiv-2510-20860:
Vishaal Udandarao leads eight co-authors on data lessons for pretraining speech language models that answer spoken questions. Several such models have appeared with strong gains, yet without controlled tests of data handling it is hard to know which choices drive the gains.

The team runs a data centric study of raw web audio processing and curation, asking how to clean it, how mixes of sources matter, and how quality filters change results. Controlled ablations separate real drivers from folklore across the pretraining pipeline. Findings give builders a firmer recipe for spoken question answering systems, echoing data lessons that reshaped text and image model training.
arxiv-2510-20960:
Sizhe Rao leads three co-authors on EPFL, a federated learning framework for detecting falls in elderly and disabled people from wearable sensors. Falls cause heavy injury and death worldwide, and detection must stay accurate while keeping personal motion data private.

Centralized systems struggle with privacy, weak generalization, and wide variation in how people move. EPFL joins continual learning, personalized models, and a specialized weighted aggregation rule so sites learn together without pooling raw data. Sequential motion patterns are captured on device, aiming at fall alerts that adapt to each wearer while respecting data limits.
arxiv-2510-21060:
Yi He and one co-author open a theoretical study of sample complexity for differentially private policy optimization in reinforcement learning. Policy methods run in robotics, health care, and language model training, all domains where training data can be sensitive.

A definition of differential privacy tailored to policy optimization is formalized first, facing the on policy feedback loop and the subtle choice of what counts as one private unit. Sample complexity bounds then measure the data cost of privacy in this setting. Early theory here guides how private learning agents can be built without silent overcollection of experience data.
arxiv-2510-21360:
Jenny Kunz builds a question-answering benchmark that tests factual knowledge about Sweden, written by hand rather than translated from American tests. Many translated benchmarks miss facts that matter locally, so models can look strong while knowing little about Swedish people and events that rarely reach foreign media.

The questions draw on a popular radio program featuring figures from culture and media, plus major Swedish sporting events. Each item also appears in English translation, which allows checks of whether a model knows the same fact across languages. Smaller models with heavy Swedish training match a multilingual model three times their size. Extra Swedish pretraining generally helps recall, though it also erases some facts the models once knew.
arxiv-2510-21460:
Sean McGregor and ten co-authors treat benchmark failure as a risk to be managed. Tests that grade large language models steer real deployment choices. Yet bias, noise, thin coverage, or murky reporting can make their verdicts unreliable. A benchmark can mislead a user about a specific use.

The team follows a national risk management process. They study twenty-six popular benchmarks in depth. They catalog fifty-seven ways those benchmarks can fail. They pair the failure modes with one hundred ninety-six countermeasures. Those countermeasures feed a scoring tool called BenchRisk. It rates how likely a benchmark user is to draw a wrong or unsupported conclusion. The rating spans five dimensions. Every benchmark scored carries significant risk in at least one dimension. The authors read that as a map of open problems for model evaluation.
arxiv-2510-21760:
Oleg V. Ponomarev, Sergey V. Kolesov, and Michail A. Nosov recover the lost sense of up and down for seismometers resting on the ocean floor. Instruments lowered to seafloor observatories land at unknown tilts, and every later measurement of ground motion needs that orientation to mean anything, yet no diver can visit to level them.

Their method exploits a direct consequence of Newton's second law. In a certain frequency band, the vertical acceleration of the seafloor tracks the pressure wiggles above it, giving a built-in plumb line from distant earthquakes. Tested on six stations of Japan's S-net during three major quakes, including the 2024 Noto event, the recovered orientations agree with an independent method within about a degree at most stations. The trick serves velocity sensors as well as accelerometers.
arxiv-2510-21860:
Callum Sharrock and six co-authors, Lukas Petersson, Hanna Petersson, Axel Backlund, Axel Wennström, Kristoffer Nordström. Elias Aronsson, present Butter-Bench, a test of whether language models can direct robots through the mess of the physical world. Modern robot stacks let a language model handle high-level reasoning while a separate controller moves the machine, and the bench grades the reasoning layer on its own.

Humans averaged ninety-five percent on the tasks, while the best language models reached only forty percent. The models struggled most with multi-step spatial planning and with reading social situations. Extra training aimed at embodied reasoning did not raise scores. The gap, the authors argue, measures practical intelligence rather than book knowledge, and it remains wide.
arxiv-2510-21960:
Z. Martinez leads a nine-author team re-examining the chemistry of very young galaxies. Telescopes have found compact, distant galaxies with odd readings. Their glowing gas looks rich in nitrogen. But the readings assume the gas is thin. The team suspects dense gas quietly distorts the standard recipes.

The team blends spectra from the Hubble and Webb telescopes. New photoionization models span a huge density range. Thin-gas assumptions in dense regions inflate temperature readings. They also badly skew oxygen and ionization estimates. Nitrogen shifts only slightly. A multi-density model corrects the abundances across the sample. The sample reaches nearly to the dawn of galaxy formation. The work warns that early-galaxy chemistry claims stand or fall on density.
arxiv-2510-22260:
Tianhao Zhao leads a ten-author team teaching dashcam systems to forecast a crash instead of merely sensing one. Accident anticipation usually trains a model to score how risky the current frame looks. The training labels call every frame of a crash video dangerous, even the calm opening seconds, so the model learns from a lie and cries wolf.

The team's paradigm predicts accident scores at many future moments at once, from a tenth of a second to two seconds ahead, supervised by the precisely annotated instant the accident actually begins. A snippet-level encoder reads the space-time dynamics of short clips, and a Transformer decoder with dedicated time queries issues all the horizon forecasts together. A tightened evaluation protocol reports how early a correct warning arrives and how many accidents are caught, the two numbers that decide whether anticipation saves anyone.
arxiv-2510-22360:
Frédéric Bourgeois and co-author Salammbo Connolly study torsion in Legendrian contact homology, an algebraic invariant for Legendrian submanifolds in contact geometry. For knots in three dimensional space, little was known about whether torsion can appear when the homology uses integer coefficients. The pair focus on both the plain linearised version and a two input bilinearised version.

They describe which torsion can occur in the linearised invariant over the integers. For the bilinearised invariant, they give the full geography, meaning the complete range of what can appear. The results close a basic gap about these knot invariants.
arxiv-2510-22960:
Zhangkai Wu leads six researchers tackling gender bias in training-free video editing. When a prompt names a job, such editors often fall back on stereotypes for who appears on screen. Fixing that bias by brute force can break motion and weaken the match to the prompt.

Their system, FAME, adds soft debiasing tokens drawn from minority examples into the text encoder. It also tunes both time-based attention and prompt-to-region attention, with masks and time decay that protect motion. The goal is fairer casting in edited clips while keeping scenes coherent and true to the words given.
arxiv-2510-23560:
Asena Cetinkaya and Sahsene Altinkaya define a new family of analytic functions in complex analysis, built using the Mittag-Leffler function, a classic special function that extends the exponential. Their functions map the open unit disc onto a region shaped like a cardioid, a heart-like curve. Families pinned to a neat target region are a standard way to organize questions about how such functions behave.

Working with a method of Miller and Mocanu, the authors study Briot-Bouquet differential subordinations for this family. A subordination compares two functions through their values and derivatives, giving conditions under which one stays controlled by another. Results of this kind yield bounds and structural facts about the whole family at once. The study adds the cardioid-shaped case, with its Mittag-Leffler twist, to the map of known function classes.
arxiv-2510-23760:
Maxim Dvornikov studies how neutrinos change flavor in external fields, using quantum field theory instead of the usual quantum mechanics. In this approach neutrinos are virtual particles, and their mass states are Dirac fermions. Two settings are covered: matter, which neutrinos feel through weak forces, and a magnetic field acting through a transition magnetic moment.

The work builds dressed propagators for the mass states in these fields. The matter case is trickier for Dirac neutrinos than for the Majorana case treated before, and adjusting the effective potential clears that hurdle. Spin-flavor precession also differs for Dirac particles, since right-polarized states may not be observable. Dvornikov derives the matrix elements and the flavor-change probabilities for both settings. The field theory adds a small extra term to the spin-flavor probabilities, beyond the standard quantum mechanical result.
arxiv-2510-23860:
Hyung Chan Cho and three co-authors test whether a social robot can help college students study alone, acting as a peer companion rather than a tutor. Robots have proven useful in guided learning, but their value during self-study, where focus drifts and motivation dips, was largely unexplored. The team used a Wizard-of-Oz setup, where a hidden human steered the robot's support behaviors.

Students studied under three conditions: a robot giving goal reminders, one giving emotional support, and a control robot that was merely present. Both support styles made the robot feel easier to use, and the goal-reminder group showed the strongest wish to study with the robot again. Satisfaction tracked how much students perceived the robot as a social other, and that perception predicted how well they hit their study goals. The authors argue functional and emotional engagement both matter for study companions.
arxiv-2510-24560:
The XRISM Collaboration, a team of 153 authors, stacks X-ray spectra of ten galaxy clusters to search for unidentified emission lines, including the debated line near 3.5 kiloelectron volts. That line, reported in earlier low resolution studies, might come from the decay of sterile neutrinos, a warm dark matter candidate. The team combines 3.75 megaseconds of early XRISM Resolve observations.

No unidentified lines are detected in the stacked spectrum across the searched energy band. Their upper limit on the decay rate for a dark matter particle near 7.1 kiloelectron volts is three to four times lower than the limit from the Hitomi collaboration. The result tightens constraints on sterile neutrino dark matter.
arxiv-2510-24660:
Arpita Das leads a team with eight co-authors who probe a very cold gas of two part molecules. The parts are rubidium and cesium atoms bound as one unit. With lasers, they map fine splits in the energy levels of a long lived upper state as a magnet field shifts.

Those upper states are hard to reach, since the jump breaks a spin rule and gives thin lines. The team fits the lines to get spin and turn constants for the state. They also watch pulse driven swings to gauge jump strength, and time how fast the upper state gives off light on its own.
arxiv-2510-25060:
Jingzhou Liu, the sole author, tracks how key points split in the loss land of a shallow net with a leaky bent step. The net trains on squared loss, with like width in both layers and bell based inputs. A dial sets how leaky the bent step is on its low side.

With a group based degree tool, Liu sets a frame to spot splits of key points for any width from four up. A multi way split shows at zero for the dial, no matter the width. Splits come just for a dial at zero or more, and the best point stays firm past it in the work range. A five wide case shows the split in full.
arxiv-2510-25160:
Hongjin Qian and Zheng Liu set a new frame for how AI search should hand texts to a large language model. Raw web pages and files are long, loud, and loose in form, so they are not fit for a model to eat as is. Past search just fetched raw spans and left the model to stitch and think.

Their Model-Document Protocol, MDP, marks paths that turn raw texts into model fit inputs for a task. One path has an agent cure raw proof into a joined whole. One path builds notes that can be reused to ground thought. A third path codes texts into set forms. The frame rethinks search as change, not fetch.
arxiv-2510-25260:
Frank Drewes, Berthold Hoffmann, and Mark Minas study ways to state graph properties. Their 2025 paper sits in theoretical computer science. Graphs model networks of nodes and links. Such models appear across many computing fields. The authors present systems of graph formulas with variables. These systems extend earlier graph formulas by adding recursion. Recursion means rules that can refer back to themselves.

Next, they compare those systems with alternating graph automata. These automata extend classic finite-state machines to graphs. They allow both either-or states and must-hold states. The team gives translations in both directions. That proves the two tools have equal power. So logic and machines can describe the same graph languages. The result links two main ways of specifying graphs.
arxiv-2510-25360:
Mario Galici and Alessandro Montinaro classify symmetric designs. Their 2025 math paper studies flag-transitive point-imprimitive designs. Designs here are combinatorial forms with balanced settings. The settings are denoted v, k, and lambda. They focus on cases where v is below one hundred. A complete classification is their main goal.

Apart from known examples, they found new cases. Two non-isomorphic designs with settings 64, 28, 12 appeared. Earlier computer work had constructed those designs independently. Their construction here is theoretical in nature. It relies on an eight-dimensional feature over two elements. That feature comes from the group PSL2(7) action. They prove the full automorphism group is flag-transitive. The group is also point-imprimitive for these designs. Mixed with primitive case results, classification is complete. All flag-transitive designs with v below one hundred are classified.
arxiv-2510-25560:
Antonin Gagnere, Slim Essid, and Geoffroy Peeters control contrastive learning with hypotheses. Their 2025 paper applies knowledge-driven choice to beat tracking. Data ambiguities can produce diverse plausible outcomes. Beat tracking listeners may adopt varied rhythmic interpretations. None of those interpretations is necessarily incorrect musically. Standard training ignores such multiplicity of valid answers.

Hypotheses concern possible positive samples in the data. The model learns features compatible with varied hypotheses. A knowledge-based scoring function retains most plausible ones. Domain knowledge guides that choice process explicitly. Fine-tuning on labeled data follows the pretraining stage. Their model outperforms current methods on standard benchmarks. Integrating domain knowledge with multi-hypothesis choice helps. Music feature learning benefits mainly from this integration. Ambiguous tasks beyond music may suit similar methods. Equally plausible outcomes challenge many machine learning problems. Their method acknowledges ambiguity instead of forcing uniqueness.
arxiv-2510-25660:
Diego Royo led five co-authors presenting mitransient. Jorge Garcia-Pueyo, Miguel Crespo, and Guillermo Enguita helped. Oscar Pueyo-Ciutad and Diego Bielsa complete six authors. Their 2025 paper extends the Mitsuba 3 renderer. Transient light transport adds time-resolved run capability. Conventional rendering lacks a time dimension for light.

Mitransient accounts for time of flight of light. Novel transient imaging systems can be prototyped rapidly. Costly or difficult hardware is not needed first. Python modules run on CPU and GPU hardware. Just-in-time capabilities of Mitsuba 3 enable that. Physically-based runs include realistic materials and media. Participating media like fog or smoke are supported. Time-resolved polarization tracking extends the functionality further. Transient differentiable rendering is also supported now. Tools simplify non-line-of-sight imaging runs greatly. Realistic scene setups with capture noise simulate quickly. The community gains support for transient imaging methods.
arxiv-2510-25860:
Xingjian Zhang leads six co-authors in work on making language models more reliable when they rate the work of others. For subjective tasks, a plain label hides the subtle reasoning behind a human judgment. The reasoning, called a thinking trace, would help train better raters, but traces are hard to collect and clean at scale.

Zhang and the team infer traces from label only data with humans and models working together, using a rejection sampling step to keep good reconstructions. They use the traces to fine tune open raters and to write clearer guidelines for closed raters. Agreement between models and humans rose across data sets, and model to model agreement rose as well.
arxiv-2510-26060:
Sina Keshvadi, working alone, analyzes stability when network users both control congestion and choose among many paths. Path aware networks, such as SCION and proposed satellite fleets, offer endpoints tens to hundreds of verified routes. When multi path protocols greedily chase the best path, wild switching can set off large, lasting load cycles whose cost was poorly measured.

Keshvadi applies a discrete time rule based framework to the joint dynamics and derives the dynamic steady states, stable repeating cycles of the system. He proves a trade off: higher quick response improves fairness but must hurt efficiency and convergence. Efficiency, convergence, and loss avoidance can still meet at one critical lossless point, while limited path view turns cycles into lasting spatial imbalance.
arxiv-2510-26260:
Luis A. Anchordoqui leads one hundred thirteen co-authors in a letter of intent for the Forward Physics Site, a proposed cavern lab downstream of a Large Hadron Collider collision point. The far forward direction carries an intense flux of high energy neutrinos and possibly new grains that current sensors miss. A shielded cavern six hundred twenty seven meters downstream would house four matching sensors.

The experiments, named FLArE, FASERnu2, FASER2, and FORMOSA in the record, target neutrino physics, quantum strong force theory, and space particle physics, and search for dark matter and other new grains. The letter sums up the physics case, site and detector design, team structure, cost estimate, and building schedule for building and installing.
arxiv-2510-26460:
Vinicius F Lisboa, Pedro R Dieguez, Kyrylo Simonov, and Roberto M Serra build a heat engine that runs on quantum rules. A quantum switch lets the order of two steps exist in a blend of both orders at once, rather than one after the other. The team drives energy exchanges with general measurements and asks how starting links between the engine and its controller change the output.

Lisboa and his three co-authors compare three starts: no links, plain classical links, and entanglement, the strongest quantum link. Entanglement let the blended order create coherence in the working medium, and that raised both work output and efficiency beyond the other cases. They also ran a proof-of-principle test on IBM's quantum platform. The run confirmed the predicted gain from correlation-assisted blended order.
arxiv-2510-26660:
Xavier Mary, writing alone in 2025, works on pure math about monoids. A monoid is a set with a join rule and an identity, an item that changes nothing. He builds a new category, a math frame of objects and links, that matches monoids. The frame draws on the Schützenberger category of semigroups.

His frame rests on strict factorization systems, rules that split maps in one fixed way. He then extends the match to unital semigroups, sets with a join rule and identity but looser form. Added maps lift the match to two-level categories. That deep sameness is Morita equivalence, the test the paper cares about. The result helps study when two monoids count as the same in a deep sense.
arxiv-2510-26760:
Jiajie Guo, Feng-Xiao Sun, Matteo Fadel, and Qiongyi He use a measurement trick to reveal delicate quantum links. In measurement-after-interaction protocols, a state is evolved once more before it is measured, a step known to sharpen precision measurements. The team asks whether the same trick can strengthen witnesses, tests that certify quantum correlations are present.

Guo and his three co-authors show it can, for non-Gaussian states, whose statistics do not follow the usual bell curve. Using only linear measurements after the extra evolution, they detect Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering and mode entanglement, two forms of quantum correlation. The approach also tolerates significantly more noise than direct measurement. The work widens what simple readouts can certify in quantum experiments.
arxiv-2510-26960:
Elizabeth Collins-Woodfin and Han Gia Le survey fifty years of work on spin glass models, which describe magnets with mixed, frustrated links. Much past work found the limiting free energy, a quantity that sums energy and disorder, using formulas first given by Parisi. Far less is settled about how that free energy fluctuates around its limit.

The survey covers the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model and its spherical version, plus versions with several species. Results are sorted by heat range and by whether an outside field is present, including results on phase changes. For researchers entering the field, the paper maps what is proven, which methods worked, and where the open gaps in fluctuation theory still sit.
arxiv-2511-00160:
Katherine Rosenfeld, Cliff Kerr, and Jessica Lundin study automating code migration with large language models, focusing on keeping a project compatible as a dependency changes across versions. Software stacks change constantly, and updates can break dependents. Their key finding is that giving the model the diff, the record of what changed in the dependency, significantly improves migration performance over out-of-the-box use.

Metrics include test coverage and change comparisons, and diff context sometimes beats using the code itself. A dataset for the problem is also provided. Software engineering readers get a practical prompting lesson: show the model what changed, not just where the code now stands.
arxiv-2511-00260:
Linzhe Jiang and five colleagues present C3VDReg, a benchmark for matching views inside the colon during colonoscopy. Doctors need to know where a live camera view sits on a stable 3D map, but colon walls look alike, folds repeat, views are partial, and depth data is noisy. The benchmark builds matched point cloud pairs from a colonoscopy video dataset and CT scans.

More than ten thousand viewpoint-matched pairs are included, with a held-out test set and a fixed scoring protocol. Surprisingly, high overlap between views does not yield reliable matching with current methods. The main failure is sliding along the tube-like anatomy, a translation error. Stronger use of anatomy and context, the authors argue, is the way forward.
arxiv-2511-00660:
Antti Tanskanen builds a rich life cycle model of work and consumption in Finland. Such models follow a population of simulated individuals across their lifetimes, choosing jobs and spending under real rules. Finland's wide variety of employment states and life situations demands a large state space, so each agent's circumstances can be tracked faithfully through career, family, and benefit spells.

The model reproduces key statistics of the Finnish labor market. It matches employment and unemployment rates by age, the spread of effective marginal and participation tax rates people actually face, and the share of part-time work. As a policy test, Tanskanen runs the Orpo government's program through the model, tracing its effects on employment and public finances. The simulator turns reform debates into measurable forecasts.
arxiv-2511-00760:
Osamu Fujino, Taro Fujisawa, and Takashi Ono offer detailed notes on acceptable bundles, a notion that plays a basic role in the Simpson-Mochizuki theory in algebraic geometry. Their study concentrates on the case of a punctured disk, a small and concrete setting where the theory can be examined closely.

Partly expository, the notes also go beyond summary. The authors introduce a new invariant for these bundles and give arguments that differ from those used by Simpson and by Mochizuki themselves. For readers working through this difficult theory, the paper provides an alternate route into its core definitions, with the punctured disk case treated in full detail. A second part is announced as a companion.
arxiv-2511-01060:
Andrew Hallam, R. G. Gayathri, Glory Lee, and Atul Sajjanhar work on detecting cognitive workload, the mental effort a person is carrying, from recorded signals. The topic matters in health, psychology, and defense, where overload can be dangerous and underload can dull performance.

Using the COLET data set, they slice the signals into time windows and build features from each window, extending features used in earlier research. Machine learning and deep learning classifiers then assign workload levels. Deep learning models, especially designs designed for tabular data, beat traditional methods on precision, F1 score, and accuracy. The authors argue window based features plus deep learning could support real time workload assessment during complex, changing tasks.
arxiv-2511-01960:
Paul Zivich argues that two cultures of quantitative science can share one language. One culture is statistical modeling. The other is mathematical modeling. Both aim to advance knowledge. Yet each grew its own vocabulary and its own habits of inference. They often talk past each other.

The shared language, Zivich argues, is identification from causal inference. He shows what this view means for reading, comparing, and joining models. A simple pharmacodynamic model of hypertension serves as the example. He also maps where the framework should grow next. The hope is to draw the two traditions into closer conversation. That would extend causal thinking well past its usual home in statistics.
arxiv-2511-02060:
Hersh Sanghvi, Spencer Folk, Vijay Kumar, and Camillo Jose Taylor address a practical problem in drone flight: controller gains tuned by hand for one manoeuvre often perform poorly on another. Their framework, called TACO, adjusts a quadrotor's controller parameters during flight, using the upcoming reference trajectory and the craft's current state. A learned model predicts how candidate settings will perform, and a light optimiser picks gains in real time.

The same machinery can reshape a planned trajectory so the drone can actually follow it while keeping motion smooth. A parallelised simulator let the team train on many trajectory types at once. In tests, TACO beat fixed tuning, ran far faster than black-box optimisation, and flew on a real quadrotor.
arxiv-2511-02160:
Mikayla Fahrenbruch, Anthony Schlimgen, and Kade Head-Marsden fix a subtle flaw in how physicists simulate open quantum systems such as molecular spins. Master equations describe a system leaking energy into its environment, and a common single-particle shortcut can quietly break the rules of fermionic statistics, producing evolution no real system could follow. The authors derive a constraint on the system and environment parameters that prevents this.

They show the constraint for three standard equations: the recently derived unified master equation and universal Lindblad equation, and the Redfield equation where it is otherwise well-behaved. For operators that violate the constraint, they explore adding Pauli factors to restore valid statistics. The goal is trustworthy microscopic simulations for quantum technologies and realistic chemistry.
arxiv-2511-02560:
Dan Bohus, Sean Andrist, Ann Paradiso, Nick Saw, Tim Schoonbeek, and Maia Stiber release a dataset of people being coached through physical tasks by an AI assistant in mixed reality. Eighty-five sessions record untrained participants following a head-mounted agent's guidance through procedural work in the real world. The recordings are rich: the participant's and the system's audio, the view from the headset, depth maps, and tracking of head, hands, and gaze, plus annotations added afterwards.

The collection is small, about fourteen hours, and the authors are upfront about that. Its value lies in being application-driven and interactive, which surfaces research problems that scripted datasets hide: how an assistant should speak, watch, and intervene while someone works with their hands. They plan to build benchmarks for mixed-reality task assistance on top of it.
arxiv-2511-02660:
Qiang Liu, Yiming Liu, Zhi Liu, and Wang Zhou study how the eigenvalues of a volatility matrix spread out when the matrix is huge. Their 2025 paper extends classic random matrix results, which assumed neat independent samples, to spot volatility built from high-frequency price data. That data comes from watching a steady process at close time points.

They derive the limiting shape of the spectrum and a central limit theorem for linear summaries of it. Those results yield workable tests for whether the matrix is an identity or a sphere-like form. Simulations confirm the tests behave well on finite samples. The work gives risk analysts firmer tools for judging fast-moving markets, where volatility shifts from moment to moment.
arxiv-2511-02960:
Sarita de Berg, Jacobus Conradi, Ivor van der Hoog, and Eva Rotenberg solve a guarding puzzle far faster than anyone had before. The contiguous art gallery problem asks for the fewest boundary stretches of a polygon such that each stretch is fully visible from some point inside. Three teams in 2025 each gave methods with roughly the same slow running time, hinting the cost was inherent.

It was not. Their new algorithm runs in time proportional to n log n, a huge speedup over the earlier methods. A simple lower bound, reduced from the set intersection problem, matches it exactly. So the problem's true cost is now pinned down tight, a rare complete answer in computational geometry.
arxiv-2511-03060:
Riccardo Di Sipio, Jairo Diaz-Rodriguez, and Luis Serrano describe transformer language models in the language of Einstein's gravity. In their 2025 framework, queries and keys bend the space of token representations like a metric, and attention moves value vectors across tokens like parallel transport in curved space. Stacked layers act as time slices, and training by backpropagation plays the role of a least-action principle.

An analogy earns its keep only if it predicts something. Their tests show token paths through layers bend and turn in ways not explained by dimension or chance, with turning angles that vary by token and layer. Controlled edits to the surrounding text deflected the paths in meaning-consistent ways, echoing the famous eclipse test of general relativity. The authors present curvature as a real feature of attention.
arxiv-2511-03160:
Everton Abreu, Henrique Boschi-Filho, and Rafael Costa-Silva study how charged black holes in an anti-de Sitter space cool or heat when they expand, a process called Joule-Thomson expansion. Their black holes sit in Kiselev spacetime and carry a quantum correction, and their entropy follows Barrow's fractal form, set by a parameter that measures how rough the horizon is. The 2025 paper asks how that fractal parameter moves the inversion temperature, the point where cooling flips to heating.

The team solves the thermodynamics numerically for many parameter sets. They draw temperature-pressure curves showing how the inversion point shifts, plus isenthalpic curves for fixed-mass processes, the paths along which the expansion actually runs. The work extends black hole chemistry, where such phase behavior mimics ordinary fluids, into the fractal entropy setting.
arxiv-2511-03260:
Rong Wu and Yim-Sang Yu add a heat-flow idea to a medical image model so it can split organs and tissues more cleanly. Models that cut scans into regions often struggle to use wide context without heavy cost. Their design pairs fast long-range modules with operators that mimic heat spreading, placed at the narrow middle of a U-shaped network.

Blurring in that controlled way lifts out broad meaning while fine detail stays in the outer layers. On an abdomen scan data set, the model scored highest among rivals on a standard overlap measure. The authors say mixing state-space reasoning with heat-style spreading gives a path that scales well. It may help hospitals segment scans under real computing limits.
arxiv-2511-03360:
Gianluca Crippa's lecture notes open the theory of mixing in flows that cannot be compressed. Mixing asks how fast a carried dye or heat field becomes uniform under a moving fluid. Two views are set side by side: following single particles, and watching the whole field evolve as an equation.

Scales of mixing give a ruler for that progress toward uniformity. The notes prove floor limits on how fast the scale can shrink, first for smooth flows with energy tools, later for rougher flows with flow-based bounds. New results on whether those floors can be reached close the tour. Students of partial differential equations get a guided path from basic pictures to live research questions.
arxiv-2511-03560:
Thanh Xuan Hoang and colleagues overturn a common belief that breaking symmetry always weakens light trapping in patterned surfaces. In metasurfaces, perfect symmetry can protect states with huge quality factors, and breaking it usually leaks light away. Their finite arrays of Mie resonators behave the other way around.

Breaking symmetry strengthens sideways coupling paths that were dormant before, and quality factors rise instead of falling. Diffractive bands and collective supermodes turn out to spring from the same resonances yet differ in nature. Finite size itself redistributes radiation channels, reversing trends that endless-lattice theory predicts. Designers of real, finite optical chips gain a counterintuitive lever: careful asymmetry as a route to stronger confinement.
arxiv-2511-03960:
Qian Li and Xin Lyu prove lower bounds for testing whether samples come from a uniform distribution when an algorithm reads the data stream several times with limited memory. The tester must separate the uniform case from a planted case where paired outcomes are biased left or right by a small amount.

Any multi-pass tester with constant advantage faces a tradeoff linking its space, sample count, and number of passes to domain size and bias size. A hybrid argument reduces streaming to two-player communication, locating hardness in uncertainty about bias directions. A strong bound for a noisy sign-matching communication task completes the proof, extending a known one-pass result to many passes.
arxiv-2511-04060:
Masato Shimokawa, writing alone, gives a graph criterion for when a partial regression coefficient in a linear structural equation model equals a direct causal effect. Catalog evidence carried a different working title about a back-door criterion; the arXiv record gives the unified criterion title used here, and that record governs.

One broad criterion unifies d-separation, single-door, and back-door conditions, and it is, in general, the exact test for the causal reading. Post-treatment bias is then explained by mechanism and measured in numbers, replacing case-by-case treatments with one framework. Results rest on algebraic traits of acyclic directed mixed graphs, not on any chosen probability law, so they apply broadly across linear models.
arxiv-2511-04160:
Laurits Fredsgaard and Mikkel N Schmidt investigate whether deep ensembles should be tuned jointly rather than model by model. Ensembles improve prediction and uncertainty calibration, yet members are usually trained and tuned alone, even though evidence hints that joint tuning can do better.

Weight decay, temperature scaling, and early stopping were tuned together, and effects on performance and uncertainty were measured across tasks. Joint tuning generally matched or improved results, though effect sizes varied widely. A partially overlapping holdout strategy balances joint evaluation against using data for training. Code was released, and the guidance targets practitioners who must choose how much coordination an ensemble is worth.
arxiv-2511-04360:
Yucheng Wang, writing alone, proposes dynamical translational symmetry as an order principle that joins localization and topological transitions, phase changes famous for occurring without ordinary symmetry breaking. The symmetry is set not by the Hamiltonian but by the long-time motion of local measures, shifting the focus from static structure to change over time.

A time-averaged local contrast serves as the order marker, showing whether change brings back or breaks that sameness. That single value captures Anderson localization, many-body localization, and topological transitions alike, the author reports. Far apart effects become one story: each is the fresh breaking of a dynamical symmetry, pushing phase-change thinking past the equilibrium frame.
arxiv-2511-04760:
Vaibhav Singh and two colleagues study grokking when training data falls below the critical size. Grokking is delayed generalization: a model overfits first, then suddenly grasps the pattern. Below a data threshold, that jump never becomes visible.

Knowledge distillation from an already-grokked model can trigger the jump on a new distribution. It works even when the new data sits below the usual threshold. The team also trains on two distributions jointly to compare plain practice. Their findings matter for deployed models that must adapt to shifted data while examples stay scarce.
arxiv-2511-04960:
Swetamber Das and Jason Green propose new rules for how small volumes move with a flow in phase space, the space of positions and momenta. In chaotic flow, tracked volumes tend to crash flat as vectors line up with the fastest growth path.

That crash is an artifact, not a fact of the flow, so the authors build an update rule from the skew part of the stability matrix. Their rule keeps phase space volume fixed in time, even for systems that lose energy. It also gives a density law much like the quantum Liouville-von Neumann form.
arxiv-2511-05260:
Felipe Abreu and Wei Chen show that a known quantum amplitude works as a generating function for the full quantum Fisher tensor. That tensor holds both the Fisher information matrix and the mean curvature, two gauges of how a quantum state shifts with its parameters.

By taking derivatives of the amplitude, both parts drop out at once. In the pure-state case, their function matches a known geometric tensor form and clarifies fidelity and phase as sources of metric and curvature. The result unifies tools used to bound how well quantum sensors can measure.
arxiv-2511-05360:
Daniel Berio and co-authors fold long smoothing B-splines into a differentiable vector graphics pipeline, so learned image systems can draw smooth paths of any length. Vector art built from short segments tends to look jagged unless a smoothing step is added.

Their linear mapping keeps the whole chain trainable by gradient methods. Derivative-based costs let users trade fidelity for simplicity, and steer style in both shape and image terms. The team shows four uses, from art generation to vectorization work, and the pipeline fits recent tools in both fields well.
arxiv-2511-05560:
Patrick Haller, Jonas Golde, and Alan Akbik build a small language model designed to learn from little data. Their work was done under the rules of the BabyLM 2025 shared task, which limits training material. Their model, BLaLM, swaps normal self-attention for a faster linear-time mixer.

They also test light add-ons such as short convolutions and sliding window attention, plus a curated training corpus chosen for clear, teaching-style text. Adding sliding window attention to the linear mixer raised zero-shot scores on both task tracks. A newer optimizer, Muon, made training steadier and lowered perplexity compared with the standard AdamW optimizer.
arxiv-2511-05660:
Rachel Fernandes leads a large collaboration reviewing how often Earth-like planets occur in the habitable zones of Sun-like stars. That rate shapes the hunt for life, since biosignatures can only be sought where suitable planets exist. Published values still lack consensus, which the review sets out to explain.

The authors define each term that enters the rate, then compile past and current estimates with the limits behind them. They list the many factors in any calculation and show how surveys differ in sensitivity. Pinning the rate down matters for planned missions like the Habitable Worlds Observatory, which will search nearby exoplanets for signs of life. The review maps what must improve before those missions fly.
arxiv-2511-06460:
Fangnuo Wu and colleagues write guidelines for building database indexes on shared memory that is only partly cache-coherent. New interconnect technology lets many cores share memory, but coherence holds only inside core subsets, which breaks assumptions baked into ordinary single-machine software. Indexes, the structures that make lookups fast, must be rebuilt with care for this setting.

One guideline set marks which data must be synchronized and which data stays protected, making existing indexes correct again. A second set attacks the speed bottlenecks that follow, using out-of-place updates, replicated variables, and speculative reads. Two converted indexes gained up to sixteen-fold throughput and beat message-passing and disaggregated rivals.
arxiv-2511-06860:
Hung-Yang Sung and six co-authors build a speech recognition system for Taiwanese Hokkien, a language with little labeled training data. Fine-tuning on Han-character transcripts misses phonetic and tonal detail, while romanized transcripts alone lack vocabulary and syntax coverage. Their system, CLiFT-ASR, starts from Mandarin HuBERT models and adapts them in two stages.

First the model learns acoustic and tonal patterns from phonetic Tai-lo annotations, then it learns words and sentence structure from Han-character transcripts. On the TAT-MOE corpus this staged approach cut the character error rate by about a quarter relative to strong baselines. The authors present it as a parameter-efficient recipe that could transfer to other low-resource languages.
arxiv-2511-07660:
Ayano Moritaka, Shin-ichi Nakano, and Kento Tanaka define fair clustering with exact quotas. Points on a plane carry colors for groups, and each cluster must hold between a lower and upper count of every color. Many earlier methods only approximated such fairness.

For their Euclidean k-center version, the team designs a polynomial-time algorithm that finds an optimal fair clustering. Cost is minimized while every quota holds in every cluster. Exact fairness with provable optimality suits settings like facility placement where representation rules are mandatory. The work shows at least one fair clustering variant admits clean exact solutions rather than heuristics.
arxiv-2511-07860:
Geuntae Park, Jiwon Yi, and Taehyun Rhee walk an avatar with two fingers on a touchscreen. Full-body locomotion control usually needs cameras, suits, or joysticks that break immersion. Finger walking is intuitive, but two sparse fingertip traces must somehow drive legs, arms, balance, and jumps.

TouchWalker-MotionNet generates full-body motion frame by frame from the two-finger input, including airborne running phases. A compact interface maps touches to avatar-relative foot targets. Unlike trigger-based systems, motion is continuous and context aware. Casual users could direct virtual characters naturally on phones and tablets, opening animation and telepresence to non-experts.
arxiv-2511-07960:
Ken Shirakawa, Yoshihiro Nagano, and Misato Tanaka reanalyze a famous brain-to-image study and find its claims inflated. The 2024 work by Koide-Majima and colleagues reported a major advance in rebuilding seen images from brain activity with generative methods. Outside checking tells a different story.

Reported results cherry-picked the best examples at several levels. Circular metrics flattered scores without matching what people perceive. Fair baselines erase the claimed advantage of the key new ideas. The reanalysis is a credibility brief for a hype-prone field: this research needs preregistered reporting and honest metrics before headlines about reading minds.
arxiv-2511-08160:
Argyris Deligkas, Eduard Eiben, Tiger-Lily Goldsmith, and Dusan Knop study fair division of indivisible items when allocations also affect society as a whole. Each agent carries two value functions, one for personal benefit and one for social impact. The goal is to maximize total social impact while keeping the split fair by a chosen criterion, which captures school, housing, and public resource settings.

Complexity hinges on whether agents are socially aware. For unaware agents the problem is NP hard for many fairness notions, with only narrow tractable cases. When agents count social impact themselves, good allocations can be computed in polynomial time, until the awareness definition is relaxed.
arxiv-2511-08360:
Dan Liu, Nikita Dvornik, and Xue Liu introduce SLOPE, a framework that combines structured sparsity with low precision quantization for extreme neural network compression. Big networks are hard to run on small devices, and the two standard shrinking tools are usually studied apart because combining them compounds accuracy loss. SLOPE instead trains with a regularizer that aligns full precision weights with their sparse, quantized versions by angle rather than direct matching.

On ResNet-18 the method shrinks model size about twenty fold while keeping about ninety nine percent of the original accuracy. It beats leading quantization and structured sparsity methods across classification, detection, and segmentation tasks and across several architectures, including a vision transformer and Mask R-CNN.
arxiv-2511-08660:
Miguel Silva and six co-authors test whether a recent dataset can train network intrusion detectors that generalize to attacks they have never seen. The GeNIS dataset is their testbed, and the study is meant to set a baseline for later benchmarks in AI-based network defense.

Five feature selection methods combine to pick the most informative traffic features and shrink the input size. Three decision tree ensembles and two deep neural networks then learn both binary detection and multiclass attack naming. Every model reaches high accuracy and F1 scores. The tree ensembles generalize slightly better than the neural networks while costing less to run, and the results support GeNIS as sound training material.
arxiv-2511-08960:
Luz Ángela García and three co-authors try to guess which galaxies hosted the fast radio bursts whose homes are still unknown. A burst's dispersion measure, the smearing imposed by electrons along its path, correlates with distance, and several formulas compete to turn that measure into a redshift.

The team first compiles an updated catalog of bursts with confirmed hosts, one hundred seventeen unique transients gathered from the literature. Four physically motivated dispersion-redshift relations are ranked with statistical metrics and stress-tested on simulated bursts that follow the observed trends. The winning models then assign probabilities to roughly one thousand unlocalized CHIME bursts, flagging those with at least ninety-five percent probability of living in galaxies already cataloged by the Sloan survey. Future surveys from DESI and Euclid will test the predictions, and an automatic localization pipeline is the goal.
arxiv-2511-09160:
Matteo Bresciani, Mattia Dalla Brida, Leonardo Giusti, and Michele Pepe explain how they computed the QCD equation of state at extremely high temperatures. The equation links pressure, energy, and entropy in quark-gluon matter. Their non-perturbative result, reaching temperatures up to the electroweak scale, appeared earlier in Physical Review Letters.

Two ideas make the calculation feasible: tracking a finite-volume coupling across many energy scales, and shifted boundary conditions that give entropy density directly. The paper covers the numerical strategy for three massless quark flavours between 3 and 165 GeV, plus continuum extrapolation and consistency checks. Final accuracy is about one percent, and the framework extends to heavier flavours and other thermal quantities.
arxiv-2511-09260:
Eleonora Brandimarti asks how the pairing of a bachelor's and a master's degree shapes later earnings, using detailed data on Italian graduates. Students choose both levels, yet returns are usually studied for one degree at a time. She also asks how curriculum features, such as how much quantitative coursework a program has, matter.

Exploiting changes in admission requirements, she causally estimates returns for 43 degree combinations. Returns vary widely even among combinations sharing the same bachelor's degree. Pairings across different disciplines pay better, while same-field pairings perform worse, she finds. Successful combinations carry more non-quantitative content in the bachelor's, and quantitative courses alone do not explain the higher returns.
arxiv-2511-09560:
Shiri Gvishi and twelve co-authors build an interferometer that can finally read the phase of an electron wavefunction in a crystal. Photoemission reads a wavefunction's amplitude well, but its phase, rich in electronic detail, stayed out of reach. Their device uses time- and angle-resolved photoemission as a quantum-path device.

They test it on the Dirac band of a classic topological insulator. The rebuilt phase shows a resonance-linked jump and a matched momentum-phase flip that reveals the Dirac cone's helicity. Because the light's polarization controls the interferometer, phase differences become measurable, a crucial step for reading phase from interference patterns. The conditions needed are common in labs, so many materials could be studied this way.
arxiv-2511-09660:
Ethan Tregidga and three co-authors build a machine learning method that knows when not to trust itself. They then aim it at dark matter. Their goal is measuring dark matter's self-interaction cross-section from images of galaxy clusters. Two simulation suites with different physics provide training domains.

Deep compact clustering maps each cluster into a latent space where simulations form clusters positioned by their physical parameters. A mock observation lands somewhere in that space. If it resembles no training cluster, it lies outside the domain and its parameter estimates are discarded. The algorithm returns confidence estimates alongside parameter values. The authors present the approach as a blueprint for transparent, robust inference in scientific machine learning.
arxiv-2511-10260:
Yongji Zhang, Siqi Li, Kuiyang Huang, Yue Gao, and Yu Jiang present H3Former for fine-grained visual classification, telling apart categories that differ only subtly, such as bird species or car models. Feature selection and region proposal methods often miss discriminative cues or drag in category-agnostic clutter. H3Former instead builds a weighted hypergraph among image tokens, using multi-scale context, so groups of tokens relate at once rather than in pairs.

Hypergraph convolution then aggregates token features into compact region-level representations that carry high-order semantic structure. A second ingredient, a hyperbolic hierarchical contrastive loss, separates classes while respecting the category hierarchy in curved embedding space. Across four standard fine-grained benchmarks, the approach outperformed the compared approaches.
arxiv-2511-10560:
Haosong Peng and ten co-authors present OmniVGGT, a 3D vision foundation model that can actually use the geometric information cameras often provide. Most models of its kind accept only color images and throw away known camera parameters and depth maps, even when those are readily available.

A component called GeoAdapter encodes depth and camera information and feeds it into the model through zero-initialized convolutions. Training therefore stays stable, and inference speed barely changes. During training, random subsets of the extra inputs are sampled for each example, teaching the model to handle any combination at test time. OmniVGGT set state-of-the-art results on depth estimation, multi-view stereo, and camera pose tasks, and it also improved a vision-language-action model on robot benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-10660:
Qihang Zhang and four co-authors blend old and new approaches to lossless text compression. Classic compressors like gzip are fast and universal but leave compression rate on the table, while neural compressors model data better yet generalize poorly to text unlike their training data.

Their framework, a Weighted Product of Experts applied at test time, adaptively combines a universal compressor with a pretrained neural language model. The combination guarantees a compression rate at least as good as the better of the two components on any given input. Experiments show improved compression with no fine-tuning at all, and the method plugs into any autoregressive language model. The authors present it as a practical way to strengthen compression across varied data distributions.
arxiv-2511-10960:
M. Ryzhii, V. Ryzhii, and their colleagues examine how added charge carriers change a sharp switch-like behavior in holed graphene sheets. The sheet is cut into ribbons linked by narrow bridges, and those bridges act as gates for electrons and holes. Heat from the current warms the carriers, which lets more current pass, and that loop can trigger a sudden breakdown.

Doping sets how many electrons and holes sit in each ribbon, so it tilts the balance of that loop. The team shows that this balance strongly reshapes the current-voltage curve. The findings give design guidance for fast switches, light emitters, and heat sensors built this way.
arxiv-2511-11260:
Vilde Lunde, Benedicte Ofstad, and their colleagues measure the electronic and magnetic traits of light rare-earth Laves compounds, a family of cubic alloys mixing rare earths with cobalt and nickel. They use soft X-ray absorption and a magnetic contrast method, backed by density-based theory and crystal field calculations. Such alloys matter because each element carries its own magnetic moment that is hard to separate.

Transition-metal moments saturated under weak fields, while rare-earth moments did not saturate even under strong fields. Nickel carried a small finite moment, against the common assumption that it is nonmagnetic here. Rare-earth moments fell below free-ion values, and the team warns that moment formulas need care with unoccupied state counts.
arxiv-2511-11460:
Qinghao Gao, Jiahui Qu, and Wenqian Dong rethink mixture-of-experts models for remote sensing classification when a sensor channel goes missing. Satellite and airborne classifiers fuse several modalities, and failures or interference often knock one out, which degrades results badly. The authors first study representative expert-based designs under varied missing-modality settings to map their strengths and limits.

Their proposed MaMOL framework unifies all missing cases in one model through a mixture of low-rank adapters. A dual routing scheme splits shared experts, which capture modality-invariant traits, from dynamic experts keyed to whichever modalities are present. Tests on remote sensing benchmarks show strong robustness with minimal overhead, and transfer tests add support.
arxiv-2511-12160:
Wenbin Mai and five co-authors design safe motion planning for many agents moving in changing, uncertain spaces. Agents must coordinate, yet joint decisions grow costly fast, and safety must hold despite random disturbances and model errors. Reactive fixes are not enough when harm must be prevented in advance.

Their framework joins game theory with reachability analysis, framing coordination as a dynamic potential game whose equilibrium gives control strategies. A neighborhood-based iterative method lets agents compute plans from local contacts while keeping convergence guarantees in a finite number of steps. Reachability checks add proactive safety, so the team approach aims to stay both scalable and safe.
arxiv-2511-12260:
Jonas Elsborg, Emma L. Hovmand and Arghya Bhowmik turn the search for the best arrangement of atoms in alloy nanoparticles into a reinforcement learning task. In a two-metal particle, which atom sits where can change the energy a great deal, and the number of possible arrangements is huge. A learning agent can search that space by swapping atoms.

The agent uses a geometric graph view of the particle and keeps the overall composition fixed as it swaps. Trained once on randomized silver-gold particles, it finds the known ground-state structure and stays robust to different starting orders. It also transfers to unseen particle sizes, though its edge fades when more alloy elements are added.
arxiv-2511-12360:
Z. Asmaee, N. Hajirasouliha and K. Azizi calculate tensor form factors for the Delta-plus baryon, quantities that describe its inner structure and how its spin is distributed among its quarks. Form factors are defined through a matrix element of a tensor current between baryon states. A complete and consistent decomposition is needed before numbers can be extracted.

The authors present the full Lorentz decomposition for that matrix element. It includes every structure allowed by Lorentz covariance. It also respects the constraints of the Rarita-Schwinger description, and symmetries such as parity and time reversal. Comparing isovector and isoscalar currents, they find differences that reflect the distinct roles of up and down quarks inside the baryon.
arxiv-2511-12860:
Yongjoo Jang and six co-authors propose running language model token generation inside flash memory itself. Giant models strain ordinary hardware: DRAM is too small and graphics processors are costly. Their design offloads single-batch generation to a 3D NAND flash processing-in-memory device, using its dense storage to hold model weights where computation happens. They re-architect the memory array with an H-tree network and choose array sizes, tiling, and layer mappings tuned for language model workloads.

The reported results are striking: faster generation than four high-end consumer GPUs running a popular serving system, and performance comparable to four data-center accelerators with only a small latency penalty. Their area analysis shows the compute fabric fits beneath the memory array in a few square millimeters. It targets the memory wall that dominates inference cost.
arxiv-2511-12960:
Daivik Patel and Shrenik Patel present ENGRAM, a deliberately simple memory system for conversational agents. Chatbots in production must remember prior sessions, respect user preferences, and ground answers in past events. Existing systems often pile up knowledge graphs and schedulers, hard to build and reproduce. ENGRAM instead stores each conversation turn as a typed record in one of three memory kinds: episodic, semantic, and procedural, all handled by a single router and retriever.

At query time it fetches the nearest records of each type and merges them as context. On LoCoMo, a long-horizon conversational benchmark, it reached state-of-the-art results. On LongMemEval it beat the full-context baseline by fifteen points while using about one percent of the tokens. Careful memory typing plus plain dense retrieval, they claim, does the job of elaborate architectures at a fraction of the cost.
arxiv-2511-13060:
Duo Yi prices two frictions that online decision systems usually ignore: delay and order. In live systems, feedback arrives late, and the sequence of actions changes which observations even appear, so decisions do not commute. Yi takes a Bregman divergence as the loss benchmark and proves a structured lower bound on the excess loss: the ideal loss. Plus a calibrated penalty for latency, plus one for order-sensitivity, plus a term for their interaction, minus a nonconvexity penalty that vanishes under convexity assumptions. The bound extends to prox-regular and weakly convex settings.

Theory is paired with a monitoring recipe: estimate the terms with simple two-by-two randomized experiments and streaming diagnostics such as effective sample size, clipping rate, and interaction heatmaps. The framework folds messy real-world effects into one statement a team can measure.
arxiv-2511-13560:
Benjamin C. B. Symons, Abhishek Rajput, and Dan E. Browne show how to grow endless families of bivariate bicycle quantum codes from covering graphs. Starting from one code, larger and larger covers of its Tanner graph yield new codes with linked structure. Simple algebraic rules on the lattice parameters and defining polynomials decide when a code is such a cover.

Projection and lifting maps between base and cover move logical operators, and sometimes symmetries, in both directions. Many prized codes, including the gross code, turn out to be covers in this sense. A search for weight-eight check codes found new examples, and the authors prove bounds that tie a cover's size and distance to its base.
arxiv-2511-13660:
Dražen Glavan constructs the graviton propagator in de Sitter space for a one-parameter family of gauges. De Sitter space, the maximally symmetric model of an expanding universe, is a standard arena for quantum gravity loop calculations. Most past work used one simple non-covariant gauge, leaving gauge dependence hard to check.

Glavan's family generalizes that simple gauge while keeping the propagator in a relatively compact form. A handy propagator across the family lets researchers rerun one-loop computations under varied gauges and see which results truly depend on the choice. Proposed observables in de Sitter quantum gravity can likewise be tested for gauge artifacts with the new tool.
arxiv-2511-13760:
Xiao Fan and 8 co-authors present MoETTA, a test-time adaptation method for models facing many kinds of distribution shift at once. Test-time adaptation updates a model during use, but real deployments mix natural, artistic, and adversarial shifts whose best update directions can clash. A single shared update path cannot serve them all.

MoETTA routes adaptation through a mixture of experts, giving different shifts separate parameter paths keyed by entropy signals. Two new benchmarks, potpourri and potpourri plus, mix broad shift types and even source-domain samples to test forgetting. Across three mixed-shift settings the method beat strong baselines throughout, setting new best results and showing the value of expert-level diversity.
arxiv-2511-13860:
James Bono reports the first randomized controlled trial of an AI helper for sorting reported phishing emails. Security teams face a flood of user reports and must judge each one fast without missing real threats. The trial tested Microsoft's Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent, giving some analysts the agent and others no help.

Analysts with the agent found up to six and a half times as many true threats per minute, and their verdicts were far more accurate than the control group's. The agent's queue ordering and written reasons drove much of the gain. Helped analysts also spent more time on truly harmful mail and did not just rubber-stamp the agent's calls.
arxiv-2511-13960:
Cooper Bruno, Tiago Cecchi, Joseph A. Pugar, and two co-authors turn CT scans of the aorta into numbers that predict disease. In aortic dissection, the shape of the torn inner channels guides whether a stent repair is likely to succeed. The team defines a descriptor called the topographical pair correlation function, which tracks how surface curvature measures vary together across a meshed scan.

Features drawn from these correlation curves classify cases with high accuracy. When the function is organized by shape index, the area under its curve alone helped reach about ninety-five percent accuracy for disease presence or likely repair success. The method beats single-point shape statistics and may generalize to other anatomical structures.
arxiv-2511-14060:
Arpita Roddanavar, Satoshi Inoue, and four co-authors simulate how a large magnetic flux rope formed during a major solar flare. On September 6, 2011, active region 11283 produced an X2.1 flare with an eruption, a preflare S-shaped structure, a circular ribbon, and distant brightenings. The team ran data-constrained magnetohydrodynamic simulations starting from the measured preflare field.

The simulations show reconnection between the sigmoid field, a neighboring fan dome, and large loops. That reconnection transfers magnetic twist and builds the big flux rope, whose footpoints land where the circular ribbon was seen. The fan-spine structure expands with the rope, matching the observed eruption layout in detail.
arxiv-2511-14160:
Laura Musgrave, Arnab Bhattacharjee, and Tapan Kumar Saha run a case study on cutting a university campus's cooling bill with reinforcement learning. The Australian campus system serves nine buildings and uses about two gigawatt-hours of electricity a year. The team first refreshed the chillers' efficiency curves and built a demand model from historical operating data.

A proximal policy optimization agent then schedules the chillers inside a receding horizon control loop, with a reward function that prioritizes respecting operating constraints. Against the existing reactive rule-based control, the learned controller saved up to twenty-eight percent of electricity just by adjusting chiller bank flow rates, with minimal constraint violations.
arxiv-2511-14360:
Sihan Jiao and 25 co-authors map the Andromeda galaxy's giant molecular clouds in unprecedented submillimeter depth. Using the JCMT's SCUBA-2 camera, the Deep Andromeda survey imaged the nearest large spiral at roughly fifty-parsec resolution, near the confusion limit. The catalog holds hundreds of clouds tied to the spiral arms plus a newly revealed population of compact inter-arm clouds.

Inter-arm clouds turn out systematically lighter, more diffuse, and colder, with lower star-forming efficiency than their on-arm cousins. Even resolved clouds in Andromeda form stars less efficiently than clouds in typical star-forming galaxies, a clue to how galactic environments quench star formation. Combined with older data, the maps also tighten the dust opacity index.
arxiv-2511-14660:
Mauro Di Nasso and Lorenzo Luperi Baglini give a fresh proof of Rado's theorem, a core result about when linear equations must have solutions inside every finite coloring of the whole numbers. The usual route leans on van der Waerden's theorem, a heavy classic result. Their proof avoids that tool entirely.

The argument rests only on basic facts that are common knowledge in the combinatorics of numbers. One standard use of the compactness principle is the single non-elementary step. A cleaner proof matters because Rado's condition marks the exact line between equations that are partition regular and those that are not. Students and researchers gain a shorter path into the theory.
arxiv-2511-14860:
Aashish Ghimire, Jun Zeng, and seven co-authors benchmark twelve modern networks for finding tooth decay in panoramic X-rays. Early and exact outlines of decay guide treatment, but low contrast, varied shapes, and scarce labeled scans make the task hard. The study trains rival designs under the same settings on a shared data set.

Against the trend toward attention-heavy models, a convolutional design called DoubleU-Net scored best on the main overlap measures. Transformer and state-space models trailed in this test. The result is a useful caution for medical imaging: newer and larger designs do not always win, and careful head-to-head tests still matter for clinical tools.
arxiv-2511-15160:
D. Shapoval and M. Dudka compute the critical exponents of a messy magnet: an Ising model with frozen-in structural disorder and interactions that reach across long distances. Near its phase change, such a system falls into a universality class of its own for certain decay rates of the long-range force. The exponents of that class are what experiments and simulations would measure.

Working with field theory and the renormalization group, the authors push the calculation to three loops in three dimensions. Summing the unruly series with resummation tricks yields the correlation length exponent for the relevant decay rates. Sharp exponents let physicists recognize this random long-range class when it shows up in real materials.
arxiv-2511-15460:
Tijn de Vos and Mara Grilnberger study matroids that change over time, as elements are added to or removed from the ground set. A matroid is a structure that captures what it means for a set to be independent, a notion behind many optimization problems. Making that structure dynamic could generalize dynamic graph problems such as matching and measures of how densely a graph can be split into trees.

Their core result maintains a base, a largest independent set, as updates arrive. Building on it, they give deterministic algorithms that keep near-exact estimates of base packing and base covering numbers. The update cost stays modest, and one covering algorithm also works with few queries against an opponent who fixes updates in advance.
arxiv-2511-16060:
Nicholas J. Pritchard, Andreas Wicenec, and three co-authors deploy spiking neural networks on neuromorphic hardware to detect radio frequency interference for radio telescopes. New observatories produce massive data rates needing real-time processing at low power, which rules out many conventional networks. Spiking networks, whose neurons communicate in pulses, fit low-energy neuromorphic chips and suit this existential data challenge.

A greedy maximal splitting algorithm partitions large pretrained networks onto a commercial neuromorphic chip. On-chip measurements reach instrument-scale inference at very low power, and the full model leads spiking baselines in accuracy. Surprisingly, a smaller unsplit model beat larger split ones, showing hardware co-design matters more than raw size and offering a practical deployment blueprint.
arxiv-2511-16360:
Nizar Bousselmi and four co-authors study interpolation conditions for linear operators, the finite tests that say whether a set of observed inputs and outputs could come from a given class of operators. Such conditions underpin worst-case performance analysis of optimization methods.

The authors first show a limit. With only convex constraints on scalar products, one can characterize just those classes whose singular values or eigenvalues lie in a fixed subset of the real line. They then give new interpolation conditions for operators with bounded smallest and largest singular values, and for values lying in unions of subsets. The conditions are used to analyze the gradient method and the Chambolle-Pock method, producing new numerical worst-case guarantees for both.
arxiv-2511-16560:
Tirthankar Sengupta, Bishakh Chandra Ghosh, Sandip Chakraborty, and Shamik Sural tackle a trust gap between blockchains. A single ledger is tamper-proof, so transactions inside one network cannot be denied later. Cross-chain deals have no such protection: a failed or malicious network's partners could deny honest claims or invent false ones.

Their InterSnap system archives snapshots of ledger data together with cross-chain transaction receipts, creating proof of bilateral agreements that neither side can repudiate. Snapshot generation is distributed, scheduling is need-based, and archives live on decentralized storage. A prototype on Hyperledger Fabric, tested on local machines and two clouds, recovered from malicious attacks while preserving the receipts, and kept snapshot transfer overhead small as load grew.
arxiv-2511-16660:
Priyanka Kargupta and eleven co-authors ask why large language models solve hard problems yet fail on easier variants, suggesting their reasoning works very differently from human reasoning. They distill cognitive science into a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements, from reasoning invariants and metacognitive controls to representations and transformation operations.

With that vocabulary they score nearly two hundred thousand reasoning traces from eighteen models across text, vision, and audio. Human think-aloud traces are scored too. Models underuse the elements that correlate with success and collapse into rigid step-by-step processing on ill-structured problems, while humans lean on abstraction. Test-time guidance that scaffolds the successful structures improved performance by up to about two thirds on complex problems. The models own the skills but do not deploy them unprompted.
arxiv-2511-16760:
Eric Vansteenberhge presents the Pioneer Detection Method, a supervisory tool meant to keep insurance markets resilient as climate change makes extreme losses harder to price. In the underlying model, independent experts set premiums from their own risk assessments, but market segmentation and the rarity of extremes make the loss tail hard to estimate for anyone.

The method exploits temporal directional change and convergence among expert opinions, weighting more heavily the experts who spot trend shifts soon after climate stress. Simulations show it outperforms traditional pooling methods inside a Bayesian framework. Welfare in a market with few private insurers improves notably as well. The approach offers regulators a way to learn from the market's best forecasters instead of averaging everyone equally.
arxiv-2511-16860:
Tianyi Shen, Huijuan Xu, Nilesh Ahuja, Omesh Tickoo, Philip Shin, and Vijaykrishnan Narayanan address action reading from body skeletons when parts of the body are hidden. Hidden joints and dropped frames are common in real video, and graph-based models often fail then because nearby context is missing.
