Their model, Parts-Mamba, mixes a graph network with a scanning method that works part by part.

A fusion step then joins the part-level detail with context from far-apart joints, so a visible arm can still inform a hidden leg. The team tests the model on the two large NTU skeleton sets under several kinds of blocking. Reported scores hold up better than rival methods when parts are missing, which matters for real cameras in homes, streets, and clinics.
arxiv-2511-16960:
Shibshankar Dey, Sanjay Mehrotra, and Anirudh Subramanyam study optimization problems where a plan must satisfy a constraint with high probability, even though its coefficients are uncertain. They focus on uncertainty that follows a Gaussian mixture, a blend of several bell curves that can capture varied real-world risk. Their goal is to turn these chance limits into problems a solver can actually handle.

The authors build mixed-binary quadratic programs that approximate the chance constraint from inside and outside, using straight-line approximations of the normal curve. They prove how many pieces the approximation needs for a target accuracy, and show the optimality gap can be made as small as desired. In tests, problems with a thousand random coefficients were solved nearly to optimality, far beyond what sampling methods managed.
arxiv-2511-17060:
Yahan Pu, Lan Wang, Guangquan Zeng, and Lizhi Xie compare how galaxies merge in two versions of the same simulated universe. One run, TNG100, includes gas, stars, and other ordinary matter; its twin includes only dark matter. By matching the same merger events in both runs, at several resolution levels, the team can isolate what ordinary matter does to merger timing and orbits.

Pairs in the full simulation merge sooner after falling together, so their merger timescales are shorter. Their orbits start out similar in both runs but bend toward head-on paths near the end, with smaller collision angles when ordinary matter is present. The authors conclude that baryons speed mergers slightly and make them spiral in more directly, an effect that fades at lower resolution.
arxiv-2511-17160:
Marco Galoppo and Pierre Mourier study a subtlety in cosmology: the universe's clumpiness can feed back on its average expansion, an effect called backreaction. Precision cosmology needs to know whether that feedback also changes how large-scale structures grow. The authors combine spatial averaging methods with gauge-invariant perturbation theory, working with models where matter behaves as irrotational dust.

In their framework, backreaction and dynamical curvature appear as an effective fluid with pressure, added to the averaged dust. They derive the general equations for small perturbations on this effective background and examine two sensible ways to close the system. Applied to four published averaged models, three of which fit observations well, the analysis shows backreaction can matter for structure growth. Ignoring it, they warn, can bias predictions even when the background expansion looks right.
arxiv-2511-17260:
François-Xavier Wicht and four co-authors redesign the reputation system of private file-sharing communities. Private BitTorrent trackers enforce upload-to-download ratios to stop free-riding, but their reputation records are self-reported, unverifiable, and trapped on one server; when a tracker dies, members lose their standing. The authors move reputation into smart contracts and replace self-reports with cryptographic receipts that peers sign for the data pieces they receive.

If a tracker goes offline, peers fall back to a distributed hash table where stored reputation doubles as an access control system, and standing migrates between trackers in one hop. Privacy protections, including ephemeral keys and zero-knowledge membership proofs, address the risks of putting reputations on a public ledger. A prototype added less than five percent overhead, and the hybrid signature scheme cut client signing costs sharply.
arxiv-2511-17360:
Lucas Warwaruk and four co-authors write a practical guide to dripping-onto-substrate rheometry, a technique that measures how stretchy low-viscosity liquids are by watching a thinning filament break. The method is established but lacked clear statements of what it can and cannot measure. The authors define operational limits for reading extensional viscosity directly from the filament's thinning rate, and model-based bounds for extracting viscosity and the extensional relaxation time.

Using dilute polymer solutions, they probe the smallest measurable relaxation times and show values as brief as a tenth of a millisecond can be resolved when two conditions hold. The two conditions involve the fluid's own timescales and the camera's capture rate, a new figure of merit they define. They also test sensitivity to nozzle size and gravity effects. The paper gives experimentalists a quantitative roadmap for trustworthy readings of weakly elastic fluids.
arxiv-2511-17460:
Yuejie Xin and seven co-authors demonstrate a way to clean up leakage errors in a superconducting quantum processor without slowing it down. Qubits sometimes leak out of their computational states into higher levels, creating errors correlated in space and time that undermine quantum error correction. Their leakage reduction unit, adapted from a double-drive reset protocol, runs during the qubit measurement itself. It uses simultaneous drives on the qubit and its readout resonator to steer leaked population back into the computational space.

The unit removed over 98 percent of leakage while keeping state assignment fidelity above 99 percent, and it added no time overhead. Combined with neural-network decoding of the measurement results, it suppressed logical error rates in both memory and stability error-correction experiments, with no post-selection needed. The result strengthens a key practical ingredient of fault-tolerant quantum computing.
arxiv-2511-17760:
Ashley S Dale, Kangming Li, Brian DeCost, Hao Wan, Yuchen Han, Yao Fehlis, and Jason Hattrick-Simpers ask why active learning sometimes fails in materials discovery. In active learning, a model flags the samples it is most unsure about, and those get tested next, on the theory that they carry the most new information. If the uncertainty scores are badly calibrated, though, the campaign can chase the wrong samples.

The team compares uncertainty methods across ensembles of several model types on tasks such as solubility, band gap, and formation energy prediction. Calibration tricks that work on familiar data carry over unevenly to new kinds of material. Their finding is pointed: when a campaign stalls, poor uncertainty far from the training data may be the cause, not the search plan itself.
arxiv-2511-17860:
Lukas Harris and three co-authors design the front optics for tiny lensless fluorescence sensors, which could enable cheap tests at the point of care and imaging inside the body. A filter must block excitation light while letting faint fluorescent light through, but thin filters leak at steep angles.

A fiber optic plate absorbs off axis light and sharpens images. Simulations show that its light gathering angle drives tradeoffs among sensitivity, resolution, and thickness. Two built designs illustrate the range: one is far more sensitive, while the other images three colors at fine resolution over a short working distance.
arxiv-2511-17960:
Tushti Patel and V. S. Prasannaa extend a famous quantum algorithm for solving linear equations, the Harrow Hassidim Lloyd algorithm, from qubits to qutrits, units that hold three states instead of two. More states per unit could mean fewer units for the same problem, if the algorithm still works.

They design the qutrit versions of the needed building blocks and a practical implementation scheme. Tests on simple matrices match expected outcomes, and they apply the method to the energy curve of a hydrogen molecule. For a fixed precision the qutrit circuit needs fewer units and a comparable number of two unit gates than the qubit version.
arxiv-2511-18060:
Francesca Romana Crucinio and Sahani Pathiraja analyze a sampling method that combines two gradient flows into a single Wasserstein Fisher Rao flow. One flow moves particles like a fluid, and the other grows or shrinks their weights. Algorithms in practice split each step, running one part then the other, and the order might matter.

Somewhat surprisingly, with a careful step size and ordering the split scheme can converge faster, in model time, than the exact combined flow. They derive formulas for one step of each ordering and show when each should be preferred. Along the way they prove the combined flow preserves a useful concavity property with a sharp decay bound.
arxiv-2511-18460:
Anupam Gupta and Vera Traub give a simpler, better guarantee for the Steiner forest problem. Given a graph with edge costs and pairs of points that must be linked, the task is to buy the cheapest set of edges that links each pair. For over twenty years the best known bound was a factor of two over optimal, from a 1991 method.

A 2025 breakthrough nudged just past two by a tiny margin, with heavy machinery. Gupta and Traub streamline that proof and push the bound a bit further, to just under two. They keep key moves — a long moat growing run and self sufficient pair checks — and add a submodular search to pick parts to merge. The cleaner proof may ease later work.
arxiv-2511-18560:
Mehedi Hasan, Khayrul Islam, Michael T. Kio, and AKM Masud probe a puzzle in nanotube polymer mixes. A polydopamine coat on carbon nanotubes firms some mixes yet weakens others. The team test if tube curve, joined with the coat, flips the sign of energy flow and grip at the boundary.

Reactive molecular dynamics lets bonds form and break in the simulation, a must for a coat that reacts. Runs vary tube curve and coat state and track how energy crosses the boundary and how load transfers. The aim is the base mechanism: how curve shapes the flow's direction and the bond's strength. A clear rule would let builders pick curve and coat to firm a mix by design, not by trial.
arxiv-2511-18660:
Mostafa Mozafari, Farooq Ahmad Wani, Maria Sofia Bucarelli, and Fabrizio Silvestri remove the harm of corrupt training data when the raw training set is gone. Corrective unlearning scrubs a bad influence after training. Past methods need the named corrupt samples, a forget set, which cannot be built if the source data are lost.

Their method, CUTS, needs only a small proxy set of like corrupt samples, not the true ones. Task arithmetic in weight space guides a light correction: the proxy shows the corruption's direction, and the model steps away from it. The stricter source free setup is stated in formal terms. Light weight fixes suit post hoc repair of fielded models. Corruption is common; a fix that needs no archive is a real gain.
arxiv-2511-18760:
Azim Ospanov and five co-authors build Hermes, an agent that mixes free form math reasoning with checked formal proof. Loose reasoning is fast and flexible, yet it hides gaps. Formal proof in Lean checks each step by a trusted compiler, but it cramps exploration. Past math agents had no sound way to hold both strengths at once.

Hermes interleaves the two: draft steps are checked in Lean mid stream, which halts drift before errors compound. A memory module keeps proof state across long multi step runs. The team bill it as the first tool agent to weave the two modes in this explicit way. Sound exploration is the prize: wild search with a proof net under it.
arxiv-2511-18960:
Lei Xiao and eight co-authors give vision language action robot models a memory of their own past acts. Most such models read each camera frame alone, as if the task had no history. Real control is partly hidden: what was grasped or missed shapes what to do next, so a Markov view misfits the job.

AVA-VLA recasts policy learning for a partly observable world. A recurrent state stands in for the agent's belief over task history and conditions each action. On that state, Active Visual Attention reweights the current frame's visual tokens toward zones that matter given the order and the history. The robot thus looks where its own past says to look. Manipulation skill under partial sight is the aim.
arxiv-2511-19060:
Amir Omranpour and 14 co-authors study oxygen vacancies in cobalt oxide, a catalyst for liquid phase oxidation, by theory and experiment joined. A missing oxygen atom in Co3O4 reshapes its electronic life. Density functional calculations for the bulk crystal show a vacancy turns two near cobalt ions to a lower charge state and narrows the band gap.

The new ions take high spin forms in distorted sites and stay stable in atomistic dynamics at room temperature. Computed X-ray absorption spectra for clean and vacancy crystals match measured spectra well, which makes them a reference for the working catalyst. Fresh and post reaction spectra then show how vacancies act in ethylene glycol oxidation. Defect aware catalyst design is the aim.
arxiv-2511-19160:
Nguyen Minh Duc, Vu Tuan Hai, Le Bin Ho, and Tran Nguyen Lan automate the design of quantum support vector machines with a genetic algorithm. Such machines classify data through a feature map, a quantum circuit that lifts the data into a richer space, but fixed hand-designed circuits often fail to generalise across data sets. Their framework evolves the circuit: candidate maps are bred, mutated, and selected by performance, inside a configurable system where the evolutionary settings can be tuned flexibly.

Tested on digits, fashion images, wine, and breast cancer data sets, the evolved machines reach accuracy comparable to classical support vector machines and to standard quantum versions. Circuits evolved on one data set also transfer to others, the team reports. The work suggests evolution can relieve quantum designers of hand-crafting circuits for each new problem.
arxiv-2511-19460:
Sofiane Ben Amor, Guillaume Guerard, and Loup-Noé Levy present a backbone model of a generic smart grid for testing future scenarios. Modern grids join power systems, energy markets, demand management, and many new assets, which makes them hard to simulate as one whole. A systemic approach treats those parts as interacting subsystems.

The model simulates the separate pieces together so planners can check assumptions before building at human scale. Distributed optimization across subsystems schedules production and consumption while keeping flexibility and room to grow. The tool is meant as a test bench for alternative grid designs rather than a model of one specific network.
arxiv-2511-19660:
Biswaraj Palit and seven co-authors report fresh observations of Mkn 590, a galaxy whose active nucleus has changed its look and is now brightening again. In its rejuvenated state the source has risen together across X-ray, ultraviolet, optical, and centimetre radio bands. The team adds three new optical spectra from the Nordic Optical Telescope and three radio measurements at a standard centimetre frequency from the Giant Meterwave Radio Telescope, gathered since late 2024.

The most recent spectra show a clear increase in the broad hydrogen emission lines that signal fast gas near the central black hole. The core radio brightness also appears to track the X-ray swings, hinting at a link between the inflow of gas and the outflow of a jet. The authors use the data to trace how the gas around the nucleus is evolving.
arxiv-2511-20360:
Dangić proposes a spectral fingerprint for wave-like heat flow in crystals. His 2025 paper studies coherent phonon transport in lattice heat conduction. Phonons are the vibrations that carry heat through solids. In disordered or strongly shaking crystals they also tunnel coherently. Direct proof of that channel has stayed elusive.

Normal particle-like flow fades smoothly with frequency. The coherent part instead produces distinct peaks. Peaks arise when modes share the same wave vector. Copper chloride supplied the test case here. Its frequency-resolved conductivity shows clear non-monotonic bumps. Those bumps match coupled acoustic phonon modes. The effect should appear in all material classes. It grows strongest where vibrations shake hardest. Standard thermoreflectance readings get reinterpreted accordingly. Their usual reading breaks down in such crystals. Measurement routes for the spectrum are sketched. Alloys and glasses are prime targets next. Heat-flow experiments gain a coherence test.
arxiv-2511-20760:
Raffaele Tito D'Agnolo and colleagues propose in 2025 a way to hunt new physics at colliders without guessing what it looks like. A hadron collision fills a detector with hundreds of particles, so each event lives in a phase space of hundreds of dimensions, and the number of possible signals grows exponentially with dimension. Testing them one by one is hopeless. Their idea: measure the intrinsic dimension of the event manifold itself, and watch for new physics to change it.

They compute this dimension with a nearest-neighbour estimator, using the energy mover's distance to compare events, and feed in single particles, not jets. Two properties make the test attractive. It has no look-elsewhere effect growing with dimension, the penalty plaguing wide searches, and it is insensitive to energy-scale uncertainties. On simulated events, the test detected many injected signals. They frame it as a new search foundation.
arxiv-2511-20960:
Soumojit Das, Nairanjana Dasgupta, and Prashanta Dutta build in 2025 a geometric way to make classifiers say 'I am not sure' on individual cases. Calibration fixes average confidence, yet a model can be calibrated and still give no clue which prediction will fail. Their framework treats probability vectors as points on a simplex with the Fisher-Rao metric. An additive log-ratio calibration map generalises Platt scaling to many classes, and a geometric reliability score flags shaky predictions for human review.

Theory backs the method: the calibration estimator is consistent at the usual root-n rate, and reliability scores carry tight concentration bounds for planning test sets. On adeno-associated virus classification, the two-stage system caught 72.5 percent of all errors while deferring 34.5 percent of samples to humans. Automated decision error fell from 16.8 percent to 6.9 percent across the retained cases. Calibration alone barely helped; the reliability score did the work.
arxiv-2511-21160:
Running neural networks inside a database usually forces developers to pick, configure, and babysit models by hand, or accept pricey AutoML detours. Sai Wu and eleven colleagues present MorphingDB in 2025, a task-centric, AI-native database system built as a PostgreSQL extension. Users state the task, and the system stores, selects, and runs models itself. New tensor data types hold models whole or split apart, and a transfer-learning selector embeds past tasks offline, then maps new tasks onto them in real time.

For inference, shared pre-embeddings remove repeated computation, and a graph-based batch pipeline schedules work by cost. Against rival AI-native databases EvaDB, Madlib, and GaussML, plus AutoML platforms such as AutoGluon, MorphingDB won across nine public datasets of several kinds. Inference time fell by more than 70 percent versus EvaDB across three datasets. The authors claim a balance of accuracy, resource use, and selection speed.
arxiv-2511-21560:
Jack Geary, Boyan Gao, and Henry Gouk tackle the cat-and-mouse game between classifiers and the people they classify, in 2025. Deploy a loan or hiring classifier and applicants adjust their profiles to pass, shifting the data the classifier later sees. Learning robust classifiers requires computing each agent's best response, their optimal adjustment. Closed forms exist only for linear classifiers, while real systems are not.

Geary and his coauthors compute best responses by optimizing the Lagrangian dual of the agent's objective, a reformulation that sidesteps the nonlinear math. In linear settings their method reproduces the known best responses exactly, exposing weaknesses in existing schemes. For nonlinear classifiers, the responses plug into both testing, measuring how gameable a model is, and training, hardening it in advance. The work gives the field a practical defense against gaming that can corrupt allocation decisions and fairness alike.
arxiv-2511-21760:
Yuxiang Wei and five coauthors present fMRI-LM, a foundation model meant to understand brain scans through language, in 2025. Multimodal language models already reason jointly over images, audio, and video, but brain imaging has stayed outside that unification. Linking scans to meaning could give neuroscience a shared representation.

The model is built in three stages. First, a neural tokenizer converts functional MRI signals into discrete tokens sitting in a language-consistent space. Second, a pretrained language model learns to predict and describe those tokens, trained on a large synthetic corpus that translates imaging features into structured text, since natural scan-text pairs barely exist. Third, multi-task instruction tuning across paradigms adds high-level semantic skill. Experiments on seven datasets show strong zero-shot and few-shot performance. The model also adapts efficiently with light LoRA tuning, a scalable path toward one universal model of brain activity.
arxiv-2511-21860:
Cavalin and colleagues question trust in headline scores of AI language models on multiple choice tests. A model can answer correctly yet change its answer when wrong options are shuffled, suggesting guessing rather than knowledge. The team proposes CoRA, a score that rebalances plain accuracy by how consistent a model is across such altered versions of the same questions.

CoRA combines accuracy at a required consistency level with an index measuring the gap to perfect consistency. Across several benchmarks, some top-scoring models collapsed when full consistency was demanded. GPT-4o, for example, dropped by at least 0.10 in accuracy and appeared unsure on about 14 percent of the questions it had answered correctly in the reported analysis. A medical model with similar headline accuracy, MedLlama3, ended with a CoRA score less than half its original mark, which they say makes consistency checks mandatory.
arxiv-2511-22060:
Feng, Gan, Gloor, You, and Moran, chemists and physicists, demonstrate quantum key distribution using light from a two-dimensional perovskite, a layered organic-inorganic crystal whose quantum wells emit polarization-encoded photons. Conventional setups steer the photons' polarization with external optical elements. Their method instead lets the material's own exciton spin dynamics and biexciton correlations, probed by four-wave mixing on femtosecond timescales, imprint the information directly onto the emitted signal photons.

With single-photon detection they implement the BB84 quantum key distribution protocol in full, mapping polarization states onto binary bits. They transmit a 56-bit ASCII message through the perovskite's photons. Efficiency hinges on the biexciton states. Near the lower-energy biexciton resonance, one bit needs only about 10 photons, versus more than 50 photons at other wavelengths, showing how spin-dependent nonlinear optics could power future quantum communication hardware.
arxiv-2511-22260:
Woodward, Ribar, and Forsman, theoretical chemists in Australia and Sweden, model a puzzle in salty water. Surface-force measurements show like-charged surfaces in concentrated electrolytes repel each other over ranges that grow when more salt is added, the opposite of textbook screening, a phenomenon called anomalous underscreening. The team generalizes their classical density functional theory so clusters behave like living polymers, chains of variable length and charge arrangement that can polarize near charged surfaces, even forming like-charged bonds.

At full equilibrium the model still predicts only weak repulsion, even with a little like-charged bonding. The anomaly appears only under a global constraint: surfaces may be neutralized solely by dissociated ions while clusters carry zero net charge. Then even a tiny clustered fraction generates strong, long-ranged forces, and if clustering grows with added salt the force strengthens at roughly constant range, matching the experiments' signature.
arxiv-2511-22360:
Xu studies how the eigenvalues of a network behave on very large graphs that grow in a regular way. The graphs are infinite networks whose balls grow like the square of their radius, called quadratic growth. Xu looks at finite balls cut from such a graph. He also looks at a quantity built from the inverse of the Dirichlet Laplacian, an operator measuring how things spread and stop at the boundary.

Under conditions including steady volume growth, a Poincaré inequality, and a uniform local limit theorem for random walks, Xu proves a sharp growth law for this quantity. It grows like a constant times the number of vertices times its logarithm, with a relative error shrinking like one over the logarithm. For the ordinary square grid the constant comes out as two over pi, yielding a new formula that recovers pi without using pi as an input.
arxiv-2511-22460:
Lei and colleagues upgrade the first stage of Tencent's advertising system, the retrieval step shortlisting candidate ads from millions before ranking. The industry-standard design is a dual-tower network: one tower encodes the user, the other the ad, and they meet only in a final similarity score. That late meeting limits how richly user and ad features can interact, hurting accuracy, while richer models are too slow for the whole inventory.

The team brings early feature interaction into retrieval by implementing a Wide and Deep architecture there. A compressed inverted list built for GPU acceleration supports it. This was reportedly the first successful use of Wide and Deep in an industry retrieval system. Offline, the method beat existing approaches by a large margin, and after deployment in Tencent Advertising, including WeChat Moments, it delivered significant online gains in accuracy and latency.
arxiv-2511-22660:
Buahong and colleagues classify graphs drawable as arrangements of see-through rectangles. In a transparent rectangle visibility graph, each vertex is an axis-aligned rectangle. Two vertices are joined when a horizontal or vertical line runs from one rectangle's interior to the other, through any rectangles between, all being transparent. Building on work by Juntarapomdach and Kittipassorn, the authors settle which symmetric graphs admit such drawings.

They prove the complete three-partite graph with three vertices per part cannot be drawn this way, and classify all complete multipartite transparent rectangle visibility graphs. The complement of a cycle's square is not representable once the cycle has at least 15 vertices, and the edges of any multipartite example on n vertices are bounded. Finally, they introduce a variant, intersecting transparent rectangle visibility graphs, and exhibit a graph realisable in the new sense but not the original, proving the variant broader.
arxiv-2511-22860:
Sundar and colleagues build a navigation system for underwater robots, where cameras struggle. Water absorbs colours unevenly by wavelength, turbidity kills contrast, and sensor noise breaks land-proven visual odometry's assumptions. Their framework, MARVO, attacks all three: a front end correcting the physics, a back end fusing extra sensors, and a learned optimiser polishing the trajectory.

At the front, a Physics-Aware Radiance Adapter extends the LoFTR matcher, compensating colour attenuation and contrast loss so matches stay geometrically consistent in murky water. Those matches enter a GTSAM factor-graph estimator alongside inertial factors and barometric depth priors from a pressure sensor, producing full-state estimates in real time. A reinforcement-learning pose-graph optimiser then refines trajectories beyond classical least-squares local minima. Across synthetic renderings and real deployments, MARVO beat SuperGlue, LoFTR, ORB-SLAM3, and LIBVISO2 on accuracy and drift, keeping tracking where classical detectors failed.
arxiv-2511-23160:
Shah and Rebentrost give the first general, deterministic algorithm for finding the full permutation symmetry group of an arbitrary Pauli Hamiltonian. The symmetries are the relabelings of particles that leave a quantum many-body system unchanged and can shrink simulation costs. Their trick is a translation, building a coloured bipartite graph from the Hamiltonian. They prove that the Hamiltonian's symmetry group is exactly the graph's automorphism group, the relabelings that leave the graph unchanged.

For physical Hamiltonians, whose interactions involve few particles and few partners, the graph's degree stays bounded. Bounded-degree automorphism problems are solvable in polynomial time rather than the quasi-polynomial time general graphs demand. The authors verified the method on models with known symmetries, including one- and two-dimensional transverse-field Ising models. They showed that deciding whether two Hamiltonians are permutation-equivalent reduces to the graph isomorphism problem through the same construction in practice.
arxiv-2511-23460:
Paul and Mahadevan show that near-inertial waves, the ocean's near-Coriolis-frequency oscillations. Do more at a surface front than slosh water up and down reversibly, as traditionally assumed. Because submesoscale currents shift the waves' effective frequency from place to place, the surface layer periodically converges and diverges. And strong vertical shear at the front means not all pumped-down water returns, so the pumping can drive net downward transport, or subduction of tracers like oxygen.

In simulations of an unstable front at 1 kilometer resolution, modeled on Balearic Sea conditions from the CALYPSO survey. The strongest wave forcing produced a tracer deficit nearly twice that of the unforced front, direct evidence of net subduction of tracer-carrying water. Spectral analysis shows sub-inertial motions dominate the vertical tracer flux inside the mixed layer, a mechanism coarse ocean models with smoothed winds currently underestimate.
arxiv-2512-00460:
Maria Gorelik and Victor Kac wrote a 2025 paper in advanced algebra on modules over Kac-Moody superalgebras. These are large symmetry algebras that extend the Lie algebras used across math and physics. Admissible modules are a special class of representations, introduced by Kac and Wakimoto in the late 1980s.

That theory grew into a well developed subject with many uses, including the representation theory of vertex algebras. Gorelik and Serganova later set it in a more general frame. Gorelik and Kac now work on quasi-admissible modules in that wider setting. Their results extend a tool kit that algebraists use to sort and build representations.
arxiv-2512-00960:
Boran Wen and a large team work on learning from human-object interaction videos in a 2025 computer vision paper. General robots must learn from many kinds of human activity to work robustly in the real world. Ordinary internet videos of people handling objects are nearly limitless and show huge diversity.

The hard part is extracting accurate, scalable 4D interaction data from such wild footage. That means tracking people, objects, and their contact through space and time. Their monocular method uses a single camera view, which is all most online video offers. Reliable extraction could turn the web's video flood into robot training data.
arxiv-2512-01160:
Ahmad Ali rethinks how atomistic models predict energy in a 2025 paper. Density functional theory estimates the energy and behavior of molecules, but it is slow. Machine learning interatomic potentials approximate those energies and forces at a fraction of the cost. Most are trained as regressors that output one energy number.

Ali explores turning the task into classification instead. Energies are placed into categorical bins, and the model predicts a category rather than a precise scalar. The study asks whether that change improves learning for these potentials. A better formulation could make fast molecular models more accurate.
arxiv-2512-01260:
Far-off bright cores of galaxies can change in light over time. A team led by Andrew Penton and Hugh McDougall used six years of Dark Energy Survey data to track those changes. They looked for delays between light from gas near a black hole and light from the core itself.

The team found clear time delays for a set of active galaxy cores at large distances. Those delays help show how far the gas sits from the black hole. That distance is a key step toward weighing the black hole. The work adds hard cases at high distance where such tests are rare and hard to do well.
arxiv-2512-01460:
Jozef Kubik, Marek Suppa, and Martin Takac improve sentiment reading in scarce tongues. Models for mood in text are weak when data is thin. Full pre-training is too costly for most teams. Gains must come at the fine-tuning stage instead.

The team tests active learning at that stage. The method picks which texts to label next for best gain. Added schedulers guide that pick with more structure. Smart picks can lift mood scores with far fewer labeled texts. That helps tools for news and social posts in tongues with small data sets.
arxiv-2512-01760:
Anurag Bishnoi, Wouter Cames van Batenburg, and Ananthakrishnan Ravi study the chromatic number of finite projective spaces. That number is the fewest colors to paint all points with no line in one color. Projective spaces over finite fields give a clean but deep setting.

Each point and line follows strict incidence rules. Finding the exact chromatic number is hard as dimension and field size grow. Bounds and builds both advance the hunt. The problem links combinatorics, geometry, and coding theory, where line-free colorings have direct kin. Small cases anchor the hunt, since exact values for tiny spaces expose which bound or build will scale to the next dimension.
arxiv-2512-01860:
The biharmonic operator governs bending in thin plates and slow flows of thick fluids, and its boundary value problems are famously delicate. Dirk Pauly and Alberto Valli devote a 2025 note to setting these problems up correctly, so that each one has exactly one well-behaved solution.

They develop variational formulations, which recast the equation as an energy-minimization problem, alongside operator-theoretic methods. Special attention goes to Neumann-type conditions and to over- and under-determined problems, where the boundary data are too many or too few. A careful setup like this is the groundwork that later numerical methods for plates and flows must stand on.
arxiv-2512-02260:
Climate change and habitat loss are redrawing where species can live, faster than conservation teams can survey. Hammed Akande and Abdulrauf Gidado propose EcoCast in 2025, a spatio-temporal model for forecasting biodiversity and climate risk continually, with ecologically rich regions like Africa in mind.

Conservation professionals need timely, high-resolution predictions to decide where to protect land and how to intervene. A continual forecaster updates its risk maps as conditions shift, rather than freezing them at publication. Better forecasts of species movement could help limited conservation budgets arrive before the losses they aim to prevent.
arxiv-2512-02460:
Yifan Zhu and four co-authors study groups hidden inside large graphs, such as friend circles in a social network. Two tasks matter here: finding the best group for one query, and splitting a whole graph into groups. Past learning methods treat the two tasks apart, so each new task needs fresh training.

Their 2025 framework, UniCom, handles both tasks in one shared system. It also pays attention to how tight and cohesive each group is. One tool for both jobs could save time for teams that map communities in real world networks of many kinds. One shared tool also makes results from two labs much easier to compare.
arxiv-2512-02660:
Athos Georgiou improves document search so answers point to the right region, not just the right page. Late interaction models like ColPali embed each page as an image and match query words to visual patches closely. Page level results, though, give generation systems more text than they need.

Text extraction tools give exact boxes but judge relevance weakly. Georgiou propagates patch relevance into regions, joining fine matching with precise location. Region level retrieval could make question answering over manuals, forms, and reports sharper, cheaper, and easier for users to verify by eye. A hit at the region scale gives the writer the lines it needs, not the whole file to wade through.
arxiv-2512-02860:
Abdul Hannan and four co-authors revisit how to match a face with its voice across languages. The Face-Voice Association challenge for 2026 tests matching in a multilingual setting. Evaluation uses English and German face voice pairs, so models must cross language lines as well as sense lines.

Their RFOP method rethinks fusion and orthogonal projection, the steps that merge face and voice features. The design focuses the merger on relevant semantic information in both signals. Cleaner matching supports media search, dubbing checks, and identity tools that must work across borders. Pairs in two tongues are a stern test, since a match must cross both the face voice gap and the tongue gap at once.
arxiv-2512-02960:
Arthur D. Yaghjian revisits the old problem of how a charged ball moves as it radiates energy away. A charged sphere of finite size obeys a modified, causal form of the Lorentz-Abraham rule. Let its radius shrink to zero while the mass is fixed, and that rule turns into the Lorentz-Abraham-Dirac form.

Yaghjian then works out the exact terms on speed and outside force that these rules require. Under those terms, momentum and energy stay conserved, as physics demands. Radiation reaction has troubled the theory of charges and fields for a full century now. Clear terms help sort real motions from runaway artifacts that no lab will ever see.
arxiv-2512-03260:
One pixel of a sky survey telescope gets a careful check. Gregory Jaehnig and co-authors report the spectral traits of a 90 GHz CLASS pixel in this 2025 work. CLASS scans the microwave sky to probe reionization and search for inflation signals.

The survey uses telescopes tuned to four frequency bands. Knowing one pixel's exact response helps turn raw signals into clean maps. Small errors in response can mimic faint cosmic signals. Careful calibration is thus key to claims about the early universe and the physics of inflation. Pixel checks like this one underpin trust in maps made from the whole survey.
arxiv-2512-03360:
Working backward from a goal is a natural way to reason. Qingchuan Li and co-authors build a backward reasoning method for language models in this 2025 work. Most current methods reason forward, step by step from premises to conclusions.

Logical reasoning underpins science, math proof, and complex choices, so its quality matters. The authors translate parts of a problem into symbolic form, but only where it helps. Starting from a hypothesis and seeking premises could make model reasoning more focused. It may cut wasted steps in hard problems. Selective translation keeps the speed of neural reasoning where symbols are not needed.
arxiv-2512-03460:
Cell culture batches need watching to stay on track. Johnny Peng and co-authors compare learning methods for that monitoring in this 2025 work. Real-time monitoring tracks cell density, nutrients, metabolites, and product levels through a batch run.

Early detection of deviations supports timely control actions. Yet data and feedback are often limited in bioprocessing. The authors compare methods that learn from limited data and feedback. Better monitoring protects product quality in medicines and other cell-based goods, where batches are costly. Limited feedback is the norm in plants, where each batch is costly and slow.
arxiv-2512-03560:
Enterprise tasks need agents that plan and use many tools. Gianni Molinari and Fabio Ciravegna present Reason-Plan-ReAct in this 2025 work. Single-agent designs force one loop of planning and execution, which causes instability over long trajectories.

Their design splits roles across a reasoner-planner that supervises a ReAct executor. Separation of duties aims to keep complex tasks on track. Firms want agents that coordinate tools and data sources reliably. A supervised structure may reduce the drift and errors seen in monolithic agents. Supervision adds a check on the executor, which can catch tool errors before they cascade through long enterprise workflows and records.
arxiv-2512-03660:
Katsoudas and co-authors link the shape of aortic aneurysms in the belly to the blood flow tearing at their walls. Seventy-four patient aortas, one of the largest such sets, were rebuilt in this 2025 computer study. Two-scale models couple whole-body flow settings to detailed 3D flow.

From each run they took wall shear measures, plus indices for swing, dwell time, and swirling flow. Matching those against diameter, curvature, and torsion measures showed reliable shape-to-flow signatures. Certain shapes time and again foretold where shear stress would run high or stagnant. Such marks, they propose, could become imaging markers for judging which aneurysms threaten rupture.
arxiv-2512-03960:
Listing every maximal clique in a real-world network can bury the analyst in near-duplicate output. Noga Alon and five colleagues propose summarising instead in a 2025 algorithms preprint. Their object, a rho-dense aggregator, is a small set of dense clusters that together contain every maximal clique in the graph.

Unlike full enumeration, aggregators are guaranteed to stay compact. For any density below one, every graph has one of sub-exponential size. The authors give an algorithm achieving that bound. On sparse networks typical of real data, the algorithm runs in near-linear time and outputs near-linear summaries. A matching lower bound shows the sizes are essentially best possible. Tests on real networks beat the leading enumeration algorithm consistently. Median speedups passed sixfold, and the summaries were far more concise to work with.
arxiv-2512-04060:
In rich galaxies, the mid-infrared sky glows with light from aromatic carbon grains, but in metal-poor galaxies those grains are strangely scarce. Elizabeth J. Tarantino and colleagues look for them with the James Webb Space Telescope in Sextans A, a 2025 preprint reports. That small galaxy holds only about seven percent of the Sun's metal content.

Webb detected and resolved the aromatic features, a first at such low metallicity. The emitting clumps are compact, only a few parsecs across, explaining why blurrier earlier telescopes missed them. Comparing features shows the grains are small and neutral, with little radiation damage. That points to stunted growth, not destruction, as the reason metal-poor galaxies lack these grains. The clumps are probably sheltered pockets where grains grow in place. Aromatic dust, the authors conclude, can form and survive in early-universe conditions.
arxiv-2512-04160:
Perturbation theory, the workhorse of particle physics, can misbehave: its outputs sometimes go negative, refuse to sum to one, or blow up. Rikab Gambhir and Radha Mastandrea propose a repair in a 2025 preprint. Their question is whether a finite-order calculation can be completed into something a measurement could actually produce.

Their Resummed Distribution Function takes any perturbative prediction and resums it. The result is guaranteed positive, finite, and summing to one, while still matching the original order by order. The construction covers every such completion, including known completed forms as special cases. That freedom doubles as an error-bar tool: higher-order knobs can be varied and treated as nuisances. As a demonstration, the authors match the method to the thrust curve at third order. They extract the strong coupling from ALEPH data, with uncertainties from the expansion attached.
arxiv-2512-04660:
Juntong Wang, Jiarui Wang, Huiyu Duan, and co-authors built I2I-Bench, a broad test suite for models that edit one image into another. Image editors improve monthly, yet grading them stays messy. Older benchmarks cover few task kinds, score on thin criteria, and lean on hand labels that cannot scale. Their 2025 arXiv paper answers with a suite built for breadth and repeatable scoring.

The bench spans ten task categories, covering both single-image and multi-image edits. Scoring splits into thirty fine dimensions, each decoupled so a flaw in one trait cannot hide behind strength in another. Automated hybrid grading mixes specialist tools with large multimodal models as judges. The team validated that its scores track human judgment closely. A shared, strict bench lets labs compare editors honestly and spot which edit skills still lag.
arxiv-2512-05260:
Karl Dilcher and Christophe Vignat settle a family of integrals built from powers of the arcsine function. The arcsine keeps turning up in probability and analysis, and its moments — average values of its powers against suitable weights — feed into many series evaluations. Using well-chosen power series expansions, the authors determine, in closed form, the moments of the arcsine raised to arbitrary positive powers.

The consequences fan out. They evaluate several doubly infinite families of power series built from generalized multiple harmonic sums and central binomial coefficients. Specializing the free variable then yields whole classes of numerical sequences, most of them expressed in terms of powers of pi. The paper closes by extracting limit expressions for arbitrary powers of pi itself. One sharp computation thus pays off across a landscape of series that previously had to be handled one at a time.
arxiv-2512-05860:
Jordan Stone and seven co-authors present the fullest spectrum yet of a directly imaged companion that sits between planet and star. The object, HD 33632 Ab, weighs about fifty three times Jupiter and orbits an F-type star. The team observed it with the Large Binocular Telescope in the L band, around three to four microns. Its spectrum now runs from one to four microns.

Matched against free floating brown dwarfs, the companion looks like a late L dwarf, near the border where clouds begin to break up. Cloudy atmosphere models fit it best, as expected. Its precisely measured mass tightly constrains evolution models, including a narrow surface gravity value. Yet the atmosphere fits and the evolution models disagree: the gravity and radius each side infers are in significant tension. Such companions are test benches for cloud physics in giant planet atmospheres.
arxiv-2512-06160:
Wesley Quaresma Cota and Ana Cristina Vieira classify the simplest building blocks in a refined corner of algebra. Their algebras carry both a grading by a finite group and a matching involution, a mirror symmetry like transposition. Codimensions count them by degree. Minimal varieties are the atoms of the polynomial side. Subalgebras of upper triangular matrices have in the past supplied those atoms.

They classify the minimal ones of quadratic growth. The minimal ones assemble into the full classification. The polynomial growth universe is getting its periodic table. The paper fills the quadratic cell for graded involutions.
arxiv-2512-06360: Divyasree Ramachandran gives a fresh proof of a classic result in algebra, Amitsur's conjecture for a family of geometric objects tied to cyclic algebras. Roquette had settled this case long ago with algebraic tools. Ramachandran instead works with shapes, building plain and explicit links between the objects that show the needed sameness directly. The short note offers a geometric route to a result once reached only through heavy algebra.
arxiv-2512-06660:
Saleha Muzammil and four co authors help security analysts hunt threats with small language models instead of giant ones. Analysts query huge telemetry streams in Kusto Query Language, a specialist dialect that takes real expertise to write well. That skill bottleneck slows security teams. The team tests whether small models can translate plain questions into correct queries, cheaply and fast.

They tune three knobs: prompting, fine tuning, and architecture. Error aware prompting, built from a handful of mined fixes for common parser failures, proved strong at low cost. Fine tuning with distilled reasoning traces, surprisingly, did not beat it. The winning design pairs a small drafting model with a cheap larger judge that refines the draft against the database schema. Across nine models, that two stage setup topped syntax and meaning accuracy on a Microsoft evaluation set, beating every baseline at a fraction of the usual token cost.
arxiv-2512-06760:
Y Wei and four co authors strengthen the feeble interactions between neutral atoms in their ground state, a bottleneck for quantum machines built from such atoms. Neutral atoms hold quantum states for a long time, which makes them attractive, but ground state atoms barely interact, and weak interaction caps what simulations and computations they can do. Their trick uses a Rydberg ensemble, atoms excited to huge orbits, driven in a repeating Floquet rhythm.

Each cycle couples the ground states, then pulses atoms up to the Rydberg state and back. Analysis and simulation show the atoms in the ensemble settle collectively into a W state, a shared excitation spread evenly over the group, inside the ground state manifold. Fidelity stays high even when the Rydberg interaction is far below blockade strength. The team also works out its use for single photon sources.
arxiv-2512-06860:
Ewan M Wright and co-authors revisit the acousto-electric effect, where a sound wave moving through a material drags electric charge along and creates a current. Their aim is a fresh viewpoint rather than a new device. They derive an equation for the sound field that resembles an old equation for thick, sticky fluid flow. In that picture, the push and pull between sound vibrations and electrons appears as a loss and gain term.

Building on the new form, the authors connect the effect to two distant topics. One is superradiance, where a moving or spinning body can amplify waves that strike it. The other is the Zel'dovich effect, a cousin idea from work on rotating systems. Such links matter because a good analogy lets results earned in one field guide questions in another. The paper offers its reframing as insight for sound-based electronics and wave physics.
arxiv-2512-06960:
Jitendra K Tugnait builds a method for spotting what changed between two streams of time-dependent data, rather than describing either stream alone. The tool is a graph of conditional independence: links mark which series still relate once all others are accounted for. Many fields track such graphs for independent samples, but real series remember their past, so the graph must live in the frequency domain instead.

Tugnait estimates the difference between the two graphs' spectral precision structures directly, assuming the graphs are similar. He works through a penalized loss with several choices of penalty, some convex and some not, solved by a standard splitting algorithm. Conditions are given under which the estimate provably recovers the true graph in high dimensions. On synthetic data the non-convex version beat both the plain penalized version and an older method that ignored time dependence.
arxiv-2512-07060:
Payam Ghafari and co-authors hunt for fingerprints of dark energy in the oldest light in the universe. Some proposed forms of dark energy can dip to negative density, an exotic twist floated to ease the dispute over the universe's expansion rate. The team tests three models, a standard evolving parametrization plus two that allow negative energy, against the standard cosmological model. Their probes exploit the Integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect, the energy light gains or loses crossing evolving gravitational wells.

They combine galaxy correlations, a lensing-based three-point statistic, and a Planck satellite likelihood built for this effect. The models are nearly twins in the ordinary microwave spectrum at small scales, yet they part ways in the large-scale plateau of this effect and in higher-order statistics.
arxiv-2512-07560:
Carles Checa and Elisenda Feliu wrote this 2025 mathematics paper with roots in chemistry. Polynomial systems often describe how chemical reaction networks behave over time. A key question is whether such a system can settle at several positive steady states.

The authors study a family called vertically parametrized polynomial systems. They give an effective test for whether some parameter choice yields multiple positive zeros. Their method grows out of earlier algorithms from reaction network theory. The hard polynomial question becomes a feasibility check on linear systems. Equalities and inequalities, both linear, decide the answer in practice. The test always gives a necessary condition for multiple zeros to exist. When the coefficient matrix has a certain sparse pattern, the condition is also sufficient. That special case yields a full characterization of the phenomenon. Chemists and mathematicians both gain a practical screening tool.
arxiv-2512-07660:
Amandip Sangha wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on what smoothness really is. A manifold is smooth when overlapping charts fit together in a smooth way. Sangha asks whether tiny packets of information could replace those charts.

His framework uses small-scale entropy data from local probability probes instead. A short list of axioms marks which coordinate functions are allowed. The smooth atlas is then rebuilt straight from the quadratic entropy response. He proves this entropy-smooth structure equals the classical smooth structure. It also survives small perturbations without breaking apart. Products, submanifolds, immersions, and diffeomorphisms all behave as they should. Smoothness, in this telling, is an information phenomenon at heart. The paper lays the foundation for a wider program in his work. That program links entropy, diffusion, and differential geometry together. Geometers gain a new language for an old and central idea.
arxiv-2512-07860:
Mohammed Alruqimi and Luca Di Persio wrote this 2025 finance paper on forecasting asset prices. Pure deep learning can miss the jumps that real markets make without warning. Pure stochastic models can miss the patterns hiding in long price histories.

Their hybrid framework weds the two traditions in one machine. A long short-term memory network reads the sequential side of prices. A Merton-Lévy jump-diffusion model supplies sudden leaps and heavy tails. Tuning that marriage takes several optimizers working in concert. A grey wolf optimizer sets the network's hyperparameters. Three calibration routes for the jump model are compared head to head. Neural networks, a marine predators algorithm, and a software library all try the job. Brent oil, a European stock index, and an Italian index supply real data. The best hybrid beats a standard network and every rival built.
arxiv-2512-07960:
Tri Nguyen, Rutong Pei, Zhuofu Li, and many co-authors wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper. Dark matter subhalos should tug on the thin stellar streams orbiting our galaxy. Reading those tugs could reveal a subhalo's mass, size, and speed.

The team forecasts how well upcoming surveys can pull off that reading. Neural posterior estimation, an implicit likelihood method, does the inference work. Simulated streams come from particle spray models of tidal stripping. One real stream serves as the test case throughout the study. Models are trained under several observational scenarios of differing completeness. Posteriors come out accurate and well calibrated in their tests. With full positional and velocity data, mass errors shrink dramatically. Realistic data still pins masses down usefully, especially in future surveys. A catch emerges: poorly sampled streams split the inferred velocity in two. Big photometric samples plus targeted spectroscopy together resolve that split.
arxiv-2512-08060: Alexis Lucas, a number theorist, posted a short research paper on arXiv in December 2025 about primes in function fields. He studies Wieferich primes for Drinfeld modules, a recently introduced analogue of a classical prime notion, and asks how they relate to Fermat equations. He also asks whether their number is finite or infinite. Lucas then introduces Mersenne numbers for Drinfeld modules and studies the links between these two notions, extending ideas from ordinary number theory into the function field setting.
arxiv-2512-08260:
Ji Yang, Qing Zeng Yan, Yang Su, and a large team of astronomers in China posted a data release paper on arXiv in December 2025. It presents the first release of the Milky Way Imaging Scroll Painting survey, a decade long mapping of the northern galactic plane. Using a thirteen point seven meter telescope, the survey traced three forms of carbon monoxide gas, the standard tracer of cold molecular clouds where stars form.

The release covers more than two thousand square degrees in a three dimensional cube of position and velocity, the most sensitive survey of its kind. From the main cube they built a catalog of over one hundred thousand molecular clouds. Smaller numbers also show the rarer gas forms, marking denser regions. Together, the cubes and catalog give researchers a deep map of molecular gas across the northern Milky Way.
arxiv-2512-08660:
Alexander Bratus, Tatiana Yakushkina, and Vladimir Posvyanski model how new genetic types appear one after another in a population with limited resources. Their model treats the density of types as a flow through mutation space over time. Growth follows a logistic rule, types compete across the space, and the mutation rate can change with time.

When mutations move in one direction only, the authors find exact solutions and formulas for carrying capacity and mutation speed. They study how rising or falling mutation rates shape the spread of the population front. Adding reverse mutations turns the model into a diffusion type equation, and tests show those flows smooth and steady the fronts. The work links to virus change, bacterial adaptation, and tumor growth.
arxiv-2512-08860:
Amit Bendkhale presents Tri Bench, a compact benchmark that tests how reliably vision language models handle spatial reasoning about triangles. Trustworthy agent systems need geometric reasoning that can be verified and controlled. In practice, models often fail when a scene changes in realistic ways, such as a tilted camera or extra objects nearby.

The benchmark uses planar triangle problems and varies two deployment factors: camera pose and interference from everyday objects. A single fixed prompt is used, with a guardrail that describes a surrounding square border to allow a correct projective correction. Six tasks with binary and continuous targets are tested on four recent models. Average accuracy against three dimensional truth is modest, and responses align slightly more with flat image projections. All models fail almost fully on minority shape classes. Camera tilt lowers accuracy, while object interference has no clear effect. Models seem to default to image plane cues.
arxiv-2512-08960:
Yueer Zhou, Yichen Wu, and Ying Wei present PS LoRA, a method to reduce forgetting when a model learns new tasks over its lifetime. Low rank adaptation makes continual learning efficient, but adapters for new tasks often interfere destructively with old ones. Their study shows the damage comes mainly from updates that point opposite to the historical weight direction.

The method resolves such conflicts by aligning updates inside the optimization subspace. A dual regularization objective penalizes conflicting directions and also constrains how far update sizes stray from prior knowledge. A magnitude based merging strategy then consolidates sequential adapters into one robust form without retraining. Tests on language and vision benchmarks show the method beats leading alternatives. It preserves the stability of learned forms while still adapting efficiently to new domains. The work targets a core tension in lifelong learning: staying plastic enough to learn, yet stable enough to remember.
arxiv-2512-09460:
Yu-Ye Cheng and Jia-Rui Sun study an analogue of the black hole information paradox built from sound instead of light. A superfluid flowing around a Schwarzschild black hole can form an acoustic black hole, with horizons for sound alongside the optical horizon. Its analogue Hawking radiation consists of phonons, quanta of sound, emitted from the acoustic horizon.

Using the island formula, a tool for computing entanglement entropy, the authors track how the phonons' entanglement grows over time in both ordinary and extremal cases. In the ordinary case, the entropy follows the Page curve, rising then falling, thanks to the emergence of islands, and at late times it scales with the acoustic horizon's area. In the extremal case the entropy diverges and the Page time becomes ill-defined. The authors say the results verify the analogue system's unitarity and clarify how entanglement entropy connects with spacetime's causal structure.
arxiv-2512-09860:
Aaron Welters introduces the Hilbert space tools behind the mathematical theory of composite materials. Composites mix phases with unlike properties, and effective operators describe how the mixture behaves as a whole. Welters shows the core ideas and main theorems of the field follow from basic operator theory on Hilbert spaces. Central is the Z-problem, an abstract equation built from a bounded linear operator and a Hodge splitting.

The chapter covers direct and dual Z-problems, where the dual view reads the inverse of an effective operator. It states when solutions and effective operators exist and are unique. It also presents the effective operator as a Schur complement, the classic Dirichlet and Thomson energy principles, and a theorem linking multi phase composites to operator pencils. The approach recovers classic results on effective conductivity and extends to elasticity and electromagnetism.
arxiv-2512-10860:
Kehong Gong and co-authors turn a single video into an animated three-dimensional asset. Making explicit 4D meshes from monocular footage is hard, and naturally captured 4D datasets are too scarce to train a general model from nothing. Image-to-3D generators, trained on plentiful data, offer strong priors to borrow instead, if their single-image machinery can be stretched across time.

Their SWiT-4D adds a sliding-window transformer on top of any diffusion-transformer image-to-3D generator. It models space and time jointly across frames. The original single-image pass stays untouched, so videos of any length work. An optimisation-based trajectory module recovers the object's global motion for static-camera footage. Fine-tuning on one short video under ten seconds already gave faithful geometry and steady motion. And on zoo tests, C4D, Objaverse, and wild footage it beat baselines on temporal smoothness.
arxiv-2512-10960:
Ethan Obie Romero-Severson and co-authors report a pilot study that tried to measure how much an AI system helps beginners do real laboratory work. Volunteers with no wet lab experience were asked to carry out a standard task with bacteria in a biological lab. One group could use an AI reasoning model, while a control group had only internet access.

The team recorded who finished each step of the experiment and watched how people used the AI, the web, lab tools, and each other. Their results feed a wider debate about AI and biosecurity, where hands-on skill, not just knowledge, may limit misuse. The study also offers lessons for designing stronger uplift tests in future.
arxiv-2512-11060:
Chenjun Li and colleagues tackle a data shortage that blocks AI reasoning about eye scans used to spot diabetic damage. Vision language models could explain diagnoses in words, but training them needs many images paired with careful text. For scans that map retinal blood flow, such paired data barely exist.

Their framework synthesises realistic retinal vessel images with diabetic features such as vessel dropout, tiny bulges, abnormal new vessels, and twisting vessels. Matching detailed reasoning text is generated automatically alongside each image. The resulting large dataset trained a general vision language model that classified real scans well without having seen labelled real examples. Expert reviewers also judged its explanations and damage localisation on clinical data to be much improved.
arxiv-2512-11160:
Markus Schmassmann and colleagues ask what physically defines the outer edge of a sunspot. Observers usually trace the boundary by brightness, but the magnetic nature of that edge was not fully characterised. They followed one long lived sunspot through two passages across the Sun's face using data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory.

While the spot was stable, a fixed brightness contour matched a fixed magnetic field strength contour almost perfectly. The defining field value is the equipartition field, where magnetic pressure balances the surrounding gas. During the spot's decay passage, the two contours separated as the penumbra vanished, revealing a regime where granulation still works despite a stronger than equipartition field. Comparing with simulations, the authors conclude that a stable sunspot's edge is set by this invariant magnetic threshold.
arxiv-2512-11860:
Yuelian Li and Andrew Rushing Hands build a graph neural network that learns diffusion on crooked meshes without breaking physics rules. Classic solvers are swift on neat grids but can wobble on irregular domains. Yet real coupled processes, diffusion, damage, healing, live on just such meshes.

Their OCGNN-PINN passes messages along mesh edges while a consistency loss enforces the gradient divergence link through the mesh structure. Node and edge dynamics thus stay locked together over time. On evolving physical meshes and scanned real surfaces, the model beat graph and plain network baselines in stability and accuracy. It came close to Crank-Nicolson solvers, the trusted classic, on unstructured domains.
arxiv-2512-11960:
M Scialpi and a large team report first year results from Cosmic Duets, a hunt for double and lensed quasars. They use the MUSE instrument with adaptive optics on a large telescope, reaching very fine detail. Targets came from the Gaia multipeak method, which flags close double sources in the Gaia catalog.

Thirty targets were observed, at redshifts from 0.5 to 3.5. All split into at least two parts. Nineteen proved to be true active galaxy multiples: six dual systems, ten double lenses, and three quadruple lenses. Eleven were chance star alignments. The full program will observe 150 systems and allow firm counts of each type.
arxiv-2512-12060:
Tejas Panambur, Ishan Rajendrakumar Dave, and co-authors present CreativeVR, a restoration system for videos with broken structure. AI generated clips often warp faces, hands, and backgrounds and stutter in motion. Very poor real videos share the same flaws. Classic restorers fix blur and noise, not warped anatomy.

CreativeVR guides repair with a diffusion prior and one control knob: how hard to trust the input. Turn it up for faithful cleanup, down for bold rebuilding of mangled scenes. Training uses a special degradation module that fakes realistic structural failures in a time coherent way. On their AIGC54 test set it leads the field, runs near 13 frames per second at 720p, and stays competitive on standard tests.
arxiv-2512-12160:
Longyu Ma and four co-authors present JAX-in-Cell in a 2025 paper on plasma physics software. Their code simulates charged particles and fields in one space dimension and three velocity dimensions. It is written fully in JAX, a Python library, rather than in older compiled languages.

The code uses just in time compiling and vector tricks to match the speed of older codes on CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs. It solves the Vlasov Maxwell system on a staggered grid, with two solver choices and three kinds of boundary. Tests check it against standard cases. Its built in gradients also let users tune inputs by optimization.
arxiv-2512-12260:
Ege Atacan Dogan and Peter F Patel-Schneider examine ontology design through Wikidata in a 2025 paper. Ontologies are systems for sorting things into classes. Classic design forces each thing into one top class, using splits like abstract versus concrete or type versus instance.

Wikidata breaks that rule. It lets many sorting axes run at once under one root class, entity, so a thing can sit in several hierarchies at once. The authors study what that choice means for building knowledge graphs. They argue the design scales well and suits joint, changing projects where classes evolve over time.
arxiv-2512-12360:
Yufei Yin and five co-authors present VideoARM for understanding long videos in a 2025 paper. Long videos have extended time spans and dense cues in sound and image. Many systems pre-process whole videos with hand built pipelines, using huge numbers of tokens, the units models read, before reasoning can start.

VideoARM instead runs an agent loop: observe, think, act, and memorize, calling tools as needed to inspect the video from broad to fine detail. A layered memory stores clues at many levels and updates as the agent works. On common benchmarks, VideoARM beat the prior top method, DVD. It also used far fewer tokens on long videos.
arxiv-2512-12860:
Aritra Banik and co-authors study the Minimum Consistent Subset problem, which comes from picking a small labeled sample that can stand in for a large data set. Each point in the full set should share its label with a near neighbor in the chosen subset. On graphs, distance is measured by shortest paths.

Past work showed the problem stays hard even on trees, which are simple graphs. The authors give new algorithms based on two graph measures: vertex cover number and neighborhood diversity. Both algorithms run in time that is fixed-parameter tractable in those measures. They stay efficient even when the data uses very many labels.
arxiv-2512-12960:
Tom Gur, Dor Minzer, Guy Weissenberg, and Kai Zhe Zheng prove that relaxed locally decodable codes are strictly stronger than the classic kind, when both use only three queries. Such codes let a reader recover a bit of a message by checking just a few spots, even after some corruption.

They build relaxed codes of near-quadratic length for messages of a given size. Classic codes with the same limits must be far longer, by a known lower bound. That gap settles an open problem from 2006. Their build rests on new checkable proofs that need only three queries, plus a method that turns such proofs into codes.
arxiv-2512-13360:
Shuyuan Xiao and co-authors introduce UCRBench, a benchmark for recovering use cases, the structured statements of what a system should do, from source code with language models. Use cases specify functional requirements, but benchmarks for them were scarce. Worse, existing ones risk drifting from what the code truly does.

Their benchmark was built by hand-checking user-goal and subfunction use cases across nine real software projects, keeping them aligned with actual behavior. A layered scoring protocol checks actor choice, naming, path fidelity, and coverage. Models partly rebuilt system functions but varied widely by project, omitted much, and struggled to keep a steady level of abstraction.
arxiv-2512-13460:
Chethana Prasad Kabgere and Shylaja S. S. present DP-EMAR, a privacy preserving repair system for federated learning in internet of things networks. In federated learning, devices train a shared model without sending raw data. Over unstable multi-tier IoT links, transmitted weights can be silently distorted by interference, harming convergence.

DP-EMAR models typical corruption patterns and reconstructs damaged weights during aggregation, before privacy noise is added. Secure aggregation and differential privacy keep the repair from leaking private data, since the system can tell privacy noise apart from true transmission errors. Tests on sensor and graph data sets kept near baseline performance under corruption, with formal privacy guarantees.
arxiv-2512-13760:
Chunlei Liu counts numbers that satisfy the Collatz conjecture, a famous open problem in number theory. The conjecture concerns a simple iteration on whole numbers that is believed to always reach one. Liu studies the counting function for numbers in an interval that meet the conjecture's condition.

He investigates a related exponential congruence equation and gives a method to build its solutions from free variables. That construction yields at least x to the power 0.3227 Collatz numbers in the interval from 1 to x. The abstract notes the historical record exponent as 0.84, placing his result in a long line of counting work. The paper is brief and focused on that construction and its counting payoff.
arxiv-2512-13860:
Henger Li and co-authors present VGCO, a framework that rewrites tool documentation so language models call tools more accurately. Tool calling lets models act in external systems, but tool docs are written for humans and often mislead models. In industry settings, hundreds of overlapping tools add scale and ambiguity problems.

VGCO uses LLMs as editors in two stages. First, it collects real failure cases and pinpoints where tool context mismatches the tool. Second, it edits the context hierarchically, with state-aware, action-specific, verification-guided editors. Specialization can come from prompting large editors or post-training smaller ones. The authors report large gains in accuracy, robustness, and generalization across models, for the single-turn, large-scale tool-calling case.
arxiv-2512-14060:
A. L. García-Perciante, A. R. Méndez, and O. Sarbach derive general first-order constitutive equations for relativistic fluids. Such equations link dissipative fluxes, like heat flow and viscosity, to the forces that drive them. The work uses the projection method inside the Chapman-Enskog expansion of the relativistic Boltzmann equation.

They generalize the first-order correction to the distribution function to include explicit freedom in the choice of frame and form. The resulting equations couple dissipative fluxes to all derivatives of the state variables, including a weak external electric and magnetic field. Special cases of these force-flux relations have been shown to give physically sound theories for such fluids. The paper appears in a special issue on nonequilibrium thermodynamics.
arxiv-2512-14260:
Anders Eller Thomsen studies renormalization group flow in effective field theories in a 2025 paper. Recent two loop results showed unphysical divergences when computed in an on shell operator basis, which raised doubts about the method itself.

Thomsen shows the problem comes from leaving out non minimal source terms in the renormalized vacuum functional. Those terms are needed to keep the theory renormalizable and to describe how Green functions flow in an on shell frame. With them included, leftover divergences are ambiguous and point only along flavor rotations, which are unphysical. The renormalization group functions are then finite. He also examines flavor rotations and the geometry of the physical coupling space in both on shell and off shell settings.
arxiv-2512-14360:
Ankita Raj, Kaashika Prajaapat, Tapan Gandhi, and Chetan Arora mimic human visual development to train image networks in a 2025 paper. Human infants start with poor visual acuity and slowly gain fine detail, while standard convolutional networks get sharp images from the first step.

Their curriculum starts training on highly blurred images and reduces the blur over time. That pushes the network to learn global structure before fine detail, which helps under distribution shifts and noise. Mean corruption error fell by up to 8.30 percent on CIFAR 10 C and 4.43 percent on ImageNet 100 C versus standard training. The method also stacks well with CutMix and MixUp and improves natural and adversarial robustness.
arxiv-2512-14460:
Arianna Nigioni and four coauthors test the orbital stability of planets formed around double white dwarfs in a 2025 paper. Second generation planets may form in discs of ejected material around such compact binaries, and can migrate to within 1 au of the pair.

Using N body simulations over a few million years, they track resonant and non resonant multi planet systems and record catastrophic events. Two planet systems often survive intact. Systems starting with three, four, or five planets usually lose members and end with two survivors, raising the two planet share by 122 percent. Single planet systems make up 7 percent of the total. Most of those single planet systems, and a handful of multi planet ones, could be detected by the LISA mission.
arxiv-2512-14760:
Afrah Shaahid and Muzammil Behzad present AquaDiff, a 2025 method for repairing underwater photographs. Water absorbs and scatters light unevenly, so underwater shots lose color, contrast, and fine detail. That damage hampers divers, biologists, and robots that rely on cameras below the surface.

AquaDiff uses a diffusion process guided by a color correction step based on how underwater color shifts work. Cross attention blends the damaged input into each denoising step, and a new training loss checks pixel accuracy, perceived similarity, structure, and frequency content at once. On several hard underwater test sets, the authors report better color correction than traditional, CNN, GAN, and diffusion rivals, with competitive overall quality across varied conditions.
arxiv-2512-15160:
Jiaxu Wan and eight coauthors build EagleVision, a video system that reasons about space by choosing what to look at. Judging distances, directions, and layouts from video needs the right frames, yet most models swallow a fixed, evenly sampled set and cannot ask for new views mid thought. Cues that decide the answer may never enter.

EagleVision works in two stages. First, a selection method picks keyframes that jointly maximize meaning and viewpoint diversity within a token budget. Then the model reasons in a loop: it can think in text, or predict a pose on a bird's eye view map and fetch the nearest real frame to check itself. The querying policy is trained by reinforcement learning with a spatial reward, no human traces needed. On VSI-Bench and SQA3D it set the best scores among open vision language models.
arxiv-2512-15260:
André Becker and two coauthors compute exactly how two ultracold atoms scatter off a lattice of light. Kapitza-Dirac scattering diffracts matter waves on a standing light field, a workhorse probe of ultracold gases. What happens when the atoms interact strongly was an open question, since most theory treats one atom or weak contact.

Their two body description is numerically exact: two contact interacting atoms in a one dimensional harmonic trap, hit by a pulsed optical lattice. They map how interaction strength, lattice depth, wave number, and pulse length reshape the diffraction pattern in real and momentum space.
