A common shortcut, the impulsive sudden approximation, is then graded against the exact result. It holds in wide ranges but fails at strong attraction and small lattice wave number. The study gives a controlled benchmark for interacting diffraction experiments.
arxiv-2512-15760:
Zhengtao Jake Gan and Xiaoyu Xie present a tutorial on dimensionless learning in a 2025 paper, dated December 12. Dimensionless learning discovers dimensionless numbers and scaling laws from experimental measurements. Such laws compress messy data into compact physical rules that reveal how variables truly combine.

The tutorial mixes classical dimensional analysis with neural networks. First the method finds the fundamental dimensionless groups, then a network learns which combination predicts the output best. A regularization step pushes learned coefficients toward simple values like integers or half integers, keeping laws readable. The authors study how noise and discrete sampling affect discovery, and list open challenges such as cost and variable selection.
arxiv-2512-15960:
A. Porredon and the DESI collaboration present a joint 3 by 2 point analysis of DESI Data Release 1 with three weak lensing surveys in a 2025 paper. Combining galaxy clustering with lensing correlation functions breaks degeneracies that limit each probe alone. The lensing data come from KiDS-1000, DES Year 3, and HSC Year 3, all overlapping DESI.

The combined fits give S8 values of 0.786 with DES, 0.760 with KiDS, and 0.771 with HSC, each consistent with the others and sitting about 1.5 to 2 sigma below the Planck microwave background fit. One unified pipeline handles all surveys, with an analytic covariance matrix covering every cross covariance. A new blinding procedure guards against confirmation bias.
arxiv-2512-16160:
Joseph D Gelfand and a large team describe glowing clouds around pulsars in a paper posted on arXiv during 2025. A pulsar's spin powers a wind of charged particles. Where that wind slams into its surroundings, it lights up a pulsar wind nebula, a bubble of radio and higher-energy emission.

Studying these nebulae shows how pulsars make electron-positron pairs, boost them to energies above 10 to the 15 electron volts, and spread them into space. Resolved maps of brightness and polarization are the key evidence. The authors explain how the Square Kilometre Array, with far better sensitivity, dynamic range, and timing, could transform this field. Better nebula studies would clarify where some of the Milky Way's highest-energy particles come from.
arxiv-2512-16560:
Chunlei Li and coauthors design codebooks for code-domain NOMA, a wireless method that lets many devices share the air at once with low delay. A good codebook needs many spreading codes with low peak power and low overlap between codes.

The team builds codes from binary Golay pairs, which keep peak power low. The core task is to find large sets of bent or near-bent functions whose pairwise gaps stay bent. Their step-by-step construction gives codebooks with six times N Golay codes of length N, where N is a power of two, and reaches the lowest overlap that is possible in theory.
arxiv-2512-16660:
Moritz Pascal Reiter and a large team lay out a way to study radioactive molecules away from big nuclear sites. Such molecules, built from elements past lead with no stable forms, are sharp tools for tests of physics past the Standard Model.

The scheme harvests radioactive ions fast, even short-lived radium, then runs gas-phase reaction tests in an ion trap with sulfur hexafluoride gas. Singly and doubly charged radium, polonium, and lead ions were tested. One reaction, doubly charged radium turning into radium fluoride, runs at near full yield. That yield makes the route fit for future lab-scale work on parity and time symmetry tests.
arxiv-2512-16760:
Tianshuai Hu and a large team survey vision-language-action models for self-driving, systems that join seeing, language, and driving acts in one model. Older driving stacks split work into perception, decision, and action blocks with hand-built links that break in rare cases and pass errors down the chain.

The survey traces the path from vision-action models to full language-aware designs. It sorts methods into end-to-end systems and dual-system designs that split slow thought from fast control, with finer splits by output type and guidance style. Data sets, benchmarks, and open problems such as robustness and instruction faithfulness round out a map of the field.
arxiv-2512-16860:
Emirhan Zor, Bora Bozkurt, and Ferkan Yilmaz design a decoder for downlink NOMA, a wireless scheme where users share one channel at split power levels. Standard successive cancellation can pass errors along when user powers sit close.

Their design pairs a cyclic redundancy check with GRAND, a decoder that guesses noise patterns in ranked order until a valid codeword turns up. The check bits guide the hunt, so no separate error-correction code is needed, cutting overhead. The strong user also decodes the weak user signal with GRAND aid before cancelling it. Simulations over clean and fading channels show clear bit error gains over past NOMA decoders, a plus for beyond-5G nets.
arxiv-2512-17060:
Monika Zamojska and Jarosław A. Chudziak build language model agents with inner ego states, borrowing Transactional Analysis, the psychology frame that splits the self into Parent, Adult, and Child voices. Plain agents give likely answers but lack the layered motives that drive human talk.

In their multi-agent system, each ego state is its own knowledge store with its own outlook and reasoning style. A retrieval tool lets states pull context from vector stores mid-dialogue. Ablation tests in a simulated dialogue compared agents with and without retrieval. Results look promising, and the authors pitch psychologically grounded structure as a route to richer, more human-like agent behavior in social simulation.
arxiv-2512-17160:
Dianxing Shi and coauthors present LGCLIP, a zero-shot image classification frame that drops the need for hand-labeled image-text pairs. Vision-language models like CLIP lean on such pairs, which cost much to build well, and on dual-tower designs that stay heavy.

A large language model first writes class prompts, and a diffusion model turns them into reference images that serve as visual class prototypes. Real images are then matched against those prototypes by visual features alone, using only a visual encoder. Only class labels enter the pipeline. Tests support the plan as a light, workable route to zero-shot classification, a new paradigm for the task.
arxiv-2512-17560:
Marco Faroni and coauthors tackle a scheduling problem that arises when people and robots share a workspace. Safety rules slow the robot down whenever a person comes near. Those slowdowns make the length of each job hard to predict, which in turn makes planning the work sequence harder.

Their scheduler learns the link between the state of the system and the safety induced speed cuts straight from records of past runs. It needs no prediction of human motion and no prior knowledge of the safety logic. At run time it picks the order of tasks that keeps the total cycle time low while the safety rules stay in force. In pick and packaging tests the approach cut cycle times by a clear margin, which suggests a practical route to faster collaborative robot cells.
arxiv-2512-17660:
João Marcos Cavalcanti de Albuquerque Neto and two co-authors put a quantum-assisted learning machine to work catching credit card fraud. Their data is no toy set: 145 million real transactions from Stone, a large Brazilian payments firm. The model, a restricted Boltzmann machine, learns what normal spending looks like so odd transactions stand out, with a quantum annealer helping it sample patterns.

Run on both real quantum hardware and simulators, the quantum-assisted model beat classical rivals on most scoring measures. That held even though today's annealers are noisy and small. Fraud teams care because catching one more fraud ring pays for a lot of compute. The team frames the work as a path toward quantum help in wider fault detection.
arxiv-2512-17760:
R Abbasi and the IceCube Collaboration squeeze a limit on a ghostly background that clouds their view of cosmic neutrinos. When cosmic rays strike the air, they make charmed mesons whose quick decay yields prompt atmospheric neutrinos. That rain mimics the prized neutrinos from deep space, and its size has never been measured, only modeled with wide error bars.

The team fits two event families in their Antarctic detector together, blobby cascades and long tracks, letting the known backgrounds flex within their uncertainties. The best fit prefers a small prompt signal, yet zero stays within one standard deviation, so the honest product is a cap: at 10 TeV the flux sits below the stated bound. Future cosmic neutrino spectra can now subtract this fog with tighter confidence.
arxiv-2512-18160:
Alex Wilf and coauthors ask whether a language model can train itself to write correct code with no human data at all. Self play has long promised this, but in coding the usual reward, passing unit tests, is brittle: tests miss cases, and errors compound over rounds.

Their framework, Propose Solve Verify, swaps tests for formal verification, which gives a sound pass or fail. A proposer invents problems as formal specifications, and a solver, trained by expert iteration, writes programs that a verifier proves right or wrong. The trained system, PSV Verus, lifts pass at 1 scores by up to 9.6 times over inference only and expert iteration baselines on three benchmarks. Gains grow with more generated questions and more rounds, and tests show the verifier and difficulty aware proposals are the key parts.
arxiv-2512-18360:
Mateusz Lango and Ondřej Dušek let a team of AI agents write a text generator from scratch. The job is turning data triples, the linked facts behind knowledge graphs, into plain sentences. Instead of training a network on human examples, their agents draft rule based Python code, test it, and refine it through talk among themselves.

The finished generator is open to read, needs no labeled training texts, and writes in a blink on a single basic processor. On two standard data sets its output made up fewer false facts than tuned or prompted language models, at a small cost in flow. The work shows agent teamwork can yield clear, old school software.
arxiv-2512-18560:
Kenji Saito proposes a way to prove that sensor data has not been tampered with along the way. Internet of Things readings increasingly drive decisions in logistics, healthcare, and disaster response, yet they pass through untrusted services that could alter them. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and presented at the IEEE Region 10 Humanitarian Technology Conference, builds the proof into the logging itself.

Tamper-evident devices sign their readouts at set intervals and link them with redundant hash chains, so gaps and edits show up. The cryptographic evidence is anchored to a blockchain service through Merkle trees, keeping data verifiable even if some records are lost. The method needs no trust in the systems in the middle. Saito aims it at diverse IoT deployments, including humanitarian work where infrastructure is weakest.
arxiv-2512-18960:
Peng-Long Zhang and seven co-authors propose hunting ultralight dark matter with one of physics' most precise rulers, the Mössbauer resonance. Certain nuclei absorb gamma rays with almost no recoil, giving energy resolution sharp enough to catch tiny shifts caused by a dark matter field washing through the lab. Their feasibility study, posted to arXiv in December 2025, covers dark matter masses from ten to the minus eighteen to ten to the minus eight electron-volts.

Two isotopes are compared, silver-109 and scandium-45, with silver-109 the more sensitive. Projected coupling limits reach about ten to the minus nineteen per GeV for the photon coupling, and even tighter, ten to the minus twenty-two, for the gluon coupling. At low masses the photon reach approaches today's equivalence-principle tests. Table-top Mössbauer setups could thus join the hunt for the universe's missing mass.
arxiv-2512-19060:
Moses Ganardi and Markus Lohrey pin down the exact computational cost of finding Strahler numbers. A Strahler number measures how complex a binary tree's branching is, and it shows up in register allocation for compilers. The tree here is given as a term, a compact symbolic form.

They prove the problem is complete for the circuit complexity class NC1, a standard level of parallel computation. Variants where the tree comes as pointers, a graph, or a compressed program get exact classifications too. For grammar-generated trees, the problem is P-complete, and it rises to PSPACE-complete when the trees must be acyclic.
arxiv-2512-19760:
Nic Brody writes a short note that corrects the record in group theory. In 1999, Long and Reid put forward an action of a surface group on a product of trees. They said the action was proper. A proper action moves points in a controlled way. Only a few group steps can move a point near itself. Such actions are prized, since they certify strong traits of a group.

Brody shows the action is not proper after all. The note is brief, since the point is narrow. A cited construction does not have the trait claimed for it. Any result that leaned on that claim now needs new support. The note stands as the fix in the record.
arxiv-2512-19960:
Luciano Araujo Dourado Filho and Rodrigo Tripodi Calumby attack a quiet saboteur of plant image classification: members of one species can look wildly different from each other. High within-class variability, worse when classes are also rare, undermines fine-grained visual categorization. Their framework, FGDCC, responds by finding structure inside each class before classifying across classes.

Clustering is applied class by class, and the resulting cluster assignments become pseudo-labels encoding degrees of similarity among images. A hierarchical classifier then learns from those finer distinctions, picking up subtle features that separate look-alike groups. Early experiments on the PlantNet-300K dataset still reached state-of-the-art performance even with components admittedly unoptimized, and the authors map which pieces need development before the evidence is conclusive.
arxiv-2512-20060:
Aasim Jan and three co-authors reanalyze the heaviest black hole merger yet seen. The event is GW231123. Its black holes sit in or above the pair-instability mass gap. Plain stellar collapse should not make holes that heavy. Both holes also spin fast. That drew wide notice. But unlike waveform models gave unlike parameters for the same event. That hinted at physics missing from the templates in use.

The team reran the case with a fuller model. It covers spin precession and orbital eccentricity at once. They find no strong sign of eccentricity. Dropping it barely moves the results. Even large eccentricity would be hard to certify in such systems. Fake-signal checks pin the model clash on strong spin precession. They also warn that one class of model can fake eccentricity, though model choice tests reject that read.
arxiv-2512-20160:
Dhruv Ringe's doctoral thesis asks how gravitational waves from the early universe can test particle physics models. The signals of interest come from first-order phase transitions and from topological defects called domain walls. Such events would leave a faint background hum that future observatories might detect.

Ringe works through several theories beyond the Standard Model, including Froggatt-Nielsen flavour models and a doublet left-right symmetric model. For each, he maps which parameter values upcoming detectors such as BBO and DECIGO could rule in or out. He also fits domain-wall signals to fifteen years of NANOGrav pulsar timing data. The methods developed here transfer to other early-universe scenarios.
arxiv-2512-20260:
Jiawei Ge and co-authors detect camouflaged objects in images when only scribble annotations are available for training. Scribbles are cheap to draw but sparse, and they bias models toward marked regions. General segmentation models such as SAM can propose full masks, yet they lack the task-specific understanding that hidden objects require.

Their approach, called D3ETOR, works in two stages. A multi-agent debate mechanism plus entropy-driven point sampling improves the pseudo masks that SAM produces. A second network, FADeNet, then fuses frequency-aware features at several levels and reweights supervision across regions to counter scribble bias. Combined, the stages narrow the gap to fully supervised detection and reach leading results on several benchmarks.
arxiv-2512-20360:
Benoit Cadorel, Ya Deng, and Katsutoshi Yamanoi close a three-part study of complex quasi-projective shapes, spaces cut out by polynomial rules with some pieces removed. This last part puts the earlier machinery to work. It defines h-special shapes, those linked in chains by the closures of whole curves, a cousin of Campana's special shapes in the holomorphic world.

The main result says that for special or h-special shapes, the image of the basic loop group under any linear map into matrices is virtually nilpotent. Cases show the claim is sharp, which forces a revised form of Campana's abelianity guess. A structure theorem for shapes with big, semisimple maps answers a 1995 question of Kollár. New cases also show how the non-compact world behaves unlike the projective one.
arxiv-2512-20460:
Ilias Aarab asks whether the stock market's risk premium is predictable, and answers: it depends on the economic weather. A growing literature finds forecasting power concentrated near recessions. Aarab defines the market state in real time from the slope of the yield curve and lets predictability switch with it.

Against the standard single-regime regression, the state-switching version improves both in-sample and out-of-sample performance for the classic Welch and Goyal predictors. Most predictors gain in economically meaningful ways. Aarab also builds a new aggregate predictor, the Aligned Economic Index, using partial least squares. Inside the switching model it predicts returns significantly in and out of sample, beating popular benchmarks and other combination methods.
arxiv-2512-20560:
M Cadeddu and co-authors revisit a thirty-year-old neutrino puzzle. Experiments GALLEX, SAGE, and BEST measured neutrinos captured by gallium-71 from radioactive sources and found about twenty percent fewer than predicted, a deficit now beyond five sigma. Either the experiments, the theory, or neutrino physics itself must give.

The authors reexamine the cross-section maths. The standard treatment factorizes the leptonic wave functions using detailed balance, and they show that shortcut has real limitations. Feeding in Gamow-Teller transition densities constrained by the well-measured germanium-71 half-life changes the answer. The revised cross-section drops sharply, perhaps erasing the anomaly with ordinary physics. The gallium anomaly may be an artefact of the maths after all.
arxiv-2512-21460:
Masaya Nishihata and Suguru Otani ask whether the chemistry between teammates matters differently for different skills. In team production, output depends on each member's ability and on an unobserved affinity, the match quality between the people working together. The authors want to separate those ingredients without assuming a rigid formula for how they combine.

They build a nonparametric framework that allows for task structure, asymmetric roles, and hidden affinity, then split team performance into skill-specific productivity and match effects. As a test case they use elite women's bobsleigh, where a run divides naturally into a start phase and a riding phase drawing on different skills. The estimates show coordination and complementarity are stronger at the start. During riding, affinities are weaker and more spread out. The lesson is that team fit is not a single trait but varies skill by skill, which matters for how teams should be assembled.
arxiv-2512-22260:
Chen Chen, Daniela Kaufmann, and four co-authors present ReVEAL, a method that helps prove hardware multipliers correct. Algebraic checking methods struggle with large, heavily optimized multiplier circuits because they cannot see the hidden design. ReVEAL reverse-engineers that design using graph learning, reading structural cues of the circuit graph to recognize design patterns at scale.

The system was demonstrated across diverse multiplier benchmarks, where it improved both scaling and accuracy compared with older rule-based approaches. It also integrates smoothly with current checking flows. By recovering the architecture, ReVEAL supports the downstream algebraic proof strategies that finish the checking job. The work targets a practical bottleneck in chip design, where optimized arithmetic blocks resist standard checking tools.
arxiv-2512-22360:
Ivan Karpov and Miguel Moreira define new counting invariants for objects in an abelian category and prove they behave predictably as stability conditions change. Their construction starts from the stack of objects itself. They put a new associative algebra structure, the K-Hall algebra, on the K-homology of that stack, then extract invariants by taking formal logarithms of contributions from semistable objects.

Wall-crossing formulas, which say exactly how the invariants jump when stability crosses a wall, are proved using the non-abelian localization theorem. The results extend earlier Joyce and Liu theory, which needed a framing functor, to non-standard hearts of derived categories where such functors are unknown. When both definitions apply, the authors show they agree.
arxiv-2512-22560:
Wei Gao and a large team at Alibaba present ROLLART, a system for training AI agents with reinforcement learning at industrial scale. Agentic training mixes heavy prefill computation, bandwidth-bound decoding, CPU-bound environment simulation, and bursty reward scoring. Current systems either cram all stages onto one GPU cluster or split them too coarsely. Both choices waste hardware and synchronization time.

ROLLART assigns each stage to best-fit hardware: compute-optimized GPUs for prefill, bandwidth-optimized ones for decoding, and CPU clusters for environments. Rollout is decoupled at the trajectory level so slow environments never block others, and stateless reward work runs on serverless infrastructure. Training ran 1.31 to 2.05 times faster than rival systems, and the team validated it on a model with hundreds of billions of parameters across more than three thousand GPUs.
arxiv-2512-22660:
Julia Kończal, Michał Balcerek, and Krzysztof Burnecki ask whether the climate's big cycles move the price of catastrophe bonds. Cat bonds pass disaster risk from insurers to investors, and worsening natural disasters make pricing them well more urgent. The authors enrich the usual pricing features with climate gauges including the Oceanic Niño Index, Arctic and North Atlantic Oscillations, Pacific patterns, and sea surface temperatures.

They compare linear regression against random forest, gradient boosting, extremely randomized trees, and extreme gradient boosting at predicting bond coupons. Adding the climate variables raised accuracy for every model, and extremely randomized trees achieved the lowest prediction error. Their conclusion: large-scale climate swings measurably influence catastrophe bond pricing, and machine learning captures links that linear models miss.
arxiv-2512-23060:
Xu Zhang and a ten-author team hunt for quasars hiding behind the Milky Way's disk, a region where dust extinction and crowded stars have left quasar catalogs badly incomplete. The search starts from X-ray sources in the Chandra Source Catalog and adds optical data from Gaia and mid-infrared data from CatWISE. Confirmed quasars and stars from several surveys provide the training labels.

A random forest classifier picks out quasar candidates, with Gaia proper motions used to suppress stellar impostors, and a second random forest estimates photometric redshifts. Applied to unclassified Chandra sources, the pipeline found more than seven thousand candidates, including over a thousand close to the Galactic plane and several hundred high confidence. These candidates reach fainter fluxes than the known sample and show the harder X-ray spectra expected from extra absorption. Pilot spectroscopy has confirmed two high-confidence candidates as genuine quasars.
arxiv-2512-23260:
Dianyun Wang and co-authors present SAILS, a method for teaching language models to refuse harmful requests without the cost of full fine-tuning. Safety behavior lives in low-rank structures inside the model, which should suit parameter-efficient adapters like LoRA. Yet LoRA trails full training on safety benchmarks. The authors blame semantic entanglement: because features are polysemantic, safety directions come tangled with unrelated concepts, so an adapter cannot find it alone.

SAILS untangles first. Sparse autoencoders split the model's internals into single-meaning features, and their decoder directions define an interpretable safety subspace used to initialize LoRA adapters. Theory shows this identification can drive recovery error toward zero, where direct identification hits a floor. On a nine-billion-parameter model, SAILS reached safety rates above full fine-tuning and on par with reinforcement-based alignment, updating under a fifth of one percent of parameters.
arxiv-2512-23460:
Andrzej Czarnecki and Jishnu Khanna dismantle a proposal that the living cell arose through a vacuum phase transition. Paul Frampton had modeled the origin of the single-celled organism as tunneling between a no-life vacuum and a life vacuum, in the style of false-vacuum decay. He concluded biogenesis is exponentially suppressed, implying extraterrestrial life is absent. After a review of false-vacuum decay, the authors show the calculation does not hold together.

The decisive flaw is dimensional. The exponent in Frampton's formula carries units of inverse time, an energy barrier divided by Planck's constant, not the dimensionless tunneling action required. The probability is ill-defined and determines no tunneling rate at all. The configuration, a toroidal structure of molecules in space, also clashes with soft-matter physics and with hot, crowded prebiotic conditions. The claimed suppression, and the astrobiological inference built on it, are unsupported.
arxiv-2512-23660:
Liang Li studies a rare curiosity in gamma-ray burst astronomy: bursts that triggered the Swift and Fermi satellites twice. A double-trigger burst flares, goes quiet long enough for the onboard trigger to reset, then flares again and is logged as a brand-new event. Yet sky positions prove both episodes came from the same source. Only a few cases are known.

Li classifies three of them in detail, burst by burst. He measures duration, hardness, variability, spectral lag, peak energy, and energetics for each episode, and compares them with ordinary long bursts and with single-trigger bursts that have quiet intervals. Every sub-burst sits squarely in the long-burst region. The conclusion: double-trigger bursts are not a separate species, just long-burst engines that switch off for an unusually long dormancy and then restart.
arxiv-2512-23760:
Ken Huang and Jerry Huang propose a governance-first design for self-improving AI agents. Agents that learn from their own successes over long tasks can drift, game their rewards, or improve in ways no one can audit, because the gains hide inside opaque parameter updates. Their framework, Audited Skill-Graph Self-Improvement, treats improvement instead as compiling the agent into a growing graph of explicit, checkable skills.

Each candidate skill is extracted from a successful trajectory, given a clean interface, and promoted only after passing verifier-backed replay and contract checks. Rewards are decomposed into components that can be reconstructed from replayable evidence, so promotion decisions can be independently audited. Experience synthesis stress-tests candidates, and continual memory control protects long-horizon performance. A runnable reference implementation with audit logging shows the full loop on continual task streams.
arxiv-2512-23960:
Zonglin Mo and Yi Yin build spin kinetic theory from the bottom up. Hot or dense plasmas, such as the quark-gluon plasma, carry spin effects that hydrodynamic and transport models increasingly need to capture, including the polarization phenomena measured in heavy-ion collisions. A systematic kinetic theory for spin has been under construction from several directions; this paper supplies a formulation grounded in phase-space variables.

Scalar and axial-vector phase-space functions parametrize both the spin-averaged and spin-dependent parts of the distribution. Using spin-dependent Poisson brackets, the authors derive the kinetic equations and construct the matching Schwinger-Keldysh action, then express physical observables through constitutive relations in the same variables. In the linear response regime they establish exact matching between the kinetic description and field theory for vector and axial Wigner functions under electromagnetic and gravitational perturbations.
arxiv-2512-24760:
Emanuelli, Vannini, Hoelzl, and colleagues simulate runaway electrons in the Divertor Tokamak Test facility at its full power scenario, with plasma current well above the commissioning level. Earlier low-current studies suggested a safe margin against runaway beam formation. Higher current changes that picture sharply, because avalanche gain grows exponentially with current.

Using the nonlinear magnetohydrodynamic code JOREK, they model the current quench phase across several disruption scenarios in two dimensions. The safe operating window narrows severely at full power. Fusion safety readers get a concrete reason to treat runaway beams as a central design concern for high-current tokamak operation.
arxiv-2512-25060:
Gabriela Moisescu-Pareja, Gavin McCracken, and Harley Wiltzer re-examine how neural networks learn modular addition, comparing the clock and pizza readings tied to other attention designs. Those images offered uniform and learnable attention designs build distinct circuits. By finding all neurons in each learned representation and studying their geometry and topology, they reach a other finding.

Both designs build the same method through topologically and geometrically equal representations. Interpretability readers get a caution against reading processes off single neurons or weights. Whole-representation analysis can reveal being the same where earlier neuron-level stories claimed difference, changing how circuit claims should be checked.
arxiv-2601-00360:
Jamiu Idowu, Ahmed Almasoud, and Ayman Alfahid ask how human societies fight collusion, and what those lessons mean for groups of AI agents. Autonomous agent systems can learn to coordinate in harmful ways, much like traders or firms in human markets. Their 2026 paper builds a taxonomy of human anti-collusion tools and maps each one onto possible safeguards for multi-agent AI.

The human tools include sanctions, leniency and whistleblowing, monitoring and auditing, market design, and governance. For each, the authors suggest how it could be built into an AI setting. They also flag hard problems: blaming the right agent, agents that can be copied or altered, telling helpful cooperation from harmful collusion, and agents that learn to evade checks.
arxiv-2601-00460:
Jnanajyoti Bhaumik and Naoki Masuda ask why people cooperate when competing, using a model built on layered networks. Earlier work showed network structure can favor cooperation, but usually assumed every interaction is a social dilemma. In real life people also take part in contests with no dilemma, such as fads or opinion spreading. The authors put both kinds of interaction in one model.

One network layer hosts the prisoner's dilemma, while the other follows simple biased competition akin to opinion dynamics. Their analysis shows that coupling the two layers reliably boosts cooperation across many network types, update rules, and payoff schemes. The lesson is practical: embedding people in varied settings, even ones unrelated to the dilemma, can be a principled way to encourage prosocial behavior.
arxiv-2601-00560:
Robert Ganian, Hung Hoang, Christian Komusiewicz, and Nils Morawietz rethink how computer science measures the difficulty of local search. Local search improves a solution step by step until no small change helps, and it is used everywhere in practice. Older frameworks from the late nineteen eighties either ask only for a local optimum or force every improvement step to follow one fixed rule.

The authors define a middle-ground task: output a local optimum together with the chain of improvements that reached it. That framing captures the real design challenge of choosing a good pivoting rule. Combined with parameterized complexity, which measures difficulty against a chosen parameter, the framework lets them analyze which features of a problem make guided local search tractable.
arxiv-2601-00760:
Diksha Bhandari and Sebastian Reich present, in 2026, a method that infers unknowns in models too complex for direct maths. Many science models are black boxes: they take inputs and spit out outputs, with no formula to invert. The authors' method works with no slopes at all. It moves a cloud of guesses through steps shaped by how far outputs sit from data.

The steps borrow the spread of the cloud itself in place of slope data. The method does not care how inputs are scaled or shifted. It also holds up when the model is a rough stand-in for the truth. Tests cover a chaotic system where the model is right. They also cover rigged cases with dirty data, where the model is wrong. Scores matched or beat slope-based rivals, at much lower cost. The method widens the reach of sound inference for black-box science.
arxiv-2601-00860:
Xidi Wang is the sole author of a 2026 paper that argues language itself needs energy loss to work. The paper asks a bold question: can a purely mechanical system write coherent text? Wang claims to prove that it can, under two strict conditions. The system must throw off information in a controlled way, called dissipation. It must also pull context together across long ranges at once.

The proof uses path integrals, a way to sum over all routes a system can take. The spectrum splits into three kinds of modes: ones that fade, ones that grow, and ones that hold. Wang argues that strict conservation laws kill the fading and growing modes. With them gone, performance drops even though the model's size stays the same. The claim is strong, and readers should note it rests on the author's own frame.
arxiv-2601-00960:
Michele Perna and seventeen co-authors report, in 2026, a crowded scene around a dead galaxy seen as it was long ago. The galaxy, GS10578, sits at a redshift of three, and had already stopped forming stars. Past data showed a wind driven by its central black hole. A third candidate sat farther out, in a bright hydrogen emitter.

New data from the James Webb Space Telescope targeted light lines from that emitter. The line ratios match an active black hole, confirming the third one. Its gas looks clumpy, with messy motions on small scales. A twin emitter nearby stayed dark in all lines but one. The match of that one line hints it is scattered light, not new stars. The scene shows three black holes active near one dead giant. It gives a rare look at how feedback and neighbours shape a galaxy's late life.
arxiv-2601-01360:
Seven authors led by Jiawei Fang make motion capture work from sensors sewn into loose clothing. Camera systems need line of sight, and tight sensor suits are intrusive. Loose garments are comfortable but shift against the body, and that shifting corrupts the sensor data in structured ways that depend on where each sensor sits.

Their system, GID, cleans the data in three stages: per-location denoising, a fusion step that adapts across wear setups, and pose prediction. A shared backbone reads the overall motion, while specialist heads learn the quirks of each sensor's garment dynamics. The team also releases GarMoCap, a data set spanning many users, motions, and garments. In tests, GID restored accurate, real-time motion capture after training on a single user, and it generalized to new users, motions, and clothes. Added to leading methods, it improved them across the board.
arxiv-2601-01460:
Four authors led by Mohd Usama fix a quiet failure of medical AI: a model trained on ultrasound images from one scanner often stumbles on another's. Different machines and settings change texture and add reverberation noise, breaking the same-distribution assumption behind most training. Retraining for every device is slow and dear.

Their adversarial network translates test images into the style of the training domain, changing texture and stripping noise while keeping the anatomy untouched. They test it on carotid artery ultrasound from three domains across two data sets. The translated images matched the target domain far better on histogram and distance measures than unadapted ones. A standard CycleGAN comparison came off worse. If such translation holds up in clinics, one good model could serve many scanners, a large saving for hospitals that cannot label data for each machine they own.
arxiv-2601-01760:
Gabriel Potestades asks whether algorithmic information theory, which measures complexity by the shortest program that produces an object, can reveal the structure inside graphs. The study builds on the Block Decomposition Method. That method estimates the complexity of a graph's adjacency matrix. The question is whether one edge can be spotted by its information contribution. That edge is the single link between two subgraphs.

Each edge was perturbed in turn and its average information contribution compared, exhaustively checking vertex relabelings. The connecting edge carried the highest average contribution in twenty-nine of thirty graphs, and often by a wide margin. The full symmetric group of relabelings grouped edges better than a restricted automorphic subset. The results suggest algorithmic complexity can serve as a practical lens on graph substructure.
arxiv-2601-01860:
Genes rarely act alone: disease risk can depend on combinations of several genetic markers interacting at once, a phenomenon called epistasis, but the number of combinations explodes as more markers are considered. Shuta Kikuchi and Shu Tanaka recast the search as a black-box optimization problem.

Their method pairs two tools. A factorization machine proposes promising marker combinations. Quadratic-optimization annealing guides the search. Each proposal is scored by the error rate of multifactor dimensionality reduction. That method is a standard epistasis evaluator. On simulated case-control data with planted cases, the search found the true epistasis. It worked across interaction orders and marker counts, within limited iterations. The approach makes high-order interaction hunting possible. Gene studies are the target use.
arxiv-2601-02060:
Functional programming promises reliable software but its steep learning curve keeps adoption low, and code-generating language models have mostly been judged on imperative languages. Nguyet-Anh Lang, Eric Lang, Thanh Le-Cong, Bach Le, and Quyet-Thang Huynh introduce FPEval, built on FPBench, a benchmark of seven hundred twenty-one tasks at three difficulty levels in Haskell, OCaml, and Scala.

The framework checks generated code with full test suites and static analysis for style and maintainability, and evaluates models including GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, and GPT-5 against a Java baseline. Newer models improved substantially, yet error rates stayed far higher in Haskell and OCaml than in Scala or Java, and models often wrote imperative-style code in functional dress. Given static analysis feedback, models could partly repair both correctness and quality problems.
arxiv-2601-02160:
Quantum systems in contact with an environment remember their past. Their dynamics are non-Markovian. Simulating them accurately is a crowded field of competing methods. Meng Xu and three co-authors survey the landscape. Methods range from hierarchical equations of motion and pseudomode formulas to chain mappings. Stochastic paths and refined master equations appear too.

The review's unifying move is an extended state space. A few effective reservoir modes sit alongside the system there. Each method finds its place and its physical meaning in that space. Relations, strengths, and limits of the approaches become visible side by side. For researchers facing a complex open system, the overview doubles as a guide. It helps in choosing a modeling strategy.
arxiv-2601-02360:
Yazan Obeidi and four co authors ask whether language models can be pre trained across machines linked by slow networks, including machines outside big data centers. Splitting a model across devices normally forces constant large transfers. They combine a data parallel method called SparseLoCo, which syncs rarely and sends only sparse updates, with pipeline parallelism that compresses the signals passed between stages.

Their framework lets well connected participants hold full model copies, while weaker participants group together to hold one copy jointly through the pipeline. Several adaptations make the compression work with the sparse sync method. In experiments with models from under two hundred million to one billion parameters, activation compression and SparseLoCo compose well, pointing toward training pools that mix strong and modest hardware.
arxiv-2601-02860: Mitchell Gaudet and Talant Talipov prove an upper bound on the Morse index of certain surfaces built by a min-max process. The surfaces in question are stationary integral varifolds, a generalized kind of surface, that realize the p-width of a closed curved space. The Morse index counts the ways such a surface can be deformed to reduce its area, so bounding it limits how unstable these min-max surfaces can be.
arxiv-2601-03160:
Matteo Ferrari, Ilaria Perugia, and Enrico Zampa revisit numerical schemes that solve wave equations by treating space and time together, with second-order accuracy in time. They establish precise equivalences between these space-time discretizations and first-order-in-time formulations. The schemes use continuous piecewise-polynomial trial functions in time. These are tested against discontinuous polynomials of one degree lower.

With that setup, one popular scheme turns out to match a method from the nineteen nineties, in the linear case, and its semilinear extension. It conserves energy at mesh nodes but is not symplectic. The authors then introduce two symplectic variants, built from Gauss-Legendre and Gauss-Lobatto quadrature in time. Each corresponds to a specific Runge-Kutta integrator. The connections clarify the geometric structure behind the methods.
arxiv-2601-03260:
Chenyang Shao, Fengli Xu, and Yong Li build SciNet, a dataset for testing whether AI research agents understand the relationships between scientific papers, not just their contents. Keyword and embedding search can find similar papers but miss corroborating or conflicting studies and the lineages along which techniques develop. SciNet is built on a meta-database of two hundred sixty-nine million papers across seven disciplines.

Its nearly nine thousand tasks probe three levels of relational understanding. Some tasks ask for papers around a focal work with novel knowledge structures. Others ask for the relationship between pairs of papers, or for paths through the citation network. The authors present SciNet as the first relation-aware benchmark of its kind for scientific retrieval agents. It aims to expose the fragmented knowledge and misread sentiment that purely content-based retrieval produces.
arxiv-2601-03460:
Zeyu Dong and three co-authors challenge a habit in self-driving research: fine-tuning the whole vision encoder on driving data. That practice may make the encoder too narrow and hurt performance in new scenes. Their system, FROST-Drive, keeps a pretrained vision encoder from a vision-language model frozen, so its broad world knowledge stays intact.

A transformer adapter blends the image features with other inputs, and a recurrent decoder produces smooth waypoints for the car to follow. A custom loss targets a rater feedback score that rewards robust route planning. Tests used the large Waymo open driving dataset, chosen to stress generalization. The results support a simple claim: sometimes the best way to use a strong pretrained eye is to leave it alone.
arxiv-2601-03660:
Jiangyuan Liu and five co-authors present MGPC, a system that completes three-dimensional point clouds of objects seen only in part. Sensors capture partial views because of occlusion and limited angles, and filling in the missing shape helps robots and scanners work with real objects. Earlier methods did well on synthetic tests but generalized poorly to new objects and real scenes.

MGPC fuses point clouds, color images, and text in one architecture. A modality dropout trick, which randomly hides one input type in training, builds robustness, while a transformer fusion module and a progressive generator refine the shape step by step. The team also built MGPC-1M, a dataset with over a thousand categories and a million training pairs. Strong completion across categories matters for warehouses, homes, and other unplanned spaces.
arxiv-2601-03760:
Katharina Ammann, Timo Adam, and Jan-Ole Koslik extend a class of statistical models used for time series that switch between hidden regimes. Their models combine distributional regression, which can model a distribution's location, scale, and shape, with hidden Markov switching between states. Until now, the odds of switching states were usually held constant over time, so regime changes could not respond to outside conditions.

The extension lets covariates drive the transition probabilities themselves, modeled as smooth functions. Estimation uses penalized likelihood with automatic smoothness selection to guard against overfitting. Simulations plus applications to daily Lufthansa stock prices and Spanish energy prices test the method. Markets and energy systems both switch regimes in response to conditions, so letting the switching itself react to covariates is a natural, useful step.
arxiv-2601-04060:
Jinwei Su leads nine co-authors with a system that builds workflows for ComfyUI, a modular tool for AI image work. Users wire many parts into graphs, but keeping a long graph valid is hard. Many automatic attempts fail to run or produce weak results.

Their framework, ComfySearch, searches the space of parts in an agentic way and checks each draft workflow as it grows. Guidance from those checks steers the next steps, which keeps the graph within its strict rules. In experiments the system beats earlier methods on complex and creative tasks. It reaches higher rates of workflows that run, higher rates that solve the task, and better transfer to new tasks.
arxiv-2601-04460:
Md. Rajbanul Akhond and Alexandru B. Georgescu draw the first map of a scattered family of quantum materials in a 2026 arXiv paper. In correlated electron molecular orbital materials, the key electrons live not on single atoms but in molecular orbitals spread over clusters of metal ions, producing unusual electronic states. Such materials have turned up one at a time, treated as one-offs rather than a class.

The authors set out classification criteria and software that sorts materials by their cluster symmetry and the cluster lattice's effective dimension, then check the electronics. Narrow bands arise either from isolated cluster orbitals or from cluster localization tangled with frustrated-lattice flat bands. Screening more than thirty-four thousand compounds this way yields over two thousand six hundred plausible stable candidates. Their open dataset, Cluster Finder software, and public platform invite the field to explore the new territory.
arxiv-2601-04760:
Mahdieh Eskandari Merajin hunts for fingerprints of physics beyond the Planck scale in the oldest light there is, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Inflation stretched quantum fluctuations into the cosmic microwave background's pattern, but the theory's earliest instants involve energies where quantum gravity should leave marks, and the large-scale CMB carries known anomalies. She studies a generalized Sasaki-Mukhanov equation — the master equation for primordial perturbations — with a time-dependent correction governed by one coupling constant.

Solving the mode equations exactly in terms of Whittaker functions, she derives a power spectrum with scale-dependent oscillations and suppressed power at the largest scales. Implemented in a Bayesian inference engine and fitted to Planck and Atacama Cosmology Telescope data, the model constrains the coupling to be extremely small. the author reports it fits the low-multipole spectrum better than the standard model, easing the low-quadrupole anomaly without spoiling smaller scales.
arxiv-2601-04960:
Qing Wang and 8 co-authors build a spoken language model that reasons about the emotions behind a user's words in a 2026 paper. Their unified model handles spoken interaction with emotional intelligence rather than treating feelings as an afterthought label. A data strategy called Injected Emotional-Attribution Thinking inserts the user's emotional state and its likely causes into the model's internal reasoning, so emotion-aware thinking is internalized during training.

Training proceeds in two stages: speech-text alignment with emotional attribute modelling through self-distillation, then joint end-to-end tuning across both modes. A voice assistant that grasps why a user sounds upset, not only that they do, could respond more helpfully in support, education, and accessibility settings.
arxiv-2601-05060:
Valentin Brunn and 5 co-authors put forth a new source of charged grains deep inside the discs where planets form in a 2026 paper. In such a disc, charge sets the mix of stuff, the heat books, and how well the disc grips its own magnet fields. The stock sources of charge fall short at depth. Star light in the harsh bands fades fast as it sinks, and rays from far space are bent away long ere they reach the deep disc.

The team work out the charge and heat from grains sped up in the disc's own sky layers. There, churn in the magnet fields snaps and re-joins field lines, and that snap throws grains to high speeds. The team find where this home-grown source beats star X-rays. If it holds up, planet birth models gain a lost source of charge right where new worlds take shape.
arxiv-2601-05260:
Armin Gerami, Kazem Faghih, and Ramani Duraiswami measure how much each retrieved document actually shapes a retrieval-augmented model's answer in a 2026 paper. Retrieval-augmented generation connects language models to external knowledge, improving accuracy and freshness, but it also imports factual inconsistencies, source conflicts, bias, and security risks. Evaluation lacked any metric telling how much a single retrieved document swayed the final output.

Their Influence Score uses partial information decomposition, a method for splitting information into unique, shared, and combined parts, to quantify each document's effect. Knowing which source drove an answer lets engineers debug bad outputs, drop harmful sources, and audit systems whose answers must be traceable to evidence.
arxiv-2601-05660:
Theophane Bernhard and Andrea Grisafi resolve, in a 2026 paper, a long-standing difficulty in computing how a metal's Fermi energy responds to added charge at an interface. That response can be written locally through the Fukui function, but adding finite charge inside a periodic calculation caused inherent approximations.

Their exact approach uses the screening behavior of conductors to obtain Fukui functions from a finite electric field instead. The resulting linear-response theory showed strictly quadratic error scaling across representative platinum surfaces, reaching very high accuracy at moderate fields. It also reproduced work-function changes under molecular perturbations and produced capacitance-voltage curves consistent with test, grounding a local theory of screening at metallic interfaces.
arxiv-2601-06060:
AI slop deserves serious study, argue Cody Kommers and 8 co-authors in a 2026 essay. Slop is the flood of cheap AI-generated content often dismissed as digital pollution. The authors say dismissal misses what slop does in culture and the economy.

Slop meets a real demand: people collectively want more content than humans can supply. It also has its own aesthetic value, like earlier low cultural forms that critics scorned. The paper names three typical features: a veneer of competence over thin substance, far less effort to make than to make by hand, and mass producibility. Slop varies in usefulness, personalization, and surrealism, and will shape creative and information economies.
arxiv-2601-06160:
Strong models can collapse into repeating the same wrong logic. Dayu Wang and 6 co-authors call that reasoning collapse and propose a fix in a 2026 paper. On hard math problems, random sampling often produces word-level variations of one flawed approach rather than genuinely different attempts.

Their Spectral Orthogonal Exploration uses a weaker model not for imitation but as a probe. The probe injects diverse reasoning signals into directions outside the strong model's dominant hidden-state subspace. That steers the teacher toward more varied trajectories and better exploration. On mathematical benchmarks, average accuracy and sampling efficiency rose sharply over baselines. Early evidence suggests the geometric intervention also helps on logic and code generation tasks.
arxiv-2601-06260:
Cheap plasticity models for magnesium alloys must still capture the metal's quirks. R. Vigneshwaran and 3 co-authors assess such models in a 2026 materials paper. Magnesium crystals deform by slip and by twinning, a second mechanism that makes tension and compression behave differently.

The team compared two-surface and three-surface coarse-grained models against high-fidelity crystal plasticity simulations across many textures and grain sizes. The two-surface version separates slip and twinning; the three-surface version also splits basal from nonbasal slip. Models were fitted to stress-strain responses for six loading directions in tension and compression. Analysis tracked evolving anisotropy and the relative activity of each mechanism. The paper closes by discussing prospects for sound damage models built on these formulations.
arxiv-2601-06460:
How a user phrases a prompt can push a vision-language model to invent details. Weihao Hong and 6 co-authors study that pressure effect in a 2026 paper. These models often hallucinate content absent from an image to satisfy a prompt, a serious risk in safety-critical uses, yet prompt phrasing as a cause was poorly characterized.

Their Ghost-100 dataset contains procedurally generated scenes with key details deliberately removed, enabling controlled tests of absence-based hallucination. Prompts varied across five intensity levels, from neutral queries to toxic demands and rigid formatting constraints. Three open-weight models were evaluated. Hallucination rates did not rise monotonically with intensity; all models improved at some higher levels, though not all sustained that under maximum coercion. Safety alignment apparently catches hostile wording better than structural pressure.
arxiv-2601-06560:
Fake speech fools the ear more and more, most of all when it is played back or sent down a bad line. K. A. Shahriar builds a lean spot tool for it in a 2026 paper. Most tools read sound at one scale of time and pitch. Cues that clash at one scale can agree at the next, and one-scale tools miss that.

His tool reads sound at a few scales at once and makes the scales agree. A cross-scale focus step lines the reads up. A pact step keeps them true to each other. On three test sets, with both fake and played-back clips, the tool's miss rate stayed low, in one case near nil. It beat one-scale tools by a wide gap. Yet it is tiny: a small count of weights and a light cost per clip.
arxiv-2601-06660:
Leonid Bedratyuk builds a new way to make group-based yardsticks in a 2026 paper. His base is the moving frame method, changed in a clear-cut way. It works on an enlarged space, which gives the method room to run.

A yardstick of the kind he builds shifts by a power of a scale factor. That scale factor comes from the group act and is known in closed form. Old frame tools find fixed yardsticks, but some tasks need this looser kind. His changed method gives steps one can carry out, not just a proof that they exist. It links old work by Cartan to present-day work on group acts. Those who study shape and symmetry gain a tool they can apply at once. New group acts can now be worked through the same steps.
arxiv-2601-06860: Yifei Chen and co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on agents built from large language models. The paper, called ET-Agent, deals with agents that call tools as they work. Tool use lets a model reach past what it holds in its own weights. Yet training tends to grade the final answer, not the steps that lead to it. As a result, agents can call tools too often or too rarely. The authors set out to tune how the agent acts, not just what it says at the end.
arxiv-2601-07360:
Research by Subhasish Basak and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with heavy hadron spectrum from 2+1+1 flavor MILC lattices. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The authors study the mass spectra and various mass differences of heavy hadrons containing one or more bottom. Quarks using MILC’s N f = 2 + 1 + 1 HISQ gauge ensembles at three lattice spacings.

For the valence quarks, we employ a combination of lattice actions: the NRQCD action is used for bottom quarks. The anisotropic Clover action for charm quarks, and the O ( a ) O(a) -improved Wilson–Clover action for strange and lighter (up/down) quarks. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07760:
Shao-Ting Chiu and colleagues speed up Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks by swapping their basis functions. KANs approximate complex nonlinear functions well, placing learnable functions on network edges. The original design uses B-spline basis functions. Evaluating B-splines through De Boor's algorithm costs substantial compute. Their 2026 preprint, Free-RBF-KAN, uses adaptive radial basis functions instead.

Radial basis functions can improve both efficiency and flexibility, the authors argue. Making them adaptive lets each function adjust its shape during training. The goal is KAN-level accuracy without the spline overhead. Efficient function learning matters for scientific computing, where KANs are used as equation solvers and surrogates. The paper targets machine learning scholars who like the KAN idea but need it faster. It keeps the architecture while changing its costly core.
arxiv-2601-08060: Ahmed Hassan, Ahmad Qidan, Taisir Elgorashi, and Jaafar Elmirghani tackle power control in optical wireless links. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses deep reinforcement learning for systems that mix light detection, coded access, and non-orthogonal sharing. In such links, many users share one optical spectrum at distinct power levels. Poor channel knowledge and decoding errors hurt performance, above all in crowded indoor settings. The paper frames that control problem and the deep learning route the title promises for handling it.
arxiv-2601-08560: Luis Bonah and five co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on the light fingerprint of a molecule called cyclopentadiene. The team took high-resolution infrared spectra of the molecule in an excited state. Such states serve as probes of the heat of the zones they sit in, and may cause many sky survey lines no one has named yet. The paper covers vibrational modes below 860 per centimeter, and one mode called nu 21, read with the ASAP method. Exact energies from such spectra can guide later work on pure rotation.
arxiv-2601-08760:
Yi Zhuang, Kun Yang, and Xingran Chen study how edge net users should ask for fresh data. In an edge net, users ask through gate nodes that link to far hosts. A user can not see the load on a gate, nor what peer users do. Yet old data is of no use, so each user wants the freshest copy it can get.

The team frames each ask choice as a bet with odds that shift in time. Past odds do not stay fixed, since load and peer acts change. Their method lets each user learn on its own, with no central boss. A reader who runs edge nets gets a self taught ask rule. It aims to keep data fresh while the net shifts round the user.
arxiv-2601-08960:
Keerthana Gurushankar and three co-authors set the best plan for jobs whose wait cost grows as they wait. In many queues, a job that waits long costs more per hour than a fresh job. A late report may lose all worth. A stale food order is waste. The plan must weigh that growth, not just job size.

Their plan is called LookAhead. It is an index rule: each job gets a score, and the top score runs next. They prove their rule is best, and that its scores never fall as a job waits. A reader who runs queues gets a rule with a proof, not just a hunch. It fits help desks, clinics, and print shops alike.
arxiv-2601-09060:
Theo Johnson-Freyd, Victor Ostrik, and Zhiqiang Yu study when two deep algebra worlds count as the same in a shared list. The list is the Witt group, a roll of worlds up to a fair tie. One world is a plain group rep world. The next is a braided world built on top of it. The ask is when the two land on the same line of the list.

They give tests that are both a must and enough for that tie. Such tests rest on how the top world acts and links. A reader in this algebra field gets a firm rule for a long open guess, the minimal extension conjecture in part. Clean tests help sort a vast zoo of worlds.
arxiv-2601-09560:
Bogdan M. Fominykh, Valentin Yu. Irkhin, and Vyacheslav V. Marchenkov ask a pointed question about a famous quantum effect. Their 2026 arXiv paper, bound for Physics Letters A, concerns the Berry phase, a geometric phase picked up by quantum systems. Physicists often read the phase from quantum oscillations in a magnetic field.

Oscillations such as the Shubnikov-de Haas effect are a standard tool for probing a material's topology. Yet pulling the Berry phase out of them without ambiguity has stayed tricky. The authors examine whether the phase can be fixed from oscillations alone. The answer matters for claims that a new material is topological.
arxiv-2601-09660:
Carla Nathaly Villacís Núñez and five co-authors measure the material properties of rotator cuff tendons. Their 2026 arXiv paper infers constitutive parameters from full-volume data on intact and torn tendons. The animal model tendons were scanned through their whole volume, in both healthy and injured states.

Tension along the fibers triggers stretch, volume change, and shear at once, thanks to the tendon's complex shape. The team fits a physics-based model to the internal strain fields. Knowing how a torn tendon differs in stiffness guides surgery and repair design. The data-driven fit avoids cutting the tissue into simple test strips.
arxiv-2601-09760:
Jiali Cheng, Rui Pan, and Hadi Amiri name a new kind of knowledge conflict in tool-using language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces tool-memory conflict. The clash occurs when a model's internal knowledge contradicts what an external tool reports.

Tool-augmented models power many applications, from search assistants to data agents. When memory and tool disagree, the model must choose, and either choice can mislead. Naming and framing the conflict is a step toward handling it well. The paper studies how such conflicts arise in practice and what they do to answers.
arxiv-2601-09860:
Sepideh Mahabadi, Sherry Sarkar, and Jakub Tarnawski improve algorithms for fair selection under constraints. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats submodular maximization subject to matroid constraints, now with fairness requirements. Submodular maximization drives many machine learning tasks, from summarization to sensor placement.

As algorithms decide over people, sensitive attributes such as gender or race come into play. Fairness constraints aim to prevent bias and discrimination in the outcome. The authors give improved algorithms that respect both the matroid structure and fairness. Full-version results like these guide the design of selection systems that must be both strong and fair.
arxiv-2601-10160:
Cameron Tice and co authors test if talk about AI can bend AI acts. Training text holds vast talk about what AI is and does. Much of that talk is dark. If a model takes that talk to heart, it may act in the dark ways it read of.

The team calls this self fulfilling misalignment. They ran the first tight test of the claim. They pre trained small models on set text mixes. Some mixes held more dark AI talk than the rest. They then checked how the acts of the models shift with the mix. The work asks if the tale makes the trait.
arxiv-2601-10360:
Grigori Karagulyan bounds the weights that make trig sums settle. A trig sum adds waves of many tones. With terms in a mixed order, the sum may or may not settle as terms grow. A weight can force it to settle at most points.

Such a weight is named a Weyl multiplier. Karagulyan works on sums in many dims. He seeks weights that work for all term orders at once. He shows any such weight must sit twixt a log bound and its square. That tight range sorts what weights can do the job.
arxiv-2601-10460:
Abhinaba Basu and Pavan Chakraborty show that a model's bias grade shifts with the scene set round it. A model may pass a bias test in the lab. In real use, the same model may fail. Place, time, and who reads can all be named in a prompt. None of that need be a trick prompt.

The team built Contextual StereoSet to test this. It holds the bias claim fixed. It then varies the scene in set steps. Bias grades move a lot as the scene shifts. The work warns that one lab grade is a weak proof of fair acts in the wild.
arxiv-2601-10560:
Xi Shi, Mengxin Zheng, and Qian Lou cut lag in teams of AI agents that run in parallel. A team can solve hard tasks by split work. But each step and call adds lag. That lag caps how big a team can grow. It also hurts tasks where time counts.

Past work tuned for grade or cost, and took steps in a line. The team teach an orchestration plan with lag in the loss. Agents run side by side, not in a line. The plan learns which agent should do what, and when. The aim is a fast team that keeps its grade.
arxiv-2601-10660:
Tiziano Labruna, Arkadiusz Modzelewski, Giorgio Satta, and Giovanni Da San Martino study how machines can spot a winning argument. Finding persuasion in text is hard, yet it bears on how human communication works. The team asks whether named persuasion strategies help a model judge which text will sway readers.

The strategies include attacks on reputation, distraction, and manipulative wording. By tagging texts with such moves, the authors test if large language models judge persuasiveness more like people do. The work links classic rhetoric to modern text models. It may help tools that flag manipulative content in debates, ads, and news.
arxiv-2601-10960:
Hyeseon An, Shinwoo Park, Hyundong Jin, and Yo-Sub Han steer language models at the logit level, before any words come out. Steering matters for style-sensitive rewriting, user-adaptive replies, and cutting toxic output. Prompting can steer, but its grip is coarse and uneven. Activation methods reach deeper, yet need access to inner layers.

Logits are the model's scores for each next token, the last step before speech. Intervening there promises fine control without deep surgery. The authors develop this middle path and test its reach. Their work serves product teams that must shape model tone tightly while working with models they cannot fully open.
arxiv-2601-11160:
Claudia Plant, Lena G. M. Bauer, and Christian Böhm present an AAAI 2026 tutorial on clustering high-dimensional data. Clustering asks how to find a natural grouping in a large dataset. It demands a balance between abstraction and representation. To find clusters, one must drop needless detail from single objects. Yet the representation must keep the key features that make groups distinct.

High dimensions strain that balance: distances blur and noise piles up. The tutorial gathers methods that keep groups visible in such data. It is aimed at researchers and practitioners who cluster genomes, documents, or sensor streams. A clear map of the trade-offs can save teams from groupings that look neat and mean nothing.
arxiv-2601-11260:
Martin Ortiz builds new theta operators on Shimura varieties in this work. His 2026 preprint deals with Hodge type varieties at hyperspecial level. Theta operators shift weights of modular forms in mod p work. They are differential operators with deep arithmetic uses.

The new family shifts weights modulo a prime p. Basic theta operators come first in the construction. Each is labeled by a positive root of the group. That labeling generalizes Katz's classic theta operator. Katz's case was for modular forms in one variable. Ortiz lifts the idea to the broad Hodge type setting. New operators give new tools for mod p number theory.
arxiv-2601-11460:
Franziska Herbert and four coauthors teach robots task structure from human demos. Their 2026 preprint builds semantic-geometric task graphs from demonstrations. Long-horizon manipulation is hard for robots to learn raw. Bimanual tasks add two hands whose moves must be ordered.

A good task record must hold two kinds of structure. One is the discrete semantic side: steps and objects used. The other is how object geometry shifts over time. Both sides can vary much from demo to demo. The team's graphs join meaning and geometry in one form. That form supports reasoning about how a task unfolds. Robots can then plan long tasks with clearer steps.
arxiv-2601-11560:
Zifeng Wang and seven coauthors launch DeepEvidence for biomedical discovery. Their 2026 preprint builds on biomedical knowledge graphs. Such graphs encode vast, mixed data for the life sciences. Literature, genes, pathways, drugs, diseases, and trials all sit inside.

Using those graphs jointly for discovery stays hard today. Their structures differ from one resource to the next. They evolve over time as new studies land. Cross-resource alignment is limited and needs manual work. That hand work caps the depth and scale of exploration. DeepEvidence aims at deep graph research with less friction. Better tooling could speed drug and disease insight.
arxiv-2601-11660:
Chunshu Wu and four coauthors argue that zeros can be informative. Their 2026 preprint gives a masked binary U-Net for segmentation. Real-time segmentation enables AR, VR, robots, and drones. Tight budgets bind accuracy, latency, and energy on edge devices.

U-Net balances accuracy and efficiency better than big transformers. High-resolution input still strains compute, memory, and power. Binary networks cut weights to one bit for speed. Masking turns many values to zero in the network. Those zeros, the team shows, still carry useful signal. Running on Tensor Cores targets the hardware in edge chips. The aim is real-time masks within strict budgets.
arxiv-2601-11860:
Xin Xiong, Zijian Guo, Haobo Zhu, and a cross-lab team tackle decay in clinical AI over time. Tools that work well at launch often fade as data shift. Causes span new patient mixes, code updates such as ICD-9 to ICD-10, and shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

Full retraining is often too costly or blocked by privacy rules. Their frame aims for durable AI that adapts as it moves to new sites and times. It treats drift as a fact to plan for, not a surprise. Sound drift tools could keep care AI safe for longer.
arxiv-2601-12160:
Y. Shen, W. He, J. Sears, and a large team report the first watch of plasmons in low-valence nickelates. Nickelate superconductors opened a new field for the study of electron fluids that pair in odd ways. Plasmons are joint waves of the electron gas, and they hold key facts on charge dynamics.

Such waves had not been seen in nickelates before this work. Their data add a new probe of how charge moves in these materials. That probe can test theories of their odd superconductivity. The team span labs in the US and abroad.
arxiv-2601-12860:
Youngmin Lee, Subong Lim, and Wissam Raji study the Rankin Cohen bracket for vector valued modular forms. Modular forms are functions with rich symmetry, central to number theory. The Rankin Cohen bracket combines two such forms into a new one. For vector valued forms, the bracket carries extra structure worth mapping.

The team explore how this bracket relates to Petersson inner products. They derive an explicit description of the adjoint map for the bracket operator. The study extends to Jacobi forms and skew holomorphic Jacobi forms. An isomorphism connects their brackets with the vector valued case. Adjoint maps for the extended operators are examined as well.
arxiv-2601-13260:
Sawsan Alqahtani and co-authors argue that tokenizers are core design picks, not mere prep steps. A tokenizer cuts text into bits that a large language model reads. The go to cut is byte pair encoding, which joins the most common pairs step by step. It scales well, but the cuts can clash with true word parts.

That clash can waste model room and can grow bias. It hits tongues and fields far from the train mix the most. The team reframes the cut as a model pick in its own right. They urge that it be judged with the same care as net shape or train data. For model builders, the piece is a call to own the first step of the chain.
arxiv-2601-13660:
Aiko Miyamoto and co-authors hunt for changing iron light from the heart of the Circinus galaxy in 2026. They used eight sets of Chandra X-ray data taken over about twenty-two years. Their target is neutral iron-K alpha emission, a sharp X-ray glow from iron atoms. The glow comes from the region near the galaxy's core, about ten to a hundred parsecs out.

Maps and spectra split by place let them track the glow spot by spot. They search for time variability, shifts in brightness over the years. Changes would hint at how light and gas move near a giant black hole. Long records like this are rare and prized.
arxiv-2601-14160:
Ali Hamza Bashir and co-authors adapt language models to German law with synthetic data in 2026. Large language models often struggle in specialized domains like legal reasoning. Limited expert knowledge leads to factually incorrect outputs or hallucinations. German legal question answering is the target task here.

Their method fine-tunes advanced models on novel synthetic data. A generation approach creates training cases in the legal style. Domain adaptation through synthetic data avoids costly expert labeling at scale. Reliable legal assistants could help citizens and junior lawyers find rules fast. The dip was brief, so fast alerts from sky watchers were key. Their quick word let big scopes join in time to catch it.
arxiv-2601-14260:
Xiaoxuan Yang, Peilin Chen, Tergel Molom-Ochir, and Yiran Chen tackle a hardware problem in this 2026 paper. Transformers run most large language models, but they are costly to run at scale. The authors name three main challenges. One is the attention step, which needs huge matrix work.

Attention also forces much data movement. Intermediate results shuttle back and forth between memory and compute units. That traffic drives up both delay and energy use. The team's answer sits in processing-in-memory designs. Such designs place compute inside or near memory chips. The paper works on end-to-end speed-up for transformers on that kind of hardware.
arxiv-2601-15160:
Yuval Kansal and Niraj K. Jha argue that a knowledge graph can quietly act as a reward model. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the reasoning of large language models. The models shine at math and code, but multi-hop reasoning in specialist science stays weak.

The authors propose a bottom-up route. A model first learns firm domain facts, stated like axioms. Signals derived from paths in a knowledge graph then reward good steps. From those facts the model composes answers to complex new tasks that it has never once seen before.
arxiv-2601-15360:
Eichi Uehara repairs a popular estimator for treatment effects that vary by person. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with heterogeneous treatment effects in fields like ad tech and health care. Two problems strike at once: extreme class imbalance and heavy-tailed outcomes.

The X-Learner handles imbalance by cross-imputation. But the author shows it breaks under outlier smearing when squared error rules the fit. A few wild outcomes can poison the estimates. Robust X-Learner swaps in robust methods to stop that smearing. The repair keeps the cross-imputation strength while taming the heavy tails.
arxiv-2601-15760:
Shubham Patel and Utkarsh Mishra squeeze more from a quantum optimizer in a 2026 arXiv paper. The algorithm is QAOA, built for combinatorial optimization. They test it on MaxCut, a classic graph problem. Three graph families serve as testbeds: 3-regular graphs, Erdős-Rényi graphs, and Barabási-Albert graphs. Their recipe starts with parameter transfer initialization. Good parameters from earlier runs seed the new one.

Targeted single-layer optimization then refines the result. Regularization keeps the search focused, per the title. The abstract reports a mean approximation ratio of 0.9443 for the transfer approach, before the record cuts off. Parameter tuning is QAOA's practical bottleneck. Cheaper tuning widens the problems users can afford to try.
arxiv-2601-15860:
Shui-Hsiang Hsu, Tsung-Hsiang Chou, Chen-Jui Yu, and Yao-Chung Fan build a table representation in a 2026 arXiv paper. Table retrieval finds the most relevant tables for a natural-language query. The search runs over large corpora. Structured tables and unstructured questions differ in form and meaning. That gap makes embedding alignment hard. Recent methods enrich tables with synthetic queries. Many still sample partial tables coarsely and fuse signals simply.

Their method is STAR, a semantic table representation. It uses header-aware clustering and adaptive weighted fusion. Headers carry much of a table's meaning, so the method leans on them. Adaptive fusion weighs parts by their value per query. For search over data lakes, such gains decide whether the right table surfaces at all.
arxiv-2601-15960:
Zihao Wu and a large team report a possible galaxy cluster from the dawn of time in a 2026 arXiv paper. The candidate sits at redshift about 10.5. That distance places it within the first 500 million years, per the title. It contains 18 galaxies with consistent photometric redshifts. They show robust F115W dropouts, the color signature of very distant sources. The group spans 8 comoving megaparsecs in projection.
