The data come from the JADES survey with JWST. An overdensity this early is a strong claim. Structure needs time to grow, and 500 million years is little time. A confirmed cluster that young would strain formation models. The authors present it as a candidate, inviting the spectroscopic checks that can settle it.
arxiv-2601-16360:
Tom Moshaiov and Shaul Zemel give curve forms for group marks on cycles. Their 2026 preprint deals with the symmetric group and its marks. Past work by Cohen and Zemel showed a key size is a curve in n. That size is the span of a group form tied to a set split. The split has a fixed small part and a part that grows with n.

The pair now give like curve forms for marks on cycles. Marks and sizes both turn out as curves of set grade. Curve forms let teams work values for big n at once. No step by step sum is then needed for each n. The work adds firm forms to group maths.
arxiv-2601-16560:
Ruisheng Shi and coauthors test eclipse hits on the Ethereum peer net. Their 2026 preprint deals with hits that cut a node off from true peers. A hit node sees just foe peers and their false tale. Past hits were well read in Bitcoin and Monero nets. How they fare on Ethereum post Merge was far less known.

The team tests if the same tricks can take Ethereum nodes. Post Merge shifts in the peer rules may block or aid hits. Clear risk maps help node hosts set peer guards. Such guards keep the chain tale true for all users. The work brings a known hit to a new net.
arxiv-2601-16960:
Olivia Pal, Veda Duddu, Agam Goyal, Drishti Goel, and Koustuv Saha study student trust in AI answers. Trust and use are oft read as one linked pair. Tune trust right, and fit use should follow, folks say. Their 2026 preprint doubts that link in school work. Students now ask bots for help on a daily basis.

The team frames the doubt as shared mind-read skill. Each side models what the next side knows. Misfit models can leave trust high but use poor. Or trust low while use stays fit. Their work can guide school tools that earn apt trust. It warns grades based on trust polls alone.
arxiv-2601-18260:
Eytan Kats and co-authors teach a model to locate organs inside the body from a photo of its surface. Their 2026 preprint deals with depth images of the patient's outside. Automated patient positioning matters in medical scanning. A well-placed patient shortens the scan and improves throughput and comfort. If a system can infer where organs sit from the surface shape, the scanner can be set up before any imaging dose is spent.

Learning that inside-outside map is the paper's core task. Surface depth is cheap and safe to capture. Organ position varies with body shape, so the map must be learned, not ruled. The work joins computer vision with radiology workflow.
arxiv-2601-18360:
Weikang Qian and three colleagues study the shape of a set of plans that show up in hard choice tasks. The sets pair a kind of curved cost rule with caps on how much of each group can be picked. Such sets sit inside tasks in ports, power grids, and work plans. The shape of the set tells a solver which cuts will trim the search with no loss.

The team find a new class of sharp cuts for two such sets. They build the cuts by a step trick that lifts a small true claim to a large one. Sharp cuts can cut run time a lot on real tasks. Their work gives solver teams new tools to add to the kit. It also maps the form of these sets with more care than past work did.
arxiv-2601-18460:
Francisco Gancedo and four colleagues study what can go wrong where two fluids of unlike weight meet and move. The heavy fluid sits on top of the light one in their setup. That stack is not calm: the edge between the fluids tends to grow wild with time. Thick rules of flow, with drag, set how the edge moves.

The team prove that the wild growth does not stop. In their setup the edge grows in length or in curl for all time, with no cap. A proof of that kind rules out hopes that drag alone would calm the stack. It also maps a hard case for teams who model oil, water, or air in tanks. Such proofs keep models honest about what they can and cannot tame.
arxiv-2601-18660:
Jaume de Haro gives a fresh, clear path to a set of marks used to chart a fall into a black hole. The marks are named for Novikov. They ride with bits that fall in a straight line toward the hole. In the chart, time and place are set by those falls, so the chart fits how a fall feels from in-side. Past paths to the marks were long and hard to read.

De Haro starts from falls with a twist: the bits bear a kind of charge that past work tags as less than none. Those falls form a full set that spans the whole of the hole's world, in-side and out. From them the marks drop out in a short, plain way. A clear path could help teach the chart and use it in new work on how holes grow and fade.
arxiv-2601-18760:
Henry Bell and three colleagues argue that the rules used to train language models should rest on why people hold their views, not just on which reply they pick. In the main path now, a model is taught to match a set of writ rules. Those rules are set by a small team. It is not clear how the rules could be set in a fair way with wide voice from all who are touched by the tools.

Picks alone hide the grounds of a view. Two folk may pick the same reply for quite unlike grounds. A rule built on picks may thus miss what folk prize most. The team set out a path that learns rules from grounds and worths. Such rules could claim a fairer base. They could also be checked in the open, ground by ground.
arxiv-2601-18960:
Sofia Cocciaretto and Vittorio Giovannetti study how much quantum data a lossy channel can carry. Most quantum link work rests on qubits, units with two states. Higher level units, called qudits, may carry more and compute better, a point fresh results stress.

They study a family of channels that model energy decay for such multi level signals. The work asks what the quantum capacity of these channels is, that is, how much quantum data can pass safely. Knowing the cap for real loss shapes helps plan links that use bigger units, not just qubits.
arxiv-2601-19060:
Jeonghwan Kim and ten co-authors teach a visual model to fetch facts tied to the exact spot in a photo. Answering questions about images often needs both sharp sight and outside facts. Past systems that fetch facts lack an inner rule for when to fetch and how to aim the search.

Their model, PixSearch, joins region level sight with fetch based reasoning in one end to end system. It can point at the part of the image the question is about, then pull facts for that part. Grounded fetching could cut the made up answers that plague visual question answering today.
arxiv-2601-19360:
Diego Rossini and Lonneke van der Plas find multiword expressions in text with a light, language aware model. Multiword expressions, like idioms, act as one unit of meaning spread over several words. Spotting all their types is a known hard step for language tools.

Their method labels each token as inside or outside an expression, adds linguistic features, and grows the training data by augmentation. Their model tops the prior best on its test set, ahead of far larger systems. A light model that wins on skill, not size, suits real pipelines that process text at scale.
arxiv-2601-19760:
Yuya Koshiba and colleagues report a laser that fires short, strong pulses in the infrared. The device uses a thin disk of holmium-doped YAG crystal, pumped by laser diodes. It was run in two modes: Q-switching and cavity dumping, two standard ways to store and release light in bursts. The output wavelength sits near two micrometres.

The pulses carry more than six millijoules of energy and last only a few nanoseconds. That combination gives a peak power above a megawatt. The beam quality is near the diffraction limit, meaning it stays tight and clean. Such sources serve in materials processing, sensing, and further laser stages. The work shows what thin-disk designs can reach in this wavelength range.
arxiv-2601-20260:
Xingxin Xu and four colleagues present a diffusion method for fusing images from different sensors into one picture. Fusion aims to keep fine detail and high visual quality while joining the strengths of each source image. Diffusion models generate sharp images, but they often lose detail when used for fusion.

The authors design a reversible, efficient diffusion process to cut that loss. Their goal is a fused image that keeps the texture of the inputs, not a smoothed version of them. Better fusion supports night vision, medical scans, and remote sensing, where each sensor alone sees only part of the scene.
arxiv-2601-20760:
Sarvesh Shashidhar, Abhishek Mishra, and Madhav Kotecha question a basic assumption in how AI models learn from human feedback. Their 2026 paper is about RLHF, the method that trains models with human ratings. RLHF has been effective for AI alignment, the task of making models act as people wish. But it treats all raters as if they respond in the same way.

Real users differ, and the authors put that heterogeneity at the center. If raters want different things, one reward signal may fit no one well. The paper explores what changes when feedback comes from a mixed crowd. It asks how training should handle clashing tastes and values. The work speaks to builders who want models that serve varied users, not an average one.
arxiv-2601-20860:
Babak Vakili asks whether quantum teleportation still works in a universe that expands. The 2026 paper studies teleportation in Friedmann-Robertson-Walker spacetime, the standard model of an expanding cosmos. Two scenarios take center stage. One is a power-law expansion, steady and simple. The other is the de Sitter universe, which expands at an ever-quickening rate. The approach is field-theoretical.

Two comoving observers share an entangled mode of a scalar field. Comoving means they drift along with the expansion. Vakili analyzes the quantum correlations between them. Expansion can stretch and weaken those correlations. The study asks how much fidelity teleportation keeps under such strain. The results matter for quantum information in curved spacetime, a field that joins gravity with quantum rules.
arxiv-2601-21060:
Zhuoyan Li and a large team of co-authors put humans and language models on the same feature-building team. Their 2026 paper studies feature engineering for tabular learning. Feature engineering turns raw columns into inputs a model can use well. Large language models are increasingly used to automate that craft. Given task details, an LLM can propose diverse transformations. Those proposals aim to enhance downstream performance.

The paper's twist is collaboration. Humans and models each bring strengths to the table. Models offer breadth and speed; humans offer judgment and context. The study examines how the pair should work together. Good features often decide whether a tabular model succeeds. This human-LLM workflow could make that step faster and better. The work serves data teams that live in spreadsheets and databases.
arxiv-2601-21160:
Michael Ibrahim, Nagi Gebraeel, and Weijun Xie study clustering when data stays split across many separate clients. No one knows in advance how many groups exist across all clients. Each client also holds its own mix, and the mixes can overlap or differ.

The authors build a shared learning method that works without pooling the raw data. It extends a classic expectation and maximization routine to the split-data setting. The method has to guess the total number of groups while it learns them. That makes it useful for settings where data must stay local, such as hospitals or banks that cannot share records.
arxiv-2601-21660:
Jingyang Zhao and Mingyu Xiao improve approximation algorithms for vehicle routing with capacity limits. In this classic problem, vans leave a depot to serve customers who each demand some load. Every van has a fixed capacity, and routes should be as short as possible.

The unsplittable version bars splitting one customer's demand across vans, which matches real practice. The authors give better guarantees on how close their routes come to optimal. Routing sits under delivery, repair, and transit services everywhere. Even small gains in the guarantee translate into large savings when the method runs at city scale every day.
arxiv-2601-21760:
Ruian Tie, Wenbo Xiong, and five co-authors downscale climate data to fine grids without any paired training examples. Supervised downscaling learns from matched coarse and fine data, which ties it to the models it trained on. New climate models break that pairing and expose domain gaps.

Zero-shot methods exist but can violate physics or lose their gradient signal at large scale factors. The authors use diffusion posterior sampling to stay both physical and stable. Fine local detail is what impact studies need, from flood risk to heat planning. A method that transfers across climate models saves retraining for every new release.
arxiv-2601-21960:
Aref Farhadipour and a large team lay out the rules for a shared contest in speaker verification. Systems that confirm a speaker's identity degrade badly when the language changes between enrollment and testing. The field's reliance on English-centered data makes that weakness worse.

The TidyVoice 2026 Challenge, described in this evaluation plan, is designed to confront the language mismatch problem head-on. The plan spells out how systems will be tested so results can be compared fairly. Challenges like this matter because voice verification guards bank accounts and devices worldwide. And a system that fails on non-English speakers fails a large part of the world.
arxiv-2601-22260:
Tom Gajecki, Jonas Althoff, and Waldo Nogueira work on a clear need: help cochlear implant users pick out one voice in noise. Their 2026 preprint uses brain wave cues to learn which speaker the user wants to hear. An implant turns sound into small electric pulses for the ear.

Their network joins the mixed sound with the brain wave cues in one light step. It then builds a pulse pattern for the wanted voice alone. The method also solves a mix-up that pure sound tools face. It points to implants that track the mind, not just the ear.
arxiv-2601-22360:
B. J. P. Jones works out how light hydrogen atoms bounce off helium at near-freezing cold. His 2026 preprint covers all three forms of hydrogen: plain, heavy, and the rare radioactive form. Both light forms of helium serve as targets.

The rates span a vast range, from near absolute zero up to room heat. The work is driven by a real need: sources of cold tritium for tests of the neutrino's mass. At such cold, each bounce can shift the atoms' paths and spins. Firm rates help teams design those sources with care.
arxiv-2601-22660:
Evan Gibson Smith and Bashima Islam train deep binary networks by freezing layers in stages, with no gradient shortcut. Binary networks use one-bit weights and activations, which makes them tiny and fast. Their 2026 preprint tests progressive freezing in place of the straight-through estimator, the usual trick that fakes a gradient.

Plain global freezing works for binary weights, they find, but fails for full binary nets. Blocked gradients through activations are the cause. The find maps where the trick can and cannot go. Tiny nets matter for phones and sensors. Honest limits guide the design.
arxiv-2601-23060:
Luo-Jia Kang builds a complete operator basis for the Standard Model Effective Field Theory with modular flavor symmetry. The effective theory extends the Standard Model with higher-dimensional operators that capture unknown heavy physics. Modular symmetries organize the flavor patterns of quarks and leptons.

The setup uses two copies of an A4 flavor group, one for quarks and one for leptons, with separate moduli. Right-handed quarks carry the simplest modular weights. A complete basis tells model builders exactly which operators the symmetry allows. Distinct moduli for the quark and lepton sectors let the symmetry treat the two flavor puzzles separately.
arxiv-2602-02460:
J. Roberto Viana and 4 co-authors solve a 2D magnetic model by growing clusters step by step, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The spin-3/2 Ising model places magnetic moments with four possible states on a lattice. Computing its partition function directly grows exponentially, reaching four-to-the-N possibilities.

Their hierarchical method builds finite magnetic clusters generation by generation. Each site's effective state in the next generation comes from the local magnetization of a cluster in the previous one. Systems of effectively enormous size become reachable. Applied to the ferromagnetic model on a honeycomb lattice, the setup models monolayer chromium triiodide, a real 2D magnet. Calibrated to the measured transition temperature near forty-five kelvin, it reproduces the magnetization curve and the broad specific-heat peak. Entropy calculations show a finite low-temperature residue matching the system's double degeneracy.
arxiv-2602-02660:
Automating AI research itself is the goal of a 2026 system from Jiefeng Chen and 5 co-authors. Machine learning engineering differs from ordinary coding: evaluation means expensive model training, and knowing which change caused a gain is opaque. Language-model agents tend to write monolithic scripts that ignore both problems.

Their framework, MARS, rests on three pillars. Budget-aware planning searches with Monte Carlo tree search under explicit cost constraints. Modular construction follows a design-decompose-implement pipeline suited to complex research repositories. Comparative reflective memory tackles credit assignment by analyzing differences between solutions and distilling high-signal lessons. On MLE-Bench the system reached the best performance among open-source frameworks and stayed competitive with top leaderboard methods. Most lessons the agent actually used came from transferring insights across different search branches.
arxiv-2602-03160:
Steering a model's values to a chosen intensity is the goal of Woojin Kim, joined by 3 collaborators, in their system VALUEFLOW. Aligning language models with diverse human values remains central and hard. Preference methods often miss deeper motivational principles. Value-based methods are more principled, yet extraction ignores hierarchy, review detects presence without intensity, and steerability is poorly understood across models and theories.

VALUEFLOW unifies extraction, review, and steering with calibrated intensity control. A hierarchical vector space captures form within and across value theories. A large database of value-labeled texts supplies intensity figures. An anchor-based evaluator scores outputs against those panels. A large study across ten models and four theories found asymmetries in steerability and composition patterns for multi-value control.
arxiv-2602-03360:
Rockfalls fragment by a universal law regardless of rock type, according to Alvaro Vergara, with 2 co-authors, in runs validated against field data. Impact fragmentation is a fundamental dissipative process in geosciences, yet its stochastic nature makes debris evolution hard to predict. Their discrete element system resolves fragmentation mechanics across diverse lithologies, from high-strength siliciclastic units to massive carbonates, using high-detail data from documented rockfall events to check the breakage patterns the model produces.

Fragment size spreads follow a Weibull scaling law for every lithology and any starting kinetic energy. A relative breakage index collapses the data onto a single statistical signature. That signature acts as a proxy for lithological sensitivity, showing how efficiently kinetic energy becomes new fracture surface. Energy partitioning between surviving blocks and fine debris supports better gallery design.
arxiv-2602-03760:
Camera pipelines polish images for human eyes and throw away sensor detail that machines could use. Mishal Fatima and 4 co-authors release RAWDet-7 in a 2026 paper, a benchmark built on raw, unprocessed images instead. The dataset holds roughly 25,000 training and 7,600 test images from varied cameras, lighting, and environments.

Seven object categories are densely annotated following established conventions, and each object also carries a description derived from the matching high-resolution processed image. Simulated four-, six-, and eight-bit quantization mirrors real sensor constraints. The benchmark supports studying detection performance, description quality, and generalization in low-bit raw processing. It asks how much object-level information survives when the usual image pipeline is stripped away.
arxiv-2602-03860:
Yifeng Gao and 2 co-authors improve a closed-form model for estimating nonlinear interference in optical fiber links. Their 2026 paper refines the GN polynomial closed-form model. Network engineers use that tool to predict how signals distort each other over long fiber spans. Earlier versions leaned on machine-learning correction factors to stay accurate.

The new coherent model folds in the spectral power density of the interference and its coherent accumulation along the link. It evaluates the interference accurately over any rectangular integration domain, the island of spectrum being analyzed, without those correction factors. The improvement holds even in low-dispersion and low-baud-rate subcarrier systems, the regimes where the older model struggled most. Closed-form speed with broader accuracy widens the model's practical reach.
arxiv-2602-04060:
Do poor countries catch up to rich ones? M Hashem Pesaran and 1 co-author revisit the output convergence debate with modern panel methods in a 2026 paper. Popular regression tools assume parallel trends and uniform dynamics across countries, assumptions the authors show are badly wrong.

Those tools substantially understate convergence speed and mislead inference. Dynamic common correlated effects estimators handle nonparallel trends, correlated differences, breaks, and unit roots properly. Applied to Penn World Table data, they find almost no sign that per capita output converges, and only slow growth convergence, and a route to estimating slow-moving growth factors. The paper is a warning about method-driven conclusions in growth economics.
arxiv-2602-04360:
What minimal change would flip a hypergraph model's decision? Fabiano Veglianti and 2 co-authors answer with what-if explanations for hypergraph neural networks in a 2026 paper. Hypergraphs capture group interactions that ordinary graphs miss, but the models built on them resist being explained.

Their explainer edits only node-hyperedge incidences or whole hyperedges, keeping changes doable and structurally meaningful. Tests on benchmark datasets produced valid, concise counterfactuals. The edits spotlight the higher-order relations most key to each prediction. For high-stakes uses, knowing the smallest change that flips an outcome supports audits, appeals, and model fixing alike.
arxiv-2602-06160:
The edge of a geometric space can hold deep clues about the space itself. Suzhen Han and Qing Liu study a special kind of edge called the Morse boundary. They define a trait for it, named uniform perfectness, and give a plain account of what it means.

Their main result says the Morse boundary of any finitely made, non-elementary group is uniformly perfect whenever it exists at all. That covers wide families, including acylindrically hyperbolic groups, Artin groups, and hierarchically hyperbolic groups. They also prove a rigidity result: maps between such edges come from coarse distance-preserving maps exactly when they meet any of several natural tests.
arxiv-2602-06560:
Erasing one bit of memory costs a minimum amount of energy, according to Landauer's principle, at least in equilibrium. Salambô Dago and Ludovic Bellon show experimentally how to slip below that bound with a clever feedback trick. Their bit is a micro-resonator held in a virtual potential shaped by feedback, with hysteresis built into the shaping.

Tuning the hysteresis creates a non-equilibrium steady state whose effective temperature can be tuned. Erasure then consumed substantially less than the Landauer limit, by more than a fifth in their measurements. The hysteresis acts as an embedded Maxwell demon, using temporal and spatial information to cut the system's entropy and the cost of transformation. The platform offers a playground for feedback, information, and energy trade-offs.
arxiv-2602-06960:
Yuchen Yan and nine co-authors tackle the cost of long chains of thought in reasoning models. Stretching a chain grows cost in a quadratic way, hits context limits, and lets key facts get lost in the middle. Summing up thoughts at intervals helps, but old methods do not learn when to sum up, what to keep, or how to pick back up. Their system, InftyThink+, learns the whole iterative path by reward training.

Training runs in two stages: a taught cold start, then path-level reward learning, so the model learns smart summing-up and continuation choices. On a distilled reasoning model it lifted accuracy on a math test by 21 percent and clearly beat usual long-chain reward learning, while carrying over better to out-of-distribution tests. It also cut run-time lag and sped up training, pairing stronger reasoning with better efficiency.
arxiv-2602-07060:
Haochen Wang and eight co-authors improve short-time muon scattering tomography, a non-invasive inspection technique that images the interior of objects using cosmic-ray muons. Practical use is limited by poor image quality when only a short exposure is possible, because few muons arrive. The team trains a U-Net framework on simulated point-of-closest-approach images to enhance low-statistics reconstructions.

Applied to experimental data, the framework raised structural similarity from about 0.72 to about 0.97 and cut a perceptual dissimilarity measure from about 0.36 to about 0.03. Those gains show the method can effectively rescue images from sparse muon data, paving the way for practical deployment of short-time muon tomography in inspection tasks where long exposures are infeasible.
arxiv-2602-07460:
Detecting tiny nonlinearities in resonators calls for sensors whose response sharpens near special points.  Ya-Wei Zeng and four co-authors propose a scheme based on a three-mode anti-parity-time-symmetric cavity-magnon-waveguide system, where tuning optical gain controls the linewidth suppression point.

Even when the two dissipative magnonic modes decay strongly, the scheme senses weak anharmonicities in both cavity and magnonic modes with similarly high sensitivity, and a detuned laser drive improves it further.  The design generalizes to other physical systems with nonlinearities.  Quantum sensing teams get a flexible, gain-tuned route to measuring effects that usual sensors would miss.
arxiv-2602-07660:
Telling regular from chaotic motion usually needs variational equations or neighboring trajectories, but a simpler test may suffice. Javier Jiménez-López and one co-author study the time-averaged phase space arclength of a trajectory, expressed through a normalized Lagrangian descriptor, as a chaos indicator.

It needs only integrating the motion plus one scalar running sum, with no variational tools. Regular quasiperiodic paths and well-mixed chaotic ones show different finite-time behavior even though it converges in both cases. Quasiperiodic paths settle as one over time, while chaotic ones wobble at a slower rate. Tests on the Hénon-Heiles and Fermi-Pasta-Ulam systems back the claim, with SALI as the reference chaos check. Motion experts get a cheap, single-path test for chaos grounded in ergodic theory.
arxiv-2602-07860:
Rebuilding a 3D shape from a still photo is well studied, but ultra-fast motion blur, as with a spinning machine part or a ball in flight, defeats standard multi-view methods. Fei Yu and five co-authors propose an inverse-rendering approach that recovers geometry directly from severely blurred images.

Standard blur simulation averages many frames and repeatedly recomputes barycentric weights, a costly bottleneck. Their fast barycentric solver cuts that overhead for speedups up to 4.57 times, enabling efficient photorealistic simulation of high-speed motion, and the whole pipeline is differentiable so shape can be optimized from the blurred evidence. The work opens 3D reconstruction to scenes where the camera or object simply moves too fast for ordinary methods.
arxiv-2602-08060:
Running language models on edge devices demands low latency, and speculative decoding, drafting tokens quickly then verifying them, helps, but integrating it into compiler workflows on heterogeneous chips is tricky. Alejandro Ruiz y Mesa and four co-authors address both problems with an analytical cost model that guides partitioning of model subgraphs across a system-on-chip's varied processors.

The model predicts when speculative sampling plus heterogeneous execution jointly pay off, especially for the short inputs typical at the edge. It is validated on a device with a hexacore ARM CPU and a Mali GPU. Edge AI engineers gain a sound way to decide how to split work across cores and accelerators instead of guessing, a step toward safe, responsive on-device language models.
arxiv-2602-08360:
A galaxy cluster that looked like it was rotating turns out to be an optical illusion. Yicheng Li and seventeen co-authors analyze the cluster RXCJ0110.0+1358 with deep imaging, survey photometry, spectra, and X-ray data. Their arXiv paper is the second in a survey series, and it resolves a puzzle between the optical and X-ray views.

Optically the cluster looks bimodal with strong substructure, yet X-rays show one smooth blob centered on the brightest galaxy. Weak lensing settles it: nearly all the mass sits in the southeast, while the northwestern clump is almost massless. The apparent second clump is a projected filament mistaken for members. Readers get a cautionary tale about rotation claims and a clean lensing mass map.
arxiv-2602-08560:
Estimating a hidden state from noisy measurements is routine when the dynamics are known, but many real processes offer no model at all. Fredrik Cumlin and two co-authors propose DNS, a data-driven nonlinear smoother that works without any state-transition model. Their arXiv paper targets model-free dynamical processes observed through linear measurements.

A recurrent architecture yields a closed-form posterior for the hidden sequence given the measurements, and training needs only measurement data, never state data. Tests on several stochastic processes, including the Lorenz benchmark, show DNS beating a deep Kalman smoother and an iterative data-driven smoother by clear margins. Readers get an unsupervised smoother for processes too complex to model.
arxiv-2602-08660:
Models that make images and text can amplify bias in society, yet fairness rules borrowed from classification miss the point: they balance group frequencies while ignoring how good the output is. Alexandre Verine and two co-authors show such rules can be met even when groups are modeled with wildly varied quality. Their arXiv paper introduces equalized generative treatment, which asks for comparable output quality across sensitive groups.

Quality is judged by a reference divergence, and enforcing fairness ties overall quality to the hardest group to approximate. That insight motivates a simple min-max fine-tuning method that balances divergences across groups. Tests on image and text tasks show fairer outcomes at competitive overall quality. Readers get a fairness definition that measures what truly matters to the people depicted.
arxiv-2602-09260:
V. A. Souza Alves and three co-authors study correlation functions with fractional-mode excitations of R-symmetry currents in the D1-D5 conformal field theory. Fractional modes lift to the covering surface as specific sums of integer modes, with coefficients fixed exactly by the covering map through Bell polynomials. That lifting is the paper's central technical device.

Four-point functions are derived for fractional excitations of chiral and anti-chiral Neveu-Schwarz fields, Ramond ground states, and the twist-two scalar modulus operator that moves the theory away from its free point. Twist structures include (n)-(2)-(2)-(n) and double-cycle cases. Final answers depend only on the lifted cross-ratio, with discussion of Hurwitz blocks, operator-product channels, and fusion rules.
arxiv-2602-09760:
Lexical semantic change is the phenomenon in which a word's meaning shifts over time. Kohei Oda and three co-authors note that most studies improve estimates of the degree of change, yet struggle to show how meaning actually changes. Enhancing interpretability is a significant challenge, since it could yield novel insights. Their 2026 paper proposes mapping the semantic space of contextualized word embeddings from a pretrained language model onto a neurobiological feature space.

In that space, each dimension marks a primitive feature of words, with its value showing the feature's intensity. Humans can thus interpret semantic change systematically. Used to estimate the degree of change, the method beats most previous methods. Given its high interpretability, several analyses follow, uncovering interesting change types overlooked in prior studies and effectively finding words with specific change types.
arxiv-2602-09860:
Sang-Jun Park studies k-plus and Schmidt numbers for linear maps and two-part states showing sym folds in his 2026 paper. Two cases are studied: maps matching under flipping by unitary sym grids, and two-part states fixed under sym tensor actions, each set by two knobs. An account of k-plus and splitting rules for these maps is given, with Schmidt numbers found for the linked two-part states.

Analysis yields plus-partial-transpose states with Schmidt number half the size. It also gives first plain builds of k-plus whole maps for any k up to half the size minus one, reaching the best bounds. Two uses follow. The plus-partial-transpose-squared guess holds within sym-matching and mirror-sym-matching maps. A guess of Pal and Vertesi on the lower bound of the Sindici-Piani semi program for plus-partial-transpose linking is settled.
arxiv-2602-09960:
Sixth-generation networks promise coverage for remote regions from the sky, but drone base stations are few and power-hungry. A 2026 paper led by Arman Azizi, with four co-authors, joins drones with a high-altitude platform carrying a reconfigurable intelligent surface, or HAPS-RIS. The framework treats the two layers as one system rather than rivals.

The design serves as many users as possible through the platform, uses as few drones as possible, and trims average drone path loss, all under service and resource limits. A low-complexity method ties path loss to clustering and gives a closed-form surface design. Simulations show platform-only coverage at low rates, drones indispensable at higher rates, and the joint design beating either layer alone.
arxiv-2602-10060:
Networks can tip suddenly when a giant connected piece appears or vanishes, and finite size blurs the warning signs. A 2026 paper by A. V. Goltsev and S. N. Dorogovtsev offers susceptibility as an early warning sign for percolation shifts in complex networks. The method plants watchers, randomly chosen nodes that monitor local links.

The authors write down exact rules for susceptibility and trace its key pattern near smooth and mixed-order shifts. Tests cover random networks with one-way or two-way links, networks with dependency links, and network cores. Landau theory backs the shared pattern of that behavior, suggesting a sharp rise in susceptibility reliably heralds an approaching shift.
arxiv-2602-10360:
Private continual release of distinct-item counts in turnstile streams, where items insert and delete, carries a polynomial additive error floor that has seemed fundamental. A 2026 paper led by Anders Aamand, with two co-authors, shows that floor can be dodged by letting estimates with both additive and multiplicative error. It reaches polylogarithmic multiplicative and additive error for continual distinct-element counts.

A similar pattern holds for the second frequency moment of a turnstile stream, reaching near-one multiplicative and polylogarithmic additive error. Both results use polylogarithmic space where prior approaches used polynomial space. With sublinear space, some multiplicative error is needed even without privacy, and the paper raises open questions on additive-multiplicative error trade-offs in private continual release.
arxiv-2602-10660:
Kiarash Ghasemzadeh and Sedigheh Dehghani present a real-time multi-task network for driving perception in a 2026 paper. Self-driving cars could cut accidents and congestion, but steady perception remains a major challenge. Multi-task networks help by sharing runs across tasks, improving speed and transfer.

Their network, AurigaNet, integrates object finding, lane finding, and drivable-area segmentation in one system. Trained and tested on the BDD100K dataset, known for its driving diversity, the system targets real-time urban work. The paper places the unified design as a useful step toward perception stacks. Such stacks see the road's actors, markings, and free space jointly, fast enough to drive on.
arxiv-2602-10960:
Bank shocks rarely travel down one road alone. Ilias Aarab and four co-authors build a euro-area bank network with several layers, one for each way trouble can spread. The layers cover long and short credit, shared bond holdings, short secured funding, and overlapping outside portfolios.

All layers sit on one shared set of large banking groups, with balance-sheet detail added for tuning. The authors show that the layers differ sharply in links and key players. Flattening them into one map can hide real structure and name the wrong firms as central. A centrality test and a small agent model run on real exposures show how the layered map can guide risk checks and stress tests across markets.
arxiv-2602-11360:
Clinical risk models can wobble when trained on other samples from one population. Sara Matijevic and Christopher Yau propose a bootstrapping-based control frame that builds resampling straight into deep network training. It constrains forecast variability across resampled data sets, yielding a single stable model.

Tests on simulated data and three clinical data sets show improved balance, with smaller mean absolute differences and far fewer strongly deviating forecasts. Discriminative results and trait importance consistency hold up, with high links between models. Ensembles prove more stable still, but at the cost of clarity, since each member uses predictors differently. The method offers trustworthy, reproducible risk models for data-limited care settings.
arxiv-2602-11560:
Asteroid families are born when a parent body shatters, but sorting true fragments from neighbors and stray interlopers is painstaking work. David Vokrouhlicky and two co-authors use their own catalog of asteroid orbits to re-examine the Karin family. A standard clustering pass names 3863 candidates, yet that list mixes in members of nearby families and older Koronis strays. Tracing orbits backward in time isolates 2161 objects whose paths converge on the parent body Karin.

That convergence dates the breakup to about five point seven million years ago and links ejection speeds to a new convergence measure. Small members show drift tied to heat-driven forces and spin tilt, and Karin sizes follow a steep power law. The neighboring Koronis2 family proves harder to pin down. Matching its large members to Koronis would need an age above 10 million years, a claim the authors say still needs direct numerical checking.
arxiv-2602-11760:
Feature ranking methods promise to turn predictive models into tools for scientific discovery. Flexible models, however, can be unstable: sampling noise and algorithmic randomness distort their scores, a serious flaw for biomedical uses. Joseph Paillard and three co-authors ask a practical question. Should researchers explain one ensemble model, or aggregate explanations from individual models? The curved nature of these scores makes the choice hard to settle, and it remains little studied.

Their theory, built to cover complex modern models, shows the choice hinges mainly on excess risk. Against earlier claims, ensembling at the model level gives better variable scores, especially for flexible models, by shrinking the leading error term. Tests on classical benchmarks and a large proteomic study from the UK Biobank confirm the finding.
arxiv-2602-11960:
Document parsing feeds retrieval systems, so transcription and layout errors propagate downstream. Bruno Rigal and four co-authors evaluate PDF-to-Markdown conversion with recent vision-language models on challenging French documents. Existing benchmarks skew toward English or Chinese and punish benign formatting choices, like line breaks or list splits, that barely matter for downstream use.

The authors build a French-focused benchmark of difficult pages, chosen by model-disagreement sampling from a corpus of 60,000 documents, spanning handwritten forms, complex layouts, dense tables, and graphics-rich pages. Unit-test-style checks target concrete failures, such as text presence, reading order, and local table constraints, with normalization that discounts presentation-only variance. Across 15 models, the strongest proprietary systems prove most robust on handwriting and forms, while several open-weights systems stay competitive on standard printed layouts.
arxiv-2602-12260:
Decentralised protocols promise fixed rules, yet many hide emergency brakes such as freezes, pauses, and account quarantines. Oghenekaro Elem led this work with one co-author, Nimrod Talmon, asking when such overrides save trust and when they look like illegitimate power. With about 10 billion dollars in exploit losses potentially open to on-chain action since 2016, the stakes are high and current designs are ad hoc.

The paper maps emergency designs on two axes: scope precision and trigger authority. It then models trade-offs among standing centralisation cost, containment speed, and collateral harm. Across 705 exploit cases, containment time varies with authority type. Losses skew toward rare catastrophes, and narrower account or module actions match broader ones on success while running slightly faster at the median.
arxiv-2602-12360:
Autonomous systems often see only part of their surroundings, through narrow sensors, occlusions, or failures, yet they must still act safely. Knut Peterson led this work with one co-author, David Han, testing deep learning for predicting dynamic map states from limited field-of-view time series. The challenge is to infer nearby states from partial, changing sensor data.

By packing spatial and temporal information into a single-image format, the team can use a wide range of existing image-to-image models for the task. Tests across diverse sensing scenarios show high accuracy in predicting map states from limited views. The approach turns a hard partial-observation problem into a familiar image prediction problem, without bespoke model design for each sensor setup.
arxiv-2602-12460:
The first stars, Population III, shaped the early universe through radiation and explosions, yet their feedback is hard to model at scale. Bocheng Zhu led this work with one co-author, Liang Gao, presenting SPARK, a Population III plus Population II subgrid framework in the moving-mesh code AREPO. It joins primordial non-equilibrium chemistry, metal-line cooling, IMF-sampled stellar evolution with supernova feedback, and approximate Lyman-Werner and ionising radiation transport.

Simulations in a 1 megaparsec per h box run from redshift 127 to 10, with fiducial gas mass resolution near 10 suns and spatial resolution near 4 parsecs. The model reproduces Population II star formation rate density from earlier work, with metal-enriched gas filling 0.5 to 2 percent of volume by redshift 10. Convergence arrives once subhalos above about 3 million suns are resolved, and a fiducial run costs about 10,000 CPU hours, making larger studies tractable.
arxiv-2602-12560:
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons are the main contributors to aromatic infrared bands seen widely in space, yet analysing those bands is hard because the PAH family spans immense structural diversity. Guoqing Tang led this work with three co-authors, building a graph neural network frame that predicts PAH absorption spectra up to 10,000 times faster than traditional quantum chemical methods. Reliable reference spectra are otherwise difficult to compute for so many structures.

Four designs were evaluated: graph convolutional networks, graph attention networks, message passing networks, and attentive fingerprint models. The attentive fingerprint model performs best overall, and training it with five spectral distance metrics as losses shows Jensen-Shannon divergence gives the most accurate, stable results. Performance peaks for PAHs with 20 to 40 carbon atoms, falling for larger molecules where training data are scarce, offering fast approximate reference spectra for small to medium PAHs.
arxiv-2602-12760:
Quantum walks spread a particle across a graph by scattering at each vertex, and random phases can pin the particle down, a phenomenon called dynamical localisation. Alain Joye, Andreas Schaefer, and Simone Warzel study walks on arbitrary infinite graphs, where each vertex carries its own scattering matrix. Multiplying those matrices by independent random phases creates a random scattering walk.

The authors prove that localisation holds in a strong-disorder regime, where randomness is large. The proof rests on a link between fractional moment estimates and eigenfunction correlators, a result of independent interest for general random unitary operators. By working on arbitrary graphs rather than neat lattices, the paper extends localisation theory to a much wider class of quantum walks.
arxiv-2602-13360:
Models of colliding nuclei guide heavy-ion physics, and a newer model built at JINR for the NICA project aims at energies of several GeV per nucleon. This paper asks whether that model, DCM-QGSM-SMM, also works lower down. Its predictions are compared with FRAGM and FIRST/GSI experimental data from 300 MeV per nucleon upward, alongside rival models in the same range.

Nuclear fragmentation, the breakup of nuclei in collision, is the test case, since its patterns expose how interaction mechanisms behave across energies. The comparison gauges whether mechanisms tuned for higher energies carry over to the intermediate range. M. A. Martemianov leads the work with six co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14160:
Chaeeun Lee and three co-authors present a 2026 arXiv system for clinical reasoning with multiple agents. Clinical choices need nuanced reasoning over mixed evidence, with traceable justifications. Most multi-agent language systems chase final accuracy while neglecting whether the reasoning path follows clinical standards.

The test case is gene-disease validity curation, where experts weigh diverse biomedical evidence for a causal gene-disease link. The authors train a supervisor agent with GRPO, adding process-level supervision to outcome rewards within a hierarchical multi-agent setup. On the ClinGen dataset, outcome-only training lifted accuracy from 0.195 to 0.732 but scored only 0.392 F1 on process alignment, a gap the combined rewards aim to close.
arxiv-2602-14260:
Robert Edwards and seven co-authors compute a 2026 arXiv quantity from lattice QCD: the gluon momentum fraction of the nucleon. A nonperturbative renormalization method based on gradient flow anchors the calculation. The result comes from a single Wilson-clover ensemble with 2+1 flavors, pion mass 358 MeV, and lattice spacing 0.094 fm.

A variational method cuts excited-state contamination, while the distillation framework supports a large operator basis. Bayesian model averaging over all fits reduces systematic uncertainty. Matching coefficients then convert flow-time lattice results to the MS scheme at 2 GeV. The final value is 0.482, with a statistical uncertainty of 0.035, a precise lattice handle on gluon momentum.
arxiv-2602-14360:
Zuyuan Zhang and two co-authors propose a 2026 arXiv planner for service function chaining under network drift. Edge-cloud convergence demands continuous placement and scheduling of virtual network function chains under compute, bandwidth, and end-to-end quality constraints. Most optimizers assume static networks and degrade when topology and resources change over time.

LiSFC is a Lipschitz lifelong planner that carries Monte Carlo tree search stats across shifting net setups, using an MDP-distance cap. The problem becomes a sequence of Markov decision processes indexed by network graph and constraints, with a graph-drift metric bounding the LiZero distance. That transfer imports bias and sample-efficiency guarantees, while LiSFC-Search, a service-chain-aware unified tree search with adaptive UCT, puts the theory to work.
arxiv-2602-14460:
Shiva Sheybani and two co-authors set up a 2026 arXiv set of integral inequalities for numerical radius and operator norm. Bounded linear maps on Hilbert spaces are the setting, and the results sharpen old triangle-type and map matrix bounds through convex mixes and sum averaging. Several follow-ons come out, including new identities, tighter bounds, and match rules.

Those follow-ons show deeper shape links between number radius and map norm, two gauges of map size that grasp varied sides of acts. The sum averaging trick offers a flexible tool for tightening known bounds, with match cases pinning when the new gauges are exact.
arxiv-2602-14760:
Jonathan Lys and others find a fault line in transformers where short paths and next-word aims pull apart. Short paths tie each step's signal to the word in hand, while training aims at the next word, so a poor guide word can send wrong news onward.

The team traces this shift with decoding paths over tied word spaces and like-measures, and finds hidden signals flip from in-word ties to out-word ties deep in the net. A fix follows from that find. The paper names a quiet flaw in the build all large language models share.
arxiv-2602-14960:
Kasela and colleagues present DRAMA, a framework for neural web search that cuts energy and parameter costs without giving up accuracy across domains. Training a separate model per domain is wasteful. One unified model often generalizes poorly. DRAMA instead pairs domain-specific adapter modules with a gating step that picks the most relevant domain knowledge for each query.

New domains join through light adapter training alone, with no full retraining. Across several web retrieval benchmarks, the system matches domain-specific models while using only a fraction of their parameters and compute. The authors argue that energy-aware design of this kind can make large-scale neural retrieval both more scalable and more sustainable.
arxiv-2602-15160:
Baêta and Cai establish a new family of sharp analytic inequalities known as chord Sobolev inequalities. Paired with Almgren and Lieb's fractional Sobolev results, the new family makes up a full class of this kind. These results connect closely to chord isoperimetric results from integral geometry, via a functional extension of the chord power integrals.

The team also derives the limiting cases, and one of those gives a result of logarithmic Sobolev type. Alongside work by Bourgain, Brezis, and Mironescu, these results finish the picture for chord Sobolev results, endpoint cases included.
arxiv-2602-15260:
Zhang and colleagues propose on-policy prefix distillation, a fast tweak of on-policy distillation. On-policy distillation draws paths from the student model and has a teacher check them token by token. It avoids reliance solely on proven final rewards, and can transfer better than off-policy distillation. Costly live sampling of the student policy while training sharply raises training cost, above all for long answers.

An early look shows training signals often cluster in the prefix of each output. Even a short teacher-generated prefix can greatly help the student produce the correct answer. Building on these findings, the team applies the training objective only to prefixes of student outputs and stops each sampling early. Tests on AI-for-Math and out-of-domain test sets show it matches full on-policy distillation while cutting training FLOP 2 to 47 times.
arxiv-2602-15560:
Cho and colleagues bridge the gap between black hole horizons and whole galaxies. How supermassive black holes feed back into their host galaxies spans a vast range of scales, and small-domain simulations cannot safely be stretched to galactic scales. The team runs long multizone GRMHD simulations that track inflow and outflow from the horizon out to the Bondi scale, across spins from zero to 0.9 and a wide range of Bondi radii.

From those runs they derive spin-dependent subgrid recipes for hot, low-rate accretion, with compact fits for accretion rate and feedback power, plus lognormal spreads for both that widen at larger Bondi radii. They also find spin-up scaling that implies a very long spin-down time, so spins stay near frozen during quiet accretion. Cosmological modellers gain recipes built from first principles rather than extrapolation.
arxiv-2602-15660:
Exler and colleagues ease a bottleneck in large-scale medical imaging: picking models and tuning settings for 3D segmentation and classification, where manual analysis is impractical. Their 3D data Analysis Optimization Pipeline uses Bayesian optimisation in two stages. First, it selects a segmentation model and tunes postprocessing on a domain-adapted synthetic benchmark, guided by a new segmentation quality metric as its objective.

Second, it tunes classifier design choices, including encoder and head architectures, use of prior knowledge, and pretraining strategies. An assisted annotation workflow in that stage pulls predicted instances from segmentation results and shows them to the operator in sequence, removing the need for manual tracking. Four case studies show the pipeline efficiently finding effective model and parameter choices for each data set, cutting the manual effort that usually gates 3D biomedical analysis.
arxiv-2602-15760:
Szulc and colleagues explain why micro-focused Brillouin light scattering still sees forward volume spin waves despite symmetry-based blocking hopes. A reciprocity-theorem model with vector diffraction-limited focus names the lengthwise focal-field part, which is far from small, as the key to response in forward volume setup. Full polarisation analysis through polar maps of spin waves excited in step adds information beyond the usual crossed readout.

In a BiYIG thin film, seen maps show Stokes and anti-Stokes polar asymmetries and odd patterns arising from quadratic magneto-optical coupling terms. Fitting with a model including Voigt and Cotton-Mouton parts yields a working Cotton-Mouton constant and shows the second-order response matching the linear Voigt part. The work clears up signal making for forward volume spin waves and gives lab workers a fuller polar toolkit.
arxiv-2602-15860:
Gong works alone on Maniscope, a shape ranking method using shortest-path gaps on k-near surfaces over fetched picks. Current net ranking methods for search-based making rely on cross-encoders or large language models, needing heavy compute and showing lags of 3 to 5 seconds per query. Maniscope joins whole cosine likeness with near surface shape to capture meaning structure flat metrics miss.

Evaluating on eight BEIR benchmark data sets, 1,233 queries, Maniscope beats an HNSW graph-based rival on the three hardest data sets. Gains in NDCG at 3 are NFCorpus plus 7 point 0 percent, TREC-COVID plus 1 point 6 percent, and AorB plus 2 point 8 percent. It runs 3 point 2 times faster, 4 point 7 ms against 14 point 8 ms average. Against cross-encoder rerankers, Maniscope achieves within 2 percent scores at far lower latency. On TREC-COVID, an LLM reranker provides only plus 0 point 5 percent NDCG at 3 gain over Maniscope at 840 times higher latency.
arxiv-2602-15960:
Clarke and Pospelov probe light dark matter with spin dependent links to nucleons, using the SNO experiment as their detector. Heavy water reactors can create pairs of MeV scale dark matter particles through neutron capture on deuterium. The authors work out the expected rate in the simplest interaction models.

Because the reaction releases ample energy, many of the created particles can split deuterium at SNO, adding to its neutral current signal. Running the numbers for a CANDU reactor feeding SNO rules out proton cross sections above a stated threshold for masses up to about one and a half MeV. A mirror reaction in the Sun excludes a further slice of parameter space, and small detectors placed near a reactor would add only weaker sensitivity.
arxiv-2602-16060:
Jayme Brickley and Xueyu Song study how liquid-liquid phase separation may shape viscosity in a supercooled glass-forming model. They use a recently introduced order parameter, the weighted coordination number, to track separation in the Kob-Andersen binary Lennard-Jones system, a standard glass former. First they rebuild the gas-liquid binodal line with this parameter, then extend the same approach to the liquid-liquid binodal.

Systems at varied densities are quenched swiftly from high to low temperature, where liquid-liquid separation appears. Densities and compositions of each liquid state check out against the lever rule, and density and pressure profiles support local equilibrium at the separation. A Markov network model then links interfacial information to temperature-dependent viscosity, tying coarsening of the interface to the steep, super-Arrhenius rise seen on cooling.
arxiv-2602-16160:
Patrick Poggi leads a team of four researchers cutting the cost of transformer-based visual tracking without sacrificing accuracy. Such trackers lead on accuracy but run their full encoder-decoder stack on every frame. That wastes compute on long stretches of video where frames change little. Their method, UncL-STARK, preserves the design while enabling dynamic, uncertainty-aware depth adaptation.

The model is fine-tuned to stay robust at multiple intermediate depths. Random-depth training with knowledge distillation allows safe truncation at inference time. At runtime, a light estimate of uncertainty drawn from corner localization heatmaps drives a feedback policy. It picks encoder and decoder depth for the next frame based on prediction confidence. Tests on two benchmarks report double-digit percentage cuts in compute, latency, and energy, while accuracy stays within a fraction of a percent of the full-depth baseline.
arxiv-2602-16360:
Leonard Günzel leads eight coauthors on docking work for an underwater vehicle that stays on site. Ocean knowledge stays limited because observations are sparse and infrequent. Underwater monitoring is held back by high cost and effort, relying on sporadic surveys or long-term measurements at fixed spots. Such work therefore needs persistent, autonomous operation without surface support, yet resident vehicles remain uncommon, challenged by autonomy, resilience, and robustness in harsh, remote deployment.

The team presents a resident setup: a docking station with a mini-class vehicle at ninety metres depth. The vehicle navigates alone with USBL signals, docks through ArUco marker-based visual localisation via an Extended Kalman Filter, and runs local surveys. It reached ninety percent autonomous docking success and finished full inspection missions within four minutes, validating acoustic and visual navigation. The results show reliable untethered work at depth is feasible, pointing toward scalable sea monitoring.
arxiv-2602-16460:
G. P. Galdi leads four others on uniqueness and structural stability of Couette-Poiseuille flow in a channel for any flux values. They establish this for a class of flows in a straight, endless channel, under perturbations with globally or locally bounded Dirichlet integrals. The key feature is that no restriction on the size of the flux is required.

Extending and refining an approach introduced by J. B. McLeod, the authors demonstrate smooth invertibility of the linearized operator at a generic Couette-Poiseuille solution without flow reversal. From this they deduce local uniqueness of such flows and their nonlinear stability under small external forces. They also prove this for a certain class of such solutions in the large, within symmetric solutions. Finally, an example shows that if that assumption is violated, it is no longer invertible, marking it as essential.
arxiv-2602-16760:
Michael Cunningham presents a practical system for privacy-aware language model inference split across a trusted local GPU and an untrusted cloud GPU. Only intermediate activations travel over the network. The design tackles autoregressive decoding over high-latency wide-area networks, where round trips dominate cost.

An asymmetric layer split keeps embedding and unembedding layers local, so raw tokens never leave the trusted device. Lookahead decoding is applied to split inference for the first time, amortizing latency across several tokens per round. An inversion attack study shows split depth trades privacy against speed, while n-gram speculation accepts over one token per step on average. Formal checks prove lookahead output matches sequential decoding under greedy choice, with no quality loss.
arxiv-2602-16860:
Adam Reddy, Asma Karami, and Hussein Nassar give complete closed-form solutions for inextensional bending of surfaces of translation and origami tessellations. Plates admit six deformation modes: three high-energy membrane modes that stretch the midsurface, and three low-energy bending modes that bend it without stretching. For origami tessellations and other corrugated compliant thin shells, modes mix and it is unclear which, if any, are low-energy in the inextensional sense.

By direct construction, the paper shows that when the midsurface is a surface of translation, three infinitesimally inextensional modes exist. They correspond to stretching with an effective Poisson effect, bending with an effective synclastic or anti-clastic effect, and twisting. The expressions hold regardless of surface regularity and properly handle creases, straight or curved. The results benchmark numerical methods and clarify elastic stiffness of thin corrugated shells.
arxiv-2602-16960:
Kolter Bradshaw and co-authors capture second kinetic instabilities in three-dimensional dayside reconnection using an improved gradient-based closure. Magnetic reconnection is highly dynamic, exciting a wide variety of kinetic waves and instabilities. Transverse current sheet events such as lower-hybrid drift and second drift-kink events have been shown by kinetic simulations to modify the process and introduce churn and mixing to the layer.

Using the Gkeyll software frame, the team simulates asymmetric reconnection based on the October 2015 MMS crossing of a diffusion region, the Burch event. An improved gradient-based heat flux closure shows significant improvement in second kinetic instabilities growing in the current sheet, which generate churn leading to second magnetic islands and flux ropes.
arxiv-2602-17260:
Hung Mai led a nine-author team on catching AI-generated video. Modern video generators now produce highly realistic synthetic clips, exposing the limits of detectors built on shallow embedding paths, image-based tricks, or heavy multimodal models. The paper proposes EA-Swin, an Embedding-Agnostic Swin Transformer that models space-time links directly on pretrained video embeddings through factorized windowed attention, fitting generic patch-based encoders.

The team also built EA-Video, a benchmark of well over a hundred thousand clips mixing new samples with curated sets across commercial and open-source generators, including unseen-generator splits for tough cross-distribution tests. EA-Swin scored near-perfect accuracy across major generators, beating prior best methods by a clear margin while generalizing to unseen sources. The result is a scalable, robust detector for modern synthetic video.
arxiv-2602-17360:
Sámuel G. Balogh led a three-author team showing that non-drug interventions can flip which immunization plan works best. Herd immunity depends not only on a pathogen's infection capacity or a population's contact structure, but also on how and when people gain immunity. Immunization plans interact with interventions that cut social contacts, and those interactions can produce unexpectedly strong, counterintuitive effects on herd immunity.

On spatially embedded contact networks, the team uncovers a reversal in the relative success of disease-induced versus vaccine-induced immunity, with average contact numbers as the critical driver. In sparse geometric networks with limited degree variety, uniform vaccination wins, but as average contacts rise, naturally gained immunity ultimately becomes the better plan. The pattern appears not only in synthetic networks but also in real-world mixing networks observed during intervention periods across multiple United States states.
arxiv-2602-17460:
Baradhwaj Coleppa led a team on neutral scalar signatures at a muon collider in the Z3 Three Higgs Doublet Model. Extending the Standard Model scalar sector is a route to new physics. The team studies Three Higgs Doublet Model phenomenology at a muon collider. Its spectrum holds three CP-even, two CP-odd, and two charged states.

For Higgs pair production via muon-antimuon annihilation, the paper studies production and decay of neutral scalar states. It assumes the Standard Model-like CP-even Higgs is the lightest state. Several benchmarks lead to four-bottom-quark and two-bottom-two-tau final states, analyzed by cut-and-count at three teraelectronvolts. Results show such a collider offers a setting for testing Higgs sectors. Neutral scalar states from two hundred to four hundred gigaelectronvolts are discoverable at five sigma for luminosities of one to four inverse attobarns.
arxiv-2602-17760:
Naomi McWilliam and team improve neural net removal of stellar activity signals in radial velocity work. Stellar activity limits radial velocity mass measures. It adds near-regular wobble that must be removed to expose exoplanet signals. Prior nets used white light cross correlation functions on HARPS-N solar data. This paper extends that work.

The team trains a net on six years of HARPS-N solar data. Added activity signs include color cross correlation functions, line shape metrics, spectral activity signs, total solar irradiance curves, and light slopes. Bisector inverse slope and sodium D matching widths add little. Unsigned magnet flux, light and its slope, S-index, H-alpha matching width, color functions and contrast improve scatter prediction. The new model cuts held-out scatter markedly, near supergranulation noise levels. Better granulation tracers will be key to sizing up Earth twins.
arxiv-2602-17960:
Zhou Fan and team establish local laws for sample covariance matrices built from free random vectors with a common spread. Prior work largely covered the separable model, where a vector equals a covariance root times independent entries, yet that structure rarely appears in uses with linked or changed data.

Under a concentration assumption for quadratic forms, they prove an optimal averaged law: the Stieltjes transform converges to its fixed limit uniformly down to the optimal scale. Under an added structural rule on cumulant tensors, which bridges the highly structured independent-entry case and generic dependence, they prove the full anisotropic local law. That gives entrywise control of the resolvent in all ways. They discuss several non-separable examples meeting their rules. These include mean-zero distributions, the random features model, and Gaussian measures with tilting. Proofs offer a tensor network frame for fluctuation averaging amid higher-order structure.
arxiv-2602-18160:
Shahaf Bassan and two co-authors unify two ways of explaining machine-learning predictions. Their 2026 paper treats sufficient reasons, small sets of inputs that lock in a prediction, and contrastive reasons, small sets whose change flips it. Earlier studies handled these in scattered settings, from chance-based to fixed frameworks and from single cases to whole models.

The team shows every case can be read through minimizing one shared chance-based value function. Whether that function is easy to compute turns on three traits: monotonicity, submodularity, and supermodularity. Surprisingly, whole-model functions carry these traits while single-case ones carry none of them. That split yields fast, guaranteed methods for whole-model explanations across neural nets, trees, and tree groups, while even stripped-down single-case explanations stay hard to compute.
arxiv-2602-18360:
Sandip Maiti and three co-authors map the phase diagram of a lattice fermion model with symmetric mass generation. Their 2026 paper studies two flavors of massless staggered fermions with two independent four-fermion couplings on a three-dimensional Euclidean spacetime lattice. At one coupling set to zero, the model shows a direct second-order transition between a massless phase and a symmetric-mass-generation phase.

Turning on a small second coupling splits that single exotic transition into two ordinary ones, separated by a middle phase where masses arise by spontaneous symmetry breaking. The first is a Gross-Neveu transition from the massless phase to the symmetry-breaking phase. Second comes a three-dimensional XY transition to the symmetric-mass phase. Fermion-bag Monte Carlo checks confirm critical exponents match the literature, giving a quantitative portrait of the phase structure.
arxiv-2602-18460:
Gabriela Aránguiz Dias and six co-authors examine why agentic AI in healthcare stays under human control. Their 2026 paper notes agentic AI systems are promoted as able to act on their own, yet in practice they stay under near-total human oversight. Safety, regulatory, and liability constraints make autonomous clinical reasoning unworkable in high-stakes settings. Market enthusiasm suggests a revolution, but the assumptions and accountability structures behind these systems remain underexamined.

The team presents a qualitative study based on interviews with twenty stakeholders, including developers, implementers, and end users. Analysis finds three linked tensions. First, people disagree on what agentic means. Second, sales promises outrun what the systems actually do. Third, evaluation favors technical benchmarks over sociotechnical safety. The authors argue agentic AI is a contested concept where technical hopes, business incentives, and clinical limits meet, with real consequences for patient safety and who takes the blame.
arxiv-2602-18660:
Brandon Victor Syiem and one co-author argue for better stats on survey ratings. Their 2026 paper notes ordinal measures such as Likert items are widespread in human-computer interaction research, yet researchers agree little on which methods fit such data. Parametric and non-parametric methods both see extensive use, with limited reflection on assumptions and fitness.

The authors examine recent human-computer interaction works reporting statistical analyses of ordinal measures, highlight prevalent methods, discuss limits, and spotlight assumptions and oversights that weaken insights drawn. They champion and detail cumulative link mixed models for ordinal data, with worked examples applying them in R to open datasets. The work aims at better understanding of ordinal-data stats and consolidated practices.
arxiv-2602-18860:
Noise is usually seen as the enemy of quantum work extraction, but it may sometimes help. Mohammad B. Arjmandi, writing alone in 2026, studies ergotropy, the maximum extractable work, split into incoherent and coherent parts under typical Markovian noise.

For single qubits, explicit conditions mark when coherent ergotropy freezes or grows. It cannot exceed half the state's quantum coherence. For Bell-diagonal two-qubit states, the work that can be drawn equals the mean of geometric quantum and classical correlations. Coherent ergotropy cannot grow there, though freezing occurs under some noise. For separable states with local coherence, it can grow under all considered noise channels. With more qubits, the growth and its range increase. Entanglement does not block the effect.
arxiv-2602-19060:
A three-spin trimer with Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interaction bridges quantum and classical physics. Robert Wieser, with one co-author, studies that bridge in 2026 within one Hamiltonian frame. A modified Gisin-Schrödinger equation tunes the balance. Quantum weight falls as mean-field weight rises.

The resulting motion is summarised in a ground-state diagram. It shows spin motion evolving from fully quantum to semiclassical as the interaction is treated at different treatment levels. Chiral spin dynamics proposed by Da-Wei Wang and colleagues are then examined theoretically. Their behaviour at the quantum-classical boundary gets special attention. The work thus links two descriptions of spin motion that are often treated apart.
arxiv-2602-19160:
Can language models reason inside strict rule systems? Maciej Świechowski, with two co-authors, tests that question in 2026 through General Game Playing. Four models face forward-play tasks, including next-state and multi-step formulation and legal action generation, across diverse game instances. Rule-governed environments expose reasoning cleanly.

Games are characterised by dozens of structural features, and feature-score correlations are analysed. Obfuscation tests probe the role of linguistic semantics and prior exposure during training. Three models generally perform well across settings. Performance degrades as horizons lengthen, with more game steps. Case analysis reveals common errors, including hallucinated rules, redundant state facts, and syntactic slips. Formal thought in contemporary models shows clear progress, with horizon length as the key limit.
arxiv-2602-19360:
Studying sensitive data together without pooling raw data sets is the promise of federated data work. Natallia Kokash and two co-authors note that real adoption lags, because access policies, regulations, and long-running workflows differ across organizations. Their paper presents a framework for compliance-aware federated processing that joins policy-as-code, workflow control, and compliance help from a large language model.

A working prototype shows legal and group requirements being gathered and converted into machine-ready policies in shared networks. Rather than treating compliance as an afterthought, the framework bakes it into how work is planned and run. Readers get a practical design for collaboration that respects rules across group boundaries.
arxiv-2602-19560:
Ableist language feeds harmful stereotypes and shut-outs, though its nuance makes it hard to spot and address. Kynnedy Simone Smith and two co-authors study whether large language models, namely ChatGPT, can fix ableist language and teach welcoming talk. GPT-4o outputs were set beside crowd notes from trained members of the disability community, then disabled readers rated both.

Readers agreed as much with human and AI notes but liked the AI far more, citing steady story flow and a plain style. They still prized the heart and lived-culture roots of human notes. The findings highlight both the promise and limits of language models in handling ableist language with care.
arxiv-2602-19660:
Battery storage can lift welfare in power markets, yet a profit-chasing operator may not match a central planner's gains. Zhile Jiang and two co-authors compare the two in a broad continuous-time random setting, with batteries following adaptive, forward-looking policies under periodicity and general convex limits. They measure efficiency loss as the ratio of planner gains to profit-maximizer gains.

For linear prices the ratio is tightly capped at 4/3, a structural invariant that survives any random demand process and general convex operating limits. With general convex prices the loss can run unbounded even in a simple discrete-demand benchmark, so convexity alone cannot promise market efficiency. For monomial prices the loss grows with degree but stays under 2, and with n rival batteries it shrinks toward 1.
arxiv-2602-19760:
How evenly a finite set of points fills a cube can be measured by discrepancy, and the extreme Lp version is a classic gauge of irregularity. A 2026 arXiv paper by Erich Novak and Friedrich Pillichshammer finds a matching integration problem whose worst-case error equals exactly that discrepancy.

Studying the dual problem, the authors show the discrepancy falls prey to the curse of dimensionality for every exponent strictly between one and infinity: costs grow exponentially with dimension. The problem was already known to be tractable at infinity, while the endpoint case of one stays open. The paper thus settles the middle range and leaves a single sharp question for future work.
arxiv-2602-20160:
Rebuilding three-dimensional scenes from images usually needs many views and heavy compute. Long image sequences strain context limits. A 2026 arXiv paper by Chen Wang and eight co-authors proposes tttLRM, a large three-dimensional model. It uses a test-time training layer for long-context, step-by-step rebuilding with linear complexity.

The framework packs many image views into the test-time training layer's fast weights. That forms an implicit three-dimensional model in latent space. It decodes into direct formats such as Gaussian Splats for downstream use. An online learning variant supports rebuilding and polish from streaming views. Early training on novel view creation transfers well to direct three-dimensional building, raising rebuilding quality with faster learning. Broad experiments show better one-pass three-dimensional Gaussian rebuilding, beating leading approaches on both objects and scenes.
arxiv-2602-20360:
Runlong Liao and five co-authors introduce Momentum Guidance, a plug-and-play guidance method for flow models. Pretrained flow models give high-fidelity samples, yet without guidance their image samples often look diffuse and lack fine detail. Existing guidance such as classifier-free guidance improves fidelity but cuts sample diversity. Momentum Guidance instead extrapolates the current velocity away from an exponential moving average of past velocities along the ODE path, at no extra cost per step.

The method gains beyond classifier-free guidance, improving the precision-recall frontier. On ImageNet-256, it improves FID by about thirty-seven percent without classifier-free guidance and about twenty-five percent with it, on average across sampling settings, reaching a low score at sixteen sampling steps. Tests on large flow models, including Stable Diffusion 3 and FLUX.1-dev, confirm gains across standard metrics. The approach offers better samples without paying for extra model calls.
arxiv-2602-20760:
Arnab Chaudhuri asks what happens when a hidden dark sector runs hotter than ordinary matter in the early universe. Using a simple Higgs-portal model, he lets the dark sector stay warmer at the electroweak epoch while still fitting limits on extra radiation.
