That heat gap reshapes the energy landscape and changes how bubbles of the new phase form, with no need for strong couplings or extreme cooling. The result boosts the gravitational wave signal more than tenfold and shifts its peak into the millihertz band, bringing it much closer to what future space detectors could sense.
arxiv-2602-21060:
Commuting Hopf algebras and affine group schemes carry a rich category-level structure. David Forsman proves in this 2026 arXiv paper that the class of commuting Hopf algebras over a field is co-semi-abelian. That result implies the class of affine group schemes over that field is semi-abelian. Coregularity comes from spotting a clean split-up of onto maps and truly flat into maps.

Coexactness follows from Takeuchi's match between normal Hopf ideals and Hopf parts of commuting Hopf algebras. Readers get a shape-level result that places affine group schemes inside a well-run category-level setup. The proof is short on tools beyond the split-up and the match it builds on.
arxiv-2602-21160:
Safety-key sorters need doubt split by class, not just totaled. Mame Diarra Toure and David Stephens split mutual facts into per-class shares in this 2026 arXiv paper. A second-order Taylor spread of entropy yields the split, with inverse-mean weighting that fixes edge damping and keeps rare and common classes matched.

A partner skew check flags inputs where the near form worsens. On diabetes eye disease picking prediction, key-class doubt cuts picking risk by nearly thirty-five percent over mutual facts and about fifty-six percent over variance base cases. Out-of-spread spotting and label-noise studies further show per-class views baring shifts and touchiness that totals hide. After-data quality shapes results at least as much as metric choice.
arxiv-2603-01360:
Gong Chen and Yingmo Zhang study long waves with a strong nonlinear term in this 2026 math work. Their equation, a quintic form of the Benjamin-Bona-Mahony model, tracks how such waves evolve over time. The main question is whether small, smooth waves settle down and act like simple linear waves in the long run.

Using a space-time resonance method, they prove that small smooth solutions do scatter to the linear flow. The strong term makes some parts of the proof easier than in a weaker quartic case. Other parts grow harder, since key patterns that held before fail at some resonance points. Careful estimates near those points close the proof, which adds a firm case to the study of wave decay.
arxiv-2603-02060:
Stefano Burrello, Carmelo Piazza, Rui Wang, and Maria Colonna test the stability of warm, dilute nuclear matter with light clusters present. Their 2026 work uses a generalized mean-field framework at finite temperature and symmetric isospin. Clusters like light nuclei count as degrees of freedom beside single nucleons here.

Free-energy curvature decides where the matter turns mechanically unstable, the spinodal region. An infrared momentum cutoff models Pauli blocking, which thins low-momentum states inside the medium. When that cutoff depends on density, thermodynamic consistency forces extra terms in chemical potentials and hydrodynamics. Those terms shift the spinodal boundary and reshape the unstable modes themselves. With a stiff enough cutoff, clusters can fluctuate out of phase with nucleons, a reversal of the pattern found when medium effects are ignored.
arxiv-2603-02260:
Ethan Chu, Yiyang Guo, and Jan Hoffmann extend automatic cost analysis to programs that jump around in this 2026 paper. Many tools can read code and derive bounds on time or memory use. They struggle when control jumps far, as with exceptions or effect handlers. A handler can catch a thrown effect from deep inside a program.

Their analysis is the first to bound costs across such jumps. It extends a type-based method built on amortized analysis, where costs are prepaid by data. New type rules cover exceptions and handlers, and a soundness proof checks them against a stack machine. Tests show the method handles programs older tools cannot. Overhead from supporting handlers stays low in their trials.
arxiv-2603-02360:
Edsel Peña, Dip Das, and Yuexuan Wu use tennis scoring to teach probability in this 2026 paper. Tennis has a nested scoring system of points, games, tiebreaks, sets, and matches. Their simple model gives each player a fixed chance to win each service point. Points are treated as independent across the whole match.

From those serve chances, they derive win chances at every level of the system. Big problems split into small ones, then recombine into full answers. The method showcases total probability and iterated rules for means and spreads. Fun questions include whether matches surely end and whether serving first helps equal players. Scoring systems act as decision tools that can crown the weaker player. The paper compares systems on that error risk as well.
arxiv-2603-02460:
Gabriel Melo, Thibaut de Saivre, Anna Calissano, and Florence d'Alché-Buc add error bounds to graph prediction in this 2026 paper. Some tasks output whole graphs, not single numbers. Honest error ranges for such outputs have been scarce. Their method gives coverage promises that need no assumptions about the data spread.

A distance between graphs anchors the method's mismatch score. That distance compares graphs no matter how their nodes are ordered. A quantile method then adapts the prediction set to each input's difficulty. Graphs are kept or dropped by their distance to the predicted one. The authors test the approach on a synthetic task. Such promises for structured outputs could matter wherever graph forecasts guide real choices.
arxiv-2603-02860:
Fermín Moscoso del Prado Martín and Suchir Salhan explain the pattern of sound frequencies across the world's languages. Every language uses its phonemes, its basic speech sounds, at uneven rates. Their 2026 paper models that uneven spread at two scales, using information theory.

At the large scale, rank-frequency curves match a simple random model whose single setting grows steadily with the size of a language's sound inventory. Larger inventories show lower relative entropy, a balancing effect the model captures. At the small scale, a maximum-entropy model using articulation, sound-combination, and word-structure rules predicts each language's exact sound rates well. Together the two views give one account of a pattern found in every spoken language.
arxiv-2603-02960:
Nahema Marchal, Stephanie Chan, Matija Franklin, and colleagues argue that AI systems have become knowledge agents and must be governed as such. Large language models now curate what people read, answer specialized questions, and shape shared knowledge. Their 2026 paper warns that badly calibrated agents could dull human skills and slowly drift public knowledge off course.

The authors propose a trust framework with three parts: build agents that are genuinely trustworthy, align them with human knowledge goals, and strengthen the surrounding knowledge infrastructure. Trustworthy agents should show competence, openness to being proven wrong, and honest habits, backed by provenance tracking and protected knowledge sanctuaries. The roadmap aims at a human-AI ecosystem where machine help sharpens, rather than replaces, collective judgment.
arxiv-2603-03260:
Wanqi Liu and Rong Zhao test whether a new café lifts the value of homes around it, or merely follows rising neighborhoods. Restaurants and cafés visibly mark gentrification, but cause and effect are tangled. Their 2026 study exploits the staggered timing of over twenty-one thousand openings across nearly five thousand small London areas.

An event study with area-specific trends, which passes pre-trend checks, tracks prices around each opening. Prices rose steadily afterward, reaching about four percent higher after four years. Matching openings to price-tier data shows the effect comes from upmarket arrivals, not budget ones, whose patterns look unreliable. The quality of commercial clustering, not its mere presence, drives the neighborhood premium.
arxiv-2603-03660:
Hai-Long Zhen and three colleagues ask how a quantum-gravity correction would repaint a black hole's portrait. The extended uncertainty principle modifies quantum mechanics at large scales. Their 2026 paper first builds an explicit bridge between that principle and spacetime geometry. It converts the principle's modified temperature function into a modified metric for the Schwarzschild black hole, then derives its thermodynamics from that metric.

One quantity refuses to move: the event horizon sits exactly where Einstein put it. The photon sphere, where light orbits, grows as the correction parameter rises, while the visible shadow shrinks, an optical shift with no change in the horizon itself. Comparing the predicted shadow with Event Horizon Telescope observations of the galactic center black hole, Sagittarius A-star, sets fresh constraints on how large the correction can be.
arxiv-2603-03760:
Seungha Hong and five others compress time series datasets in the frequency domain, where their rhythm lives. Forecasting trains on terabytes of sensor data, and dataset distillation, synthesizing a tiny dataset that trains like the huge one, promises relief. Generic distillation, though, overfits one architecture and scales badly on sequences. Their 2026 method, HDT, is built for time series from the start.

Each series is decomposed into sinusoidal components by the fast Fourier transform. A step called Harmonic Matching aligns the core periodic structure between the synthetic and real data. Because updates happen in the frequency domain, they apply globally across the whole series at once, never tearing the temporal dependencies that forecasting depends on. Extensive tests show strong generalization across architectures the distillation never saw, plus the scalability real deployments need.
arxiv-2603-03860:
Jiansheng Yao and Yingkui Zhao present a particle-grid simulation method for inviscid compressible flows with shocks and strong vortices. Such flows are hard for particle-grid methods because moving discontinuities, cell-crossing noise, and quadrature damage under deformation all cause trouble. Working from a combined FLIP and APIC framework with vorticity-aware artificial viscosity, the authors identify a long-time failure in Rayleigh-Taylor instability tests. Particles drain from spike heads, quadrature degrades, and nonphysical void-like dents appear.

Their fix adds conservative split resampling, which replenishes depleted cells while exactly conserving mass, momentum, and internal energy. It also adds a soft switch that weakens only the affine part of the update where particle support is thin. Tests on the Sod shock tube and Rayleigh-Taylor cases remove the voids while preserving vortex roll-up and matching reference growth measures.
arxiv-2605-00560:
V Venktesh, Mandeep Rathee, and Avishek Anand argue that in modern search, the costly problem is not inventing extra versions of a query but choosing among them. Reformulating a query many ways can raise recall sharply. Yet merging and reranking everything is prohibitively expensive, and stray reformulations drag results off topic, a failure called query drift. Their framework, ReformIR, is built around a strict inference budget.

ReformIR treats each reformulation as a first-class feature and builds one large candidate pool from all of them. A light surrogate model, taught online by a strong reranker, estimates each document's utility from reformulation-specific signals. Under the budget, the system spends teacher reranking where it pays most, anchored to the original query to suppress drift. On standard passage and deep-learning benchmarks it beat existing reformulation strategies, with the gap growing as reformulations multiply and rivals degrade.
arxiv-2605-00660:
SangHyun Park proves that a directed seven-dimensional torus, a grid of points on a seven-dimensional doughnut with wraparound edges, can be decomposed into directed Hamiltonian cycles for every odd side length. A Hamilton decomposition splits all the directed edges into cycles that each visit every vertex exactly once. Such decompositions are prized in network design, giving balanced routing patterns.

Park's proof has two engines. The first is a root-flat certificate: three local conditions on one flat slice, Latinness of rows, bijectivity between layers, and primitivity of return maps, which together guarantee a full decomposition. The second is a uniform construction for all larger odd moduli, using prefix coordinates and explicit count matrices to produce all seven Hamiltonian factors with no search. The two smallest moduli defeat that construction provably, so they are settled by finite certificates checked in the Lean proof assistant, inside one formal development.
arxiv-2605-00960:
Chirag Shinde introduces energy-based constraint networks, an architecture that learns structural coherence across modalities and assigns it a scalar energy. Frozen encoder embeddings pass through a state-space model with dual-head attention, producing one energy for overall consistency and per-position scores that localize violations. Independently trained branches detect different violation types and can be combined at inference without interference.

In text, the system scores well on both trained and unseen corruption types using a frozen BERT encoder. In vision, the same design gives strong deepfake detection without training data from one test set. Changing domain requires only new corruption strategies. Changing encoder requires only a new input layer, which supports flexible reuse.
arxiv-2605-01160:
Sabry E. Farrag argues that AI coding assistants create a Productivity-Reliability Paradox in software development. Trials report large output gains on well-scoped tasks, while a careful randomized trial records a slowdown for experienced coders. Large telemetry shows many more pull requests but much longer review times with flat delivery. Farrag defines the paradox in formal terms through a multivocal review of dozens of sources.

Three moderating variables and two amplifying mechanisms structure it. A scheme sorts six methodologies under three AI adoption tiers, and a Specification Governance Model grounded in transaction cost economics offers a practical decision guide. Two tools are tested as model examples in a four-month pilot. Specification discipline, not model capability, is named the binding constraint.
arxiv-2605-01260:
Xin Liang and six co-authors survey write-read decoupling in modern large-scale search engines. Frequent index updates keep results fresh, yet in the dominant Lucene-based architecture, segment merges triggered by writes compete with queries for CPU, disk, and cache, inflating latency. The survey systematically examines architectural solutions developed across industry and academia to separate write pressure from read latency.

Five principal patterns are identified, from node-level separation and compute-storage separation to full in-memory indexing, log-structured write paths, and in-place partial updates. Representative systems from major companies are surveyed. An emerging synthesis architecture combines several patterns with per-field update routing, sending simple fields through fast in-place updates while full-text fields follow a segment path. Open challenges include hybrid retrieval and serverless deployment.
arxiv-2605-01760:
Sebastian M Cioabă, Lele Liu, and Yi Wang close a conjecture about how a graph's Laplacian spectrum can shift when edges change. The Laplacian matching roots of a graph blend two spectra. Earlier work had defined the integral variation of those roots and shown a one-place change to be impossible. The two-place case was ruled out only for graphs whose cycles are sparse relative to their girth.

Wang, Cui, and Cioabă had conjectured the two-place variation never happens in any connected graph. This paper confirms that conjecture in full. The proof joins a structural relation from the earlier work to two new power-sum identities for Laplacian matching roots. Results of this stamp matter because spectral fingerprints are used to tell graphs apart and to certify network traits; knowing which variations cannot occur tightens every argument built on them.
arxiv-2605-01960:
Pranay Mundra, Adam Sealfon, Ziteng Sun, and Quanquan Liu consider answering database queries privately when the queries arrive as a stream. Real workloads are predictable, with recurring jobs and templates, even if their order is unknown. The authors ask whether predictions about future queries can improve accuracy under one shared privacy budget, without failing badly when predictions are wrong.

Their system, LAPRAS, uses a predicted query set to guide spending. Predicted queries get the best offline method, while the rest are answered online from what budget remains. A smooth allocation rule paces spending across an unknown number of surprise queries. The design aims to gain from good forecasts while staying robust to bad ones.
arxiv-2605-02060:
Maksim Kazanskii extends stochastic neighbor embedding, a method that maps high-dimensional data to a low-dimensional picture while keeping neighbours close. Such maps can badly distort how dense points are in a local area. Kazanskii adds a regulariser that aligns a profile of local concentration, based on inverse neighbourhood scale, between the source and the map.

The new method, DR-SNE, keeps that relative concentration while staying unchanged under global rescaling of the map. Across real and synthetic data, it generally improved concentration preservation with controlled loss of neighbourhood fidelity. Tests show a steady trade-off as the regulariser grows stronger. The work suits cases where local density itself carries meaning.
arxiv-2605-02160:
Xueyin Wang proves a continuity result for the Lyapunov exponent of quasi-periodic cocycles in a Gevrey class. The Lyapunov exponent measures the average growth rate of products of matrices that vary in a quasi-periodic way. Whether that rate varies continuously with the system is a basic question, and Gevrey regularity, which sits between smooth and analytic, sets the setting here.

Wang works with frequencies in a subexponential Brjuno class. Under a numeric condition linking the Gevrey index and the frequency parameter, the sum of the two lying between one and two, the Lyapunov exponent is continuous. The note is short and states the result with its precise assumptions, adding a case to the known continuity theory.
arxiv-2605-02660:
Dasari Naga Raju tests whether biological knowledge about tumor geography can help a model read a genetic trait from routine cancer slides. The trait is microsatellite instability in colorectal cancer, normally found by molecular testing. Models that read stained slide images often fail at a new hospital, because slides carry site-specific texture along with real biology.

Raju builds priors from known patterns: immune reaction at the tumor's invasive edge, and the local ratio of immune cells to tumor cells near each tile. These priors enter a transformer aggregator before attention, over features from large foundation models. Six reference combinations of model and aggregator set the baseline. The study asks whether steering features toward known biology yields signs that travel better across sites.
arxiv-2605-02860:
Mohamad Khajezade, Fatemeh H. Fard, and Mohamed Sami Shehata distill a large reasoning model into small open models that can detect code clones across programming languages. Equivalent programs in different languages often look nothing alike, so surface matching fails. Large models reason well about such pairs, but black-box use raises cost, privacy, and format problems, and small models often fumble reasoning-style prompts.

Training pairs come from a public multilingual code archive, with reasoning-style synthetic data built for teaching. Two compact students are fine-tuned with low-rank adapters. Stabilization tricks include forced-conclusion prompts and added classification heads that map output cleanly to a clone verdict. Across several language pairs, distillation consistently helped, and both raw accuracy and response reliability were tracked.
arxiv-2605-03060:
Andrea Panarotto, Riccardo De Santis, and Livio Finos build confidence intervals for generalized linear models that stay valid when the variance model is wrong. Standard intervals trust the mean-variance link, yet excess spread and uneven variability in biomedical data often break that trust and shrink coverage.

Their method flips the signs of single score parts to form tests, then inverts them with a bisection search to find interval bounds. Theory gives broad validity, and simulations show reliable coverage where Wald intervals fail. An RNA sequencing cancer study shows the method at work.
arxiv-2605-03160:
Michael A. Riegler and Birk Sebastian Frostelid Torpmann-Hagen warn that labeling sparse autoencoder features from top contexts alone can misname what a feature does. Standard checks steer one feature at one strength, which samples just one cell of a wider steering grid.

On three instruction-tuned models, features labeled as AI self-disclaimers switched voice form under steering, so the label named a regime, not a causal axis. Three near-orthogonal features proved jointly needed for grounded work, and matched random controls showed the damage came from direction, not size. The study urges grid-wide checks before trusting feature labels.
arxiv-2605-03260:
Shugen Song, Wenjie Mei, and Chengyan Zhao improve path tracking for vehicles by pairing sampling-based predictive control with continuous-time residual learning. The Model Predictive Path Integral method is strong for nonlinear systems, but its results hinge on how accurate the built-in dynamics model is.

Their ICODE-MPPI framework learns the missing dynamics with neural ordinary differential equations that respect time continuity across the prediction window. In high-fidelity simulations on complex paths, tracking error under steady disturbances fell by up to about two thirds versus standard control. Steering also grew smoother, with far less chattering in the commands.
arxiv-2605-03560:
Zijiang Yang shows that free-text medical notes carry strong signal for predicting death after hospital discharge, despite their messy, repetitive quality. Electronic health records hold vast unstructured notes that many models ignore in favor of clean coded fields.

Across prediction windows from fifteen days to a year, models using note information scored well above those without it. A deep network with a pooling mechanism that learns from the most informative notes beat traditional tree-based models by clear margins at every horizon. The models also surface keyword and document patterns linked to patient severity, consistent with prior clinical findings.
arxiv-2605-04660:
Xiaoteng Zhang and three co-authors present a high-order numerical scheme for simulating compressible fluid flow in two dimensions in a Lagrangian frame, where the computational mesh moves with the fluid. Accurate, robust schemes of this kind underpin simulations of shocks and extreme flows.

Their method combines a multi-moment finite volume approach, which evolves both point values at cell corners and cell averages to guarantee conservation, with a new two-dimensional nodal Riemann solver. The solver's fresh jump and balance conditions connect surface pressures to mesh motion in a way that stays compatible with the numerical fluxes. The result keeps third-order accuracy while inheriting the nodal solver's robustness.
arxiv-2605-04860:
Jacob Mercer studies particle systems where particles branch, move like Brownian motion, and are removed according to their rank among the group. Such branching-selection systems are known models for fronts and spreading populations. Mercer asks what large-scale equation describes the whole system as particle numbers grow large.

He shows the limit is a reaction-diffusion equation whose reaction term is determined by the rank-based killing rule. The result generalises a well-known special case and connects the particle picture with travelling waves of the equation. Mercer also gives conditions for a steady spreading speed and describes that speed closely, providing a partial weak selection principle.
arxiv-2605-04960:
Song Yu, Li Li, Wenwen Zhao, and Zhisheng Yang improve group-based reinforcement learning used to train language models on tasks with checkable answers. The standard method, GRPO, grades a whole group of answers together. The authors identify three credit failures: all tokens graded alike, correct steps sometimes punished, and groups with no score spread losing their learning signal.

Their EP-GRPO mines the model's own information flow for denser guidance, using entropy to spotlight key decision tokens and progress-based signals for step-level feedback. It needs no external reward model. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, EP-GRPO beat GRPO and its variants on both accuracy and efficiency in their experiments.
arxiv-2605-05360:
CopyCop is a method by Rahul Nandakumar and Deepayan Chakrabarti for proving that one graph neural network was copied from another. A thief can train a network to mimic the outputs of a target model, then disguise it by changing its shape, weights, or output size. Watermarks and fingerprints often fail under those tricks.

CopyCop still detects the copy under these harsh conditions, and the authors give theory to back the test. In trials on 14 datasets and five network designs, it stayed accurate against many attacks and disguises. The work gives model owners a practical way to defend their property.
arxiv-2605-05660:
Balancing several goals at once is hard enough before the data start shifting. Yufeng Yang and four co-authors define distributionally robust multi-objective optimization, where each goal is judged under its own worst-case data law. Standard forms ignore such shift entirely.

They propose Pareto-style solution concepts for the robust problem and build multi-gradient descent methods with provable guarantees. A Lagrangian dual form yields a double-loop method that estimates dual variables internally. Sample cost bounds come with the method. The setup targets learning systems that must stay good on several criteria even when the world moves.
arxiv-2605-05860:
Atsushi Hori and Kazuyuki Sekitani write on a known weak point in data envelopment analysis, a method used to score how well units use inputs. The Russell graph measure, a standard model in that field, breaks down at the edge of the allowed range. Earlier fixes can miss good targets or lose traits that a sound measure should keep.

The authors add a closer target setting approach to the model, with production trade offs included. They show the new measure avoids the edge problem and has stronger traits than past models. Its scores can be found by solving a series of linear programs. A test on real data suggests its targets are more realistic in practice.
arxiv-2605-06060:
Peihao Li, Nadia Dahmani, and Wenqi Cai ask when arbitrage can be trusted to keep automated market maker prices stable. Such pools quote prices from their own state, and traders profit by correcting any drift from a reference price. Much of decentralized finance rests on the hope that this correction is strong and fast enough.

The authors model the price gap as a stochastic tracking error, with arbitrage as the corrective input and blockchain execution inside the loop. Fees, block timing, ordering, and failed trades all shape how much correction lands in each block. Under a block level correction condition they prove the error settles in a stable pattern. A constant product example maps fees and liquidity into the no trade band.
arxiv-2605-06460:
Weien Li and ten co-authors propose MINER, a plug-in that makes single-vector document retrieval stronger without giving up its efficiency. Visual document search needs compact indexes. Late-interaction retrievers match pages in fine detail but store hundreds of vectors per page, while single-vector methods are cheap yet compress everything into one final-layer embedding and lag in quality.

A layerwise diagnostic shows useful signal lives in internal transformer layers, not just the last one. MINER probes each layer, masks weak neurons adaptively, and fuses the surviving signals into one embedding. Across the ViDoRe benchmarks it beats comparable dense retrievers and sometimes nearly matches late-interaction quality.
arxiv-2605-06660:
Yuhang Lai, Jiazhan Feng, Yee Whye Teh, and Ning Miao introduce VHG, a framework that generates hard new math problems for training language models. Models solve problems well but struggle to create ones that are valid, challenging, and novel. Naive self-play generation often yields invalid problems because the setter exploits weak rewards, a failure called reward hacking.

VHG adds an independent verifier to the usual setter-solver pair, so the setter's reward depends jointly on validity, judged by the verifier, and difficulty, judged by the solver. Two verifier types are tested, one symbolic and one model-based. On integral tasks and general math reasoning, VHG beats all baselines clearly.
arxiv-2605-06860:
Manuel Emiliano Monreal Cancino and Angel Sánchez derive the propagator of a massive charged vector boson in a constant magnetic field. Propagators are the building blocks for computing particle interactions, and a background field quantizes motion into Landau levels with spin structure that must be handled carefully. Working in unitary gauge, they use the Ritus eigenfunction method for an explicit treatment.

The paper analyzes polarization vectors for all Landau levels and derives the LSZ reduction formula for such bosons in the field, a tool for self-energy and radiative correction calculations. It also connects the Ritus representation to Schwinger's proper-time form, exhibits the Schwinger phase, and flags a small discrepancy with earlier literature caused by gauge and spin treatment.
arxiv-2605-07260:
Youngsik Yoon and three co-authors check whether mixture-of-experts language models send each token to the right experts. These models route every token to a few specialists, but routing quality is rarely tested directly. Holding the model fixed, the authors compare the chosen route against equal-cost alternatives for the same token.

On confident tokens the standard router aligns well with route usefulness. On fragile tokens that drive hard reasoning it is uninformative, and better routes go unchosen. A small update to only the final layer's router shifted scores on hard math contest sets. Part of the failure, they argue, is fixable routing rather than limited expert capacity.
arxiv-2605-07360:
Keisuke Taga solves the Kuramoto model exactly for three identical coupled oscillators, a case that had resisted closed-form solution. The Kuramoto model is the standard picture of sync, from fireflies to power grids. Yet exact phase paths from any starting point existed only for two units. Taga builds special eigenfunctions of the Koopman operator for the system.

Those functions relate the oscillator phases to time and reduce the dynamics to time-dependent quartic formulas. Choosing the branch in the formula that matches the starting state rebuilds each phase path in full. The result gives the first global exact solution for the three-oscillator identical Kuramoto system.
arxiv-2605-07860:
Usevalad Milasheuski and three co-authors sort out how generative models should be shared in federated maintenance. Factories keep sensor data on site but want shared anomaly detection for time series. Autoencoders, GANs, and diffusion models each offer unsupervised detection, yet federated versions face bandwidth limits and mismatched data across sites.

Comparing full federation, where whole models are shared, with partial federation, where only parts move, they find distinct trade-offs in utility, stability, and scale. Full federation stabilized the GAN setups but they stayed least robust; for diffusion models, sharing only the decoder beat sharing everything in bandwidth-tight, uneven data settings. The paper proposes a scheme making partial sharing a sound route to tailoring.
arxiv-2605-08060:
Jiayuan Liu, Tianqin Li, Shiyi Du, Xin Luo, and coauthors report a counterintuitive failure of language model agents. Giving an agent a longer memory of past rounds is usually treated as a pure upgrade. Across seven models and four social dilemma games played over five hundred rounds, longer recall instead reduced cooperation in most settings, a pattern the authors call the memory curse.

Analysis of hundreds of thousands of reasoning traces links the decay to fading forward-looking intent, not rising suspicion. Replacing visible history with synthetic cooperative records restored cooperation at the same prompt length, showing that memory content, not length, drives the effect. Targeted fine-tuning on forward-looking traces also reduced the decay.
arxiv-2605-08160:
Girmaw Abebe Tadesse and colleagues built WATCH. The system watches old sites from space and dates damage to the month. Guarding heritage at scale is hard. Damage cues in satellite images are subtle, and labeled cases are rare.

WATCH works with PlanetScope mosaics from 2017 to 2024. It covers 1,943 sites in Afghanistan. It offers three scoring routes. One is a training-free temporal embedding distance. One is a self-taught ensemble of signals. One is a weakly guided model trained on sparse event labels. The team tests embeddings from six foundation models beside handcrafted features. The result is a practical toolkit for heritage monitors.
arxiv-2605-08360:
Carter Blair, Ariel Procaccia, and Milind Tambe argue that group decisions from free-form text need embeddings of preference, not of meaning. Citizens state views in their own words. A natural plan places the texts in a vector space. Fair clustering and facility location tools can then be brought to bear. Those tools need distances that mean disagreement. Plain embeddings measure topic likeness instead.

Standard embeddings do carry a coarse preference signal. Similar wording often tracks a similar stance. But the signal breaks when that link fails. The authors frame the fix as an invariance problem. A good representation keeps stance and values. It discards semantic detail that does not bear on preference.
arxiv-2605-08460:
Ziwen Cai, Yihe Zhang, and Xiali Hei follow a compromise as it spreads through a network of AI agents. Modern agent systems delegate work to freshly spawned subagents, and a child agent typically inherits memory from its parent. Planted instructions, stale state, or unintended rules inside that memory can ride along, turning one breach into many.

The authors model contemporary multi-agent networks through this inheritance channel and analyze how a local compromise propagates across agent boundaries. Their study complements work on single-agent attacks such as prompt injection and poisoned retrieval by examining the aftermath inside the network, where spawn and memory sharing decide whether an incident stays small.
arxiv-2605-08560:
Shapourian and three colleagues present a compact mixture of experts vision language system built on their own language model ZAYA1-8B. Even at this compact size, it matches leading base models and surpasses several rivals on image understanding, reasoning and counting benchmarks. The report details the full training pipeline, including data composition, sequence packing, and the attention masking scheme.

Two design innovations stand out: vision specific LoRA adapters inside the language model, which add modality specific capacity without adding experts. The second is bidirectional attention over image tokens inside the language model, which sharpens visual understanding. The model totals 9 point 2 billion parameters, with 1 point 4 billion active including the vision encoder. The system, ZAYA1-VL-8B, is publicly available, giving researchers a compact yet competitive vision language system to build on. The technical report frames compact design, not sheer scale, as the route to strong multimodal performance.
arxiv-2605-08760:
Qijun Hou, Yuchen Shi, Pingyi Fan, and Khaled Letaief work on joint training where clients keep their data at home. Each client's data is a mix of a few shared hidden types. Grouping like clients helps, but groups still hold mixed types inside. Full custom fits for each client waste what clients share. Their FedGMI plan usesVAE style models to learn the shared types. It then works out each client's mix.

The plan gives custom fits with joint gains kept. Tests show it finds the hidden types cleanly. It also finds each mix with care. It holds up when the talk budget is tight. Joint training gains a sound mid path, between one fit for all and one fit per client.
arxiv-2605-08860:
Leandro Dognini and Constantino Tsallis rework how firm states come from a broad entropy max. The broad entropy has an index q in it. The mean energy rule can weigh states with a second index. That makes a clan of max tasks whose best spreads need care. The team sets terms for best spreads to be there, to be firm, and to be the sole ones. A claim lets some be worked out in closed form.

Two stock cases in the field grow clear. A new third case joins them. Just the stock cases give the famed q-exp shapes. A Clausius style heat scale and free energy come out too. The zeroth law of heat stands in this broad frame.
arxiv-2605-08960:
Chengqian Zhang and five coauthors teach gem growth models what holds a gem up. Growth models learn how firm gems look. They get thin word on why gems hold. Probes show a wide gap twixt growth codes and trained force models. A plain training time line up shuts the gap. Their CrystalREPA plan pulls the growth coder's atom states to a frozen force model's states. An atom wise match loss does the pull.

Cross three growth plans, ten force guides, and two test sets, gems gain in firm hold, sound form, and true shape. There is no cost at use time. Guide worth tracks how clear its atom states are, not its board rank.
arxiv-2605-09060:
J de Curtò, Mauro Liz, and I de Zarzà probe why multilingual vision-language models work better in some languages than others. The gap could come from the part that sees images, the part that reads text, or the way the two interact, and the team designed a test to separate these causes.

They hold the image encoder fixed and swap only the text branch across thirteen languages, using two model sizes. Low-resource languages such as Arabic, Basque, and Luxembourgish scored worse at both sizes, which points the blame at the text side. Bigger image encoders even widened some gaps. The failure, they show, is mostly misplaced attention on the image, not a total loss of signal.
arxiv-2605-09460:
Zheng shows the cost of keeping faces true in image generation, built on many-step diffusion backbones, is often unnecessary for identity-conditioned FLUX. A frozen InfuseNet adapter trained with FLUX.1-dev moves directly to the distilled FLUX.1-schnell backbone. A two-line change, swapping the backbone and disabling classifier-free guidance, cuts latency 5 point 9 times. It improves ArcFace identity scores by 0 point 028 and LPIPS by minus 0 point 016 over the 28-step FLUX.1-dev baseline.

Denoising path analysis finds identity fidelity entering an early effective regime, often within 4 to 8 steps, while later steps refine detail, sharpness, and contrast. Adapter ablations confirm identity formation depends on the identity adapter, and norm probes suggest conditioning share falls as sampling proceeds. Style and object adapter tests on SDXL and SD1.5 show fading returns after middle steps. Distilled backbone replacement is a simple, training-free strategy for the efficiency-fidelity tradeoff of face-true generation.
arxiv-2605-09660:
Romano derives multimessenger consistency checks for cosmological models. They link gravitational wave and electromagnetic luminosity distances within the Friedmann frame. With gravitational wave detections now routine, cosmologists can test the standard model in new ways. But claims about dark energy often hinge on the chosen parametrization. Tests that use only observed distances avoid that bias. Romano first looks at the flatness guess common in gravitational wave parameter estimation.

He derives a general link for the curvature parameter from flatness biased gravitational wave distances and electromagnetic distances. He adds a consistency check for the Friedmann model valid regardless of the dark energy equation of state. He then derives a second check for the cosmological constant that needs no flatness guess at all. Together, the checks let distance data alone probe curvature, the Friedmann model, and the cosmological constant.
arxiv-2605-09760:
Yu and eight colleagues improved resume-job matching with ConFit v3, adding language-model re-ranking to fast embedding retrieval. Embedding systems like ConFit retrieve candidates at scale but offer little control or explanation, while LLM re-rankers promise reasoning yet were trained on short documents unlike messy recruiting data. The team first dissected the re-ranker training pipeline: inference design, reinforcement-learning choice, data cleaning, and distillation.

They found four moves that mattered: multi-pass re-ranking, listwise reinforcement objectives, removing noisy samples, and distilling from a stronger model before reinforcement learning. Bundled into ConFit v3, built on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B, the recipe beat existing person-job fit systems on real-world recruiting data. It also beat strong general models including GPT-5 and Claude Opus-4.5, as the authors report.
arxiv-2605-09860:
Li and five colleagues study a neglected choice in long-horizon machine reasoning. It is not just which move to make, but how many moves to run blind before looking again. That number, called commitment depth, trades replanning cost against errors that pile up while acting without fresh input. Most systems fix it by hand, but the authors make it a learnable, state-dependent part of the policy itself, inside a vision-language model.

On the Sliding Puzzle and Sokoban puzzle tasks, the adaptive policy beat every fixed-depth baseline that was not degenerate. It gained up to twelve and a half points of solve rate while using about a quarter fewer moves per episode. Despite a seven-billion-parameter backbone, it also outscored much larger commercial models on both tasks. Every tested open-weight vision-language model failed outright without task-specific training, scoring zero.
arxiv-2605-10060:
Kuvalekar, writing alone, models how rising skill premia reshape pre-marital skill investment in a decentralised marriage market with search frictions and non-transferable utility. Even in a symmetric environment, the market can settle into asymmetric equilibria, with one gender putting more into skills than the other. In some environments that asymmetric outcome is unique. Household utility maximisation, modelled from microfoundations, traces the switch.

As labour-market wages for high-skilled workers rise, the skill premium drives a shift from symmetric equilibrium, unique at first, to a unique asymmetric one. One gender ends up investing fully while the other invests far less. The paper speaks to two literatures at once, since both labour-market and marriage-market returns shape pre-marital education choices. Rising premia therefore do more than reward skill; they can reorganise who invests, and by how much, before marriage.
arxiv-2605-10260:
Yukun Du and seven colleagues shift the focus of meta black-box optimization from how to search to where to search. Existing methods train a neural policy to control a low-level optimizer, but they largely ignore which region deserves attention. Their 2026 paper presents MetaSG-SAEA, a bi-level framework for expensive constrained multi-objective problems, where each evaluation is costly.

A meta-policy guides a surrogate-assisted evolutionary algorithm, which replaces most costly evaluations with cheap predictions. The guidance rests on Max-Min Constraint-Calibrated Inequality, a compact region abstraction that maps varied constraint scores onto an ordered scalar level. Diffusion-based population initialization then turns region guidance into starting solutions. Across diverse benchmarks MetaSG-SAEA beat state-of-the-art baselines and generalized across problem distributions.
arxiv-2605-10660:
Ainna Yue Moreno-Locubiche and co-authors propose a joint design of tunable smart surface settings and zero-forcing pre-coding for multi-user multiple-input single-output downlink sending in mm-wave bands. Zero-forcing suits mm-wave systems because it cuts inter-user crosstalk by using large antenna arrays and sparse aimed channels. This enables good spatial sharing at modest cost. Careful design is needed to overcome rank gaps when users have very different channel gains or align with the transmitter.

Deploying a tunable surface adds artificial scattering that addresses those situations. The authors explore the joint design under perfect channel knowledge and assess how imperfect channel guesses affect bit error rate. They propose a robust pilot design that equalises multi-user crosstalk across users despite channel errors in the pre-coder. Tests show the advantages of tuned surface-aided zero-forcing sending for next-generation wireless downlinks.
arxiv-2605-10860:
Ruimin Shi and four colleagues measure how close real compilers come to portable speed on RISC-V vector hardware. The RISC-V Vector Extension promises lasting compute for science and machine learning, but compiler support and performance counters for version 1.0 hardware are still maturing.

Assembly microbenchmarks on Banana Pi F3 hardware calibrate the counters and expose predication overhead and strided loads as bottlenecks that compiler cost models miss. Across six applications, GCC 15 beats Clang 21 in four, with Clang ahead only on two dense matrix kernels, and a new vector backend for Google's Qsim simulator shows the same pattern. Chip and compiler teams get a calibrated map of where the gap still lies.
arxiv-2605-10960:
A statistical study tests two Hebrew folk proverbs that tie rainy lunar-calendar anchor days to rainy months, using 75 years of Israeli rainfall data from 1950 to 2024. One proverb names Rosh Chodesh, the new month's first day, and the other names Shabbat Mevarechim, the Saturday before it.

Across seven cities in three climate regions, a rainy anchor day lifts the chance of a rainy month from about 22 percent to about 39 percent. Both proverbs show nearly identical effects. The signal fades with longer lags and weakens over recent decades as rainfall patterns shift. Folklore researchers get proof that the old sayings encode real atmospheric persistence, now eroding with climate change.
arxiv-2605-11160:
Alexandre Ern and Ruma R. Maity build an energy-decreasing algorithm for the finite element approximation of two-dimensional ferronematic equilibrium states. Ferronematics mix magnetic nanoparticles into a nematic liquid crystal, where coupling between nematic order and magnetism boosts susceptibility.

The task is to cut the harmonic energy of two 2D vector fields, both with fixed length, plus a nonlinear rule on how the two vectors point. The finite element setup uses piecewise continuous trial functions on a weakly acute triangulation. It uses a decomposition-coordination frame with a Uzawa-like iteration. Tests show how the scheme performs. Applied math readers get a scheme whose energy always drops for ferronematic equilibria.
arxiv-2605-11260:
Jincheng Cao and three co-authors propose Curriculum Learning-Guided Progressive Distillation, or CLPD, for large language models. Knowledge distillation transfers large-model skills into smaller, efficient student models. But current methods overlook learning order of training data and capacity mismatch between teacher and student. This caps performance and yields the odd pattern where stronger teachers still fail to turn out better students.

CLPD handles both factors by matching data difficulty to teacher strength. It builds an explicit curriculum that orders training examples from easy to hard, while an implicit plan over supervision signals brings in teachers of growing size in stages. The framework is modular and plugs into standard algorithms with minimal overhead. On reasoning benchmarks, CLPD consistently beats standard methods, data ordering alone, and teacher order alone across multiple settings. Users get a unified method that treats both together.
arxiv-2605-12160: Joonha Park, Jiseung Jeong, and Taesik Gong present Premover, a light add-on letting VLA robots start moving before the user finishes speaking. Robot policies wait for the full instruction, wasting seconds, though partial instructions often hold enough to begin. Premover maps the partial instruction onto the scene with a focus map, and a readiness gate decides when to start, leaving the main policy untouched. On the SO-101 robot it cut task time by 17.9 percent, from 60.5 to 49.7 seconds, with success rates held. In LIBERO simulation it cut time by 8.3 percent.
arxiv-2605-12360: Avraham-Re'em and Kosloff classify a subtle asymmetry in the analysis of countable groups. The left and right regular actions give two Dirichlet spaces that need not match, even though the two actions are unitarily equivalent. Their main result says the spaces agree exactly when the group is an FC-group, for countable amenable groups. The proof builds a skewed Følner mechanism, called a left scheme, and shows it concretely for the Heisenberg group and wreath products. A dynamical twin appears in nonsingular Bernoulli shifts.
arxiv-2605-13160: Oliveira builds a kernel-based theory for regularised nonlinear parametric models, trained on data gathered on the fly in Bayesian optimisation. Old work covers Gaussian process models, kernel methods, linear models and linearised nets, leaving a gap for the nonlinear models used in practice. Kernels over parameter space induce Hilbert-space structures over the model class, yielding error bars under wide classes of regularised convex losses. The bounds back convergence guarantees for nonlinear acquisition and surrogate models, including randomised policies that pick points by maximising a trained random model.
arxiv-2605-13260: Hashimoto and Iwata give one proof plan covering both physics informed neural nets and their variational kin. Earlier proofs needed tight limits like stability or linear ellipticity. Using Taylor expansion, they turn nonlinear differential operators into linear ones on a large space, then apply Koopman style maths. The result shows high rank nets can generalize well even with derivatives, while operator nonlinearity swells the bound fast.
arxiv-2605-13360: Coleman Hooper and colleagues build speculative interaction agents for real time voice style assistant work. Tool calling can add seconds of delay, breaking the sub second feel that live interaction needs. Asynchronous input output lets reasoning overlap waiting, while speculative tool calls act before the full user message is certain. Strong cloud models gain 1.3 to 1.7 fold speed with small accuracy loss, and small edge models gain 1.6 to 2.2 fold after clock based training.
arxiv-2605-13760: E. Sacchetti and colleagues develop a full test flow for new speed guesses of single-chip active pixel sensors. The flow covers signal creation in the live volume through pixel digital logic doing time-of-arrival and time-over-threshold reads. It adds pixel wells from the layout to describe leakage and punch-through currents exactly. It couples Monte Carlo Allpix Squared tests with exact SPICE circuit tests. Applied to Belle II vertex sensor upgrade MAPS, the flow's match with TJ-Monopix2 reads supports modern MAPS building.
arxiv-2605-13860: Sushant Gautam and three colleagues present the Moltbook watch Archive, a growing data quietly logging agent-only social network life. On Moltbook, posts and comments are written only by self-run AI agents. Data cover agent pages, posts, comments, group labels called submolts, platform-level time-series snaps and word-rate trend totals. To their knowing, this is the first large-scale watched data of a social network filled only by self-run AI agents.
arxiv-2605-14160: Andrade and Liao study topological solitons in two-field scalar models set in round-symmetric backgrounds of any dimension. Lagrangians with canonical and generalized kinetic terms appear, and a Bogomol'nyi method is built for the cut-down theory. Local topological lumps are found, and their stability, as a rule blocked in higher dimensions by scaling instability, is enabled by radial change in the potential. First-order equations yield an integrable orbit rule that solves the problem fully, with target-space orbits shared across similar systems in other backgrounds.
arxiv-2605-14360: Harry and colleagues test whether ultra-brief written worries can enrich wearable sensing for student health. In a year-long study of 458 students wearing Oura rings, a bimonthly prompt asked their main concern, typically answered in three words. Weeks framed by academic concern came with lower physical activity. Weeks with emotional-exhaustion language came with poorer sleep and lower heart-rate variability. General pretrained embeddings matched or beat domain-adapted models, suggesting emotional register beats topic labels as signal, though many links faded after correction for multiple comparisons.
arxiv-2605-14660: Bandara and team propose MindGap, an on-device conversational AI framework for upstream neuroplastic rehabilitation in post-traumatic stress disorder. Where exposure and cognitive therapies work downstream, after distress has arisen, MindGap targets the gap between a pre-cognitive feeling tone and the reactive elaboration that follows. Three progressive layers of observation guide patients to notice the bare signal, see it as self-arising, and spot the conditioned belief beneath it.
arxiv-2605-14860: Angino and team propose a non-monotone trust-region method for neural network training. Domain splitting divides a network into subdomains trained in parallel, linked by a global trust-region rule. Building on the APTS strategy, the variant adds a nonlinear Schwarz preconditioner. It combines parallel fixes with global coarse directions. A windowed rule allows controlled rises, avoiding needless rejection of good coarse steps. Accuracy holds while CPU time falls thirty percent and rejected steps drop to one third.
arxiv-2605-15260: Ludwig M. Böss and four colleagues advance the Entity particle-in-cell code for plasma astrophysics with higher-order shape functions and generalized field stencils. Since plasma phenomena grow from small instabilities, codes must suppress noise so growth is physical. Their current-deposit scheme reaches up to eleventh-order interpolation, and tunable field stencils suppress numerical dispersion. Tests confirm charge conservation, stability against numerical heating, better energy conservation, and damping of numerical Cherenkov effects, with scaling benchmarks for the performance cost.
arxiv-2605-15560: Jijia Tian, Hao Wang, Mu Jia, Yi Wang, Junting Chen, and Pooi-Yuen Kam guard shared radio-map learning. Shared model updates can still leak where transmitters sit, though raw readings stay local. Their plan spreads a fixed noise budget across upload groups that leak most. Those groups come from the RadioUNet build. Group noise is tuned from small upload stats just before send. Under a matched budget it gives the best privacy shield and the best rebuild quality of all noise guards.
arxiv-2605-15960: Logan Mondal Bhamidipaty and four colleagues define model exploitation in reinforcement learning. A world model is exploitable if it implies one policy should be strictly preferred over another while the true transition model implies the reverse. They link it to reward hacking, but the prior inevitability proof does not transfer. A general theory proves exploitation essentially unavoidable on large policy sets, with the hacking claim as a special case. Finite-set unhackability conditions have no counterpart precluding exploitation, so the authors relax the notion and derive a safe horizon.
arxiv-2605-16360: Li, Lou, and Li present ProxyKV, a cross-model proxy pruning tool for efficient long-context language-model inference. The key-value cache memory wall forces a choice between fast heuristics that lose precision and precise reconstruction methods with costly prefilling. ProxyKV offloads importance scoring to a small intra-family proxy model run beside the large target model, with a mapper bridging heterogeneous models and a loss that targets relative ranking consistency. It matches KVZip accuracy while delivering up to 3.21-fold prefilling speedup on Llama-3.1-8B.
arxiv-2605-16560: Jhawar and Baccelli study a cellular network whose base stations move at constant speed in random directions, modeled as a Poisson point process. A user connects to the nearest station and hands over as stations move, with signal and interference shifting throughout. The authors derive closed or integral formulas for coverage probability and Shannon rate at key moments, including handovers and closest approaches. They frame signal swings as seasons of Shannon rate and sketch a lift to three-dimensional drone and high-altitude networks.
arxiv-2605-16860: Tran and colleagues propose PhysioSeq2Seq, a hybrid digital twin and Seq2Seq LSTM for long-horizon glucose forecasting in type 1 diabetes. Recursive LSTMs show negative bias at long horizons from compounding, while population ODE models fail across individuals. For each glucose segment, twin matching searches 300 digital twins for the best fit from 3 hours of monitoring history. The matched twin's 10 ODE variables feed both encoder and decoder. Simultaneous 48-step prediction removes compounding. At 240 minutes, mean absolute error is 39.28 mg/dL, beating recursive LSTM bias by 13.89 and ODE twin error by 28.62.
arxiv-2605-17160: Chaymae Yahyati and colleagues show that shrinking a model through quantization can break algorithmic recourse, even when accuracy survives. A small change that flips a full-precision decision may fail or grow costly after compression. They define validity drop and recourse gap to measure the damage, then propose counterfactual-faithful quantization, which preserves recourse points during training and cuts both measures at matched accuracy and bit budget.
arxiv-2605-17260: Kim and colleagues present LiteFrame, a compact vision encoder that lets video language models scale to far more frames. Their compressed token distillation trains a small student to predict dense, compressed views from a large teacher, skipping redundant per-frame work. Paired with language-model adaptation, it cuts end-to-end latency 35 percent against InternVL3-8B while handling eight times more frames and lifting average accuracy.
arxiv-2605-17560: Mallick and colleagues apply topological data analysis to space-time signs of intermittency in helically rotating turbulence. Vorticity magnitude and eddy-size fields serve as scalar readouts, with shifting shape tracked through persistence diagrams and Wasserstein-distance metrics. The frame proves more sensitive than standard stats to local, short-lived flow changes. Sharp changes in heatmaps give direct signs of strong turbulent fluctuations across space and time.
arxiv-2605-17660: Raphaël Barboni and three colleagues build a rigorous math picture of transformer training as depth and width grow without bound. ResNet training behaves like steering a neural ordinary differential equation, while transformer training steers a neural partial differential equation, since attention couples many token distributions. Their mean-field model tracks token distributions and attention weights across layers. They prove the forward pass is well-posed and derive the Wasserstein gradient of training risk. Gradient flow, they show, reaches global minima when starting loss is small enough, given kernel injectivity.
arxiv-2605-17760: Yuichi Yoshida gives tolerant testers for Unique Games with sublinear query counts in the adjacency-list model. Earlier tolerant testers needed structural assumptions like expansion or clusterability. His tester separates instances where at most an epsilon fraction of constraints are violated from those where at least a rho fraction are, under a stated epsilon-log-n condition. It uses query counts scaling like the square root of m times powers of rho. He also gives a sharper specialized tester for bipartiteness, the two-label transposition case, exploiting its signed structure.
arxiv-2605-17860: Sicheng Jin, Dipankar Srirag, and Aditya Joshi introduce PAREDA, a speech dataset built from discussions of natural language processing papers. Speakers with Australian, Indian-English, and Chinese English accents give spontaneous summaries and question-and-answer exchanges. Tests show speech recognition models struggle zero-shot on PAREDA, confirming difficulty, especially with mixed accents and faster speech. Fine-tuning on PAREDA cuts word error rate sharply, showing the set captures traits missing from standard corpora. PAREDA offers a new resource for robust speech recognition in real-world settings.
arxiv-2605-17960: Md Navid Bin Islam and Sajal Saha link network attack detection to action. Detection systems classify attacks well but leave analysts asking what to do next. Their framework classifies traffic as benign, denial of service, or distributed denial of service with three binary deep neural networks. It scores 99.84% on CICIDS2018 and 95.30% on UNSW-NB15. A retrieval-augmented generation pipeline builds prompts from the top five anomalous features. It directs a local language model to write structured, citation-grounded mitigation reports, beating vanilla outputs on all metrics.
arxiv-2605-18260: Jonathan Joás Zapata Campos's 2026 paper predicts ultra-compact sub-stellar objects made of strange quark matter. A Bayesian sweep of the MIT bag-model space accounts for finite-size and curvature effects at low baryon number. It confines self-gravitating sequences to masses near one hundredth to one tenth of the Sun. Their radii run to thousands of kilometres. Rapid rotation inflates equatorial radii toward massive exoplanets, yet the objects keep their density. A density gap separates them from planets and brown dwarfs, offering microlensing targets.
arxiv-2605-18360: Wanchen Li and three colleagues introduce Nested-GPT, a hierarchical autoregressive Transformer that simulates parton-shower histories with a varying emission count. Unlike a flow-matching baseline, which needs the final count fixed in advance, Nested-GPT predicts emissions in order and learns when to stop. On gap-fraction observables in the 2026 tests, its samples match a reference Monte Carlo dipole shower within statistical uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-18460: MKA Ariyaratne and three co-authors present a centroid-guided Firefly Algorithm variant in a 2026 paper for data clustering, tackling K-Means gaps with uneven shapes, densities, and unknown cluster counts. A centroid-shift plan plus a multi-goal fitness score weighing tightness, separation, and a TSP-based travel penalty auto-picks the cluster count and shifts bounds. On robotic sensor nets it lifts clustering quality and shortens in-cluster paths over K-Means.
arxiv-2605-18660: Shi Ding and Sijian Tan propose TCR, a 2026 scheme for judging human-AI interaction with tutoring software as the test case. Aggregate scores like accuracy and fluency, they argue, miss traits that matter face to face: steady behavior across turns and step-by-step improvement. TCR stresses openness, consistency, and refinement, with set prompts and sample exchanges. The aim is human-centered review that adds to aggregate scores and judge-based review for interactive systems.
arxiv-2605-19060: Xinhe Zhang and five colleagues build LiFT, a method for making three-dimensional medical scans from two-dimensional slice generators. Rather than modelling a whole volume at once, it treats the volume as an ordered path, tracking how body structures appear, shift, and vanish with depth. A loss function aligns generated slices with real scans, while a mixing step keeps neighbouring slices coherent across scan types. Tests on brain imaging show slice quality preserved at far lower computing cost.
arxiv-2605-19260: Yuankai Li and colleagues cut the visual cost of GUI agents, which feed high-resolution screenshots to large multimodal models. Screenshots waste tokens on blank regions while text and icons still need fine detail, and older fixes need retraining or ignore screen layout. Their AQuaUI builds an adaptive quadtree per screenshot, keeping one merged token per leaf and preserving positions, then reuses past quadtrees for steadier work. On a leading GUI model it runs up to 13.22 percent faster with 29.52 percent fewer tokens while keeping 99.06 percent of full-token performance.
arxiv-2605-19460: Terashima and Yamaguchi prove the Gang-Kim-Yoon integrality conjecture for torus knots: sums of powers of adjoint Reidemeister torsions are integers. The proof holds for every torus knot and every non-negative power index. It introduces Verlinde numbers for torus knots through the modular S-matrix, with recursion formulas and initial values that yield integrality. The authors also build a birational model of the character variety for a torus knot and show how its defining polynomial, via its Hessian, recovers the adjoint torsion.
arxiv-2605-19660: Su and team propose OScaR, a lightweight framework for extreme key-value cache quantization. Per-channel quantization handles key-tensor outliers but falters under extreme compression. Their analysis names token norm imbalance as the bottleneck: shared quantization parameters spanning token groups amplify errors. OScaR advances the per-channel paradigm with canalized rotation and omni-token scaling, cutting variance. Across text-only and multimodal models it beats rivals at INT2, and against a BF16 baseline it reaches 3.0 times faster decoding, 5.3 times less memory and 4.1 times more throughput.
arxiv-2605-20360: Thomas and four co-workers track line-shape changes in WD J005311, the remnant of the 1181 supernova, thought to come from two merged white dwarfs. Broad shifts across the strong O VI line, about 10 percent of line flux, likely come from wind instabilities like those in Wolf-Rayet stars. A hint of order in those shifts fits rotation over about two hours, though features fade within one cycle. Narrow shifts near line centre point to an unstable disk tied to the remnant's rotating magnetosphere.
arxiv-2605-21260: Yue Zhang and colleagues develop a learning-theoretic account of chain of thought, modeled as interaction between an answer map and a chain rule that generates intermediate questions in sequence. Reasoning risk splits into two opposing terms: oracle-trajectory risk, capturing chain-of-thought benefit, and trajectory-mismatch risk, capturing cost from error buildup along mismatched trajectories. Without stability in loss, answer map, or chain rule, mismatch risk can grow without bound even when benefit risk is zero. Under stability, a tight upper bound on mismatch risk follows.
arxiv-2605-21760: Farjam Karim and co-authors analyze passive reconfigurable intelligent surfaces under short-packet, finite-blocklength sending, with surface-element thermal noise. Standard infinite-blocklength studies miss this noise, and the authors build a single model for block-error rate and goodput under uniform and non-uniform reflection settings. Leaving out surface thermal noise overstates reliability, with the gap growing as element count rises. Larger surfaces do not always help, notably at low transmit power where built-up noise rules, showing simple surface models need the noise term for honest testing.
arxiv-2605-21860: Valentio Iverson and coauthors present empirical sensitivity, a robustness measure. An estimator has bounded sensitivity if changing at most eta of its points usually moves the estimate slightly. For Gaussian mean estimation they prove lower bounds. Any estimator with optimal square-root-of-dimension-over-n error has sensitivity of order eta plus square root of eta times dimension over n. The two terms come from mean and variance obstructions via Efron-Stein. The bound is tight up to log factors, using recent robust mean estimation results.
arxiv-2605-21960: Sanjiang Li presents dSABRE, a router in the SABRE style for multi-core distributed quantum computers that minimizes EPR consumption, the dominant routing cost. Each lookahead-driven iteration first settles intra-core front-layer gates with SWAP scores, falling back to inter-core teleportation candidates only when the intra-core front is empty. Across 18 MQT-Bench circuits at 25, 36, and 64 logical qubits, it cuts geometric-mean EPR use by 41 to 44 percent over TeleSABRE and by 16 to 68 percent over pytket-dqc. A large QFT sweep at 100 to 360 qubits confirms it scales.
arxiv-2605-22660: Skórski asks whether machine translation keeps subtle moral meaning intact when moving morally annotated posts from Polish into English. Using about 50,000 annotated social media posts and a four method validation pipeline, he finds direct translation preserves moral cues well enough for cross lingual learning. Accuracy gaps across moral foundations stay tiny, though slang, vulgarity and culture bound phrases still suffer. The result frames translation as a practical cheap route to moral research in under resourced languages, with Polish standing in for related Slavic tongues.
arxiv-2605-22860: Ebode Atangana and Ndognkon Manga give a short, self-contained proof that every signed planar graph is 5-choosable, meaning each vertex can be colored from any list of five colors respecting edge signs. Their signature-blind induction inserts one sign factor uniformly, so it reduces to Thomassen's classic proof when all signs are positive. The same argument yields refinements, including 3-choosability for outerplanar signed graphs and a fast list-coloring algorithm.
arxiv-2605-23260: Papazafeiropoulos develops a unified model for the MISO downlink with fluid antenna users. Fluid antenna access lets each user switch among several closely spaced ports and pick the strongest signal. He shows the per-port signal-to-interference ratio follows a Beta-prime shape with settings Meff and L. He derives closed-form total distribution functions for both cases, plus cross-port links. Number results confirm the distributions and outage bounds, and show maximum ratio sending achieves weaker port links and larger selection gains than zero-forcing.
arxiv-2605-23960: Wang and four colleagues untangle protein representations so that structure maps more cleanly onto function. Their framework, ProtDiS, splits pretrained embeddings of protein micro-environments into grounded, task-relevant parts, balancing detail against compression in the spirit of the information bottleneck. The split features prove more specific, independent, and information-efficient, and lift scores across twelve downstream tasks, mainly when splits follow structure. Protein- and residue-level checks show it separates proteins with similar folds but different functions and catches fine biophysical signals.
arxiv-2605-24060: Panthi and Abdelfattah show that scoring-target choice can silently flip conversational-memory benchmark verdicts. Their audit, TIAP, regrades saved ranked outputs without rerunning retrieval, crediting Raw, Source, or Canonical in turn. Switching only the credited target changed nDCG on 83.4 to 94.0 percent of shared queries, flipped target orderings on transfer runs, and reversed parser-density recommendations. A 1,902-case semantic audit found relaxed source-linked credit fully justified only 29.2 percent of the time. Memory papers, they urge, should define and report the scoring target explicitly.
arxiv-2605-24160: Campbell settles a question Crandall left open in 2012 about the binary digits of the Erdos-Borwein constant, the irrational sum of reciprocals of one less than powers of two. Crandall asked whether the string 11 recurs infinitely often in the constant's base-two expansion, a problem Shallit later noted as well. Campbell proves it does, combining a congruence construction in the spirit of Erdos with a prime-counting estimate of Alford, Granville, and Pomerance for primes in arithmetic progressions. The argument grew out of extensive exchanges with GPT-5.5 Pro.
arxiv-2605-25060: Sanjeev Kumar, Sung Min Jo, Alessandro Munafò, and Marco Panesi study non-equilibrium radiation in a high-enthalpy plasma wind tunnel. There, radiative transfer is often ignored or cut down to see-through. Their framework joins a plasma-flow model with a spectral radiative transport solver. Runs cover nitrogen and air plasmas across pressure and power ranges at Plasmatron X. Radiative losses depend strongly on pressure: tiny at low pressure, main at high pressure, about 32 percent of input power for nitrogen and 22 percent for air.
arxiv-2605-25160: Guohong Liu and colleagues offer ScaleWoB, a way to synthesize interactive environments for testing agents that operate graphical interfaces. The fake environments run as plain web pages needing no backend, so they start fast and cost little. They cover mobile, desktop, and car interfaces with over one hundred environments and one thousand checkable tasks. On a mobile benchmark of 120 tasks across 63 apps, leading agents average only 27.92 percent success against 92.08 percent for people.
arxiv-2605-25460: Mengda Li, Zeng Li, and Jianfeng Yao remove mean-shift noise from PCA by adding knockoff noise on purpose. Standard PCA breaks when shifted samples skew leading components, and existing robust methods cannot handle this mixture contamination in high dimensions. Random-matrix theory shows the mean-shift spikes separate spectrally from stable eigenvalues. The original eigenspace stays invariant in the limit whatever the mixture weight. The team exploits this stability in a two-stage algorithm that adds knockoff mean and identifies the shifted component using only standard PCA operations.
arxiv-2605-25660: Albano, Facchini, Mazzotta and Stefanelli give methods for building Yang-Baxter solutions from right groups. Their form follows set theory with left non-degeneracy. They offer left RG-semibraces, new algebraic systems that contain left cancellative semibraces as a proper part. The work thus extends the toolkit for solution work, placing plain left ones inside a wider right-group frame.
arxiv-2605-25960: Sen and Mandal study a spin-half chain with trimerised couplings, a pattern relevant to the compound Na2Cu3Ge4O12. At low energy, the chain behaves like a simpler Heisenberg chain built from three-spin units. That mapping gives exact spinon excitations through the Bethe ansatz, a classic exact method. For higher energies, the authors build a self-consistent mean-field theory that yields three fermion bands. The theory also reproduces a one-third magnetisation plateau and predicts measurable magnetic and heat responses.
arxiv-2605-26060: Hou, Hu and Liu prove the matching conjecture for four-uniform hypergraphs at matching number 6004 and above. A matching is a set of disjoint edges, and the conjecture caps edges in hypergraphs lacking a larger one. Their proof cuts the global claim to a lower-uniformity bound plus a fixed finite optimisation. For four-uniform hypergraphs the board has 19 vertices, split into 19-, 15- and 11-vertex layers. The hardest layer falls to exact rational certificates and fixed integer searches.
arxiv-2605-26360: Luis Avilés and three colleagues extend Weyl transformations in first-order gravity with one new parameter, defining a conformally coupled scalar sector with torsion. In the resulting Einstein-Cartan-Maxwell theory, they derive static solutions in asymptotically flat and locally anti-de Sitter spacetimes. Depending on constants and the deformation parameter, they describe regular black holes, scalar-dressed black holes, and traversable wormholes. Torsion can regularize the scalar field and improve singularity structure, while topological black holes in anti-de Sitter space need nonzero electric charge, in a 2026 paper.
arxiv-2605-26660: Nguyen and five others present WINDQuant, a controller that assigns bit widths for squeezing large language models. Ultra-low-bit squeezing usually wrecks accuracy or demands costly retraining, while coarse sensitivity maps miss fine variation inside weight matrices. WINDQuant learns, chunk by chunk under a global storage budget, which widths and treatments each column slice gets, using reinforcement learning with activation-aware calibration. On LLaMA models it holds competitive accuracy at tiny bit widths with less tuning cost than retraining.

arxiv-2606-04060:
Zhonggai Wang, Kai Fang, and Guangyu Gao present in 2026 a method for teaching image segmentation systems new classes step by step when only weak labels are available. The known failure is drift: noisy labels slowly corrupt what the model remembers, so new classes overwrite old ones.

Their system, SASA, fights drift on two fronts. Learnable anchor tokens pin down each class's identity over time, while a flexible adjustment layer still lets the model adapt to each image. A spatial arbitration rule then filters unreliable label signals and enforces one class per object. Across standard benchmarks, the method beat prior approaches, with the clearest gains in long, multi-step learning sequences where drift usually hurts most.
arxiv-2606-04160:
Anna Marbut, Travis Wheeler, and Daniel Olson dissect in 2026 how refusal behavior, the trained habit of declining harmful requests, is distributed inside mixture-of-experts language models. In these models, each input is routed to a few specialized sub-networks called experts.

A steering vector can suppress refusal in ordinary dense models; the team extended the technique to three open mixture-of-experts systems. Steering worked just as well despite the routing complexity. A single expert, free to choose its location, recovered over three quarters of the full steering effect on average, but barely half when forced to the location full-layer steering uses. The refusal signals also differed from the signals that drive routing. Refusal, they conclude, is spread unevenly rather than run by one switch.
arxiv-2606-04260:
Šimon Schierreich and Ildikó Schlotter study in 2026 the majority illusion, a social network trap where a minority opinion looks dominant because the minority happens to hold the best-connected seats. Agents then misread their community and may act on the false picture.

Their question is detection: given a network, can some labeling of opinions produce the illusion for a chosen fraction of agents? They map how the network's structural properties move this decision problem between tractable and intractable. The result is a detailed complexity map for the parameterized problem, showing which structural restrictions make detection efficient and which leave it hard. Such maps matter because a platform that cannot even detect an illusion-prone network cannot hope to correct one.
arxiv-2606-04560:
