Yoo and colleagues recycle the practice runs that reinforcement learning usually throws away, in a 2026 arXiv paper on training reasoning models. GRPO is a standard method for post-training with verifiable rewards. It uses each rollout for one gradient update and discards it. That is sample inefficient. Naive replay fails because the policy drifts quickly. Stored rollouts go stale and destabilize training. Their buffer stores and samples individual rollouts rather than whole groups. It adds safeguards against staleness.

Rollouts older than a fixed age are evicted. Each training batch anchors on fresh on-policy rollouts. It then adds replayed ones, prioritized by the size of each rollout's advantage. The team tested three Qwen3-Base scales on five math benchmarks. The method beat GRPO and naive replay baselines. Gains appeared at every scale and grew with model size. The largest gain was 4.35 percentage points on the five-benchmark average at 4B.
arxiv-2606-04960:
Chen and Jin prove that a charged gas in a bounded container settles into a unique steady state and returns to it after small disturbances, in a 2026 arXiv analysis paper. The Vlasov-Poisson-Boltzmann system couples particle transport, a self-consistent electric field, and Boltzmann collisions. For the stationary problem in a bounded convex domain, they construct a unique stationary solution. The key difficulty is regularity, because the electric field and collision operator are coupled.

They overcome it with a bootstrap framework. For the dynamical system near the stationary solution, they prove global existence and uniqueness for small perturbations, plus exponential convergence back to the steady state.
arxiv-2606-05060:
Genyue Liu and colleagues demonstrate high-fidelity neutral atom gates calibrated by low-rank Hessian optimization in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum optimal control can design fast, robust multi-qubit gates, but the resulting high-dimensional waveforms are hard to calibrate in the lab because direct searches converge slowly. The team exploits the low-rank structure of quantum control landscapes, where only a few waveform directions strongly affect fidelity.

Their method finds those sensitive directions, whose number is set by the accessible leakage and error channels, and optimizes only within that small space using closed-loop experimental feedback. Applied to an amplitude-robust controlled-Z gate on metastable ytterbium-171 nuclear-spin qubits, the optimized gate reached a raw fidelity of 0.9959, rising to 0.99902 after postselection on no detected loss, and performance barely changed under laser-power swings of up to 20 percent. The same directions could also correct certain Hamiltonian parameter errors.
arxiv-2606-05360:
Dmitrii Kolotkov, Sergey Belov, and Mohamed Sherif hunt for observable fingerprints of the entropy mode in the solar corona in this 2026 arXiv paper. Magnetohydrodynamic waves in coronal loops are prized seismological tools, and the fast and slow magnetoacoustic modes are exploited. The entropy mode, the third eigenmode of the system, has stayed inaccessible because it neither propagates nor oscillates.

Working in the corona's non-adiabatic conditions, where the entropy mode couples closely to the compressive slow mode, the authors model a one-dimensional coronal loop. The entropy mode decays faster than the slow mode, and that superposition of two exponential decays leaves distinct marks. The marks are a non-exponential damping profile during the first oscillation cycles, and an asymmetry between the upper and lower envelopes of the temperature and density swings. There are also deviations from the canonical quarter-period phase shift between temperature and velocity perturbations.
arxiv-2606-05460:
Lavsen Dahal and colleagues present ORACLE-CT in this 2026 arXiv paper, an anatomy-aware method for classifying diseases in abdominal CT scans. Most classifiers pool features from the whole volume. That lets evidence for a liver label leak in from anywhere and breaks the link between a prediction and its basis.

ORACLE-CT uses multi-organ segmentation to define an anatomical support for each label, the region where evidence for that disease may live, and restricts attention pooling to it. The framework is encoder-agnostic and was tested with three representation families: a vision transformer, a 3D convolutional network, and a radiology foundation encoder. It was trained on one dataset and checked on two external ones. Support-masked pooling improved discrimination on the benchmark and transferred better externally. It lifted one encoder's external scores on both test sets, while keeping every prediction traceable to its evidence.
arxiv-2606-05560:
Takuo Matsubara and co-authors extend a classic forecasting tool to streams of distributions in a 2026 arXiv paper. Exponential smoothing blends past values with fading weights and often beats fancier forecast tools. It was built for plain numbers, though. Some modern series record a whole distribution at each step, like the spread of returns within an hour. The team rebuilds smoothing inside Wasserstein space, where distance measures how much mass must move to turn one distribution into another.

The generalized method keeps the old tool's prized simplicity, with a single smoothing parameter. The authors show that parameter can be estimated consistently by minimizing a Wasserstein distance to the data. Theory backs the claim, and practice confirms it. Tests on high-frequency financial returns and household electricity demand showed the method works well. The paper gives distribution-valued series a forecaster as light as the classic one.
arxiv-2606-05860:
Poikarayil and colleagues let a language model design time-series networks on demand in a 2026 arXiv paper. Forecasting and anomaly detection models are usually hand-built per dataset. Classic AutoML searches fixed menus that fit varied data poorly. GenAutoML turns user requirements in plain words into runnable PyTorch code. A sandboxed loop runs the code, reads the errors, and repairs it alone.

A signature-aware runtime keeps generated models within promised shapes. A normalization wrapper guards against drifting, non-stationary inputs. Tests on transformer temperature and weather datasets showed the agent inventing fresh layouts per dataset. One generated model, WaveInterferenceNet, answered in under a hundredth of a millisecond per sample. That latency set a state-of-the-art mark while giant foundation models lagged on speed. The framework trades their brute accuracy for tailored, deployable speed. Industrial monitoring, where milliseconds matter, is the stated target.
arxiv-2606-06460:
Thamilvendhan Munirathinam proposes a polite way to bar AI agents from servers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Autonomous agents now hold real credentials and run infrastructure unsupervised. Access control today is binary: the agent gets in, or it is hard blocked like any intruder. There is no standard way to say this resource is off limits to agents, please leave. His Recuse Signal is that message, sent through channels the protocol already has.

He defines the signal as an open mini standard and built adapters for SSH banners, a PostgreSQL proxy, and a Kubernetes webhook, deployed on a live host. Fresh agents given a benign task were then watched. In the SSH pilot with GPT 4o models and Claude Code, the signal produced one hundred percent recusal, against full task completion with no signal. It stayed a cooperative signal, though: an explicit operator authorization framing flipped the strongest model to proceed.
arxiv-2606-06660:
Long robot tasks often fail slowly, with one bad move making the next ones worse. Chen proposes a safety switch for that problem in this 2026 arXiv paper. The system, called AEGIS, watches the inner signals of a working robot policy, the rules the robot uses to pick actions. A cheap probe reads those signals and warns that failure is likely soon.

When the probe flags a risky step, control passes to a stronger backup policy for just those steps. On the LIBERO-Spatial test suite, AEGIS rescued about ten percent of the runs the weak policy lost, roughly double the rescue rate of blind switching at the same cost. The backup was active on only thirty eight percent of steps, and the warning probe scored well within the first third of each run, before any switch took place.
arxiv-2606-06760:
A medical AI that chats about a scan but cannot point at the problem is half useful. Aofei Chang and co-authors close that gap with MedSIGHT in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system joins a large vision language model, which reads images and text together, to pixel level segmentation, the outlining of exact regions in an image, inside one unified design.

A new part called the Region Perceiver turns areas of the image into region tokens the language model can reason over. A medical codebook adds region codes to the model's vocabulary, so it can name a body part or a lesion as a symbol and later decode that symbol back into an outline. Training proceeds in stages so the parts align stably. Using only seventy two thousand instruction examples, MedSIGHT reached state of the art results on medical question answering and segmentation across many imaging types.
arxiv-2606-07360:
Bayard solves a geometric boundary-value problem inside anti-de Sitter space in this 2026 arXiv paper. Anti-de Sitter space is a universe with constant negative curvature, central to geometry and theoretical physics. The question concerns spacelike hypersurfaces, slices that behave like space at an instant, whose scalar curvature is prescribed. The Dirichlet problem asks whether a surface exists matching the value and boundary data, expressed through a nonlinear equation.

Bayard proves the problem has a solution when the data are convex. That convexity condition, requiring boundary and target data to bend outward together, gives the estimates needed to control the equation. The result adds to the theory of prescribed-curvature problems, which extend classical questions about which shapes can realize a given function. Such problems connect differential geometry with the study of initial data in general relativity, where spacelike slices with controlled shape model space at a moment.
arxiv-2606-07560:
Wang shows that attention heads in language models contain two opposing factions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Function-vector heads are the parts credited with carrying out rules learned from examples, and researchers identify them by their causal contribution, treating the set as one class. Using a sign-preserving attribution method, Wang finds the population splits. Writers push the correct answer's score up, while cancellers push it down, and removing both shifts the output less than either group alone would suggest.

The split proved causal and reproducible across model-task pairs spanning 3 architectures and 6 model sizes. A shuffled null test rejected the single-class story. Size-only ranking cannot see the split, so function vectors average a promoter with a suppressor. Ablating the cancellers improved the correct label's score in every test cell and raised accuracy. Cancellers matched none of the head types, making them a characterized mechanism.
arxiv-2606-07760:
Andersson and a large team introduce scCBGM, a generative model that edits single cells in ways biologists can read and steer, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Single-cell RNA sequencing profiles each cell's active genes, but the space of drug and genetic perturbations is too large to test exhaustively. A useful model must predict how a cell would look under untried conditions, and explain itself in named concepts.

The design routes generation through a concept bottleneck, a layer of interpretable concepts, with skip connections and a penalty that keeps the concepts disentangled. A flow-matching version extends the idea from editing measured cells to generating new ones. To judge counterfactual edits fairly, the team built a synthetic benchmark where the true edited cells are known by construction. Across real datasets the model led in combinatorial generalisation, predicting responses to unseen condition combinations, and in counterfactual accuracy at cell and population level.
arxiv-2606-08060:
Toshiharu Harada, Tetsuo Handa, Masaki Hashimoto, and Hidehiko Tanaka present TOMOYO Linux, a security system that judges access requests by what a program has been doing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Conventional access control looks only at the pair asking: which application, which file. It ignores the application's intent and history, so a compromised or misused program inherits its full permissions.

Their mandatory access control keys decisions to the application's execution state: the chain of programs that led to this request. A request that fits the program's history can be allowed, while the same request arriving through an abnormal path can be denied. Administrators thus reduce damage from malicious attempts and mistakes without hand-writing rules for every file. The paper covers the concept, the Linux implementation design, and a brief evaluation. It is an English translation of the authors' earlier Japanese journal paper.
arxiv-2606-08260:
Qi Liu and colleagues present a single model that both edits and generates video in this 2026 arXiv paper. Video diffusion models, which build footage by gradually removing noise, have advanced quickly, yet editing and generation usually live in separate task-specific models. A unified framework is hard because tasks feed the model different mixes of inputs: a source video, reference images, or text instructions. Earlier unified attempts needed extra encoders or could not tell these conditioning tokens apart reliably.

Their framework, TIDE, integrates instruction-based editing, reference-guided editing, and multi-reference generation in one system. Its core device is the per-token task embedding, a small learned tag attached to every input token stating which task role it plays. With each token labeled, the model can explicitly tell apart target, source, and reference material even as their number and type vary across tasks.
arxiv-2606-08360:
Lingkai Kong and colleagues tackle a planning problem in public health outreach, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Peer-referral recruitment is key for studying and reaching hidden populations hit by infectious diseases. Agencies must allocate limited referral resources adaptively across many rounds. Each round's decisions shape both how many people arrive next and who they are. Prior work simplified this by assuming recruits are drawn independently from a uniform population.

That assumption ignores homophily, the tendency of people to refer others like themselves. The authors instead condition arrivals on the observable traits of current recruits. They build a generative frontier planning approach that looks ahead under this dependence. Planning must balance reaching more people against learning the population's structure, since today's referrals determine tomorrow's pool. The method is meant for field teams that must act fast with small budgets and hard limits.
arxiv-2606-08460:
Xunye Tian and colleagues turn a statistical weakness, having very few test samples, into a strength, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Two-sample testing asks whether two samples come from the same distribution. Data-adaptive versions learn a discrepancy measure from the data itself. Such methods usually split data to keep learning separate from testing. That suits few-shot settings poorly, where imbalance is severe: abundant reference samples on one side, a handful of query samples on the other. Their method, LOTTERY, exploits the imbalance constructively.

Using the abundant reference data, the method learns representations that summarize the salient structure of the reference distribution, giving signals for detecting departures with very few query points. Families of representations capture global and local structure, weighted adaptively using only reference samples. They prove control of the type I error rate, the probability of a false alarm, plus consistency guarantees.
arxiv-2606-08760:
Alejandro Mata Ali presents software for seeing the structure of quantum and tensor-network computations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tensor networks and quantum circuits are structural objects whose meaning depends on connectivity and contraction order. They are easier to reason about visually than as code. Yet in Python they are commonly built through backend-specific objects, making structural mistakes hard to notice.

One package supports visual debugging and structural inspection of tensor networks and traced contraction workflows. A second provides visual-to-code authoring, generating backend code from diagrams while preserving designs as data. A third renders quantum circuits clearly for inspection and side-by-side comparison. The packages are deliberately not simulators. They sit between the researcher and the simulation libraries, catching wiring errors that numerical output cannot reveal.
arxiv-2606-08960:
Zhong and colleagues automate the arms race between cheating agents and their checkers, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agent benchmarks grade work with outcome verifiers, programs checking whether a task was done. Hand-written verifiers are brittle, so agents reward-hack them with shortcuts like deleting failing tests. Auditing 1,968 tasks across 5 terminal-agent benchmarks, the authors found 323, or 16 percent, hackable by frontier models given the task description.

Their hacker-fixer loop sets three language-model agents against each other. A hacker tries to pass without solving the task. A fixer patches the verifier against each exploit, and a solver confirms solutions still pass. On KernelBench the loop drove attack success from 62 percent to zero on held-out exploits. Weaker defenders sufficed: a loop run by Gemini 3 Flash cut Gemini 3.1 Pro's attack success from 76 percent to zero. The team releases the 323 hackable environments as the Terminal Wrench dataset.
arxiv-2606-09160:
Thapa and Pandyea build a phone-based farming advisor for Nepal that forecasts weather, recommends crops, and answers farmers' questions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. About two-thirds of Nepal's population farms, mostly at subsistence level, and planting still rests on experience and coarse forecasts. The system predicts weather 30 days ahead for 1,359 locations using two graph neural network models, which learn from places as a graph, capturing variation across space and time.

The spatio-temporal graph convolutional model beat the transformer-based model, its mean squared error near 0.011 against 0.013. Forecasts combine with soil properties, pH, moisture, and organic content, in a scoring algorithm matching crops to their preferred conditions. A retrieval-augmented chatbot, mixing SPLADE sparse retrieval with dense vectors, answers farming questions from domain documents. The system ships as a mobile app giving real-time suggestions. User feedback confirmed its relevance in rural settings, where personalized guidance is scarce.
arxiv-2606-09760:
Dushmanta Sahu and Captain Singh study how a magnetic field can set the hottest matter in the lab spinning in this 2026 arXiv paper. The matter is quark-gluon plasma, the melted state made in heavy-ion crashes. The effect is the Einstein-de Haas effect: when spins line up in a field, the whole body turns to keep total spin balanced. It is known in solids, less so in plasma.

The pair use a quasiparticle model of the expanding fireball. The induced spin rate grows with proper time, the clock of the fireball itself. Hotter plasma damps the effect, since heat fights alignment. Near the crossover heat, where plasma turns to normal matter, the rate grows large enough to matter. Curves for strong and weak fields cross at one heat. That cross splits a spin-led regime from an inertia-led one.
arxiv-2606-09960:
Vila-Cruz and colleagues design a continual learning system for small devices, in a 2026 arXiv paper on efficient machine learning. Class-incremental learning teaches a model new categories over time without forgetting old ones. Most methods need powerful hardware and long retraining cycles. Robots and edge devices, by contrast, must adapt quickly with limited energy and memory, which motivates a lighter design.

Their system, HydraCIL, freezes the feature-extraction backbone and creates a small task-specific classifier head for each new task, avoiding costly retraining. Features are extracted once, and prototype matching, which compares inputs against stored class averages, selects the right head at prediction time. On CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100, CoRe50, and Flowers102, HydraCIL matched or beat leading class-incremental methods. It also cut training time and carbon footprint sharply, suiting embedded settings where rapid adaptation matters most.
arxiv-2606-10160:
Matsuoka and colleagues use the James Webb telescope to check whether six distant galaxies hide active black holes, in a 2026 arXiv paper on astronomy. The galaxies, at redshift near six, came from the SHELLQs survey as candidate obscured quasars: they shine brightly in narrow hydrogen emission but lack the broad lines typical of quasars. Two objects show a broad component in their Balmer lines, direct evidence of active galactic nuclei.

The remaining four show similar profiles in permitted and forbidden lines, arguing against hidden broad-line regions. Combining these with similar objects reported earlier, broad lines correlate strongly with hydrogen luminosity. The inferred active fraction exceeds seventy-seven percent above a luminosity threshold and falls below fifteen percent beneath it, figures the authors report from the combined sample. Dust corrections from the Balmer decrement would imply unrealistically high hydrogen luminosities, suggesting the emitting gas has multiple zones.
arxiv-2606-10360:
Khanh and his team present a pretrained speech model built just for Vietnamese, in a 2026 arXiv paper on speech technology. Vietnamese is under-served by speech models trained mainly on English, so they pretrain on seventeen thousand hours of unlabeled Vietnamese speech. Their model, ViP-VL, uses vector-quantization learning within a ChunkFormer design, adding acoustic stacking and receptive field matching to enable an eightfold subsampling rate that keeps processing fast.

The released model sets new state-of-the-art results across four downstream tasks in their tests: automatic speech recognition, speech emotion recognition, dialect sorting, and speaker checks. Pretraining weights and the code are released to support future Vietnamese speech research. The work shows that language-specific self-supervised pretraining, with design changes tuned for speed, can beat general multilingual models on a mid-resource language. That pattern is useful for many languages still poorly served by speech tech.
arxiv-2606-10460:
Wang and a large team of co-authors introduce LakeQA in this 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark for question answering where the evidence is not handed to the model. Real questions often require searching a vast data lake, a mixed collection of files, before any reasoning can start. LakeQA is built over roughly 9.5 terabytes of Wikipedia and open government data. Each task was annotated by at least one doctoral-level expert and needs multi-step reasoning across several sources.

Seven frontier language models were tested, and the benchmark proved hard. GPT-5.2, the strongest named result, reaches an exact-match score of only 18.37 percent on LakeQA tasks. Performance drops as tasks need longer reasoning chains and more evidence sources. Tracing the failures shows the main bottleneck is document discovery: models often never find and open the documents, and cautious search strategies with high precision but low recall are punished heavily.
arxiv-2606-10860:
Bolliger and Jäger teach language models to respect instruction pecking orders in this 2026 arXiv paper. Deployed models get instructions from platform, developer, user, and retrieved content, yet treat every token as equally authoritative, which is what prompt injection exploits. The authors formalize a five-level hierarchy, with ten pairwise priority relations, and train on conflicts between levels.

Their method, Gravity-Weighted DPO, weights each training example by the structural distance between the clashing levels, with a bilateral schedule that also counts the victim level's rank. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct it beats standard DPO on priority adherence while keeping over-refusal at about half the standard rate. Five levels generalize worse than three: a breadth-versus-depth tradeoff.
arxiv-2606-11260:
Hongyu Jin and thirteen co-authors introduce RAIL in a 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark for the auditory intelligence of large audio-language models. Humans process rich soundscapes through skills like perception, reasoning, and memory. Scoring of audio models is largely task- or domain-centric, measuring final scores while ignoring underlying behaviors, which limits fit with human goals.

RAIL is grounded in the Cattell-Horn-Carroll framework, which structures auditory cognition into five core skills, developed into structured tasks with principled curation and human-aligned protocols. Evaluating 26 models reveals strong performance on knowledge-related tasks but weak perception and memory, reflecting reliance on language-based pretraining. Thinking in audio settings is also limited, with too much of it spent at the cost of efficiency. Six models exceed human performance in general, yet their sound processing lags behind humans. The authors argue progress requires targeting broad cognitive abilities directly.
arxiv-2606-11560:
Khan, Sun, and Huang survey how large language models and graphs can strengthen each other in a 2026 arXiv tutorial paper. Language models have advanced rapidly, but their limits in structured and multi-hop reasoning motivate graph-native, combined AI systems. Graph data underpins work across social, biological, financial, transportation, web, and knowledge domains.

It synthesizes three synergies. First, language models augmented with graph computation for retrieval. Second, two-way integration with knowledge graphs, where models help construct and curate graphs while graphs enforce semantic constraints and factual agreement. Third, AI agents strengthened by graph algorithms for planning, decisions, and multi-step reasoning. In parallel, language models serve graph data management and graph machine learning through natural language interfaces and hybrid pipelines. The authors offer data mining researchers a unified view of these converging directions and their design principles.
arxiv-2606-11660:
Lucia Quirke and eight colleagues release a software library for data attribution in this 2026 arXiv paper. Data attribution asks a causal question: how did each training example shape a model's behaviour? The answers help debug odd outputs, catch mislabelled data and curate better training sets. Doing this at the scale of large language models demands heavy engineering, and many leading methods had no open tools.

Their library, Bergson, supports gradient stores kept on disk, a necessity when gradients for huge datasets cannot fit in memory, and computation spread across multiple machines. It includes quality-of-life tools for researchers. The team also provides the first open-source implementations of three leading attribution methods, named MAGIC, SOURCE and TrackStar, plus a scalable version of unrolled differentiation, which replays training steps to trace influence. They hope shared, scalable tooling lets more researchers study how training data drives model behaviour.
arxiv-2606-11860:
Christoph Koller, Johannes Fürnkranz and Timo Betram teach a model the meaning of chess positions without playing games in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most chess AI learns through reinforcement learning or hand-built knowledge. Their architecture, RePAIR, instead learns representations by repairing damage: large parts of a sequence of board positions are masked, hidden, and a small predictor must restore them in a compressed latent space.

The design blends masked autoencoders, which reconstruct hidden inputs, with joint-embedding predictive methods, which predict in representation space rather than raw detail. After training, meaningful chess concepts cluster naturally in the learned space, and unmasking a hidden position shows the model reasoning about how pieces move. Game trajectories traced through this space let analysts dissect matches intuitively. The authors present chess as a testbed for a broader claim: masking and repairing latent sequences can extract semantic structure from sequential data.
arxiv-2606-11960:
Aparajita Dasgupta and Uttam Kumar Dolai solve a nonlinear heat equation in refined function spaces in this 2026 arXiv paper. The equation is of Hartree type: its nonlinearity couples each point to the whole solution through a convolution. Its diffusion is driven by a fractional anharmonic oscillator, a quantum oscillator with fractional powers and growing potential. The natural habitat is weighted modulation spaces, which measure a function's time-frequency content with a smoothness weight.

The authors first derive Strichartz-type estimates for the heat semigroup. With those, small initial data yield global solutions, existing for all time. A first argument uses the algebra property of the space when smoothness is high enough. Refined trilinear estimates then bypass that algebraic structure entirely, extending global well-posedness to all non-negative smoothness. The paper thus gives a complete small-data theory for this nonlocal heat flow.
arxiv-2606-12160:
Sun stress-tests popular tricks for making language models answer more truthfully, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Decoding-time methods tweak how a frozen model picks its next words, contrasting layers, steering internal signals, or adding small learned adapters. On older base models they reportedly gained ten to thirty points on TruthfulQA, a benchmark of questions that invite false answers. Modern instruction-tuned models, already trained to follow directions, start far higher, between 61 and 76 percent.

Sun applies six strict controls across five models, three benchmarks, and fifteen methods, checking contamination, judge choice, and plain statistical noise. On the full TruthfulQA set of 817 questions, no word-level method improves scores by a statistically significant margin. The best learned adapter lands two points below plain greedy decoding. Chain-of-thought prompting, which asks the model to reason first, proves far more robust, gaining between about six and nineteen points across benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-12460:
Vallarino treats Latin American debt crises like avalanches in a sandpile, and finds the metaphor earns its keep, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Using monthly sovereign bond spreads for eleven countries from 2007 to 2026, he defines stress events as spread jumps past country-specific thresholds. A regional avalanche counts how many countries stress in the same month. Avalanche sizes follow a heavy-tailed power law with exponent near 1.77, the signature of finite-size criticality.

A reshuffling placebo proves synchronization is real: countries stress together far more than independent timing allows. Large avalanches coincide with denser correlation networks among spreads. But after filtering out common factors through partial correlations, the extra structure vanishes. The co-movement is a shared regional factor, not country-to-country contagion propagating conditionally. Network metrics, Vallarino cautions, describe stress regimes as they happen; they are not early-warning signals.
arxiv-2606-12560:
Arbalestrier and co-authors prove that in higher-form gauge theories, every state is a defect, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Defects are extended objects where a theory is modified; states are what the theory can be in. A direct map between them sounds unlikely, since it leans on conformal symmetry. These theories are generally not conformal. The bridge is symmetry of a newer kind: higher-form symmetries, acting on lines and surfaces, not points.

Electric and magnetic higher-form symmetries have a mixed anomaly, a mismatch, which yields endless conserved charges. In p-form Maxwell theory, the charges generate a Kac-Moody algebra acting on states and operators. The algebra sorts the Hilbert space, on a product of spheres, into highest-weight representations. That sorting identifies states with p-dimensional defects. Wilson-'t Hooft defects dressed with operators correspond to squeezed energy eigenstates. The construction survives in nonlinear electrodynamics.
arxiv-2606-13060:
Kouroudis and colleagues build a green solvent screening tool based on uncertainty-aware, transformer-boosted transfer learning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Machine learning could predict solubility descriptors for candidate solvents, but data on them is scarce, which limits model quality exactly where new materials are in play.

The pipeline transfers a model pretrained on QM9 targets to solvent screening with minimal data needs, and adds uncertainty quantification so users can gauge prediction confidence. As a baseline, it predicts Hansen solubility parameters and dielectric constants, for which data banks exist. It reaches high performance on Gutmann donor and acceptor numbers, measures where data is limited. Overall the tool augments data on solubility descriptors by up to 2 orders of magnitude with high-quality predictions. The tool found known green solvent alternatives again and offered new candidates.
arxiv-2606-13160:
Hassler and Vajnovszki present ranking and unranking methods for permutations avoiding a pattern of length 3, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ranking maps a combinatorial object to its position in an ordered list of its class; unranking inverts the map, returning the object at a given position. For permutations avoiding any pattern of length 3, the class is enumerated by the Catalan numbers, making these classes nontrivial testbeds for order-based algorithms.

Such algorithms have practical effects beyond enumeration. Iterating the unranking function builds the whole ordered list, and applying it to a random index yields a uniform random sampler for the class. Combining ranking with unranking computes the successor of any given permutation. For the Catalan classes of 3-pattern-avoiding permutations, ranking and unranking exploit the decomposition structure that the pattern avoidance imposes. That connects the order statistics of the class to its Catalan enumeration.
arxiv-2606-13460:
Xian and colleagues present VISA in this 2026 arXiv paper, a training-time method for auditing the semantics of 3D occupancy models. Such models divide space into voxels labelled by category, giving cars and robots a world state for reasoning and collision checking. Errors on objects and rare classes can corrupt all of that. A fix aligns voxel features with image-caption embeddings, but the authors show this improves text similarity without reliably improving occupancy accuracy. VISA asks a vision-language model to audit each object.

For a crop of an object instance, the auditing model returns hypotheses, confusions, a reliability judgement, attributes, and evidence. That audit propagates along the object's track through time and is grounded to the voxels. Reliability-weighted losses distil the audit into the model's outputs, while inference stays unchanged. The approach targets the rare-class and object errors that endanger driving decisions.
arxiv-2606-14060:
Khan and Andrews detect machine-written text by forcing an attacker to fool several detectors at once. Paraphrasing and style transfer degrade single-signal detectors, and trained classifiers can be confidently wrong on new attacks. Their 2026 arXiv paper extracts multiple views of each document: stylistic, likelihood and rank-order, and structural features. A Gaussian process ensemble aggregates evidence per view. An attack hiding one signal may leave others intact, raising evasion cost.

The design brings two benefits. Gaussian processes yield calibrated probabilities, so confidence means something, and they support principled abstention on out-of-distribution inputs. Tests ran on three benchmarks spanning many generators and attacks: DetectRL, RAID, and PAN 2025. The detector held strong and beat existing approaches on held-out attacks. It also learned from small amounts of target data. Rather than one universal detector, the authors favor detectors tuned for specific settings, with uncertainty marking where they work.
arxiv-2606-14160:
Seo and colleagues teach a legged robot to judge which of its own sensors to trust, moment by moment. Proprioceptive state estimation fuses inertial readings with leg kinematics, but leg data is reliable only when that foot touches ground, and contact-aided estimators break when feet slip. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes GAIT. Inertial and per-leg readings become separate tokens in an attention network. It learns to reweight each by the current contact condition, with no contact estimator and no stationary-contact assumption.

Trained only in simulation, on trotting data, it was tested on a real Unitree Go1 quadruped. The tests covered debris terrain never modeled in simulation and gaits never seen in training. GAIT beat existing learning-based estimators under the unseen gaits and outperformed the conventional contact-aided model-based estimator. Attention weights showed how it shifts trust between inertial and leg tokens under novel contact conditions.
arxiv-2606-14860:
Ojeda-Díaz and co-authors characterize the galaxy NGC 1313 in a 2026 arXiv paper. NGC 1313 is a nearby barred spiral galaxy. Signs suggest it has interacted with a smaller companion. Such encounters can stir gas, spark star birth, and mix chemical elements. The team studied nineteen regions across the galaxy, including its complex southwest part.

Spectra from the GMOS-S instrument gave oxygen abundances and gas densities. The oxygen level is low and mostly flat across the galaxy. A flat gradient points to gas mixing from the past interaction. Star-forming regions are young, with ages from about two point seven to six million years. Wolf-Rayet bumps in two regions confirm very young, massive stars. Hydrogen gas motions in the north are messy, with asymmetric line profiles. The galaxy serves as a lab for how minor encounters reshape small spirals.
arxiv-2606-15560:
Roy studies quadratic one-forms on the moduli of logarithmic Higgs bundles in 2026, working over a compact Riemann surface of genus at least two with marked points. A Higgs bundle pairs a bundle with a Higgs field; in the logarithmic setting the field may have poles at those points, with nilpotent residues. Roy asks what one-form the squared Higgs field defines on the pointed Teichmüller space.

The key step is elementary: for invariant polynomials, nilpotency of the residue cancels the leading pole term. In degree two this places the Higgs field square inside the cotangent space of pointed Teichmüller space, yielding the logarithmic quadratic one-form. Roy relates the form to the variation of energy for tame nilpotent harmonic bundles, under a decay assumption near the punctures. He writes compact formulae for classical groups and standard real forms, tying the construction to nonabelian Hodge theory.
arxiv-2606-15760:
Koulakis and Seibold build a test framework in 2026 for measuring the shape of data manifolds, the curved thin structures deep learning theory assumes data live on. Error bounds lean on numbers like intrinsic dimension, curvature, and reach, yet they could not be measured reliably: analytic manifolds are too simple, and real datasets allow only coarse guesses.

The framework extends two classic datasets, dSprites and COIL-20, with extra transformation dimensions and dense, axis-aligned sampling, so the true shape is known. Paired finite-difference tools then recover curvature, reach, and volume almost exactly in regimes where general estimators fail. Two studies show the testbed at work: checking how published generalisation bounds actually scale, and tracking how an autoencoder's layer shapes change during training. As a calibration sandbox for theory, the framework gives manifold-based learning something it lacked: measurements it can trust.
arxiv-2606-15860:
Mizuno reports new lower bounds for the degree/diameter problem in 2026, obtained through a six-day interaction with ChatGPT's standard web interface. The problem asks for the largest graph with given maximum degree and diameter; exact values are unknown for most parameter pairs. No agent framework, search loop, or proof assistant was set up: the construction emerged from dialogue, steered by general constraints, not hints about its components.

The resulting graphs give at least 34,992 vertices for degree 12 and diameter 5, up from 29,621. For degree 16 and diameter 5 they give at least 147,456, up from 132,496. More vertices at fixed degree and diameter means cheaper, shorter networks, which is what designers care about. Mizuno also analyses the transcript, marking the meta-level interventions and where the construction's abstraction first appeared. The account doubles as a case study in conversational steering of a language model on a hard search.
arxiv-2606-15960:
Demirer and colleagues build a theory of AI automation in 2026, modelling production as a sequence of steps, each done manually, augmented with AI, or fully automated. Automated steps bunch into contiguous chains, verified by a human only at the end. Firms bundle steps into tasks and jobs, trading specialisation gains against coordination costs. How should bundling change as AI improves?

Chaining breaks the standard logic: step-level comparative advantage can fail to decide who does what, because a step's neighbours matter. Productivity gains are non-linear, arriving in jumps when a quality threshold triggers a discrete reorganisation of jobs, the J-curve pattern of technology adoption. The model still aggregates to a standard CES form at the macro level. Its three key predictions hold empirically: AI steps co-occur in chains, dispersed AI exposure lowers job-level AI use, and adjacency raises a step's chance of automation.
arxiv-2606-16360:
Lin and co-authors give language models a typed toolbox for silent reasoning in 2026, deciding at each step whether to think in words or in vectors. Chain-of-thought prompting externalizes reasoning as text, which adds redundancy and inference cost. Latent reasoning computes in continuous representations instead, but earlier methods fixed in advance when it runs and how much it gets. Their framework, Tyler, makes those choices online during decoding.

A learned policy picks, at each decoding step, between emitting a text token and invoking a latent computation module. Three typed operators cover global planning, local state updates, and reusable procedural abstraction. A budget-aware rule decides how much latent compute each invocation receives. Across three backbone models, Tyler improves average performance by up to 14.49 points over chain-of-thought and up to 4.30 points over the strongest rival baseline, per the report. It also forgets least in sequential adaptation tests.
arxiv-2606-16460:
Wu and co-authors cluster gene expression samples in 2026 with a model that respects how genes work in modules, aiming to find disease subtypes hidden in the data. High-throughput expression data are high-dimensional, strongly correlated between genes, and uneven across patients, a hard mix for clustering. Their module-based mixture factor model layers finite mixture modeling over low-rank latent factors defined at the level of gene modules. Mean and covariance structure both carry the module information, so clusters respect gene groupings.

Expression spread splits into global gene-specific effects, cluster-level module shifts, latent links inside modules, and gene-level noise. An EM-type algorithm fits the model with stable, scalable fitting. Applied to a large clinical transcriptomic dataset covering two autoimmune diseases, the framework identifies disease-linked molecular subtypes. Code and data are public. Such subtypes could one day guide treatment choice.
arxiv-2606-17260:
Wang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on faster algorithms for smooth convex optimisation, the workhorse problem of minimising a well-behaved curved function. Their route runs through Hamiltonian dynamics, the physics of systems that trade height and motion energy while conserving the total. Earlier dynamics-based methods gave acceleration only for quadratic objectives, or only on average over random runs, leaving firm guarantees for general smooth problems open until now.

The trick is to use contraction of averaged flow paths rather than demanding contraction at the path endpoints. That shift lets the authors prove deterministic accelerated rates for an idealised continuous-time algorithm first. Practical discrete-time versions follow, with optimal first-order complexity in the number of gradient steps needed. The work presents this dynamics as a sound primitive for building accelerated optimisers with firm guarantees.
arxiv-2606-17360:
Mann and colleagues present a 2026 workshop paper on how computing's guiding words can quietly shrink what practitioners imagine is possible. Concepts such as innovation, efficiency, resilience, and professionalism start as reflective ideals, then drift into tools that limit behaviour and deflect responsibility. The authors call that drift weaponisation, and they study it through shared self-study across education, justice, public administration, research management, and computing itself, comparing notes across those fields.

Recurring mechanisms include simplification, blaming single persons, binary framing, metric substitution, hero scripts, and organised ignorance. Against them, the paper proposes reframing: small, practice-ready shifts of language and attention that restore nuance and surface hidden assumptions. Each reframing pairs with a do-now prompt usable without formal authority over the workplace. The toolkit aims at day-to-day practice that makes more room for care, sufficiency, and justice.
arxiv-2606-17560:
Chen presents a 2026 arXiv paper building intertwining operators on the spectral side of the Langlands programme, mirroring a classic construction from the theory of group representations. Classically, such operators move between representations of a p-adic group induced from two parabolic subgroups sharing one Levi subgroup. Normalising them so that compositions behave is a famous subtlety, measured by L-functions. Chen defines spectral analogues acting between Eisenstein series attached to the two subgroups, aiming for the same clean formal properties.

A normalised spectral operator with the key transitivity property is constructed, plus an unnormalised partner defined through an analogue of the Bruhat-Mackey filtration. The two differ by a ratio of L-functions, as the classical picture predicts up to units. Under any proposed categorical form of the local Langlands correspondence, the spectral operators match the classical ones. The analogy thereby becomes a proved bridge between the two sides.
arxiv-2606-17660:
Luo and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on TuneAhead, a lightweight system for predicting how a fine-tuning run will turn out before the full training bill arrives. Fine-tuning outcomes swing with data quality and settings, and bad runs can leave a model worse than it started. TuneAhead describes each candidate run by static facts about the data set plus dynamic features from a short standard probe run. It then maps that profile to a predicted score for the finished model.

Attribution analysis shows which features drive each prediction, giving users a diagnosis rather than a bare number. Across more than thirteen hundred runs, the system beat strong baselines including early-stop extrapolation and proxy models. Nearly all held-out predictions landed within a few points of the true score. Such screening supports go or no-go calls that skip doomed runs while keeping most of the promising ones.
arxiv-2606-17760:
The ATLAS collaboration reports a 2026 measurement of rare collision events that pair one isolated photon with two jets of particles. Data came from proton and lead-nucleus collisions recorded by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, both at the same collision energy. Photons with high transverse momentum, balanced by at least two jets, let physicists probe how fast partons lose energy in hot nuclear matter.

Three quantities are measured: one tracks the total energy loss of the multi-parton system, one compares the loss between the two jets, and one watches their opening angle. A new mixing technique removes background from unrelated jet pairs. Comparing lead collisions with proton ones shows how the dense medium created in heavy-ion crashes drains and reshapes the jets, a core clue about quark-gluon plasma.
arxiv-2606-17860:
Knight and colleagues bring logic to a classic puzzle of coordination over bad phone lines, in a 2026 paper. In the coordinated attack problem, two generals must strike together, but messengers may be lost, and the task is provably impossible to guarantee. A randomized version, where generals flip coins, can succeed, yet it had never been studied with probabilistic epistemic logic, the logic of who knows what.

The authors build a general framework for randomized algorithms that run a bounded number of rounds on changing communication graphs. Processes may lose messages to an adversary, and the logic tracks nested knowledge under uncertainty. Applied to coordinated attack, the frame closed gaps between known upper and lower bounds. It also fits consensus and approximate agreement, giving distributed computing a sharper language for randomized protocols.
arxiv-2606-17960:
Sohail and Wei compute the typical entanglement of states drawn from a special random ensemble, in a 2026 quantum information paper. Random quantum states underpin much of modern quantum science, and one natural way to generate them uses the Bogoliubov-Kubo-Mori metric, a geometry built from entropy itself. The team asks how much entanglement such states carry on average.

They derive an exact, explicit formula for the average entanglement entropy over this ensemble. Strikingly, the derivation uses only facts about the ensemble's normalization constant, sidestepping the correlation kernel that other ensemble calculations depend on. That shortcut matters beyond the single number. The same route could open the way to higher-order statistics of the ensemble, such as spread and skew. Those remain out of reach for some rival ensembles.
arxiv-2606-18360:
Correia, Varizi, and Carvalho develop a unified way to describe how isolated quantum systems settle toward equilibrium, in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. A closed quantum system never truly stops evolving, yet the part an observer can access often looks steady over time. Existing theory treated that effect for subsystems and for restricted readings.

Their framework describes whatever an observer can access as the output of a quantum channel acting on the full microscopic state, which they call a generalized subsystem. They prove bounds showing such descriptions equilibrate whenever the accessible part is small compared with the effective size of what is thrown away. Typical starting states in large spaces meet that condition. The familiar subsystem and reading results fall out as special cases. A finite-resolution energy channel shows the idea, showing how blurred energy readings leave some coherence visible while still strengthening equilibration.
arxiv-2606-18460:
Seeba and colleagues present the first fully machine-learned approach to reconstructing hadronically decaying tau leptons for a future collider, in a 2026 particle physics paper. The planned TeraZ program will produce enormous numbers of Z bosons decaying to tau pairs, but taus decay instantly, with undetected neutrinos, so their properties must be inferred from visible remains.

The team formulates reconstruction as several linked tasks: identifying the tau, classifying its decay mode, recovering its charge, and regressing its full momentum. They compare dedicated models for each task with one unified multi-task model on simulated collisions. Both reached mis-identification rates at the per-mille level at high efficiency, strong decay-mode scores for the main channels, and charge errors far below a conventional estimator. Dedicated models reconstructed kinematics best, while the unified model classified slightly better using only about a quarter of the parameters.
arxiv-2606-18560:
Jang and colleagues tackle a familiar failure of few-shot fine-tuning for audio-language models in a 2026 machine learning paper. Adapting to labeled examples of known classes quietly wrecks performance on classes never seen in training. They trace the problem to drift in the text embedding space, where tuning distorts the relationships between classes and pulls adapted embeddings away from their pretrained anchors.

Their method, Subspace Tuning, constrains that drift in two ways: a structured subspace parameterization limits how the embedding geometry can deform, and residual anchoring stabilizes adaptation around the original zero-shot representations. A gating step at inference further suppresses negative transfer for weakly aligned unseen classes. Across eleven audio benchmarks the method delivered strong few-shot generalization while staying efficient. The authors frame controlled, geometry-aware adaptation as the principle behind the gains.
arxiv-2606-18860:
Jebril and the team measure uncertainty in medical image segmentation, by probing the model for weak spots, in a 2026 medical AI paper. Clinicians need pixel-level doubt to monitor lesions over time, and tell true growth from artifacts. But standard networks are miscalibrated and overconfident. They hide their flaws exactly at subtle pathological boundaries, where errors matter most.

Their post-hoc scheme QUAM-SM runs a targeted adversarial search for the pixels whose calls are fragile. Those are the ones small perturbations can flip. The method treats those as the uncertain regions. It also splits the two sources: epistemic uncertainty, from limited knowledge, and aleatoric uncertainty, from built-in ambiguity and annotator disagreement. On two public datasets with multiple expert annotations, it beat standard and recent methods in reliability and boundary response. Its aleatoric part tracked inter-rater spread more strongly than total doubt did, supporting safer longitudinal monitoring.
arxiv-2606-19560:
Alireza Jafari and four colleagues compare forecasting models on flu data in 2026 to learn what time series foundation models do well. Seasonal influenza sickens millions in the United States each year, so short-term forecasts guide vaccine timing and hospital staffing. The team test regional forecasts of flu-like illness and hospital stays, one to four weeks ahead.

Classical neural networks, numerical transformers, pretrained foundation models, and language-model forecasters all face the same tasks. Both time-based and place-based generalisation settings check whether skill travels. A mixture-of-experts model that fuses several pretrained forecasters performs best overall. Pretraining helps most at longer horizons, above all when the pretraining domain matches flu dynamics. Language-model methods lag numerical forecasters in this setting. Hospital data help in selected cases, both as extra input and as pretraining material. The results give health agencies concrete guidance on model choice.
arxiv-2606-19760:
Md Rokibul Hasan and Pratim Guha Niyogi model the full spread of daily physical activity in 2026. Step counts and averages hide how activity intensity is distributed across a day. The pair instead build hazard curves from wrist accelerometer data, borrowing tools from survival analysis.

Minute-level movement data cover 4,297 adults with seven full wear days from the 2011 to 2012 national health survey. Each person yields an activity-intensity hazard curve on a shared intensity grid. Functional principal component analysis then extracts the main modes of variation across people. Group mean curves barely differ at low intensity but split widely at high intensity. Women, older adults, and participants with obesity or hypertension show more hazard at high levels. The first component explains about sixty to seventy percent of all variation. Hazard-based curves expose group gaps that means alone would miss.
arxiv-2606-19860:
Mohammad Elsayed and Sara Najem detect shocks in Norwegian board networks with heat kernel curvature in 2026. Directors and their company seats form a network tracked monthly over nine years. Simplicial complexes model the web, with directors as nodes and companies as faces.

Three measures face off: Euler characteristic, torsion, and higher-order clustering. Their own curvature comes from coefficients of the heat kernel expansion in time. Euler characteristic folds curvature into one number, losing local detail. Torsion can swing hard without marking real shocks, and tree counts mislead as well. Curvature instead registers the board changes forced by new representation law. Its inflection points align with outside forcing, and its minima mark shock arrivals. Geometry thus sees legal shocks that cruder topology misses.
arxiv-2606-20060:
Nubius Brandner, Frank Hellmann, Hans Würfel, Jürgen Kurths, Anton Plietzsch, and Anna Büttner model cascading failures in power grids with full dynamics in 2026. Blackouts grow through chains of component failures, yet most physics studies treat line overloads in a static snapshot. The new model couples node and line failures to an oscillator description of grid synchronization, letting failures and dynamics drive each other for the first time.

Two counterintuitive fragilities emerge. High inertia, usually protective against frequency swings, can enlarge cascades unless other settings adjust with it. Making individual nodes more robust can also paradoxically worsen cascades, a new form of Braess's paradox, where local improvement harms the whole. Grid planners designing renewable-heavy networks must weigh these collective effects.
arxiv-2606-20560:
Joshua Engels and a large team of coauthors ask how inspectable the reasoning of DiffusionGemma really is. Their 2026 paper notes that this model performs a larger fraction of its computation in a continuous latent space than ordinary language models. Latent computation might make its reasoning harder to inspect, a problem for debugging and for catching misuse.

The authors split openness into components, starting with variable transparency: whether intermediate snapshots of the model's computation can be understood. The study tests whether diffusion-style generation hides the model's intermediate steps from standard inspection tools. If latent reasoning resists inspection, transparency techniques must be rebuilt for this model class. The paper gives the field a framework for asking the question precisely.
arxiv-2606-20660:
Fabian Schwab and seven colleagues study learning control for a soft robotic swimmer in 2026. The robot is a platform for embodied intelligence, or intelligence shaped by a body. The robot swims by waving its body and tail, but its flexible body is hard to control when water flow changes. Standard proportional-integral-derivative feedback, a classic control method, holds rhythm in still water yet develops delay and uneven trials as flow grows.

The team adds a linear repetitive learning estimation scheme, which generalizes integral action for repeating reference signals and avoids long-term instability seen in older repetitive controls. Closed-loop tests in a flow tank cover five speeds from still water to 32.6 centimeters per second. Results point to recovered accuracy and repeatability under dynamic flow. Better control matters for studying animal locomotion and robots in moving water.
arxiv-2606-20760:
Supriya Khadka and Sanchari Das study privacy-preserving compliance on public blockchains in 2026, where transparency clashes with data minimization rules. Public ledgers prove integrity by showing data openly. Compliance checks often need the opposite: prove a fact without revealing it. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a path, but smart contract settings add risks. Off-chain proof creation and on-chain submission are decoupled, opening front-running and proof reuse attacks.

Khadka and Das formalize Selective Disclosure Authorization Schemes, a cryptographic tool for granular, revocable checks. Their security model adds attribute unlinkability and context-aware sender binding. A valid proof stays bound to its intended authorization context. They also build ZK-Compliance, an Ethereum system with a grant, verify, and revoke lifecycle. User control over disclosure could let regulated services use public ledgers without exposing the underlying witness data to every observer.
arxiv-2606-20960:
Mingyang Liu, Gabriele Farina, and Asuman Ozdaglar study game equilibria with internal transfers in 2026, where players pay each other to improve incentives before play. Nash equilibrium comes from selfish choices. Its social welfare can be far from optimal. Computing it can also be intractable. Their augmented games add budget-balanced peer transfers that are paid only if the recipient follows a prescribed strategy.

Their Self-Enforcing Transfer Equilibrium sustains strong outcomes. For polymatrix games, every stationary point of social welfare can be sustained, including the social optimum. A polynomial-time algorithm and a decentralized learning dynamic compute such equilibria. A mediated variant makes offers binding through a mediator. Transfers inside a game could align selfish agents without an external enforcer, a pattern of interest for markets, protocols, and multi-agent AI systems that must cooperate without central control.
arxiv-2606-21160:
Arun Seshadri and three colleagues investigate star formation in 2026 at the edge of a molecular superbubble, in the cloud complex G12.79+0.43. Infrared and radio-bright regions line an irregular rim. A central zone shows diffuse emission at longer wavelengths. Carbon monoxide line data reveal three distinct velocity components along the line of sight. Low-frequency radio data fill the enclosed central region.

Seventy compact radio sources and six ionized hydrogen regions are identified across the complex. They are likely powered by early B-type young stars. Infrared data yield dozens of young stellar object candidates, including many deeply embedded Class I sources. On larger scales, gas motion places the complex on the rim of a superbubble about fifty parsecs wide. The picture supports triggered star formation, where an expanding bubble compresses gas at its edge and seeds a new generation of stars.
arxiv-2606-21260:
Eyal Vayness and Maxime Sangnier study subsampling for kernel-based learning in 2026, asking which training points to keep when data are too plentiful to use whole. Their setting is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, a space of functions defined by a similarity kernel. The estimator reweights the kept points in Horvitz-Thompson fashion to correct for the sampling. Training on a chosen subset cuts compute time, energy use, and cost.

By analyzing the estimator's long-run behavior, they identify a subsampling scheme that is optimal for the trace of the covariance operator, a summary of total variance. The scheme can be estimated from the data itself and plugged in directly. Tests on synthetic and real datasets show the approach is practical and beneficial, keeping accuracy while shrinking the training set.
arxiv-2606-21460:
Jumana Alsubhi and seven colleagues benchmark twelve small language models on Arabic in 2026, a language where compact models are rarely tested carefully. Their benchmark holds 240 Arabic test items across eight domains and ten language skills, mixing comprehension and generation tasks. Every model faced the same Arabic-only prompt in a zero-shot setting, and three different judge models scored the answers, with scores pooled across judges.

Gemma 3 at twelve billion parameters topped the table at 4.548 out of five, followed by Aya and a C4AI Command Arabic model. Size alone did not explain the ranking; models with stronger Arabic alignment and steadier instruction following did better. Weak models leaked prompts, drifted into other languages, or stopped early. The benchmark gives builders a structured reference for compact Arabic systems.
arxiv-2606-22560:
Fei Wang and Zebai Tian design a trustworthy gateway for language model services in this 2026 preprint. Third-party gateways sit between applications and model providers, choosing routes, handling fallbacks, and issuing billing records. Because the operator authors those records, clients cannot tell honest mediation from route substitution, hidden fallback, or forged provenance.

Their architecture separates the operator's control plane from an attested execution plane. Inside it, a measured Attested Gateway Runtime alone may decrypt requests and apply path rules, build upstream calls, and sign evidence. Clients check the signed release metadata and a new attestation, then encrypt requests only to keys tied to that runtime. The runtime then enforces routing and fallback constraints, returns encrypted streams, and signs evidence tying policy, route, and completion data together. A Rust prototype on AWS Nitro Enclaves showed modest overhead and fail-closed detection of tampering outside the runtime.
arxiv-2606-23060:
Jan Jasiński and colleagues compare three ways of catching invented speech transcripts in a 2026 paper. Speech recognition systems sometimes hallucinate, producing fluent text with no basis in the audio. The team studies the Whisper large v3 model on real speech with human-labeled errors. Their first approach scores the output text with standard text metrics. The second asks a large language model to judge the transcript. The third probes Whisper's own internal decoder states for warning signs.

Jasiński and colleagues find that text classifiers catch many hallucinations but weaken when no reference transcript exists. The language model judge improves precision with domain-tuned prompts, yet still trails the lightweight text methods. Probing internal states works best of all without any reference, showing hallucination traits spread across middle decoding layers. A final combined classifier merging text and internal signals achieves the strongest overall detection.
arxiv-2606-23560:
Baran and Bergmann extend a classic optimization method so it can handle outliers and constraints on curved spaces, in a 2026 paper on numerical optimization. The Levenberg Marquardt method solves least squares problems, where a model is fitted by minimizing squared errors. Its Riemannian version works on manifolds, curved spaces such as spheres or rotation spaces, instead of flat coordinates. Squared errors, though, punish outliers heavily, so one bad data point can wreck a fit.

The robust variant swaps in outlier tolerant costs and is stated block by block. The authors show how known convergence results carry over. They also discuss several ways to phrase the subproblem solved at each step. An open source implementation in Manopt.jl, a Julia toolbox for manifold optimization, is tested on geodesic regression, Procrustes analysis, and bundle adjustment. Comparisons with other nonsmooth solvers show its strengths.
arxiv-2606-23660:
Pidduck and Modigliani propose measuring how much friction users face when working with open datasets, in a 2026 paper on research data services. The FAIR principles say data should be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, and high FAIR scores are often treated as proof of usability. Yet a dataset can pass every stewardship check and still cost a new user hours before a first usable file arrives.

The Dataset Friction Framework scores friction across six dimensions. It separates engineered friction, deliberate provider choices that keep a service viable, from accidental friction, defects that need fixing. Validation uses more than eighteen thousand support tickets from a European weather forecasting centre serving two hundred eighty thousand users. Case studies show the two measures disagreeing both ways: a highly FAIR compliant dataset can carry heavy friction, and a low FAIR score can reflect anti scraping policy.
arxiv-2606-23760:
Farrell and fellow organisers report on a 2024 Lorentz Center workshop that brought two research communities together around building autonomous systems that can be trusted, in a 2026 workshop report. Autonomous systems are spreading into daily life, and engineering them reliably is an increasingly urgent problem. Two workshop series had led the discussion separately: one rooted in formal methods, the other in cognitive robotics and multi agent systems.

The report captures and expands the joint discussions across three themes. They cover techniques for verification and validation, the checking of systems against their requirements. They cover engineering real world autonomous systems, and software architectures for safe autonomy. One main outcome is a shared research agenda across the previously separate communities, recording where the fields agree and which challenges they plan to tackle together.
arxiv-2606-23860:
Guey, Bougault, Zhang, de Moura, and Gomes map China's proposed World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization into the crowded field of global AI governance, in a 2026 paper on international institutions. AI governance has shifted from ethics principles to standing bodies, and WAICO, announced by China in 2025, is the most consequential new proposal and the least studied. The authors code fifteen international AI instruments and institutions on membership, organization, and priorities.

WAICO's design combines three features no existing multilateral body combines. Membership would be open to any sovereign state, with no values test for entry. Its agenda centers on development and the global capability divide. Bodies led by the West restrict membership to states sharing their values, while United Nations bodies are open but rights anchored. The authors read WAICO as a proposed second pole of AI governance.
arxiv-2606-23960:
Xu and colleagues build artificial magnetic fields for light spanning nearly a full octave of frequencies and ten thousand modes at once, in a 2026 paper on photonics. Photons ignore real magnetic fields, so researchers fake them: artificial gauge fields make light behave as if charged, unlocking quantum Hall physics for optics. Every earlier realization worked in a narrow band. The team develops a general theory of broadband, multimodal, dispersion corrected gauge fields and implements it in integrated photonics.

Their devices realize over one hundred distinct gauge fields hosting more than ten thousand modes, the first frequency comb version of an integer quantum Hall model built for photons. Kerr nonlinearity grants single shot control of the field pattern. The behavior stays robust against wafer scale fabrication variations, pointing to manufacturable photonic applications.
arxiv-2606-24060:
Salgado Neto and co-authors test how artificial intelligence changes the earliest step of building software: gathering requirements from the people who will use it. Stakeholders must explain needs, argue over priorities, and turn discussion into documents developers can follow. Their 2026 mixed-method experiment compares four routes, from plain group discussion to a language model writing requirements directly from transcripts.

One route pairs group work with the Strateegia platform and its GPT-powered writing applet, which drafts documents from the discussion. Another hands transcripts to a language model with no live collaboration at all. Judges scored the outputs against the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 quality standard, and participants rated each process. Combining stakeholder discussion with AI drafting produced the highest-rated documents and felt clearer and easier to run. Salgado's team concludes that generative tools work best reshaping human discussion, not replacing it.
arxiv-2606-24160:
Elias Bareinboim, with Junzhe Zhang and Sanghack Lee, introduces causal reinforcement learning. The new field joins two areas that grew up almost entirely apart. Causal inference combines data with knowledge about a setting. It answers counterfactual questions, meaning questions about what would have happened under other choices. Reinforcement learning instead trains an agent by trial and error. The agent learns actions that raise a reward when it is deployed.

Bareinboim and colleagues model any such setting as a structural causal model. That is a graph of separate mechanisms, each with its own stable rules. Under this one view, online learning, off policy learning, and causal calculus learning fall into a single framework. The authors then show these standard modes still miss some learnable relations. They add new tasks, among them generalised policy learning and deciding where to intervene. Imitation and counterfactual learning also get a causal treatment.
arxiv-2606-24360:
Ghildiyal, Dasgupta, and Biswas measure whether quantum oscillators in sync are collectively locked, or merely pairwise aligned. Quantum sync, phase-locked oscillation in driven, dissipative quantum systems, is usually quantified for pairs. Their 2026 measure works in phase space. It rests on the first angular moments of phase distributions, taken from Husimi-Q quasiprobability functions, and extends from two qubits to three.

A new class of sync residuals subtracts what pairwise contributions predict from the collective behaviour. The residuals are modelled on subadditivity hierarchies from information theory. In a driven, lossy quantum Rabi network, the two-qubit residual stays non-negative. Collective locking never exceeds the sum of individual contributions. The three-qubit steady state breaks that pattern, with a negative tripartite gap. That signals genuinely collective phase sync, hidden from pairwise breakdown. Entropy-based residuals stay non-negative throughout. Phase-sensitive and entropic measures thus probe different things.
arxiv-2606-24460:
Somide measures what speaking an African language costs in the age of per token billing. Commercial language models charge by the token. Tokenizers chop the same meaning into far more pieces in some languages than others. Speakers thus pay a structural penalty before any model runs. With DataLens Africa Research, Somide quantifies it for twenty African languages across five families and three scripts, using parallel corpora so language, not content, explains the difference.

Every African language measured carries a tokenisation premium over English, across eleven frontier and open tokenizers. The median premium sits near double on a leading commercial tokenizer. Far higher extremes appear for the N'Ko script. Ethiopic and N'Ko scripts suffer most, reaching seven to ninefold token counts. The penalty is nearly identical across corpora: a tokenizer property, not a data artefact. In deployment terms, the tax means severalfold inference costs and shrunken context.
arxiv-2606-24660:
Callum Marsh, Radek Erban, and Andreas Münch tackle an inverse problem for phase field models. Such models describe phase separation, as when alloys or polymer mixes split into regions. Their patterns depend on the bulk free energy and on an interface thickness. Both quantities are rarely known in advance. Workers must instead infer them from limited observations. The authors build a neural network method, ESPINN, for this task.

ESPINN recovers the bulk chemical potential and the unknown gradient coefficients at the same time. It works only from pairs of snapshots taken over time. Tests use the one dimensional Cahn Hilliard equation. With clean data the reconstruction is accurate and stable across runs. Much of the model can be recovered from a single snapshot pair. When noise is added, accuracy falls off gently rather than collapsing. More snapshots then cut the spread across runs and restore robustness.
arxiv-2606-24760:
Tiago Coimbra and four colleagues present a physics based method for repairing five dimensional seismic data. Prestack seismic surveys sample the earth unevenly, pick up noise, and leave coverage gaps. Those flaws weaken later imaging and inversion. Their framework rebuilds the data by stacking along traveltime surfaces derived from wave physics. A multi parameter operator based on common reflection point kinematics defines the stacking paths. All parameters are estimated straight from the data itself.

The operator is called offset continuation trajectory stacking. Its trajectories honour wavefront propagation and reflection geometry. A global search strategy finds the parameters. Missing traces are rebuilt, with no fake events added. Tests on synthetic and field datasets show better signal to noise ratio and clearer structure. Lost signal strength is recovered too. The method appeared in the Journal of Applied Geophysics.
arxiv-2606-25160:
Pruning shrinks vision language models so they can run in real time on robots, where a wearer or partner needs fast, trustworthy answers about what the camera sees. Qitong Wang and four colleagues judge pruning by a stricter standard than accuracy alone: doubly correct predictions, where the answer is right and the visual evidence behind it is right too.

Their experiments deliver a surprise. Existing pruning methods often keep the evidence localisation intact while quietly damaging the prediction itself, so a model can look at the right place and still answer wrong. The team answers with a rationale informed pruning strategy that keeps evidence and decisions aligned. On egocentric video benchmarks, their method posts the highest prediction accuracy and beats existing approaches at doubly correct prediction.
arxiv-2606-25460:
Forced alignment pins each sound in a recording to the moment it was spoken, given the transcript, and old statistical tools still set the standard. Rotem Rousso, Eyal Cohen, and Joseph Keshet replace them in 2026 with a fully trainable neural aligner. One encoder branch checks which phoneme is present while a second watches for boundaries between sounds. A decoder built on soft dynamic programming then lays out the alignment, and every part learns together end to end under a new contrastive loss.

That loss pushes steady sound regions and transition zones apart, sharpening the decisions the decoder must make. On hand labelled English benchmarks the system beat the current state of the art for phoneme alignment. It also generalised well to whole words and, notably, to languages it had never been trained on, hinting the learned cues are broadly acoustic rather than language specific.
arxiv-2606-25660:
Some symmetries cannot be undone: apply them and no reverse operation exists, a modern twist reshaping how physicists classify matter. Eric Vernier, Yuan Miao, and Masahito Yamazaki realise such a non invertible symmetry directly on a lattice in 2026, in the XXZ spin chain tuned to special root of unity points.
