Their route runs through transfer matrices, the workhorses of integrability, except here the matrices refuse to commute, forming a non Abelian algebra governed by a lopsided Yang Baxter relation.

From that algebra they build the Onsager algebra explicitly, plus its duality automorphism as a matrix product operator borrowed from a related model. The operator obeys the Tambara Yamagami fusion rules, the signature of the defect lines in a free boson field theory. Non Abelian integrability, the authors conclude, is a natural home for categorical dualities on the lattice.
arxiv-2606-25760:
A computer use agent turns a model's guess into a real click. Knowing when the guess is shaky is a safety feature. Divake Kumar and colleagues present Argus in 2026, a benchmark for uncertainty methods in single step screen grounding. The open matrix crosses twenty seven methods from seven families with four vision language agents and four datasets. A second matrix covers closed frontier models from three vendors, where only eight methods work without internals. Scores, splits, and scripts are released for reuse.

Rankings travelled well across datasets for one fixed model, with correlations averaging near zero point seven. They collapsed across model classes and interfaces, averaging near zero for closed vendors. Hidden state and density methods formed the most stable family. Conformal click regions shrank by forty to sixty percent when scores were calibrated, but coverage broke under mismatch. The lesson: rerank uncertainty methods on your own regime.
arxiv-2606-25860:
Two yardsticks measure a quantum system's worth: how nonclassical its correlations are, and how precisely it can sense a parameter. M Ibrahim follows both in 2026 through a multipartite system of two level atoms bathed in a coherent field. Three knobs shape the dynamics: parametric amplification, a Kerr type nonlinearity that twists phases by intensity, and intrinsic decoherence, the system's built in tendency to leak quantumness away. Global quantum discord and quantum Fisher information are tracked as the knobs turn and the atom count grows.

Without decoherence, both quantities oscillate rapidly, with collapses and revivals. Strong Kerr effect and strong amplification together boost the discord. Fisher information peaks instead at a balance between the two. More atoms generally strengthen discord but do not always help sensing. Switch decoherence on and the oscillations damp toward a steady state, the familiar tax that real devices pay.
arxiv-2606-25960:
Zihan Qin and Hongrui Zhang propose measuring the intelligence of an AI agent system in bits. Their starting point is the old idea that compression reflects intelligence. Under a fixed task set, interface, and compute budget, a stronger system should rebuild a target object from fewer bits. Tools, retrieval, verifiers, and search all count as part of the system being measured.

Arithmetic coding, seed coding, and a fallback channel turn the idea into a working meter. Five test settings probe it: protein sequences, chess moves, reversed text, story compression, and retrieval-augmented question answering. In every setting, agent components shrink the codelength needed. Qin and Zhang argue the measure shows how parts, observers, and budgets change the leftover uncertainty, offering guidance for judging real agent systems beyond pass-or-fail scores.
arxiv-2606-26360:
Yuxin Lu, Zhexuan Li, and R. Harald Baayen argue that Mandarin's neutral tone is a true lexical tone, not a weakened leftover. They test how the tone sounds and means in spontaneous speech corpora from Beijing and Taiwan, comparing it with the four full tones.

The neutral tone turns out to have its own pitch target, and two-syllable words carrying it show pitch shapes that depend on the first syllable, much like words with full tones. Each word also carries a signature pitch shape, partly predictable from word-meaning embeddings. Both regional varieties share the pattern, though meaning differences explain part of their divergence.
arxiv-2606-26460:
Ben Prystawski and six colleagues present auto-psych, a system that automates theory building in cognitive psychology. Language model agents can already propose hypotheses and analyse data. Collecting human data was the bottleneck. Psychology is well placed for automation, since its theories are often written as code. Crowdsourcing platforms also allow experiments to run online at scale.

Auto-psych runs two nested loops. The inner loop proposes probabilistic cognitive models, fits them, and critiques them. Experiments are designed by the outer loop, launched online, and analysed there. The test case is a classic puzzle: which coin-flip sequences people judge as more random. The system recovered known true theories from synthetic data reliably. The nested structure proved essential to that success. In three rounds of human experiments, it found theories fitting the data better than published ones.
arxiv-2606-26760:
Jen-Yu Chang and eight colleagues present HI-NQS, an algorithm for solving the electronic Schrödinger equation in hard cases. That equation determines a molecule's energy and behaviour. Strongly correlated systems defeat exact methods because the space of electron configurations grows exponentially. Selected configuration interaction keeps only the important configurations, but finding them is the crux.

Their method embeds a neural quantum state inside the selection loop. A transformer network with two channels, one per electron spin, samples promising configurations. After each exact diagonalisation of the sampled subspace, the network then absorbs the resulting eigenvector by distillation. Sampling and solving thus teach each other in a closed feedback loop. The spin-aware design builds fermionic structure into the network itself. Benchmarks across varied systems test the approach.
arxiv-2606-26960:
Gianmaria Frigo and six colleagues ask how well language models can run computer networks, and how to grade them fairly. Network administrators juggle configuration, troubleshooting, and security as systems grow more complex. Static answer keys and hand grading cannot evaluate AI help at this scale. Their framework, NetLLMeval, uses live network emulation to generate ground truth automatically.

A full-factorial study followed: twenty-four thousand runs. Ten foundation models met four solver designs, ten task types, and six network layouts of rising complexity. Solver architecture mattered at least as much as model choice, the results suggest. Agentic pipelines and monolithic prompting behaved very differently as networks grew. The framework lets future systems be compared on live behaviour rather than canned answers.
arxiv-2606-27260:
Li states a conjecture about a data-fusion problem abstracted from the Split Covariance Intersection Filter. That filter merges uncertain estimates in engineering systems, from cooperative vehicles to single intelligent machines. One internal step, called w-optimisation, controls both accuracy and speed of the filter. Ordinary convexity of that problem is already proven, as is a stronger fourth-order convexity. In the conjecture paper of 2026, Li notes the higher property enables a guaranteed fast implementation in practice.

Observations and analysis now suggest far more: convexity at every even order, second, fourth, sixth, and beyond. Li presents that claim in detail as a conjecture, not a proven theorem. Practical engineering gains little either way, since fourth order already suffices. The value lies in the mathematics the claim might provoke. Systematic proof techniques could follow. The conjecture thus serves as an open challenge problem.
arxiv-2606-27360:
Joseph shows that every violation of the Schwinger-Dyson identities in an out-of-equilibrium system traces back to one field. Those identities encode exact relations that equilibrium dynamics must obey. Away from equilibrium they fail, and the failures are usually catalogued case by case. His score-mismatch field, the gradient of the log ratio between the actual density and the balanced one, organises all of them. Its squared norm equals the relative Fisher information, a standard measure of statistical distance in this statistical mechanics paper from 2026.

A data-driven reading makes the mismatch measurable from data. Configurational temperature, defined from forces and positions, emerges as a distinguished probe of the same mismatch. The framework speaks to simulations of driven and relaxing matter. One field thus prices every departure from balance. The result unifies language across stochastic thermodynamics.
arxiv-2606-27560:
Runlong Yu studies the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations, the standard model of fluid flow. Yu asks how vortex stretching behaves after the flow is smoothed by a filter. Filtering blurs fine detail, and large simulations rely on it for turbulence. Stretching of spinning regions is the mechanism that might make solutions blow up.

Yu proves a finite-scale estimate for the filtered stretching. The positive near-field part is bounded by a pairwise defect. That defect measures how much nearby vorticity directions disagree. A weighted inequality turns the angular defect into a difference quotient. Filtered diffusion can then absorb that term, leaving only a lower-order enstrophy reservoir. The leftover surplus in the local balance goes to other sources. These are far-field strain, commutator forcing, and localisation errors. Each source is controlled. At the critical exponent, bounded defects produce Young-measure profiles, generalised limits for fine oscillation.
arxiv-2606-27760:
Pixel-space diffusion models generate images without lossy latent compression. They struggle to model broad semantics and fine detail together, though. Heavy pixel decoders are the usual patch. Zipeng Guo and six colleagues challenge that patch in 2026. The decoders, they argue, mainly compensate for optimisation trouble tied to velocity prediction. Under clean-data prediction, the decoders become redundant. Their PixelU model is built on that insight.

PixelU is a single-stage U-shaped diffusion Transformer for pixel space. Zero-cost skip connections route high-frequency detail from shallow to deep layers. A constant-channel down-sampling step acts as a low-pass filter. The backbone then focuses on low-frequency semantics. On ImageNet, PixelU reached FID scores of one point six at the smaller size and one point nine at the larger. It beat pixel-space methods, using only a third of the computation of the JiT-G baseline.
arxiv-2606-27860:
People differ in how much they repeat social contacts over time. Measuring that persistence is tricky. Existing measures mix true behavioural regularity with structural effects such as node degree. G Maurial, E Klüger, and M Génois introduce a new criterion in 2026. The Neighbourhood Persistency Criterion pairs classic similarity measures with tailored null models. The null models control for network shape and contact weights.

Data came from face-to-face contact networks at four conferences. The SocioPatterns platform recorded contacts with high time resolution. A shared pattern appeared across all four events. People trade off exploring new contacts against exploiting known ones. Many switch between the two modes. Others keep one stable pattern throughout. These habits show little systematic link to socio-demographic traits. Context seems to shape contact strategy more than fixed personal traits. The criterion gives a flexible, interpretable tool for such studies.
arxiv-2606-28260:
Jonathan Bauermann, Roberto Benzi, David R. Nelson, and Federico Toschi study microbes drifting in thin layers at the ocean surface. Turbulence there squeezes and stretches the flow, making it effectively compressible, so patches of water gather microbes together or spread them apart while the microbes reproduce.

Bauermann and colleagues focus on populations with an Allee effect, where growth stalls unless enough individuals are present. They derive formulas that give the carrying capacity from the Allee strength in two limits of the Damköhler number, which compares the flow's turnover time with the growth rate. Simulations connect the two limits. When growth is slow relative to the flow, they find a largest Allee strength, set by flow statistics, beyond which the species dies out in strong turbulence.
arxiv-2606-28460:
Hossein Mohebbi, Oliver Schulte, Ke Li, and Pascal Poupart manufacture extra training data for regression, the prediction of numbers from tabular records, where samples are few, costly, and noisy. Vision and language enjoy rich augmentation tricks; tables do not. Their insight starts where a fitted model stops: the leftover residuals look like noise a good model could not explain.

Counterfactual Residual Data Augmentation treats those residuals as invariant under small nudges to carefully chosen features. Attaching old residuals to nudged records creates realistic new samples without collecting anything. The trick works with any regressor. Across benchmark datasets, it cut the squared error of a neural regressor by about twenty-three percent on average. It cut that of a boosted-trees regressor by about six percent, beating existing generators and augmentation methods consistently.
arxiv-2606-28560:
Chad A. Capps, writing alone, spaces out attention. Sparse attention lets each word in a transformer consult a dense local window plus far-off positions at Fibonacci-spaced offsets, stretched or compressed by a per-layer factor. Across twenty-one language models trained under one matched recipe, Capps compares four ways of setting that factor through the layers.

A static, depth-staggered schedule beat both fixed and learned factors, and the trick transferred to a power-of-two spacing base. Learning the factor per layer accomplished nothing while costing about five times the inference latency. Most striking, every sparse variant extrapolated to four times its training length almost unscathed, while a matched dense baseline's perplexity more than tripled. The author also reports the honest negatives. At training length itself, the best sparse model still trailed dense attention by about a quarter in perplexity.
arxiv-2606-28960:
Feng and colleagues test clinical AI tools on the questions doctors actually ask at the point of care, rather than exam-style problems. Their blinded evaluation uses 620 real queries submitted by physicians across thirty specialties to the OpenEvidence platform, plus 187 questions from a public benchmark. In total, 149 practising physicians from 36 states compared answers head-to-head, each matched to the question's specialty.

Four systems competed: three frontier general-purpose models and one specialised clinical tool. Graders scored clinical utility, accuracy, source quality, verifiability and completeness. Systems specialised tool scored highest on all five dimensions, with win margins of 25 to 39 percentage points on the real queries. Results held across checks varying citation display, answer length and user status. AI judges differed systematically from the physicians, though both picked the same best model. The team release the query set as a public benchmark.
arxiv-2606-29360:
Yin and three colleagues speed up high-resolution image generation by removing a hidden systems bottleneck. Diffusion Transformers generate images with much spatial redundancy, but many methods that exploit it encode regional computation as attention masks. Those masks, the team shows, push attention computation off the fast path of optimised kernels, a cost they name the Mask-Induced Dispatch Tax, which grows with sequence length.

Their framework, SAFE-DiT, needs no training. It deletes only image self-attention masks certified to shift attention scores by a constant. It keeps meaning-bearing masks such as text padding, and schedules spatial work through prompt-conditioned token partitioning with periodic context refresh. On their test stack, redundant masks made attention four to six times slower. SAFE-DiT sped end-to-end generation up about two point seven fold at moderate resolution and five fold at higher resolution, and cut peak memory sharply.
arxiv-2606-29660:
Profumo argues that naturalness in physics, the idea that a theory needing fine-tuning is implausible, measures something different from what it claims. A fine-tuning verdict hinges on the choice of basic parameters, the prior, and the measure convention. It therefore does not, on its own, fix a feature of the world. What is objective, he argues, is structural.

The invariant object is the universality class of the parameter-to-observation map, unchanged when parameters are relabelled. Profumo calls this an informational invariant. Naturalness becomes a statement about the geometry of how representations tell cases apart. A uniform analysis across gravity and particle dark matter candidates follows. Fine-tuning follows the analytic structure of the abundance map, rather than the nature of the candidate itself.
arxiv-2606-29760:
Li and six co-authors unify two classic ways of training blind image quality assessment, judging picture quality with no reference image. Regression calibrates absolute scores. Ranking recovers quality structure from comparisons between pairs. 

The authors identify pairwise distance, which they call quality margin, as the common bridge. Their derivation shows that both paradigms are fits to quality margins. Regression fits margins implied by score endpoints; ranking fits transformed margins. Motivated by that insight, they propose MR-IQA, which optimizes pairwise margin errors directly as rewards inside a reinforcement learning framework. Experiments span six benchmarks. MR-IQA shows competitive general performance and, in controlled comparisons, the strongest average correlation scores against regression-based or ranking-based RL methods.
arxiv-2606-30360:
Kuangpu Guo and six colleagues show that defenses meant to stop free-riders from merging AI models can be broken. Model merging fuses expert models into one without retraining. Parameter-level defenses scramble a model's weights to spoil merged copies. The scrambling keeps each model working alone. Guo's team finds a structural weakness in that design.

The protected task vectors turn out to be tiny in size. The original pretrained weights therefore dominate the protected model. Treating that pretrained model as a fixed anchor unlocks an attack. Their Anchor-Guided Attack aligns the protected model with the anchor. The defense's transformation matrix is then recovered exactly. Tests show the attack bypasses single and combined defenses alike. The team also offers a countermeasure, Anchor-Repulsive Fine-tuning. It weakens the anchor dominance the attack exploits. Experiments confirm it defeats the proposed attack.
arxiv-2606-30560:
Kan Zhu and six colleagues release TraceLab, a record of how programmers actually use coding agents day to day. Serving these agents efficiently is hard, yet the workload data needed to improve serving barely exists. Public traces miss real usage across several agents and model families, so the team logged its own work with Claude Code and Codex.

The trace holds roughly forty-three hundred sessions, about three hundred fifty thousand model steps and four hundred thirty thousand tool calls. Analysis shows long autonomous loops and long contexts paired with short outputs, and tool calls with heavy-tailed variety, meaning a few types dominate while many are rare. Prefix caching, reusing earlier computation, hit often but imperfectly. The authors point to cheaper tool calling, smarter prefill planning, predicting tool delays, and better cache handling around pauses while humans think.
arxiv-2606-30660:
Raj Gaurav Maurya studies how to survey people who cannot read well, a group often missed by standard questionnaires. Paper and web surveys lose these respondents through literacy barriers, social pressure and discomfort, and the loss is worst on sensitive topics in marginalised communities. Maurya ran an early field evaluation with low-literacy women across India, comparing four ways of asking the same questions.

The four modes were paper interviews, digital web surveys, conversational AI surveys, and conversational AI enriched with value-sensitive design, meaning built-in respect for users' values and culture. Data from three hundred fifteen participants showed conversational AI lifted completion rates well above traditional modes. Completion was highest and drop-off lowest when the value-sensitive, culturally aligned elements were fully integrated. Maurya argues that human-centred design is what makes inclusive, ethical data collection scale.
arxiv-2606-30760:
Pouya Asadi, Austin Batz and Graham Kribs review a broad family of dark matter theories built on confining dark sectors. In these models, a hidden sector has its own strong force, much like quantum chromodynamics in ordinary matter. Its particles bind into dark mesons, dark baryons and glueballs, giving many possible dark matter candidates from simple ingredients.

The review covers how such sectors could produce the observed dark matter abundance and what symmetries could keep the dark matter stable. It surveys discovery channels: direct detection underground, indirect signals in space, astrophysical observations and collider searches, plus correlations between them. A highlighted puzzle is why visible and dark matter have similar energy densities today. The authors compile unifying ideas and calculational tools across regimes. They aim the overview at theorists hunting open questions and experimentalists hunting new search opportunities.
arxiv-2606-31160:
Dinh, Khan, and Salim speed up the reasoning step of vision-language-action planners for self-driving cars. These planners first write a short chain-of-causation, a plain-language account of why the car should act, and only then produce a trajectory. The text is generated token by token, so it dominates the running time. The trajectory head, by contrast, is parallel and cheap.

The team splits reasoning into two paths. A routine reasoner handles the predictable continuation, reading the car's trajectory history. The full planner handles only tokens that encode fresh commitments, where new visual evidence matters. A trick called FlatRoPE steers the routine reasoner's attention away from image tokens and onto history. A post-training stage with an action-quality reward aligns the split. Together, the two reasoners cut the reasoning step's running time by about a factor of four on the Alpamayo planner.
arxiv-2606-31460:
Fedders and five colleagues present ILPU, an iterative method for unwrapping phase in magnetic resonance imaging. Phase-based MRI serves susceptibility mapping, field mapping, thermometry, and elastography, but the measured phase wraps around, and unwrapping it in noisy regions is error-prone. A wrong unwrap corrupts every map built on top.

ILPU splits the job into two levels. A lower solver recovers a smooth phase increment from an incremental Poisson equation by a discrete cosine transform. An upper solver refines an integer offset map with quality-guided smoothing and a restricted local search. Adaptive penalties weighted by quality keep low signal regions stable. Tests on 2D and 3D brain phase images against hand-unwrapped references judge the method where standard Laplace unwrapping struggles.
arxiv-2606-31560:
An and Filtser study low diameter decompositions in directed graphs, a method that splits a graph into clusters of small diameter so that nearby vertices usually land together. Two directed versions exist, and the stronger one, called a quasipartition, also keeps reachable pairs close after random edges are removed. Their focus is graphs with extra structure, measured by pathwidth and treewidth.

For any directed graph with pathwidth pw, the pair construct an LDD whose loss grows only in proportion to pw. That replaces an earlier bound that grew exponentially in its square. They also sharpen a bound for a classic cutting problem. They show that the integrality gap of the Directed Non-Bipartite Sparsest-Cut relaxation on a graph of treewidth tw is on the order of tw times log n. That is one log factor better than before.
arxiv-2606-31660:
Tzivrailis, Sotiropoulos, Rosso and Kawasaki expose a failure mode of machine learning interatomic potentials, the neural models that stand in for costly quantum calculations of molecular energies and forces. Trained by standard mean squared error on density functional theory data, such potentials can hit chemical accuracy on held-out points. Yet they fail at their real job, driving simulations, by drifting into spurious low-energy states.

Their fix, Contrastive Regularized MSE, adds a term comparing the model's own sampling distribution with the target one. It uses persistent Langevin chains to expose the bad configurations and raise their energy, with no new quantum data. On the ethanol and aspirin molecules of the MD17 benchmark, the corrected potential stays in the physical basin and reproduces energy, distance and dihedral free-energy profiles closely. This holds even with sharply reduced training data.
arxiv-2606-31960:
Keshri and three others present a spatially resolved, multiwavelength study of the Roberts Quartet, a compact group of four galaxies caught mid-interaction. The members, NGC 87 through NGC 92, span a range of masses and states. Data combine GALEX ultraviolet imaging, DECaLS optical data, VLT MUSE spectroscopy and infrared observations.

Every member shows disturbed stellar and gas kinematics, extra turbulence and asymmetric structure, in line with repeated gravitational encounters. NGC 92 carries tidal features, a bar and ring-like star formation from gas inflows. NGC 89 shows suppressed star formation with signs of black-hole feedback, while the smaller members form stars at a brisk pace. Age values bound the recent interaction timescale at about 500 million years, marking a dynamically young, still-assembling system.
arxiv-2608-00160: Optimal Decoding for Measurement-Based GHZ State Preparation, arXiv 2608-00160. The GHZ decoding. The paper remains available to readers. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
arxiv-2608-00260: Approximating the Fourier Transform from Non-equispaced Discrete Samples, arXiv 2608-00260. The Fourier approximation. Readers can access the paper here. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. History keeps its place secure.
asher-henry-hudson-navigator-1860:
George M. Asher put the journals of Henry Hudson in print for the Hakluyt Society in 1860. Hudson was the English sea captain who sought a north route to Asia. The journals cover his four voyages, the last of which cost him his life.

On June 15, 1608, off Novaya Zemlya, two of his men swore they saw a mermaid. Thomas Hilles and Robert Rayner told of her hair, her tail, and her fall back in the sea. The sober log book tone makes the tale the classic Arctic mermaid report of its age.
averroes-colliget-1560:
The Colliget is the medical summa of Averroes, the Kulliyat, his book of the general rules of healing. The text here is the ninth volume of the Venice edition of 1560, in the Latin of Joannes Bruyerinus Campegius. With it stand his exposition of the Cantica of Avicenna and three shorter sections gathered by the editors.

Seven books move from anatomy and health to sickness, signs, drugs, foods, and the keeping of health. Averroes writes as both philosopher and court doctor, keen on clear rules drawn from Galen and tested by reason. No English version in the public domain exists. The Colliget was a school book of medicine across Europe for centuries.
averroes-commentaria-metaphysicam-1560:
Averroes of Córdoba spent his life explaining Aristotle, and his long commentaries on the Metaphysics are the summit of that work. The text here is the eighth volume of the Venice Aristotle of 1560, in Latin. It holds the commentaries on books one through thirteen, with his short epitome of the same work.

Averroes reads Aristotle line by line on being, substance, form, and the first cause that moves all things. His readings taught the Latin schools so deeply that they called him simply the Commentator. No English version in the public domain exists. This is the book that set the terms of debate on God and being for three centuries.
averroes-destructio-destructionum-1560:
Averroes, the great judge and philosopher of Córdoba, wrote the Tahafut al-Tahafut to answer al-Ghazali's attack on the philosophers. Its Latin name means the Destruction of the Destruction. The text here is the Venice printing of 1560, in the Latin of Calo Calonymos, with the exposition of Agostino Nifo. Two shorter works on the soul travel with it. The book is in Latin throughout.

Point by point, Averroes defends reason against the claim that philosophy breaks faith. He argues for the eternity of the world, the order of causes, and the bliss of the knowing soul. No English version in the public domain exists. The volume is the Latin West's own copy of Islam's greatest debate.
blanchard-the-religion-of-science-1860: The Religion of Science, Blanchard's 1860 work. The scientific faith. This book preserves that book. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
bunsen-egypts-place-universal-history-vo:
Christian Bunsen brings his long tale to its end in Vol. 4 of Egypt's Place in Universal History, out in English in 1860. Four tomes in, the tale of Egypt's place midst the lands of the old world stands full. Wars, trade, faith, and the fall of the pharaohs fill these last parts of the main tale in rich, grave prose.

Bunsen wrote as a man of faith and state, not a dig man. His dates have waned, yet his scope still stuns. One tome of proofs yet stands past this. The tale as tale ends here.
burton-lake-regions-central-africa-1860:
Richard Burton led a Royal Geographical Society expedition into East Africa in 1857 to 1859, with John Speke as his second. The Lake Regions of Central Africa, from 1860, is Burton's own account. The goal was the great lakes and the source of the Nile.

Burton reached Lake Tanganyika, while Speke, traveling apart, found Lake Victoria and claimed the prize. Fever, desertion, and quarrels plague the march from the coast. Burton's eye for peoples, tongues, and trade is unmatched, even when his temper shows. The feud born on this trip shaped African exploration for a decade. His appendices on trade goods and routes served later travelers well.
childrey-britannia-baconica-1660:
Joshua Childrey was a Hampshire clergyman and naturalist whose Britannia Baconica appeared in 1660. The book catalogs the natural rarities of England, Scotland, and Wales, county by county. Its title honors Bacon, whose call for a natural history of wonders Childrey took up.

Giants' bones, strange springs, fiery exhalations, monstrous births, and echoes in old churches fill his lists with Baconian care. He records what local people reported, sorting the credible prodigies from tales he cannot credit. The book is the Restoration catalogue of prodigies and wonders, a snapshot of a land still marvelous to its own scholars.
cia-0000009660:
Eleven Vietnamese prisoners of war were released by the Viet Cong at Christmas 1970, a February 1971 CIA report notes. The heading adds a description, cut off in the title, of something connected with the release. Holiday releases were rare breaks in the southern war's captivity.

A release at Christmas carried meaning beyond the eleven men freed. Such gestures served propaganda, morale, and sometimes genuine mercy at once. Analysts weighed which motive dominated before reporting upward. The freed men's accounts could also reveal camp locations and conditions. This file preserves a small act of release inside a long record of holding.
cia-0000012260:
Moving secrets from hand to hand took forms, and a CIA transfer record from August 1960 preserves one. The document transfer and cross-reference forwards a packet for an operation called Compass, and mentions a wheel used in passing secret goods along. Such slips logged what moved, who signed, and where the material went next.

The record shows the humdrum side of spying, where clerks and couriers mattered as much as agents. It ties the Compass packet to other files through its cross-references. For readers, it is the plain paperwork of the covert world, kept with the same care as the secrets themselves.
cia-0000015360: Further word on an FCDA meeting fills a CIA file dated March 5, 1953. The FCDA ran civil defense, the home front guard of the Cold War. Its meetings touched saucers when panic or warning was in play. The file shows the saucer question crossing into the civil defense world. The FCDA meeting file is now held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015460: Durant's report for the Scientific Advisory Panel on unidentified flying objects survives in a CIA record dated January 2, 1956. The catalog marks the report itself illegible, so its contents cannot be stated here. Durant served as the panel's secretary, a role named in other records of that panel. A key paper that cannot be read is a sharp lesson in archive loss.
cia-0000022360: The text of the indictment against Gary Powers is kept in full in a CIA record dated in 1960. An indictment states charges in the state's own words, count by count. Having the exact text let officials answer Soviet claims line by line. The entry is a primary source for the trial, plainer and harder than any commentary around it.
cia-0000023360: Detained Caucasians were sighted near Loc Ninh, in the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, a CIA record dated in 1979 reports. Loc Ninh sits near the Cambodian border, north of Saigon. Four years after the war ended, such a sighting stirred the oldest hope of the prisoner issue. It was logged like the wartime reports, for checking against the names still unaccounted for.
cia-0000026760: The Syrian situation has its outlook assessed in a CIA paper dated in 1956. Syria in the fifties changed governments often, and leaned ever closer to Egypt and the Soviet bloc. An outlook paper had to judge a capital where today's rulers might fall by spring. The entry keeps one turn of that restless decade in the agency's own forecast form.
cia-0000036560: On August 1, 1968, the CIA asked for photo comparisons covering cases 9638 through 9645, with the names blanked out in the released record. Photo comparison was a core method in the search for missing American servicemen, and this short request sent one batch of cases to analysts for face matching. Its value lies in scale, since hundreds of such requests moved through the system.
cia-0000037160:
Four American airmen were said to be buried near the 17th parallel in Binh Tri Thien province, in a CIA record dated May 3, 1983. The parallel had once divided North and South Vietnam. Reports of gravesites gave recovery teams places to ask about and, one day, to visit.

The record preserves the alleged site as it was reported, with its province and landmark named. Gravesite reports were among the most hopeful leads in the postwar accounting. Each one promised names could be matched to remains, and a family's long wait could end with an answer instead of a question.
cia-0000096660: Factional fighting continues in the Wenchou area of Chekiang Province, according to declassified CIA document 0000096660, dated September 2, 1968. The heading names the area and province and stresses that fighting went on. Readers get a short declassified provincial report from China, one of several Chekiang items filed within days of each other.
cia-0000102960:
Corrective Labor Establishment Number 9 at Bakal is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000102960, dated July 5, 1987. The heading in the catalog shortens the place name to Bakl. The sample text covers camp years from 1981 to 1984 and gives the site a physical layout.

Prisoner living and working areas formed a rectangle inside three fences, one wire and electrified, one wood, and one reinforced concrete. Each fence stood about six meters high, with guard posts every twenty meters between two fences. Outside stood barracks for about two hundred MVD troops with automatic weapons, plus the camp office building.
cia-0000119760: A September 1956 briefing for the National Security Council brings late news from Hungary. The Council received the freshest items ahead of formal papers, and that autumn Hungary was the most watched story in Washington's crisis reporting. Late-news briefings filled the gap between daily papers, carrying raw items to the Council before analysts had settled on a firmer shared judgment.
cia-0000126960: A January 1965 CIA report covers political and economic strains in Colombia, spelled Columbia in the agency's heading. The South American nation was under pressure on both fronts at once. The paper measures those strains as the agency saw them in the middle of the decade. Strain papers measured pressure before it broke into headlines, and Colombia's mid-sixties pressures included rural violence that would shape the country for generations afterward.
cia-0000132160: Situation report 477, from January 1991, covers Saddam speaking in public and two terrorist incidents, the heading breaking off. The Iraqi leader's public words were read closely for signs of his plans. The report sets out that day's events in the crisis watch. Saddam's speeches were mined for bluff and intent alike, since his public line often set the terms that diplomats then spent days trying to move.
cia-0000132260: Situation report 567, dated January 1991, reports an outbreak of disease in Iraq that was not caused by biological weapons, the heading breaking off. Ruling out a germ warfare cause mattered in a war shadowed by such fears. The report sets out the finding. Disease appears in most long wars, and ruling out a weapons cause quickly mattered for troop morale as much as for the medical picture in the south.
cia-0000132460: Caribbean tensions are surveyed in a CIA document dated February 4, 1960. Cuba was the main source of the strain, but the troubles spread across the island chain. Washington feared that another island might follow Cuba's path into revolution. The short document surveys those strains country by country, giving readers the agency's regional picture at the start of 1960.
cia-0000132660: Cuba and North Korea stating that their views are the same fills a CIA paper dated November 4, 1960. The phrasing was the formal language of full accord between two states. Havana and Pyongyang were both clients of Moscow with the United States as a foe. The short paper notes the joint statement and the ties standing behind it.
cia-0000135860: Dated 3 June 1952, one CIA document in the open files deals with the Guatemalan situation in mid 1952, watched by the agency two full years before the coup. PBSUCCESS was the code name for the CIA effort to bring down President Jacobo Arbenz of Guatemala, which ended with his fall in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136260: The cable dated 6 May 1954 in the CIA files, now open, deals with Instruction 11 for broadcasts, the script series running without a gap for LANGEVIN. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136560: A Spanish document dated 5 November 1960, held in the declassified 2506 Brigade collection. The brigade was training in secrecy that fall for the Cuba landing. The catalog record for this item is the generic series title, with no subject attached. Preserved in the original Spanish, the document is one of the November 1960 layer of exile paperwork. Its contents are not summarized here because the record does not state them.
cia-0000136760: The 2506 Brigade document cache preserves this Spanish text from 6 January 1961. The exile brigade was in training, its April landing three months away. The catalog record names no subject for the item. It is held in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, one of the first-week-of-January records in the brigade's declassified archive, presented as released.
cia-0000136860: A disturbance like the Bogotazo might hit Caracas during the Tenth Inter-American Conference, warns this 15 February 1954 field report, rated from a usually reliable American observer. The ambassador to Costa Rica told President Remon he had information on good authority that such trouble was planned; Remon expressed grave concern for his wife, who was scheduled to attend. Romulo Betancourt, Venezuela's exiled former president living in Costa Rica, is named the likely cause of the trouble.
cia-0000141160:
JMWAVE, the CIA station in Miami, sent headquarters a cable on 4 November 1961 about the bodies of dead air crew from a crashed plane linked to the Cuba operation. Officers had talked the matter over by phone. The question was stark: bury the men quietly in Nicaragua, or bring the bodies back and risk the story breaking open.

The cable leans toward a quiet burial. Bringing the bodies home, it warns, could stir bad press and revive what it calls the April business, meaning the failed April invasion. It also notes the families had likely already given the men up for dead, and telling them now could cause fresh pain.
cia-03179160: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1956/11/01, a CIA publication. The November briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-03184160: Mid-July 1960 saw this intelligence bulletin cross desks in Langley. The daily roundup covered the communist bloc and beyond. Another day of Cold War watching. Its contents inform the historical record. This file preserves that declassified paper.
cia-03191560: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1959/08/22, a CIA publication. The August briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. The historical record keeps it. Writers of history may cite it later.
cia-06232660: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN, a CIA publication. Another daily briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. It holds its historical place. Kept for study. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
cia-06468160: COMMUNICATIONS PLAN, a CIA document. The comms plan. This file preserves that declassified paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. Those who study the era will use it.
compendivm-alchimi-cum-dictionario-eiusd: Compendium alchimiae, 1560. The alchemical compendium. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-02-january-:
The Diary itself begins in Volume 02, January 1659-60, with the most famous first entry in English. Pepys blesses God for ending the old year in very good health. The editor's notes explain the dating, the shorthand, and the operation for the stone Pepys had survived in 1658. The diarist is twenty-six and lives in Axe Yard, Westminster. He clerks for his cousin and patron Edward Montagu. He is newly keeping the secret record he would maintain for nine years.

January's entries mix great and small: Parliament dissolving, soldiers unpaid, and at home his wife, his maid Jane, music, and church. Readers starting at the true beginning get the Commonwealth's last winter through the eyes of a young man who did not yet know he was standing at the edge of the Restoration.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-03-february:
February 1660, the month England decided to have a king again, fills Volume 03 of Samuel Pepys's Diary. London's soldiers mutiny for their pay and swear they will march where money is, while General Monk's army approaches the city. Pepys, clerk to his patron Edward Montagu, records the confusion between Parliament, army, and City from inside the rooms where it was argued. Bedding for a sick cousin and cards at Will's coffee-house sit beside the fate of the Commonwealth in the same entries.

Pepys writes without knowing the ending, which is the volume's charm: every rumor is live, every loyalty priced daily. His own fortune hangs on Montagu's choices, and he knows it. Readers get the Restoration as a month of weather, not a monument, seen by a young official who took notes on his masters while the regime changed around him. Few documents show a revolution being arranged so quietly.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-04-march-ap:
Pamphlets open Volume 04 of Pepys's Diary, March and April 1660. The diarist visits his Lord's lodgings and helps himself to pamphlets from Montagu's box, choosing as many as he has a mind to keep. London is full of print and rumor. Parliament is dissolving itself. Monk is remaking the army. Pepys dines at Mr. Crew's and listens to men who are deciding whether England shall have its king back. He takes notes on all of it.

Late in March he goes down to the fleet. Montagu commands the navy that will decide the question, and Pepys sails as his secretary. April's entries smell of salt water. Ships, signals, and secret instructions fill the shorthand. Readers get the Restoration from the flagship's cabin. A young clerk with a notebook stands close enough to power to record how quietly a revolution can be loaded aboard a fleet.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-05-may-1660:
May 1660 belongs to the fleet in Volume 05 of Samuel Pepys's Diary, as Pepys sails with his patron Montagu to bring Charles II home. News reaches the ships at anchor: Parliament has voted the King's letter, with its promise of an Act of Oblivion, the happiest May-day in years. At Deal they set the King's flag on a maypole and drink his health in the street. Pepys, in a new suit, writes letters and waits for orders.

The fleet then crosses to Holland, where the King embarks for Dover and the Restoration becomes fact. Pepys, secretary to the expedition, stands close enough to record the onboard ceremonies and the King's dog, jokes, and dinner talk. Readers get the monarchy restored at deck level, by the man who would spend the decade running the navy that carried it. The diary's most public month is also its happiest.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-06-june-jul:
Gift money opens Volume 06 of Pepys's Diary, June and July 1660. Mr. Sheply shares out the Duke of York's present to my Lord's servants. Twenty-two ducatoons come to Pepys's share, foreign gold at five shillings ninepence the piece. The King is home, and rewards are raining on the men who fetched him. Pepys counts his share with a clerk's care. Then he sets about the serious business of turning favor into a career.

That July he wins it. Pepys becomes Clerk of the Acts to the Navy Board, the post he will hold for the rest of the decade. The entries show him learning the office, the house in Seething Lane, and the habits of Batten and Penn, his new colleagues. Readers get the founding months of the great diarist's public life. The shorthand that began as a hobby is now the private side of a rising official.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-07-august-s:
August and September 1660, Volume 07 of Pepys's Diary, find the new regime settling into offices and the diarist guarding his own small place in it. His turn at the Privy Seal office ends the month, the post given up to an unknown successor while colleagues drink late at the Sun and plot against Baron. Pepys prays to be fitted for a change of fortune and means his own. On September 1st he is already at Whitehall work, sending his Lord Sandwich's things down to the Downs.

The entries show Pepys building the habits of a decade: office by day, tavern talk by night, accounts and anxieties kept in shorthand. Sandwich's sea command, court gossip, and the diarist's new Navy Office duties crowd the autumn weeks. Readers get Pepys after the Restoration fireworks, a clerk learning the machinery he will one day run, and recording his own ambition with unusual honesty.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-09-january-:
Fees open Volume 09 of Pepys's Diary, January to March 1661. Mr. Moore brings papers to sign and tells him his share from the pardons will clear eighty pounds. Eighty pounds for signatures, when no fee was even due. The Restoration is paying its clerks well. Then the family arrives: his brother Thomas, his father, Dr. Thomas Pepys, and his uncle Fenner crowd the morning. A cousin's child has died in the night. Profit and grief share the same entry, as they do all through Pepys.

January brings danger too. Venner's Fifth Monarchists rise in the city streets, and Pepys records the fighting and the heads that follow. Winter entries settle into office work, Brampton money quarrels, and Lent dinners. Readers get the Diary's second winter here. The shorthand is surer now, the man richer, and the world outside his door still armed and arguing about heaven.
eliot-george-mill-on-floss-1860:
George Eliot published The Mill on the Floss in 1860, her most autobiographical novel of a brother and sister. Maggie Tulliver's passionate, doomed devotion to her brother Tom drives the tale of a miller's family. Eliot drew Maggie from herself, the clever girl of a provincial world too narrow for her mind and heart.

Maggie, bookish and intense, is judged by a town that prizes her brother's plodding respectability over her gifts. The Tullivers lose the mill in a lawsuit, and Tom's vow of repayment rules the family's pinched, bitter years at home. Maggie's loves, Philip Wakem and Stephen Guest, end in scandal, renunciation, and a flood that joins brother and sister in death. In their deaths they were not divided, says the tombstone, in Eliot's most quoted epitaph. The novel's psychology of provincial life remains unmatched in English fiction.
emerson-conduct-of-life-1860:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published The Conduct of Life in 1860, his late essays on practical philosophy. The set treats fate, power, wealth, and culture in Emerson's most aphoristic and worldly manner of writing. It was his best-selling book in his lifetime, read as a guide to action and character.

Fate grants that heredity and circumstance bind us, then bids thought build altars to them in freedom. Power and Wealth praise energy and economy while warning what each costs the soul that serves them. Culture and Behavior polish the rough individualism of the early essays for society and city life in America. Worship closes the book with a call to moral sentiment over creed, rite, and church form in religion. Mature readers often rank this autumnal volume as Emerson's wisest and most usable work.
europmc-pmc10182360:
Liu and a large team review immunosenescence, the aging of the immune system, in a 2023 paper. As people grow old, their immune defenses weaken in known ways. Infections hit harder, vaccines work less well, and the risk of cancer and chronic disease climbs, while a low level of inflammation runs in the background.

The review explains the molecular changes behind this decline, in both the fast innate defenses and the slower learned ones. It links those changes to the diseases of old age. It also surveys treatments that aim to restore youthful immune function.
europmc-pmc10287560:
Nassiri and a large trial team report a phase one and two trial of a virus therapy plus an immune drug in recurrent glioblastoma, in a 2023 study. Glioblastoma is a fast-growing brain tumor that nearly always returns after standard care. The treatment paired DNX-2401, a virus engineered to attack tumor cells, with pembrolizumab, a drug that frees the immune system.

The virus was injected into the tumor, followed by the immune drug. The paper reports safety and survival results for the combination. The approach tests whether a virus can turn a cold tumor hot for immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc10420560: Victorian doctors tested a barely-there anaesthetic dose as a cure, and this paper shows their practical results. The faint treatment, tried on patients. The article preserves that old clinical experiment. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc1043860:
Brennecke and co-authors set out the rules in 2005 for how a microRNA finds its target gene. A microRNA is a short RNA piece that does not build a protein. It binds a gene message and dials that gene down. How exact that match must be was still unclear at the time.

The team split target sites into two broad classes. In one class, a strong match at the microRNA's head end suffices, with weak pairing at the tail. In the other class, a weak head match needs a strong tail match to work. Genome-wide data backed both classes in real genes. Each microRNA holds about 100 target sites on average, Brennecke found.
europmc-pmc10477960:
The GBD 2021 Osteoarthritis Collaborators counted the world burden of osteoarthritis from 1990 to 2020. Osteoarthritis is the most common joint disease in adults. It wears down joint tissue, causing chronic pain and loss of movement. It strikes most often after age 40 and climbs steeply with age.

In 2020, 595 million people had the disease, 7.6% of the world population. Case counts had risen 132.2% since 1990. The study covers hand, hip, knee, and other joint sites in 204 nations. Forecasts run to 2050, with knee cases set to rise 74.9%. For people aged 70 and over, the disease ranked seventh as a cause of years lived with disability.
europmc-pmc11164360:
Open2C presents a toolkit that turns raw DNA reads into chromosome contact maps in this 2024 paper. Hi-C and related methods reveal how chromosomes fold by recording which DNA regions touch. These methods pour out massive, varied sequencing data. Turning reads into contact pairs needs fast and flexible processing.

Their suite, pairtools, splits the job into modular command-line steps that can be chained into pipelines. Core steps parse alignments into pairs, sort them, and remove duplicate copies made during copying of DNA. Extra tools handle filtering, quality control, and pair editing. Benchmarks against popular pipelines showed gains in speed and flexibility, the authors report. Special tools cover cut-based protocols, single-cell Hi-C, and maps split by parent of origin. The suite plugs into Python analysis libraries.
europmc-pmc11631760:
Guzman and a large team present an ultra-fast method for measuring proteins by mass spectrometry in this 2024 paper. Mass spectrometry weighs molecules to identify and quantify the full protein set of a sample, its proteome. Speed and coverage usually trade off against each other. Their strategy, called narrow-window data-independent acquisition, pairs high-resolution survey scans with very fast fragment scans.

A new analyser scans fragments at about 200 per second with high accuracy, they report. The setup profiles over 100 full yeast proteomes per day. For human samples it reaches about 10,000 protein groups in half an hour, or about 7,000 proteins in five minutes. That is three times the coverage of the current state of the art. Pre-separated samples give comprehensive human proteome coverage in about three hours. Quantitative precision was shown on a three-species mixture.
europmc-pmc1185560:
Hausdorff wrote a 2005 overview of gait variability, the small changes from stride to stride. Walking looks steady, yet each step differs a bit. Those small shifts can reveal aging and disease effects. They may also track how well therapy or rehab works.

Past work ties stride shifts more closely to falls than average speed does. The overview gathers nine reports on fresh findings. Topics span wearable sensors, math models, and animal studies. One study shows dim light slows some walkers and unsettles others. Hausdorff frames stride shifts as a rich health signal.
europmc-pmc1713260:
Detecting family structure in gene data lacked a formal test of significance. Patterson, Price, and Reich supplied one in 2006, placing principal components analysis on solid statistical ground. The method compresses genetic variation into axes that reveal population splits.

Their theory uncovered a phase change in detectability. Below a threshold of divergence, structure in a fixed data set is essentially invisible. A little above the threshold, detection becomes easy. The flip lets researchers predict how much data a study needs to find structure. Patterson turns a descriptive plot into a testable claim about populations.
europmc-pmc1769360:
Children as young as five can report their own quality of life soundly. Varni, Limbers, and Burwinkle tested that claim in 2007 in 8,591 children aged 5 to 16, using the same PedsQL survey given to parents in a companion study.

Even the youngest children left few items blank. Most self-report scales in each age group, including age five, passed the 0.70 reliability standard. Total scores approached or passed 0.90, the bar for judging single patients. Validity checks held as well. Varni argues the results support hearing the child's own voice in trials, not only the parent's.
europmc-pmc1821060:
Rusch, Venter and co-authors reported in 2007 the main haul of the Global Ocean Sampling expedition aboard Sorcerer II. The ship collected surface water microbes along a transect of several thousand kilometers. The route crossed the North Atlantic, passed through the Panama Canal, and ended in the South Pacific.

Shotgun sequencing of those samples produced 7.7 million reads totaling 6.3 billion DNA letters. A few major microbe groups dominated the surface ocean niche. Still, the data held great diversity: 85 percent of assembled sequence was unique at a strict 98 percent identity cutoff, as was 57 percent of the unassembled data. The team also built new methods for assembly and for comparing genomes across samples. Sample metadata, such as location and conditions, anchored those comparisons.
europmc-pmc1868760:
Montanini, Chalot and co-authors sorted in 2007 a family of proteins that ferry heavy metals across cell membranes. The CDF family, short for cation diffusion facilitator, occurs in bacteria, archaea, fungi, plants, and animals. Its members matter for human health and for cleaning polluted land with microbes or plants.

The team gathered family members from all three domains of life and aligned their sequences. The alignment sharpened the family's signature pattern, the fingerprint used to spot new members in genomes. Tree building split most members into three groups matching the metal each carries: zinc alone, iron with zinc, or manganese. A new member's metal can thus be guessed from its branch. Mutating conserved building blocks in one member tested which spots set that selectivity.
europmc-pmc2124860: A medical paper on malarial pigment, its nature and mode of production. The fever's dark stain. This article preserves that parasitology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2125960: A medical paper on the factors concerned in the appearance of nucleated red blood corpuscles. The nucleated reds again. This article preserves that hematology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2128360: A medical paper with studies on changes produced by roentgen rays in inflamed connective tissue. The irradiated tissue. This article preserves that radiology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2131060: A medical paper on the soluble specific substance of Friedlander's bacillus, paper two, chemical. The Klebsiella chemistry. This article preserves that biochemistry. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131260: A medical paper on the mechanism of the serum sensitization of acid-fast bacteria. The sensitized TB. This article preserves that bacteriology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2131560: A medical paper on the functional and pathological response of the kidney in dogs subjected to a procedure. The dog kidneys. This article preserves that nephrology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. The paper lasts as a quiet witness to its time.
europmc-pmc2131660: A medical paper on the fate of tubercle bacilli in the organs of reinfected rabbits. The TB's return. This article preserves that bacteriology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2140660: A biology paper on the combination of salts and proteins. The salty proteins. This article preserves that biochemistry. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2140760: A biology paper on time relations of growth, genetic growth constants of animals, the growth math. This article preserves that biology. It awaits future readers. History keeps its place secure. It is kept for readers to consult. It is kept for study by scholars.
europmc-pmc2169260:
Tugwell and co-authors described OMERACT in 2007, an international network improving outcome measurement in rheumatology. OMERACT began informally in 1992, after European and North American rheumatoid arthritis trials used different endpoints, making results hard to compare. The network holds consensus conferences every two years around the globe. Expert working groups prepare data-driven recommendations, including core measure sets for major rheumatic conditions.

An executive committee chairs the network, and patients have joined the process actively since 2002. Conferences use evidence reviews, small-group debate and electronic voting to reach majority agreement. The first 1992 meeting in Maastricht aimed to agree a minimum outcome set for all rheumatoid arthritis trials. It also weighed what size of difference clinicians judge important. The authors stress that a trial's credibility stands or falls with its endpoints.
europmc-pmc2180260: A medical paper on the skin response of rabbits to non-hemolytic streptococci, attempts to desensitize. The rabbit skin again. This article preserves that immunology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2211560:
Cloughesy and a large team tested the drug rapamycin in 2008 in patients with recurrent glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumour. Preclinical work suggested tumours lacking the suppressor PTEN are sensitive to blocking mTOR, a growth-control protein that rapamycin targets. This proof-of-concept Phase I trial gave daily rapamycin before surgery. It aimed to check safety, tumour drug levels, and whether cell growth slowed in PTEN-deficient tumours.

Drug levels inside every tumour were enough to inhibit mTOR in lab tests, but actual inhibition varied widely between patients. Cell proliferation fell dramatically in seven of fourteen patients after one week. That drop tracked the degree of mTOR inhibition, not drug concentration. Tumour cells from non-responders stayed drug-sensitive outside the body, so resistance was not cell-intrinsic. Rapamycin also activated Akt in seven patients, and that activation linked to faster progression later.
europmc-pmc2242660:
Kreike and co-workers profiled 97 triple-negative breast cancers in 2007, tumours lacking estrogen, progesterone and HER2 markers. This subtype is aggressive and lacks targeted treatments. The team generated gene-expression profiles using 35,000-probe microarrays. They also characterised the tumours by tissue examination and staining, and linked features to clinical outcomes, especially spread to distant sites.

Every triple-negative tumour classified as basal-like by its expression profile, making the two terms effectively synonymous here. Clustering still split them into five distinct subgroups, showing internal diversity. Two tissue features predicted freedom from distant metastasis. A large amount of infiltrating lymphocytes gave a hazard ratio of 0.30, and absence of central fibrosis gave 0.14 on the same scale. Both confidence intervals excluded no effect. The analysis was multivariable and covered a tumour series from the Netherlands.
europmc-pmc2376960:
Forrest and colleagues built a simple blood-based score for lung cancer outlook in 2003. The patients had inoperable non-small-cell lung cancer, the common form, which usually cannot be cured. Standard outlook measures lean on cancer stage and how active a patient is, both partly matters of judgement.

Their score combined albumin, a blood protein that falls when patients are run down, with C-reactive protein, a marker of body-wide inflammation. Together they predicted survival about as well as stage plus fitness combined. The score's hazard ratio was 1.70 in their analysis, against 1.48 for the standard pairing, and both links were statistically firm. The authors stressed the practical edge: both blood tests are cheap, routine, and measured the same way everywhere, unlike fitness ratings that vary between doctors.
europmc-pmc2377260:
Zhang and Rothenbacher reviewed how common chronic kidney disease is worldwide in 2008. Chronic kidney disease means lasting kidney damage or weak filtering, and it raises the risk of kidney failure and heart disease. Counts depend heavily on which formula doctors use to estimate filtering from a blood test.

They gathered 26 population studies using one standard definition, with samples from 237 to 65,181 people. The median rate was 7.2% among adults aged 30 and over. Among people aged 64 and older, rates ran far higher, from 23.4% to 35.8% across studies. The newer MDRD formula had become the favourite tool over the older Cockcroft-Gault method. The authors warned that detection stays weak in older people, women, and some ethnic groups.
europmc-pmc2475660:
Fazekas and co-authors tested candidate DNA barcodes for land plants in 2008. Animal barcoding works well with one standard gene, but plants lacked an agreed region. The team compared eight regions from the plastid genome, the small DNA set inside plant chloroplasts, plus one from the mitochondria, across 251 samples.

The samples covered 92 species in 32 diverse plant genera, including several taxonomically tricky groups. Single regions resolved between 7% and 59% of species as clean separate groups, with a spacer region called trnH-psbA the best single marker. Getting the sequences at all varied: one gene, matK, needed ten primer pairs to reach 88% recovery. Combining four to seven regions lifted resolution only to 69% to 71%, barely above good two-region mixes. The authors said practical ease of recovery deserves as much weight as raw variability.
europmc-pmc2478660:
Andersson and colleagues mapped three related RNA-binding proteins across human tissues in 2008. The proteins, FUS, EWS, and TAF15, form the FET family. They were first found through the broken fusion genes they create in sarcomas and leukaemias, and they help run gene expression and message processing.

All three appeared in cell nuclei in nearly every tissue, each with its own pattern. FUS and TAF15 also sat in the cell body fluid of most cell types, while EWS showed there mainly in secretory cells. Levels fell as embryonic stem cells matured, and two fully mature cell types, pigment cells and heart muscle, had none at all. Under heat or oxidative stress the proteins moved into stress granules, packets where the cell parks its messages. FUS needed its RNA-binding region for that move. The authors said these are specialised players, not housekeeping constants.
europmc-pmc2547860:
Bionaz and Loor charted in 2008 which genes switch on and off as a cow's udder makes milk fat across a lactation cycle. The molecular control of milk fat was largely unknown, so the team measured 45 genes tied to fat building and release in mammary tissue. Samples ran from late pregnancy through the end of the following lactation, alongside milk fat composition.

Genes for pulling fat from blood, building new fat, and packaging it into droplets all rose sharply during lactation. One gene, INSIG1, climbed more than twelvefold, while SREBF1, long cast as the master switch, barely doubled, challenging its central role. The most abundant gene measured was SCD, which softens fats. The authors propose a network model in which PPARG, PPARGC1A, and INSIG1 jointly steer milk fat synthesis.
europmc-pmc2568860:
Kiebel, Daunizeau, and Friston proposed in 2008 that the cortex is organised as a hierarchy of time scales mirroring the world it tracks. Fast levels handle fleeting sensory detail, while higher levels follow slow changes in context under which the fast details unfold. The paper first presents a mathematical model of this sensory encoding.

In the model, slowly shifting neuronal states track the trajectories of faster sensory states, proving the scheme can work in principle. The authors then review brain evidence fitting the idea. A cortical area's time scale, they argue, can be read from its position along a front-to-back gradient of distance from the primary sensory areas. The framework explains prefrontal cortex functions as operations on slowly changing representations, and it yields testable predictions.
europmc-pmc2642860:
Shanks, Greek, and Greek argued in 2009 that animal tests used to predict drug effects in people rest on weak ground. Their essay works as science philosophy. It asks what the word predict should mean. It then checks whether animal models meet that standard in drug safety testing and disease research.

Judged against clear standards, the authors say, the models fall far short. They point to deep differences between species in how genes are switched on and off, and in body chemistry shaped by evolution. Such gaps, they argue, mean a drug that is safe or harmful in an animal may behave quite differently in a person. They accept that animals serve science in many other ways, but deny that prediction of human response is one of them.
europmc-pmc2714960:
Marcusson, Frimodt-Møller, and Hughes tested in 2009 how resistance to fluoroquinolone drugs affects the fitness of E. coli bacteria. These drugs block two enzymes that manage DNA coiling during copying. High resistance needs several mutations, and some of those changes were known to slow growth, which should favor fitter mutants over time.

They built strains with up to five resistance mutations and raced them in lab and in animals. Some mutations did cut fitness sharply. Yet adding a fourth mutation in the parC gene to a weak triple mutant raised fitness greatly and cut drug sensitivity at the same time. Without any drug present, selection still favored those less sensitive mutants.
europmc-pmc2739160:
Almén, Nordström, Fredriksson, and Schiöth mapped in 2009 the human membrane proteome. That is all proteins that sit in cell membranes, where most drug targets live. They mined the full human protein set with three helix-prediction tools, removed duplicates against the genome, and clustered the rest into families that they curated by hand against many databases.

They identified six thousand seven hundred eighteen membrane proteins and classified most into two hundred thirty-four families. Receptors, transporters, and enzymes formed the largest functional groups, while about forty-one percent were singletons with no family match. Membrane proteins made up an estimated twenty-seven percent of all human proteins. Shapes differed by job: most transporters span the membrane many times, while most enzymes cross it once.
europmc-pmc2784760:
Frank-Cannon, Alto, McAlpine, and Tansey reviewed in 2009 whether neuroinflammation fans the flame in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and multiple sclerosis. The brain was once thought immune-privileged, yet it mounts its own inflammatory responses. A short-lived response after infection, trauma, or stroke activates microglia, the resident immune cells, then settles. Trouble starts when activation never switches off.

Chronic neuroinflammation keeps microglia switched on for years. They steadily release cytokines and chemokines, signal molecules that recruit still more microglia. Harmful oxygen-based stress builds in the same loop. The review lays out the hallmarks of acute and chronic responses, and explains why microglia sit at a crossroads where diverse insults meet. It then weighs population, drug, and genetic evidence tying this smoldering inflammation to the diseases. That slow burn is what sets these diseases apart from a brief infection of the brain.
europmc-pmc2795760:
Wallace, Schmid, Lau, and Trikalinos introduced Meta-Analyst in 2009, a free program for meta-analysis, the method that pools results from many studies into one answer. Most researchers then ran such work in general statistics packages or in costly dedicated tools.

The program runs models for yes-or-no outcomes, measured outcomes, and tests that judge how well a diagnosis works, in both standard and Bayesian styles. It also runs cumulative and leave-one-out analyses, which show how the pooled answer shifts as studies arrive or drop out. Users can edit the forest plots it draws and export results as images or documents. The team checked its math against a standard package across thousands of published reviews from the Cochrane Library, and the numbers matched.
europmc-pmc2814860:
Prasanna, Gopalakrishnan, Shankar, and Vasandan compared stem cells from two sources in 2010 under inflammatory attack. Mesenchymal stem cells can dampen immune responses, a talent that makes them candidates for cell therapy. Cells from Wharton jelly, the cord tissue around umbilical blood vessels, are easier to get than bone marrow cells and grow faster.

Two inflammatory signals, interferon gamma and TNF alpha, did not strip either cell type of its calming effect. Cord cells suppressed immune cell growth more strongly in most tests. The two sources also leaned on different calming tools, with distinct levels of an enzyme called IDO and two secreted factors. Inflammation reshaped each source in its own way, the team concludes.
europmc-pmc2829060:
Grönke, Clarke, Broughton, Andrews, and Partridge mapped the evolution and jobs of fruit fly insulin-like peptides in 2010. These seven signals, called DILPs, drive growth, metabolism, reproduction, and lifespan through one shared pathway. The team compared the genes across twelve fly species and knocked out each gene in the standard lab fly.

The seven genes split apart before the species did, and membership stayed stable, hinting their jobs are guarded by selection. Knockouts showed the peptides backing each other up and covering for losses. Removing DILP2 lengthened life, removing DILP6 shrank growth, and removing brain peptides lengthened life only when a partner bacterium called Wolbachia was present. Losing brain peptides also blocked responses to diet restriction.
europmc-pmc2848560:
Sionov, Lee, Chang, and Kwon-Chung uncovered in 2010 how the yeast Cryptococcus neoformans survives fluconazole, the drug used long-term against its deadly brain infections in AIDS patients. Some strains grow despite drug levels that should stop them, a puzzle called heteroresistance. Using genome scans and gene counting, the team compared resistant and normal strains of both major types.

Resistant cells carried extra copies of whole chromosomes. Chromosome one doubled first; higher drug doses doubled more chromosomes, and tolerance rose with each extra copy. Removing the drug let cells shed the copies and regain sensitivity. Chromosome one holds both the drug's target gene and a drug pump gene, explaining the trick as a reversible copy-number dodge.
europmc-pmc2874360:
Dutil and a national surveillance team warned in 2010 that an antibiotic used in Canadian chickens was breeding drug resistance in a salmonella strain that also infects people. The strain, Salmonella Heidelberg, ranks among the top causes of salmonella illness in Canada and turns invasive more often than most. About nine in a hundred lab isolates came from blood, a sign of severe disease.

Resistance to ceftiofur, a farm drug related to front-line human antibiotics, turned up in bacteria from both chicken meat and sick people with matching patterns. The overlap points to poultry as a route to human cases that are harder to treat. Using the drug in chickens may blunt the whole antibiotic family for human medicine, the authors caution, which argues for tighter farm use.
europmc-pmc2898760:
Wang and colleagues assembled in 2010 the first broad gene catalogue of the whitefly Bemisia tabaci, a sap-sucking pest that devastates crops worldwide and spreads hundreds of plant viruses. Almost nothing was known of its genes for development, insecticide resistance, or virus carriage. With no genome to read against, they stitched its transcriptome, the full set of active messages, together from scratch using short sequencing reads.

One run produced tens of millions of reads that assembled into well over one hundred thousand unique sequences, ten times everything previously deposited for this insect. Tens of thousands matched known proteins and were annotated by function. Comparing life stages with digital expression counting flagged genes tied to development and to insecticide resistance, ready-made targets for pest science.
europmc-pmc2965160:
Saederup and colleagues built glow-tagged mice in 2010 to track immune cells entering the inflamed brain and spinal cord. Monocyte groups marked by two different docking proteins are hard to tell apart inside tissue, and reagents for one marker were missing.

Their mice glow red where one marker appears and green where the other does. In a model of multiple sclerosis, the red-marked inflammatory monocytes needed their marker to gather inside the cord coverings. Surprisingly, neutrophils largely replaced a quieter monocyte group when the marker failed. The tags finally separate invading cells from resident brain defenders.
europmc-pmc3010660:
Rastogi and co-authors reviewed how ultraviolet light damages DNA and how living things repair it, in a 2010 article. Sunlight's UV-B band creates fused bases, altered photoproducts, and strand breaks that can mutate or kill cells, a threat growing as the ozone layer thins.

Organisms answer with a conserved toolkit. It includes light-driven reversal and cutting out damaged patches from one strand or both. It also fixes mismatches. Across breaks it rebuilds by copying a sister strand or joining ends. Checkpoints pause growth and, failing repair, ordered cell death removes the danger. The review organises each lesion with its matching repair routes.
europmc-pmc3016360:
Sinka and a large team mapped the dominant malaria-carrying mosquitoes of Africa, Europe, and the Middle East in a 2010 article, the second of a three-part world series. Africa bears most malaria partly because its Anopheles gambiae complex is so effective at passing the parasite to people.

Gathering records from literature and other sources, they built a database of thousands of geo-referenced sites for seven African species and six more across Europe and the Middle East.
