Infections inside the abdomen led the causes, followed by gastrointestinal bleeding, bowel obstruction, and perforation. Despite avoiding surgery, ten of the sixteen patients died in hospital. Two laboratory values split the groups sharply: non-survivors had lower serum albumin and higher procalcitonin, an infection marker, while a heart strain marker showed only weak association. The authors treat the sign as a manifestation to interpret, not a disease itself.
pmc-13254860:
Yuval Avidan and colleagues test how accurately primary care doctors read smartwatch ECGs for atrial fibrillation in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Watches now record medical-grade single-lead tracings, and guidelines say a physician with rhythm expertise must confirm any diagnosis, without defining what expertise suffices. Family doctors increasingly inherit these tracings with little specific training.

Recruited across Israel in June 2025 through professional networks, the doctors completed a web survey built from forty real smartwatch recordings. The set was evenly balanced among true positives, true negatives, and cases where the watch's own algorithm had called the rhythm wrongly in each direction, all verified by consultant cardiologists. Each tracing kept the watch's automated verdict attached, mirroring real visits, and came with a short vignette of a seventy-year-old man with palpitations. The study was designed to expose which features of the tracing trip up frontline readers.
pmc-13254960:
Christian Graesser and colleagues report a 2026 study of patients treated for STEMI, a severe heart attack caused by a blocked artery. The team asked whether inflammation that stays raised several days after the attack goes together with larger areas of dead heart muscle. They also tracked how patients fared over time after treatment.

The researchers drew on records for 1,781 patients treated at two Munich heart centers, plus blood studies in smaller patient groups and experiments in mice. White blood cell counts that remained high on day three were linked to bigger infarcts and poorer outcomes. The findings suggest that checking whether inflammation settles may help doctors identify patients who need closer follow-up.
pmc-13255060:
Osama A. Shoair and colleagues measured research output in a 2026 study of pharmacy faculty who do not teach pharmacy practice. The group covered 1,613 faculty at 142 United States pharmacy schools, split between biomedical-pharmaceutical sciences and social-administrative sciences. Publications from 2019 through 2023 were gathered from Web of Science.

Output averaged about three and a half papers per person per year, yet the spread was wide. Just fifteen percent of faculty produced half of all publications. Biomedical scientists published more than their social-science colleagues, and output ran higher at senior ranks, public institutions, and well-funded schools with graduate programs. Original research articles made up about two-thirds of the total. The authors offer the figures as national benchmarks for judging faculty and institutional performance.
pmc-13255460:
Xiaohong Hou and colleagues report a 2026 feeding study on tryptophan, an essential amino acid, in newly weaned piglets. Weaning stresses young pigs and often brings diarrhea and gut inflammation. The team used 27 Bama miniature pigs, a genetically uniform breed, split into three diet groups for 21 days.

One group ate a standard diet while the others received half-fold or one-and-a-half-fold extra tryptophan. Both supplemented groups had significantly fewer diarrhea cases and healthier intestinal structure. Gene, microbe, and metabolite profiling showed the amino acid reshaped gut microbial communities and calmed immune activity, lowering inflammatory signals while raising a protective one. The authors conclude that dietary tryptophan eases weaning gut problems through combined microbial and immune effects.
pmc-13255760:
Su and colleagues traced why Hulunbuir sheep are born with short tails, using single-cell sequencing of embryos from the short-tailed breed and from long-tailed Hu sheep. The short tail traces to a loss-of-function change in the T gene, a master regulator of body axis development. Embryos were profiled at two early stages, and a mouse model carrying the same mutation provided cross-species checks.

Mutant embryos showed signs that the apical ectodermal ridge, a signaling strip guiding tail outgrowth, regresses too early. Bone morphogenetic signaling rose while a key growth factor fell, undermining ridge survival. The same mutation killed mouse embryos outright, underlining species differences. The work nominates markers for tail-length breeding.
pmc-13256260:
Zhao, Strober, Hou, and co-authors present a method that measures how much of a disease's heritability is shared with other diseases through pleiotropy. Earlier work estimated genetic links one helper disease at a time. Their PHBC method instead uses a whole matrix of links, with a Monte Carlo fix for sampling noise, across United Kingdom Biobank diseases.

Across fifteen diseases, about twenty-seven percent of heritability was shared with a modest helper set. Expanding to sixty-two diseases and traits pushed the share to roughly half. Dropping even the most useful disease groups lowered the figure only slightly, and genetic pleiotropy topped what shared symptoms alone would predict. The authors conclude pleiotropy runs through common disease genetics.
pmc-13256560:
Samat Kozhakhmetov and a large team present a 2026 shotgun-sequencing study of the cervicovaginal microbial mix in 311 Kazakhstani women at routine cervical screening. Most microbiome research ignores fungi and Central Asian populations; this study covered both. Samples were typed for HPV, sorted by bacterial pattern, and checked for fungi from the same data.

Fungal makeup differed sharply by HPV status. Candida yeast showed up far more often with high-risk alpha-9 HPV types, even in women with normal cytology. Two bacterial patterns, one led by Lactobacillus iners and one by Gardnerella, tripled Candida albicans rates and showed depleted lactate and peroxide capacity. The authors cast L. iners as a permissive neighbor rather than a protector, and propose cross-kingdom signatures as candidate markers of HPV risk.
pmc-13257160:
Wang compared five ways of drying Polygonatum cyrtonema, a medicinal rhizome, weighing speed against quality. Hot air, infrared, microwave, freeze, and vacuum drying were tested for drying kinetics, color, rehydration, microstructure, and antioxidant retention. A mathematical model was fitted to each method's moisture curve.

Microwave drying was fastest by far, taking a tiny fraction of freeze-drying's eighteen hours, but retained fewer polysaccharides. Infrared dried quickly and kept color well, yet damaged microstructure and active compounds. Freeze and vacuum drying best preserved antioxidants and flavor, though freeze-drying's energy cost limits industrial use. The author judges vacuum drying the best overall balance for production.
pmc-13257660:
Zhenyu Bao and co-authors model how ultra-high-performance concrete cracks under pulling forces. Ordinary models fit stress-strain curves but ignore the fibers that give this concrete its toughness. Their 2026 approach listens to the material instead, using acoustic emission signals as a running measure of damage.

Tensile tests varied steel fiber length and dose while sensors counted tiny cracking sounds. A fiber factor fed those signals into a damage equation checked against fourteen published datasets. After correction, predictions landed within a few percent of measured values. Built into beam simulations, the model matched real load-bending behavior well.
pmc-13258660:
Saleh Alzughaibi and coauthors test wear of additively built stainless steel in a 2026 study. Wire arc building creates large metal parts layer by layer, leaving mixed internal structures. Disks of the steel slid against a hard ball under loads and speeds that spanned wide ranges.

Wear volume climbed steeply as load increased. Sliding speed mattered far less across the tested range. Friction eased as load rose toward a middle value, then depended on speed at the highest load. Microscopy showed mixed ferrite and austenite patterns from the building process. Engineers using printed steel parts learn that load control matters most for wear life.
pmc-13258960:
Mariola Gepfert and colleagues follow youth badminton players over sixteen months in a 2026 development study. Thirty elite young athletes were tested five times on jump power, reactive strength, stiffness, and court speed. Players split into younger and older development groups.

Every measured quality improved steadily across the training period. Gains followed straight lines without plateau in either group. Older players stayed ahead in absolute terms throughout. Improvement rates ran parallel, so younger players did not catch up faster. Individual response patterns varied widely regardless of age. Coaches gain support for long term individual monitoring over age based expectations.
pmc-13259060:
Stamatios Baltzis and colleagues build a low cost portable brainwave device for stress self monitoring in a 2026 paper. The Arduino based prototype records scalp signals linked to anxiety states. Users can watch their own signals live and practice calming responses before stress escalates.

Analog stages amplify and clean the signal before digitizing. Open source software displays the waves in time and frequency views on a computer. Tests showed visible shifts in alpha and beta signals across rest, induced stress, and self calming phases. The device is not a clinical tool in its current form. Teachers and hobbyists gain an accessible biofeedback platform.
pmc-13259160:
Tomaž Kastelic and coauthors match mold warping guesses for thin plastic plates in a 2026 study. ABS plates were molded at two mold heat mixes and checked with care. Three sim routes then guessed the same warp from the same heat inputs.

One built in tool guessed too much warp each time. A curved path tool caught some traits yet bent in false local ways. A joined heat and force route matched shape and size best for both mixes. Fill and pack steps sim well, while cool down warp stays the hard part. Mold makers learn which tool to trust for shape calls.
pmc-13259460:
Hamza Ali and coauthors catalog a gene family tied to cell transport and light response in grapevine during a 2026 study. Twenty six family members were mapped across the genome and grouped into five branches. Expression patterns were tracked across tissues and under salt, drought, and heat stress.

One member proved to be the ultraviolet sensor known as UVR8. Boosting that gene in grape callus raised red pigment production visibly under ultraviolet light. Family members differed widely in physical traits, suggesting split duties. Several members answered stress treatments with changed activity. Vineyard science gains a pigment regulator that links sunlight sensing to grape color.
pmc-13259860:
Mengting Tian and colleagues reviewed in 2026 what is known about NINJ1, a cell-surface protein, in diseases of the brain and spinal cord. NINJ1 was first found as a molecule that rises after nerve injury. Newer work shows it carries out the final rupture of the cell membrane in several forms of cell death, spilling signals that drive inflammation.

The review covers the protein's structure, its control, and its roles in multiple sclerosis, stroke, brain and spinal cord injury, and mental and degenerative disorders. The authors note that its exact jobs may differ by cell type, a gap that still needs study. They also weigh drugs aimed at the protein, including antibodies, short peptides, and small molecules. Such drugs could one day limit damage after injury or during disease flares.
pmc-13259960:
Tongle Yin leads a 2026 study of planetary health diet scores and death risk in the United States from 1999 to 2020. The Planetary Health Diet is a eating pattern meant to be healthy for people and lighter on the planet. Scores were calculated for 55,579 adults aged nineteen and over in a national nutrition survey, using one-day diet recalls. Scores can range from 0 to 150, and the team linked them to later mortality records.

Average scores were low but rose significantly over the period, ranging between 41.2 and 46.5 across survey years. The upward trend appeared in every subgroup examined, by age, sex, background, income, and schooling. People in the highest score quarter had lower all-cause mortality than the lowest quarter, with a hazard ratio of 0.78. Cardiovascular mortality was also lower, at 0.77, in the top group.
pmc-13260160:
Jinmu Ahn and colleagues tested in 2026 whether adding the enzyme xylanase helps weaned pigs grow on feed rich in hard-to-digest plant fibers. Young pigs lack the enzymes needed to break down these fibers, which can thicken gut contents and waste nutrients. Their trial fed pigs a high-fiber diet with or without the enzyme and tracked growth and gut health.

Pigs on the enzyme gained weight faster in the first two weeks and converted feed better early on. By day 28 they digested dry matter more fully, with trends toward better energy and protein use. Gut lining measures also improved, including lower levels of an inflammatory signal. Enzyme-fed pigs showed shifts in gut fluid acidity across gut sections. The authors conclude the enzyme supports growth by improving digestion and the gut environment.
pmc-13260260:
Xinni Lin, Fernando Antoneli, and Yangyang Wang present a 2026 mathematical methods study automating the classification of homeostasis in biological networks. Homeostasis means keeping an output nearly constant despite outside disturbances. In network models, rare points where the output stops changing can be identified from network structure alone using advanced graph theory. Doing that by hand becomes impractical as networks grow, and the concepts involved are hard for biologists to use.

The team built a Python algorithm that takes only a network's connections and its input and output nodes. It finds the relevant structures and lists all homeostatic mechanisms automatically. They demonstrate it on small and large networks, with single and multiple inputs, and cases where input and output coincide. An extension lets the method handle several input nodes by converting them into one combined input.
pmc-13260960:
Sari H Goossens and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study asking whether a concise symptom history can separate two rare causes of exercise leg pain in young people. One is functional popliteal artery entrapment, where an artery behind the knee is squeezed. The other is deep posterior chronic exertional compartment syndrome, where pressure builds in a leg compartment. Both cause pain, tightness, and cramps, and neither has a gold-standard test, so diagnosis is often delayed.

Data came from sixty-nine successfully treated patients, twenty-four with the artery condition and forty-five with the compartment condition. Pain, cramp, and weakness scores did not differ between groups. High foot tingling scores, at rest and during exercise, were associated with the artery condition. High tightness scores at rest pointed toward the compartment condition. The authors say these symptom clues can aid diagnosis.
pmc-13261560: Corey Ratcliffe and co-authors publish a 2026 correction to their paper on machine learning reconstruction of 2D MRI for gauging brain shape in epilepsy. A review of stored data showed the patient subgroup labels were assigned wrongly early in the study. The group called drug-resistant idiopathic generalized epilepsy was in fact 42 people with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The drug-sensitive group was 31 people with idiopathic generalized epilepsy, 11 of them drug-sensitive. Revised tables and a renamed figure are given.
pmc-13261660:
Yifan Bai and co-authors reported in 2026, in letter form, how a tiny plant peptide switches on its receptor to trigger defense. The peptide SCREW2 helps plants fight infection and manage water loss through leaf pores. It carries a single internal sulfur bridge, and whether that bridge matters was unknown.

Binding tests showed the bridged peptide grips the receptor's outer part firmly, while versions without the bridge did not bind at all. A partner protein joined only once the peptide sat in place, completing the active complex. The bridge forms inside one molecule, not between two, even under stress signals. Cell assays echoed the pattern: no bridge, no defense signal. The authors conclude the internal bridge locks the peptide into the one shape the receptor accepts. Their structural account clarifies how this hormone family assembles its switch.
pmc-13262560:
Boon Tat Yeap and colleagues survey how lockdown life treated university staff on Borneo. Malaysia's Movement Control Order forced academics and support staff into remote work almost overnight. Their cross-sectional study collected four hundred twenty-seven responses during the order's first phase.

A standard questionnaire scored physical, psychological, social, and environmental quality of life. Scores spread widest on the environmental side, covering money, safety, and home conditions. Gender made no difference, but education, years employed, marriage, and family income all shifted results. Better-educated and longer-serving staff coped measurably better, pointing to where support should aim in future disruptions.
pmc-13263160:
Omar Lopez and colleagues present a difficult case of lung disease returning after transplant in a 2026 case report. The disease, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, fills the air sacs with fatty protein material because cleaning cells fail. A 73-year-old man developed it again more than three years after receiving two new lungs, but early tests were puzzling.

Scans showed a patchy pattern typical of the disease, and antibody tests were positive, yet washings and biopsies first came back negative. Three infections at the same time mimicked the relapse and breathing measures shifted oddly. A later washing found the telltale material. Inhaled treatment plus two whole-lung washings cleared the scans largely and eased symptoms, with partial breathing recovery.
pmc-13263760:
Tan Van Nguyen and colleagues explore whether frailty hits older Vietnamese women and men with diabetes differently. Six hundred forty-four clinic patients aged sixty and up were graded by Fried's frailty criteria across two hospitals. Their 2026 observational study then tracks six months of hospitalizations.

Three in ten participants qualified as frail, with women modestly ahead of men. Frailty raised hospitalization risk in both sexes, but the link ran stronger in women. The authors read this as grounds for sex-aware diabetes care in aging patients. Screening grandmothers and grandfathers by the same cutoffs may miss unequal danger, they suggest.
pmc-13263860:
Yi Liu and colleagues asked in 2026 whether a gene rearrangement called ROS1 marks lung adenocarcinoma patients for earlier relapse, and found the answer depends on the tumor around it. Their records covered 3,162 patients with resected invasive tumors tested between 2018 and 2020. About four and a half percent carried the rearrangement.

In stage II to III disease, and in tumors that were solid, poorly differentiated, or pathologically aggressive, carriers relapsed sooner and died earlier. In stage I disease and in gentler-looking tumors, carriers fared the same as everyone else. The rearrangement clustered with non-smoking status and with invasion into lymph vessels. Carriers also spread to bone significantly more often. The authors advise folding ROS1 status into risk estimates only alongside stage and pathology. High-risk carriers may warrant closer bone surveillance.
pmc-13264260:
Hua-Chen Chan and colleagues trace how a liver lipid signal creates harmful cholesterol particles in metabolic syndrome in a 2026 study. A strongly negative form of low-density lipoprotein drives vessel injury, yet where it originates was undefined. In liver cells, a fat breakdown product switched on a low-oxygen response factor. That factor raised two enzymes. The enzymes decorate a transport protein with sugars and sialic acid, changing how particles are handled in the blood.

Decorated particles shifted from the normal clearance receptor toward a receptor tied to vessel inflammation, favoring formation of the harmful particle types. Blood samples from syndrome patients showed the same decoration pattern. Blocking the pathway reduced the modification. The chain links liver fat handling to residual heart risk that standard treatment misses.
pmc-13264760:
Ankan Gupta and Anju George discuss rapidly spreading animal-linked ringworm and molecular diagnosis in a 2026 article. Skin fungi adapted to animals can erupt widely on human skin, unlike the slower patches typical of human-adapted species. The introduction reviews how fungal classification was rebuilt by DNA methods into seven genera and how shifting demographics, environment and behavior keep reshaping which species clinics actually see, beyond simple geography.

A cited case involved a young woman with widespread blistering spots on trunk and limbs, a similarly affected close contact and a household dog with its own infection. Tissue study showed fungal elements, and species-level identification guided care. Molecular tools resolve look-alike fungi that microscopy cannot separate, supporting targeted treatment and source control in pets.
pmc-13264860:
Jose Arturo Pineda and a large team wrote a 2026 study protocol for the EIDAR study, which tests ultrasound as an early warning for swallowing problems in intensive care patients. Swallowing faults after a breathing tube comes out can cause lung infection and death. The best checks need the tube out, so a bedside scan before removal could flag risk sooner.

The study will enroll 100 adults at Dijon University Hospital who were on a ventilator for at least 48 hours. Within three hours before tube removal, staff will scan the neck to measure tongue and throat muscle size and lift. A scope check after removal, read by a blinded specialist, gives the true result. The team will judge how well the scan sorts patients and how feasible it is in the unit.
pmc-13265160:
Changsheng Wei and colleagues study a gene regulator called SPDEF in triple-negative breast cancer, in a 2026 laboratory and tissue study. This breast cancer subtype recurs and spreads often, with poor outlook. Key regulators that could aid prognosis are still being sought. The role of SPDEF in this subtype was unclear.

SPDEF levels were markedly lower in triple-negative tumours than in other breast cancer types. Low levels linked to advanced stage and tumour return. Raising or lowering SPDEF in cancer cell lines changed growth, movement, invasion, and cell death. Spatial gene data tied SPDEF to cell-death genes within tumours. The work names SPDEF as a candidate marker and target.
pmc-13265260:
Xiaoying Wang and colleagues review SGLT2 inhibitor drugs for acute heart failure, in a 2026 narrative review. These diabetes drugs have shown clear benefits in chronic heart failure. Their use during sudden worsening is attracting attention. Evidence available up to March 2026 was summarised.

Early starting during acute episodes appears generally safe. The drugs improve fluid removal, ease congestion, and reduce later heart failure events. Findings on short-term readmission remain inconsistent. Best timing and safety in particular patient groups stay unresolved. Key trials and real-world studies are discussed to guide practice and future research.
pmc-13266260:
Yujiro Yoshihara and the team use ultra-high-field brain spectroscopy to study the excitation balance in depression across ages (2026). Balance between glutamate, which excites, and GABA, which calms, shapes circuit function. The illness involves disrupted braking control. Seven-Tesla scanning can separate the two signals better than standard machines.

A clear interplay between group and age appeared for the glutamate-to-GABA ratio in a cingulate region. The normal age-related rise in that ratio was absent in the illness. Coupling between the two chemicals stayed intact. The authors interpret the pattern as an altered calming path rather than a uniform deficit, which matters for care.
pmc-13266360:
Hyun Hwa Choi and colleagues identify anatomy-based risks for portal vein problems in dual-vein liver transplants, published in 2026. Right-lobe living donor grafts with two portal vein openings are technically demanding. Records covered 111 recipients from 2011 to 2020. Geometry, recipient traits, and surgical factors were tested.

Portal vein complications arose in more than a third of recipients, with a smaller share classed major. Wider posterior vein diameter and wider axial angle independently predicted major events. Reconstruction method showed no significant effect. Patients with major overall complications had worse long-term survival. Three-dimensional imaging and risk sorting should guide donor choice and planning.
pmc-13266660:
Ahmad G M N Abdelsamad and colleagues compare ultrasound-guided catheter clot treatment with standard care for lung artery clots, published in 2026. Whole-body clot-busting drugs carry major bleeding risk. The catheter method delivers lower doses directly, aided by ultrasound. Two hundred thirty patients in a specialist response pathway were matched by risk profile.

Eighty-one matched pairs were analysed. In-hospital death was far lower with catheter treatment, and hospital stay was shorter by several days. Major bleeding events were also fewer. Milder bleeding was more common with the catheter approach. Adjusted analysis confirmed catheter treatment as an independent survival predictor.
pmc-13268260:
Marina B Wasilewski and colleagues present a 2026 interview study of a hybrid stroke rehabilitation program in Toronto. The program mixes in-person and video sessions for outpatients, aiming to deliver therapy doses that clinics rarely sustain. The team interviewed 14 health care providers who deliver it, framing questions with an implementation science model.

Four themes emerged. Providers valued the model's flexibility. Fit with patient needs and resources mattered greatly. Hospital resources and infrastructure shaped what was possible. And confidence in video care varied widely between providers. The authors conclude that fixing virtual care processes and resources could protect access and quality. Providers wanted video care kept as a permanent part of stroke rehabilitation, with its drawbacks actively managed.
pmc-13268360:
Lucas Alves da Mota Santana and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter alerting readers to a new bat coronavirus in South America. The virus, found in a Neotropical bat species, carries a furin cleavage site, a molecular notch that helps viruses enter cells more easily. That feature was once thought limited to Old World bat virus lines.

The letter reviews why the notch matters: it boosts cell entry and spread in related viruses, and removing it weakens them in lab animals. Over 180 bat coronaviruses were already known across the Americas, none with this feature. The authors link the find to habitat damage, which stresses bats and raises shedding. They call for a One Health system joining human testing, virus genome tracking, and animal ecology before spillover, not after.
pmc-13269060:
Mubai Sun and co-authors test in 2026 a selenium-enriched red yeast as a dietary defense against oxidative damage in aging. The yeast strain was loaded with selenium, mostly in the form of selenomethionine, and analyzed for its chemistry and shape. Aging mice then received the yeast while the team tracked behavior, tissue health, gut microbes, and stress markers across gut, liver, and brain.

Treated mice kept more beneficial gut bacteria and shifted microbial metabolism, while their antioxidant defenses switched on through a known protective pathway. Cell death signals eased, gut barrier strength improved, and brain cells in a memory region were preserved. The mice also showed less anxiety-like behavior and better cognition. The authors frame the benefit as a gut-liver-brain axis effect.
pmc-13269260:
Tian Wang and co-authors show in 2026 that the APOE4 gene variant, the strongest genetic risk for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, disrupts how the female brain adapts its fuel use across menopause. They profiled brain chemistry in humanized female mice carrying different APOE versions, sampled from before to after the menopausal transition. Estrogen loss already strains brain energy systems, and APOE4 is suspected of compounding that strain.

Mice with the common APOE3 form adjusted their metabolism to meet postmenopausal demand. Mice carrying even one APOE4 copy adapted poorly and faster in the wrong direction, losing amino acids and energy cycle intermediates while fats piled up. Two copies worsened every deficit. The work offers a mechanism for why APOE4 women face earlier, higher Alzheimer's risk.
pmc-13269960:
Wei Wu, Yi Zuo, and Jing Jin published a case report in 2026 on prenatal diagnosis in a Chinese family. Their unborn child carried a small missing piece of chromosome 16, at a site called 16q24.3. Such deletions are rarely reported, so counselors have little guidance when screening finds one. The report sets out the family's diagnostic workup.

Standard chromosome techniques have limited sensitivity for tiny missing or extra pieces. The authors argue that combining ultrasound, standard chromosome testing, and a high-resolution microarray scan raises diagnostic accuracy. Genetic counseling runs through each step, helping the family interpret an uncertain finding. The case is presented as a model for handling similar rare prenatal results.
pmc-13270760:
Chi Mei Sun led a 2026 journal article using Bayesian fine-mapping, a statistical method for narrowing down gene regions, to find candidate genes for production traits in chickens. Birds came from a backcross between a White Layer line and Araucana chickens, and traits covered egg number, egg weight, and body weight.

Genome-wide scans found many regions tied to body weight and egg weight, which were strongly heritable, while egg number looked more spread across many genes. Shared regions on chromosomes 1 and 4 affected both weight traits. The fine-mapping pointed to known growth genes such as NCAPG, LCORL, and IGF2BP1, and also flagged new candidates for egg number.
pmc-13270860:
Radhika Narla led a 2026 survey study of the first year of preference signalling in internal medicine subspecialty fellowship hiring in the United States. Signalling lets applicants mark programmes they especially want, adding a new factor for applicants, mentors, and programmes in the 2025-2026 cycle.

The authors surveyed programme directors in five subspecialties at three West Coast academic centres, and 11 of 15 replied. Ten of the 11 agreed signalling helped spot applicants with genuine interest and sped interview selection, but it did not cut overall review work. Directors struggled most with reading a missing signal and deciding how much weight a signal should carry.
pmc-13271060:
Guanling Chen is lead author of a 2026 pan-cancer analysis, a study across many cancer types, of a depression-related gene signature, a set of 382 genes linked to depression. The team computed a score, called DScore, for over 10,000 tumour samples from 33 cancer types and related it to tumour biology, immune surroundings, and survival.

Higher scores appeared in several gut, brain, kidney, and hormone-related cancers, and linked to older age, later stage, and poorer survival in many cancers, though the survival link reversed in a few. In breast cancer, high scores matched an immune-suppressing tumour setting with fewer killer T cells. One gene, CACNA1H, was checked in breast tissue tests.
pmc-13271360:
Lorenzo Ghelfi is lead author of a 2026 scoping review, a mapping of a young research field, on using artificial intelligence to detect relapse in psychosis. Relapse is common in psychotic disorders, a leading cause of disability worldwide. The authors searched three databases for studies using machine learning or language processing to spot relapse early.

Only ten eligible studies were found. Most collected data through smartphones and smartwatches. They used passive tracking and frequent in-the-moment check-ins. Social media and internet searches were also used. Model accuracy varied widely across studies. Detection rates and overall scores both ranged from weak to fair. Few findings were replicated, the authors conclude.
pmc-13271460:
Laura Holdsworth is lead author of a 2026 qualitative study, one based on deep interviews, of doctors' experiences in Lesotho during the COVID-19 pandemic. Most research on health worker wellbeing in the pandemic comes from Western countries, leaving the strain on staff in African settings poorly documented.

Seven doctors described their wellbeing through the crisis. Five themes emerged: feeling under pressure, unprepared, and out of control; constant uncertainty and threat; isolation alongside connection; coping largely on their own; and new perspectives gained. The challenges spilled beyond work and harmed wellbeing, yet doctors drew support from family, friends, and colleagues, and found lessons in the experience. The authors discuss national and local support needs.
pmc-13271560:
Parthopratim Dutta Majumder writes in 2026 on how thinking errors and clinical judgment shape the care of uveitis, a group of inflammatory eye diseases. These conditions are uncommon, varied, and often tied to illness elsewhere in the body. Delayed or wrong diagnosis is a familiar problem in this field.

The essay argues that sound judgment grows only through practice, careful history taking, and full eye examination. Busy clinics, short visits, and limited training in rare eye inflammation all raise the risk of bias. Listening closely to the patient's own account remains, in the author's view, one of the most underused diagnostic tools in uveitis care.
pmc-13271960:
Yutao He and colleagues run in 2026 a randomized trial comparing a percussion massage gun with stretching for tired athlete muscles. Poor recovery after hard training can blunt the next session's performance. Stretching is standard practice, yet its benefit is debated, and massage guns are now common in locker rooms.

Thirty male athletes were split into massage gun, stretching, and rest-only groups after fatiguing squats. The massage gun group regained normal effort ratings, leg size, and strength within twenty-four hours. Stretching needed forty-eight hours, while the rest group had not fully recovered by then. The tool may speed routine recovery for athletes.
pmc-13272560:
Jacob Thurell and colleagues tested fair ways to compare long term breast cancer deaths across hospitals in a 2026 Swedish registry study. Hospitals serve different mixes of patients, so raw death rates can mislead. Adjustment for case mix is common for short term outcomes but less settled over ten years.

Using a national registry covering 10,888 patients, they built two models for death from breast cancer within ten years. A full model used age, tumor, social, and health data, while a reduced model used only age and tumor data. Both models sorted risk well and gave near alike expected death rates across twelve hospitals. Age, stage, and grade predicted most strongly. The authors say routine data alone can support fair benchmarking.
pmc-13272960:
Abdelaal Shamseldin leads a 2026 study of Egyptian soil bacteria that can break down atrazine, a widely used weed killer that pollutes farm soil. Forty-four candidate bacteria were isolated from polluted sites, and 34 could use atrazine as a nitrogen source. Two strains stood out and were tested further.

The best strains, from Klebsiella and Ochrobactrum groups, each broke down about 81 percent of atrazine and carried known degrading genes. Both made the same breakdown product. Using a statistical tuning method, breakdown rose to 94.2 percent and 96.7 percent for the two strains. The authors present this as a bio-safe option for cleaning polluted fields in Egypt.
pmc-13273660:
Bunduki and colleagues argue, in a 2026 comment article, that female genital schistosomiasis belongs inside Africa's cervical cancer agenda. The disease is caused by parasitic worms in water. It damages women's genital tissue and is often missed.

The authors note that cancer prevention in Africa now centers on HPV. Vaccines, screening, and treatment all target that virus. Yet schistosomiasis can cause lesions that mimic other conditions. These lesions may raise risks and confuse diagnosis. The comment urges health programs to test for and treat the parasite alongside HPV services. It also calls for training so clinic staff can spot the disease. Joint action, the authors argue, would protect more women.
pmc-13273760:
Xinyu Zhou and colleagues measured how mental fatigue degrades basketball play in a 2026 study. Players must decide and move in one fast flow, and long mental effort may disturb both. The team put trained players through a pass and shot sequence at three fatigue levels.

pmc-13274160:

pmc-13274460:

pmc-13274760:
Qin-Mei Lin and co-authors present a 2026 longitudinal study of fear of cancer returning in survivors of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a throat cancer common in East Asia. pmc-13275360:
Yiting Zhang and co-authors gave a comprehensive account of TGF-beta signaling in a 2026 review. pmc-13276060:

pmc-13276160:
Milan Říha and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how a predatory fish finds its way home at night. Pikeperch in a large reservoir left a stable resting spot each night to hunt across wide areas. How fish navigate dark, murky water over long distances is poorly understood.

From the very start of each return, they headed almost straight toward the refuge. Their swimming speeds stayed steady and their paths barely wandered. Final approach distances were tiny compared with the trip length, and fish showed no long searching near home. pmc-13276460:

Engagement and the practice environment improved slightly overall, with stronger gains among council members. Use of evidence-based practice stayed flat across the whole sample. The authors also measured how far the councils had become routine practice.
pmc-13276560:
Mohamed Abdulkadir Hussein and co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary on a neglected crisis among older Somali refugee returnees. pmc-13276760:
Takeshi Yamaguchi and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on daily rhythms in the brain tissue that makes cerebrospinal fluid. The choroid plexus produces this fluid and houses a strong internal clock, hinting that fluid production rises and falls across the day. The molecular basis was unknown.

pmc-13278060:

pmc-13278960:
Hamideh Frühwein and co-authors apply a five-part framework to cancer prevention in Europe, in a 2026 policy paper. pmc-13279560:

pmc-13279660:

pmc-13280060:

pmc-13280460:

pmc-13280660:

pmc-13281560:

pmc-13281760:

pmc-13281860:

pmc-13282260:

pmc-13282360:

pmc-13282860:

pmc-13282960:

pmc-13283160:

pmc-13283460:

pmc-13283860:

pmc-13284060:

pmc-13285360:

pmc-13285560:

pmc-13286860:

pmc-13286960:

pmc-13287060:

pmc-13287360:

pmc-13287760:

pmc-13288160:

pmc-13289160:

pmc-13289260:

pmc-13289360:

pmc-13289660:

pmc-13289960:

pmc-13290560:

pmc-13290760:

pmc-13290960:

pmc-13291060:

pmc-13291560:

Uses run from diagnosis to trial design. Synthetic data and reasoning support get close looks. Risks include murky logic, privacy, and weak rules. Safe, trusted rollout is the review’s core plea. Research gaps for real clinic use are flagged.
pmc-13291660:

Cell power and survival signals improved as well.
pmc-13292260:

Charts from Yokohama City University Hospital covered patients treated between 2021 and 2024.

pmc-13292460:

The team pulled out key traits, what comes before, what follows, and how the idea can be measured. Home care is where such talk gets hardest as thinking declines.

pmc-13292760:

pmc-13293260:

pmc-13293460:

Response rates for single drugs ranged from the high thirties to the high fifties in percent terms. The pooled response rate sat near forty-five percent, with no spread seen between studies. Both drug target families worked about equally, giving options for a hard-to-treat group.
pmc-13293560:

Reporting gaps blocked pooling of body-based outcomes, so the authors urge tighter study standards.
pmc-13293660:

pmc-13293760:

Notifications jumped in 2023 as COVID-19 limits eased.
pmc-13293860:

Practical limits on clinical use close the review, which still leaves several control mechanisms only partly defined.
pmc-13294060:

AI tools are spreading in imaging and care, so students need shared standards for knowledge, skill, and conduct. The framework rests on three domains: core AI ideas, practical use, and ethical professional behavior.

pmc-13294160:

pmc-13294760:
Jingran Li and colleagues ask doctors in Chongqing, China, what they know and think about shock therapy for teens in a 2026 study. The treatment, given in changed form, works well for adults with deep depression. Its use in young people stays rare and much debated.

pmc-13295160:
Yanwei Xie and co-authors build a brain-seeking antidote for organophosphate poisoning in a 2026 study. Imaging and effect studies in animals confirmed the fusion reached the brain, cleared poison lodged there, and eased nerve toxicity. The approach could improve outlooks for patients with brain-centred poisoning damage.
pmc-13295760:

pmc-13296160:

pmc-13296560:

pmc-13296760:

pmc-13296960:

pmc-13297060:

pmc-13297160:

pmc-13297360:

pmc-13297460:

pmc-13297560:

pmc-13297760:

pmc-13298160:

pmc-13298860:

pmc-13299360:

pmc-13300160:

pmc-13300560:

pmc-13300760:

pmc-13301460:

pmc-13302260:

pmc-13302460:

pmc-13302560:

pmc-13303160:

pmc-13303560:

pmc-13303760:

pmc-13304460:

pmc-13305660:

pmc-13306060:

pmc-13306360:

pmc-13306460:

pmc-13306660:

Cleaning-focused therapy and retreatment of leftover sites improved plaque, bleeding and pocket scores in reported follow-up. The gap closed on its own as teeth shifted back, and bone defects looked filled on later X-rays.
pmc-13306860:

pmc-13306960:

pmc-13307860:

pmc-13308760:
