pmc-13308960:
Eyad Jamileh, Zuha Akhtar, and Maria Babu report in 2026 stomach outlet block from pseudomyxoma peritonei, a rare mucus filling cancer, in a man aged 76 years. Tumour spread through his belly squeezed the stomach exit shut, which brought pain, sickness, and steady weight loss over time.

Five metal stents in a row gave only brief relief, as squeeze and tumour growth crushed each new stent in turn. A scope made bypass join from stomach to small bowel then gave lasting relief, with vein feeding and a nose drain as backup. Early bypass thought beats stent rounds when mucus disease spreads this wide, the team argues from this hard case.
pmc-13309460:
Wallace S Tavares da Silva and co-authors compare two native goat breeds in dry Brazil in a 2026 study. Dark-coated Canindé goats and light-coated Moxotó goats live under the same hot, dry conditions. The team asked how coat, body heat, blood values, and hormones shift between summer and winter.

Thirty goats of each breed grazed together and were checked in both seasons. The dark breed showed higher coat surface heat, thicker coat change, and wider swings in thyroid hormone and blood sugar across seasons. The light breed stayed steadier on most measures. The authors read the dark breed as more flexible and the light breed as more conservative in coping with heat.
pmc-13309560:
Zakaria Mohamed Alghzzawy and co-authors build a tiny gel carrier for a plant compound with poor water solubility in a 2026 study. The compound, silibinin, shows health promise but dissolves badly, so little reaches the body. A carrier that releases more drug in acid conditions could help target diseased tissue.

Gelatin and a synthetic polymer were joined with a low radiation dose to form the gel, after a first step that spread the drug evenly. Particles stayed under 50 nm in size and trapped 82 percent of the drug load during making. Release in acid ran threefold higher than free drug after six hours. Liver cancer cells in dishes grew less under the loaded gel.
pmc-13309960:
Cristina Morente-Montilla and colleagues review animal evidence in 2026 on whether the blood-brain barrier breaks down in models of schizophrenia and autism. The barrier is a tightly sealed lining that normally shields brain tissue from circulating substances. Their search screened thousands of records and retained twenty-six studies, most in rats and many focused on schizophrenia models.

A recurring finding was disruption of the tight junction proteins that seal the barrier, present in nearly all schizophrenia model papers surveyed. Seepage of blood proteins into brain tissue appeared across several models, and some studies tied leak extent to behaviour scores. Many other reported changes rested on a single study each, so the picture is uneven. Strengthening barrier integrity might one day complement treatment, the authors suggest. They press for standardised barrier measures so future models can be compared cleanly.
pmc-13310060:
Hamed Tahmasebi and co-authors review machine learning for finding new antimicrobial peptides in a 2026 article. Drug-resistant infections form a rising global threat, with older drugs failing against more germs each year. Peptides that kill microbes offer broad action and attack routes that germs struggle to dodge, but the search space of possible peptides is vast.

Learning models can screen millions of candidates, draft fresh sequences with predicted strength, and tune several traits at once, from killing power to safety and shelf stability. Data banks and scoring methods for this niche are surveyed in depth. Weak data and uneven testing still slow translation to clinics. The authors chart next steps for turning computer finds into real drugs.
pmc-13310660:
Qilong Wang and co-authors link salt habits to single depressive symptoms in a 2026 study. Salt intake may affect mood, but symptom-by-symptom patterns and curve shapes were uncharted. Lumping all depression into one score can hide which feelings actually move with salt.

United States survey data covered 23,753 adults from 2005 to 2023, joined by a separate Chinese clinical group of 700 people for comparison. Adding salt at the table tied to higher odds of eight of nine listed symptoms, with odds ratios from 1.24 to 1.37 across symptoms in the main data. Low self-worth, low mood, and loss of interest led the list. Curve analysis probed non-linear patterns by age, sex, schooling, and blood pressure.
pmc-13310760:
Barbara Choromańska and colleagues track tissue enzymes before and after weight loss surgery in a 2026 study. Severe obesity alters the scaffold that holds tissue together, and enzymes called metalloproteinases cut that scaffold. Their role in obesity and its health harms is still unclear.

Blood enzyme activity was higher in women with severe obesity than in lean controls, with or without metabolic syndrome. Sleeve surgery on the stomach lowered some values, but balance stayed disturbed even 12 months after surgery. Harms lasted longer in women with metabolic syndrome. Long term follow up is needed to judge full recovery of tissue balance.
pmc-13310960:
Ge Yunling and co-authors probe dietary tannins against bone cancer through large scale data in a 2026 study. Osteosarcoma is a harsh bone tumor tied to swelling and cell stress. Plant tannins fight both in lab work, yet their targets in this cancer were unclear, so gene, cell, and tissue maps were joined.

A risk score built from tannin linked genes sorted patients by outlook, with high scores tied to worse survival and fewer killer immune cells. One hub gene, TGFA, marked stem like tumor cells with strong neighbor talk. Cutting TGFA in lab cells slowed growth and spread and raised cell death, while boosting it did the reverse.
pmc-13311160:
Yuehui Zhang and colleagues map in 2026 how the protein neighbourhood of the NLRP3 inflammasome reshuffles as this inflammation machine switches on inside immune cells. The inflammasome sensor and its partner protein ASC were fished from mouse macrophages at priming and activation stages, with partners identified by mass spectrometry. A light-based labelling method added spatial detail around ASC clusters.

Profiling found nearly fifteen hundred stimulus-linked interactions collapsing to about a thousand distinct partners, reorganised stage by stage. Both capture routes converged on IMMT, a protein of the inner mitochondrial membrane, as an activation-stage partner of sensor and adaptor alike. Removing IMMT made the inflammasome fire harder: more caspase cleavage, more inflammatory cytokine release, more cell rupture. IMMT thus acts as a brake on assembly. A stimulus-resolved interaction map gives drug hunters precise points where inflammation might be tuned down.
pmc-13311660:
Reza Majdzadeh and Haniye Sadat Sajadi examine, in a 2026 study, how prolonged economic sanctions have shaped health policy in Iran. Documented analysis of how health systems respond to sanctions remains rare, so the authors first drew together seven of their own earlier studies, spanning document reviews, interviews, Delphi rounds, and policy analyses. They then applied an expanded Theory of Change framework and had an expert panel check the reconstruction.

Across the four stages of the policy cycle, Iranian authorities did adapt, but coordination was fragmented, key assumptions went untested, and structured learning was thin. Weaknesses that surfaced during implementation had often been built in at the design stage. The authors recommend stronger international legal safeguards, protected humanitarian corridors, risk-informed planning, and routine scenario testing for resilience, offering their framework as a template for other countries under long-term pressure.
pmc-13311960:
Marsha Campbell-Yeo and Lior Goldchtaub comment in a 2025 article on a narrative study of parents talking with their preterm babies in neonatal units. Both mothers' and fathers' voices and touch matter, they argue.

Babies born early face higher risk of speech, language, and social problems. Parental presence, interaction, and voice have been tied to better outcomes on cited evidence. The discussed study asked parents what helps or blocks communication with their infants. Feeling close to the baby builds parents' skill and will to interact. Staff, the commentators say, should teach both parents how much this contact counts.
pmc-13312360:
Zongyu Li's 2026 poem 'Practicing with what you left' follows a mourner rehearsing the small rituals of a household after a death. The speaker picks up the dead person's glasses from the nightstand, folds their arms as the owner would, and puts them away. Then the speaker takes them out again, seven times on the first day.

A grey sweater still holds the shape of elbows but not warmth, and smells of camphor and tobacco that are already fading. The hardest object is a pill bottle labeled in the speaker's own handwriting, holding seven tablets that could not keep the person alive. The speaker returns the pills and screws the cap tight, as if something still needed preserving, and closes not yet ready to touch the bottle again tomorrow.
pmc-13312460:
Atte Tapiola and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, whether hemoglobin levels within the normal range relate to knee joint findings in young adults. The data come from the Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1986, whose members had knee MRI scans, exams, and questionnaires at age 33, with 275 people included in the final analysis.

Cartilage lesions were somewhat more frequent in the highest hemoglobin third than the lowest. Bony osteophytes at the shin and thigh bones ran the other way, and joint fluid was more common at high hemoglobin. People with higher hemoglobin also had higher body mass index, blood sugar, cholesterol, and blood pressure. Regression models found only small effects. The authors conclude hemoglobin was not consistently tied to MRI findings in this mostly symptom-free group, apart from slightly more small cartilage lesions at higher levels.
pmc-13313260:
Elyssa M Campbell and co-authors offer a 2026 perspective on prostate cancer. They argue that the 3D folding of the genome is the missing layer in understanding treatment resistance. The androgen receptor drives these tumors, and drugs blocking it work until cancers rewire themselves. The rewiring plays out not just in chemical marks on DNA. It also plays out in how chromatin loops and folds, bringing distant enhancers into contact with genes and reshuffling transcription factor networks.

Standard epigenetic thinking, focused on linear marks, misses those spatial conversations. Drawing on recent biology and new measurement technology, the authors propose a framework built around patient-specific 3D vulnerabilities. The idea is to map how a tumor's chromatin is folded. Therapies can then attack its topology and collapse the gene programs keeping the cancer alive. The piece is a call to widen epigenetic drug development beyond flat maps of the genome.
pmc-13313660:
Ting Wu and colleagues chart, in a 2026 analysis, the research landscape linking retinoic acid receptors to diseases that destroy the brain. Retinoic acid signaling steers cell growth, specialization, and death. Its receptors have drawn growing interest as possible drug targets in brain degeneration. Searching three major databases, the team gathered 1,094 articles. They mapped output, citations, and teamwork by country, institution, author, and keyword.

The United States led clearly with 254 papers and over 17,000 citations, followed by China and Germany. American groups also sat at the center of international collaboration networks. California's university system ranked as the top institution. Core themes included brain inflammation, oxidative stress, and how neurons specialize. Newer work shifts toward microglia, the blood-brain barrier, and models aimed at the clinic. The authors read the field as dynamic and spanning many fields. They urge faster movement from mechanism studies toward clinical testing of receptor-based therapies.
pmc-13314360:
Imen Safer and colleagues measure, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how widely Q fever has spread through sheep in Algeria's Tiaret province. The bacterium Coxiella burnetii usually infects sheep silently but can trigger abortions and weak lambs, and it sickens people as well. Between December 2023 and July 2024 the team tested 184 sheep sera with a commercial antibody assay. They modeled which animal and herd traits tracked with a positive result.

More than a third of the sheep, 37.50 percent at animal level, carried antibodies, marking the infection as endemic. Age and herd size dominated the risk picture. Sheep four years or older had over four times the odds of seropositivity, and flocks above 250 animals showed higher odds still, at 37.47 in the multivariable model. Herd composition and farm type also mattered before adjustment. The authors call for tighter reproductive management, biosecurity, and surveillance under a One Health banner in this major sheep region.
pmc-13314960:
Yafeng Kang, Pengchao Li, Lu Tang, and Chao Zhang apply, in a 2026 study, chaos mathematics to fascination with Tai Chi. Practices live or die on attention, and attention behaves less like trends than like weather. Feeding daily Baidu search index data from 2014 to 2024 for four Chinese provinces through three lenses, the team asked whether the fluctuations are structured, periodic, or chaotic. The lenses were visibility graphs, neural compression, and sparse equations.

All three lenses converged. Every province showed positive chaos exponents by two estimation methods, confirming chaotic dynamics, but intensity varied by region. Beijing's attention was the most chaotic and space-filling, Shanghai's nearly periodic, and Henan's the most orderly. The sparse models recovered governing equations with only about a tenth of terms active, and beat forecasting baselines while staying interpretable. The authors offer the framework as a paradigm for attention, useful to anyone promoting practices.
pmc-13315460:
Pingping Liu and colleagues present, in a 2026 case report with review, a lymphoma hiding in a man's lip. Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the lip is rare, under one percent of extranodal cases of this lymphoma, and its swelling mimics abscesses and cysts. Their patient, a 65-year-old man, was treated for a jaw space infection while his lip swelling worsened. Ultrasound and MRI showed a vague mass, and biopsy with staining showed the germinal center subtype of the disease.

He was treated with the R-CHOP chemotherapy combination and reached remission. The authors draw lessons from the detour: a lip lesion that persists deserves lymphoma on its list of suspects, with biopsy rather than infection treatment. Rare cancers reward teams that can move a case from dental presentations to hematology care without losing time. The review places the case among those reported.
pmc-13315760:
Zifan Zhu and a large team engineered in 2026 a single-dose nanoparticle vaccine that guards against two threats at once, Pseudomonas bacteria and tetanus toxin. Wounds from trauma or disaster can admit both at the same time, no licensed Pseudomonas vaccine exists, and multi-dose courses are hard to finish in emergencies.

Built on a lumazine synthase particle, the vaccine displays a fused Pseudomonas antigen and tetanus toxin fragment C together. In mice it raised antigen uptake and dendritic cell activation, and one shot produced fast, strong antibodies plus three kinds of cytokine-making spleen cells. Lung germ counts and inflammatory signals fell after challenge.
pmc-13316160:
Cyril Salama and colleagues built a workflow in 2026 to cut red blood cell glow that confuses images of inflamed lung. Natural glow from red cells can mimic true signals in close-contact tests for protein links. That hurts counts in wax-set tissue samples.

Their method combines antigen retrieval, careful fluorophore choice, spectral unmixing, and post-processing to separate red cell glow from true IL-4 and IL-4 receptor interaction spots. Tissue structure stays intact while false positives fall. A checked, repeatable routine should let other labs image protein contacts in inflamed tissue with more confidence. Each step in the chain has a clear job to do.
pmc-13316360:
eClinicalMedicine, as issuing journal, published a 2026 editorial warning that drug-resistant infections form a hidden pandemic. Since penicillin arrived in 1928, germs have steadily learned to beat the drugs built to kill them, and the editorial ties that trend to fresh global action.

It cites 1.14 million deaths in 2021 blamed directly on resistance and a forecast of 39 million more deaths between 2025 and 2050 if trends hold. Member states at the 79th World Health Assembly adopted an updated global plan for 2026 to 2036 built on One Health thinking across people, animals, farms, and nature. Prevention, tracking, careful drug use, and steady funding form the core response it urges.
pmc-13316560:
Guy H. Neild writes with colleagues, in a 2026 letter, about families who have blood in the urine and kidney tubule disease yet lack a clear genetic answer. A United States study found harmful variants in collagen genes in only about a third of similar patients. Experience in Cyprus points the same way.

The authors describe twenty Cypriot families with no overt collagen mutations. Most affected members had microscopic bleeding at some point, blood pressure was raised in all, and protein in urine stayed low. Kidney failure still developed in a quarter of older adults. Half carried one of three common collagen variants not classed as harmful. They suggest such variants may predispose to disease alongside other genetic or environmental factors.
pmc-13316760:
Ryo Nakamichi and colleagues report 2026 mouse work on Piezo1, a force-sensing channel, and its role in keeping tendon collagen healthy under everyday loads. Tendons pass muscle force to bone, and sensing that pull helps maintain their matrix, yet the channel's baseline job was unclear.

The team deleted Piezo1 only in tendons of grown female mice, using a switchable gene system. Without it, Achilles tendons grew thinner and their collagen fibers narrower under the microscope. Gene reads showed lower activity in core matrix genes and in tendon identity factors, and staining backed the drop. Nearby muscle stayed untouched, proving the effect tendon-specific. Piezo1 thus helps set fiber build even without heavy loading.
pmc-13317860:
Fariah Mahzabeen and co-authors study, in a 2026 user project, how older adults in Bangladesh take to smartwatches, tools that could ease pressure on clinics as populations age. Most adoption research comes from rich countries, so local, mixed-income voices were missing.

Adults aged sixty or more from varied backgrounds wore a shop-bought watch through three survey rounds and focus groups. Comfort ratings climbed steeply, with those calling it very comfortable rising from 26 percent early on to 80 percent at the final check in the reported figures. Heart rate checking stayed the favorite feature. Daily use held steady while feature use grew late in the study. Missing health features and clear instructions shaped long-term engagement.
pmc-13318560:
Anna Dávidovics and co-authors describe a 2026 project translating the DREEM questionnaire, a widely used measure of the learning environment, into Hungarian for medical and health professions students. No validated Hungarian version had existed before.

Translation and cultural adaptation followed international guidance, and an online survey at the University of Pécs Medical School drew 529 valid replies from medical, dental, and pharmacy students in late 2024. Consistency was excellent and repeat testing held up well, while checks of the original five-part structure gave only partial support. The average score of 135.0 points suggested students viewed their environment positively overall. The authors back its use for benchmarking, with care around the structure findings.
pmc-13318660:
Lu Liu and colleagues present a 2026 prospective cohort study from the UK Biobank. They ask whether following the EAT-Lancet diet lowers the risk of uterine cancer. That eating pattern is promoted for both health and sustainability. No earlier study had tested the uterine cancer link.

The sample held 114,572 women with no uterine cancer at the start. All had at least one day of dietary recall on record. Follow-up averaged 13.26 years, and 694 new cancers appeared. Women with the highest adherence scores had clearly lower risk. Their hazard ratio was 0.706 against the lowest adherence group in adjusted models. Each extra index point linked to 6.9 percent lower risk in the same models.
pmc-13318760:
Sandro Vento writes a 2026 commentary on reforming medical training in low- and middle-income countries. In 2019, national health workforces were short at least 6.4 million physicians, he notes. The shortage bites hardest in low-income settings. Schools must adapt to society's needs without dropping core principles.

Public medical schools carry the central mission, Vento argues. Health ministries must plan graduate numbers and guarantee decent jobs and pay. Otherwise trained doctors leave for high-income countries. He warns schools against chasing rankings and graduation metrics. Lowering standards can fake success while graduates learn little. Accreditation paperwork should not replace serious assessment by experienced faculty. The goal is competent, compassionate doctors who serve their own countries.
pmc-13318960:
Isadora Oliveira de Sousa and co-authors describe a 2026 project building and validating a triage protocol for dental emergencies in Brazil. The protocol adapts the Manchester Triage System and regional oral health guidance. It has nine items, from personal data and pain rating to vital signs and priority class. Expert judges checked its content first.

A pilot ran with 80 patients at a university dental emergency service. Pain was reported by 93.75 percent of patients, mostly spontaneous and intense. Yellow risk labels led at 50 percent, followed by green at 45 percent in the pilot. Average wait to treatment was one hour and thirty-three minutes. Dropout was only 2.5 percent overall. Ten professionals rated the tool, with 97 percent agreement, and judged it clear and relevant.
pmc-13319260:
Daan G J Linders and colleagues introduce, in 2026, a spray-on fluorescent probe that lights up bowel tumours during surgery and endoscopy. Advanced rectal cancer is usually treated with chemoradiation then major surgery, which carries heavy side effects. Tumours are hard to see in the operating room, and judging complete response to chemoradiation is unreliable.

The probe, called PH10, stays dark until it meets the acidic environment around tumours, where it glows in near-infrared light. In mice it separated tumour from background within one minute, and on human tumour samples within ten minutes. No injection into the bloodstream or long waiting period was needed. The authors argue the approach could guide resections, support watch-and-wait decisions and extend to other acidic solid tumours.
pmc-13320260:
Haoming Wu and co-authors review mouth taken gels for lower gut illness in a 2026 article that shifts focus from disease first to microbe first design. The lower gut hosts a dense microbe world that guards the gut wall, tunes immunity, and shapes body balance. Standard drugs for gut swelling, bowel pain, and bowel cancer often dissolve poorly, wash through fast, or harm the whole body.

Soft gels that ride through the stomach and free their load in the bowel can answer many of those faults, with traits tuned to gut cues. Past work aimed gels at calming swelling, repair, or tumor kill and treated microbes as a side note. Newer plans design the gel around microbe needs first, and the review maps that shift plus the trade talks among gel, microbes, and host.
pmc-13320460:
Tekletsadik Tekleslassie Alemayehu and co-authors pool studies on poor antibiotic use in Ethiopian hospitals in a 2026 review. Wrong use of these drugs drives drug proof germs and harms patients, yet a pooled count for the country was missing. Past studies were swept from five main databases plus grey sources in a two week search in December 2025 and pooled with a model that allows for wide spread.

Twelve studies entered the pool, and the shared count put wrong use near two in five hospital patients in the estimate reported, though studies clashed very widely. Wrong reason for the drug and wrong course length were the most common faults. Other illness at the same time stood among the drivers named. The team urges stewardship drives in wards.
pmc-13321260:
Ercha Hu and colleagues survey disease germs in desert rodents and ticks in a 2026 field study from Xinjiang, China. Sampling ran from October 2024 to June 2025 on the southern edge of the Gurbantunggut Desert. Rodents and their parasites can carry germs that pass to people, yet this dry region was little studied.

Teams collected 142 gerbils and 361 ticks and tested them for Rickettsia and Bartonella gene marks. Bartonella was common in rodents, at 40.14 percent, while spotted fever group rickettsiae appeared in only 1.11 percent of tick samples in the study. Gerbils look like key Bartonella hosts, and one tick type carried Rickettsia conorii, which maps local risk.
pmc-13321360:
Mahnaz Ashrafi and co-authors add energy use to brain network maps in a 2026 study. Brain regions burn energy unevenly, with memory and attention hubs among the hungriest, yet standard connectivity maps treat all regions alike. The team built a metabolism-weighted connectome from combined PET and MRI scans in healthy volunteers.

The most energy hungry hubs anchored networks for complex thought and carried molecular signs of intense synaptic activity. Those same hubs were hit hardest in Alzheimer's disease patterns. The authors propose a unifying rule: regions most vital for cognition pay the highest energy cost, and that cost may leave them open to degeneration. Energy aware maps could guide future brain research.
pmc-13321560:
Shangwen Lu and co-authors compare ten ways to forecast monthly hepatitis B cases in China in a 2026 study. Sound forecasts guide long term disease control planning, but rival methods had rarely been judged on one national series with a fair test design. Monthly reported cases from January 2004 to December 2024 were drawn from public surveillance data.

Models trained on data to 2023 were tested against held back 2024 cases, using 252 monthly observations in all. The mean monthly reported count was 91,901 cases in the data. Classic seasonal models, machine learning models, and hybrid versions were scored on several error measures, and the best were used to project 2025 counts.
pmc-13321760:
Noel Gahamanyi and a large team assess Rwanda's national reference laboratory during the 2024 Marburg outbreak in a 2026 report. Rwanda faced its first Marburg virus disease outbreak in September 2024. The review used a World Health Organization tool for haemorrhagic fever lab capacity, plus quality checks such as turnaround time, observation, records, and staff interviews.

The laboratory scored 98 percent overall in the assessment. Every area scored full marks except lab system quality, at 89 percent, held back by a lack of external quality checks for Marburg testing. Mapping of testing sites and response records complete a picture of a fast, well run national response that other centres can learn from.
pmc-13322860:
Xichao Wu and colleagues compare incretin-based drugs for type 2 diabetes in a 2026 network meta-analysis of clinical trials. They covered 15 therapies, from single-action GLP-1 drugs to dual and triple receptor drugs, across 102 trials with 98,693 patients.

All drug classes beat placebo on blood sugar control in their analysis, with tirzepatide, orforglipron and semaglutide among the strongest for that outcome, and retatrutide strongest for weight loss. Gains also appeared for lipids, blood pressure and kidney and insulin measures. Side effects were mainly mild gut symptoms that passed, and low blood sugar stayed uncommon. Higher doses helped more but caused more side effects, so the authors back choices fitted to each patient.
pmc-13323160:
Berg and co-authors test a virtual reality animation for teaching drug absorption in this 2026 study. Absorption and bioavailability, the share of a dose reaching the blood, are hard for pharmacology students to picture. Weak pharmacology knowledge is one cause of medication errors. Students who had finished a basic pharmacology course watched the animation at five international sites.

In total 133 students completed a questionnaire, and about half said the animation changed their understanding of absorption. Thirteen medical students in Bergen also joined focus group interviews. Their comments formed three themes about linking pharmacology to other subjects, balancing engagement against overload, and learning deeply while facing exams. Berg concludes the tool works well and engages students, but it must allow self pacing so learners are not overwhelmed.
pmc-13323860:
Chun Gao and team tested an AI-guided communication plan for surgical trainees talking with patients about metabolic bariatric surgery. Their 2026 randomized study assigned 40 trainees to either the VALUE framework, which structures validation, alignment, education, and joint planning through a large language model, or self-directed learning. Each trainee then held simulated consultations with standardized patients, scored for shared decision-making, communication quality, and choice conflict.

The AI-guided group scored significantly higher on joint choices and talk quality, and lower on choice conflict, with consultation outlines rated nearly twice as good. Trainees also reported larger gains in self-trust for giving facts, using patient values, helping choices, and offering emotional support, and results held after correction for multiple comparisons. The authors call the plan promising for training, while noting that larger multi-site trials must confirm it in real clinics.
pmc-13324160:
Pooja Jadiya and team tested whether blocking calcium uptake in neurons can slow Alzheimer disease. Their 2026 study used genetic mouse models to delete the mitochondrial calcium uniporter channel in neurons of 3xTg-AD mice, a robust Alzheimer model. It probed a mechanism in which lost calcium efflux drives calcium overload in cells. Cell lab work with Mcu knockdown backed the animal work.

Losing calcium uptake in neurons reduced amyloid beta and tau pathology, synapse trouble, and cognitive decline in the mice. In cells, knockdown lowered matrix calcium, redox imbalance, and cell dysfunction, while restoring cell cleanup and protecting neurons against amyloid toxicity and death. Imaging confirmed improved structure in the treated mice. The authors propose blocking calcium uptake in neurons as a powerful therapeutic target for impeding disease progression.
pmc-13324460:
Keita Soda and co-authors test a shortcut for counting viruses in water in a 2026 methods study. Standard testing first extracts viral genetic material, a slow step that dirty samples can block.

Heat and pressure treatment breaks virus particles open directly, skipping extraction. With pepper mild mottle virus as the model, the best setting was 120 °C for 15 seconds, matching results from normal extraction. Heat above 140 °C damaged the genome and hurt accuracy. Results held up across qPCR and digital PCR and stayed steady in wastewater. The team suggests the approach could speed routine virus checks and suit automated, near real-time monitoring once more virus types are validated.
pmc-13324560:
Samanta Dodino and colleagues use camera traps and AI to track penguin breeding timing across the sub-Antarctic in a 2026 study. When birds breed shapes their fit with the environment, and warming seas may shift those dates.

A time-lapse camera network around Patagonia watched Southern Rockhopper and Macaroni Penguins, with citizen help and automated reading pulling dates from images. Rockhoppers arrived on time but left earlier, shrinking their season. Macaronis both arrived and left earlier, a shift rather than a squeeze. Dates tracked winter sea surface temperatures most closely. Breeding success stayed steady in both species, which suggests flexible timing, though hidden costs for populations remain possible.
pmc-13325160:
Karthikeyan Venkatachalam and co-authors compare powders made from tangerine peel of three Thai cultivars in a 2026 food study. The peel, a citrus byproduct, is rich in useful compounds that often go to waste.

Cho Kun, Sai Nam Phueng, and Bang Mod powders all stored well, with water activity below 0.30 in every batch. Cho Kun led on phenolics at 49.98 mg per g and flavonoids at 36.11 mg per g of dry weight. Its antioxidant scores also topped the set, and its vitamin C reached 76.78 mg per 100 g. All powders fought Bacillus cereus, with clear zones from 20.91 to 29.33 mm. D-limonene dominated the scent profile throughout.
pmc-13325360:
Thamires Martinho Prados, Leda Maria Saragiotto Colpini, and Giancarlo Alfonso Lovón-Canchumani assess the life cycle of neodymium-iron-boron magnets in Brazil in a 2026 study. These rare earth magnets drive wind turbines and electric motors, but their supply chain is dirty.

Modeling followed ISO 14040 and 14044 rules with SimaPro software and EcoInvent data. Mining hurt most, above all the roasting step, which burns much energy and emits particles and greenhouse gases. Acid leaching in oxide making added marine and radiation burdens. Machining in magnet making drove warming, ozone, and water impacts. The authors urge tighter rules, recycling loops, and cleaner power to shrink the footprint.
pmc-13325860:
Peter W. Bright and colleagues pair chemical screening with fish toxicity tests on tap water in a 2026 study from western Oregon. Unknown and emerging contaminants slip past routine water checks.

Twelve public tap samples and one bottled water went through high-resolution mass spectrometry workflows. Suspect screening named 52 likely compounds, and 13 were confirmed, including the fungicide propiconazole and a plasticizer. One confirmed find, 18β-glycyrrhetinic acid, had not been reported in drinking water before. Zebrafish embryos showed shape harm from that compound and from a phthalate mix. Behavior shifts followed one single compound and seven mixes. The paired approach widens safety screening.
pmc-13326360:
Xian Yu and a large team study the enzyme cathepsin S in macrophages after brain bleeding in a 2026 paper. Bleeding inside the brain damages white matter, and no therapy yet targets macrophage-led repair of that wiring.

A mouse model of intracerebral hemorrhage was treated with the cathepsin S blocker LY3000328. Single-cell sequencing of tissue near the clot found infiltrating macrophages, above all a fat-handling group, carrying most of the enzyme signal. Blocking the enzyme dampened that lipid program and lowered ApoE, ABCA1, and ABCG1 levels. Culture tests with precursor cells probed whether macrophage fat support for new myelin suffers, with an LXR drug used as rescue.
pmc-13326960:
Akinori Yamaguchi and team tested if a steady sodium drip added to long-term renal replacement therapy lifts results. Their 2026 re-use of past data took in 46 people with sudden kidney harm needing care for at least seven days. Of these, 24 got plain support and 22 got support plus the steady sodium drip.

People needing such long care tend to fare poorly. Steady blood flow is a key hurdle. The drip group held blood flow steadier, passed more urine, and kept a better fluid balance. Staying alive at 90 days with no need for kidney care hit 42.9% with the drip, against 12.5% with plain care in this group. Staying alive to ICU discharge hit 68.2% against 29.2%. Rates of stopping kidney care were far higher. The team holds that the sodium drip may shore up blood flow and lift stopping and staying-alive rates in this high-risk group.
pmc-13327860:
Bandar S Alharbi, Majed M Aljabri, and Endale Alemayehu Ali map mental routes into diabetes distress in a 2026 survey study from Saudi Arabia. Distress from daily diabetes care affects up to 36 percent of people with type 2 diabetes and worsens outcomes. The team surveyed 438 adults at four primary care centers.

Checked scales measured pain catastrophizing, views of illness, and distress, and modeling traced paths among them. Dwelling on pain and holding emotional views of illness both fed distress directly, and pain rumination also fed distress through the emotional route, with an indirect effect of 0.34 in their model. Grouping methods split patients into burden profiles, pointing to where counseling could help most.
pmc-13328360:
Yu Sun, Qian Liu, and Xiaona Liu study what builds employability in Chinese university students in a 2026 survey. Graduate numbers rise yearly and jobs grow more competitive, so the team tested how career planning and self-concept feed job readiness, and whether learning attitude carries their effects. Questionnaires covered 735 undergraduates in Hebei Province.

All three factors, career planning, self-concept, and learning attitude, lifted employability directly in the structural model. Learning attitude also sat in the middle, passing part of the benefit of planning and of a healthy self-concept into readiness. Universities should help students draw clear career plans and build a sound self-view, the authors advise, since attitude turns both into action.
pmc-13329660:
Isabela DeJohn and colleagues study whether preventive vancomycin by mouth stops repeat gut infection in young cancer patients in a 2026 report. Clostridioides difficile can return when broad antibiotics are given again. Adult data hint at benefit, but child data are scarce. Records covered primary infections treated from 2017 to 2024.

The starting group held 163 patients. After exclusions, 72 patients received 150 broad antibiotic courses within 6 months of their first infection. Repeat infection arose in 17.9 percent of courses without preventive treatment and 7.4 percent with it in the raw counts given. Matched analysis linked prevention to lower risk. Small size and bias risks mean the finding needs larger tests, the authors caution.
pmc-13330360:
Shiyu Li and co-authors survey low mood in fathers of preterm babies in intensive care in a 2026 study. Fathers in a Gansu hospital unit were surveyed two to three days after admission, between November 2024 and October 2025. In total, 379 fathers completed mood, personality, and family function scales.

With a mood scale cut point of 10 or more, 29.55 percent screened positive for depressive symptoms in the reported results. Higher income band, paternity leave, and mid-range birth weight each linked to lower odds in the models given. Some personality traits raised odds, while outgoing traits lowered them. Weak family function linked to far higher odds. Early support for fathers is warranted, the authors argue.
pmc-13330660:
Arkadeep Dhali and team tested GLP-1 receptor agonists for pain management in chronic pancreatitis. Their 2026 look-back cohort study from the TriNetX US Network compared adults given GLP-1 receptor agonists against controls, using one-to-one propensity matching for age, sex, race, and comorbidities over three years. Chronic pancreatitis is a crippling illness with lasting gland destruction and stubborn pain, and GLP-1 agonists showed anti-inflammatory effects in lab models, yet their patient impact here remained unknown.

GLP-1 agonist users had 41% lower hazard of starting chronic opioids and 42% lower hazard of opioid use disorder. Therapy was also linked with much lower risk of celiac plexus block, endoscopic treatments, and major pancreatic surgery, with hazard ratios of 0.51, 0.48, and 0.44 in that order. The team concludes that GLP-1 agonist use meant far fewer new opioid orders and invasive treatments, hinting these drugs may help symptom control and team-based care of chosen cases.
pmc-13331960:
Ramazan Bayat and colleagues built a near-infrared sensor for dopamine in a 2026 nanotechnology study, using single-walled carbon nanotubes wrapped in a repeating short DNA strand. Dopamine is a key brain messenger, and detecting it selectively among other body chemicals is a standing challenge.

The wrapped nanotubes glow in the near infrared. Their brightness rose as dopamine levels increased across the tested range of 10 to 100 µM, while other biological samples gave no matching response. The detection limit worked out to 4.2 × 10−5 M, with a quantification limit of 13.24 × 10−5 M. Because nanotube glow does not fade or blink like ordinary dyes, the authors see the sensor as a candidate for longer-term dopamine monitoring tasks.
pmc-13333360:
Huimin Huo and co-authors optimized a greener way to pull health-giving polyphenols out of the truffle Tuber formosanum in a 2026 study. The fungus is prized as food and medicine, yet no efficient, low-impact extraction recipe for its polyphenols existed.

Ultrasound-assisted extraction first beat older methods head to head, giving 14.7 percent more yield than hot reflux while using 7.5 times less energy. Statistical screening named power, time, temperature, and alcohol strength as the levers that matter. Surface modeling fixed the best recipe at 95 minutes, 210 W, 70 °C, and 60 percent ethanol, lifting total polyphenol content to 2.72 mg/g, a gain of 16.24 percent. Importance analysis confirmed power as the dominant factor. The optimized extract also scavenged radicals and reduced iron more strongly in standard antioxidant tests. The authors present the recipe plus its explainable modeling as a template for other rare fungi.
pmc-13333460:
Andreea-Emanuela Baciu and colleagues ask whether fluid collecting between a trauma patient's brain hemispheres forecasts later hydrocephalus, in a 2026 retrospective study. Removing part of the skull saves lives after severe head injury, but in half of survivors the injured brain later swells with trapped fluid, sometimes needing a shunt.

The trauma-center review covered 104 patients older than 15 who had decompressive craniectomy for head injury between 2011 and 2025. Half developed radiological hydrocephalus. On multivariable analysis, the thickness of the interhemispheric hygroma, the fluid pocket between the hemispheres, tracked the diagnosis independently, with odds rising 19 percent per millimetre, and it also predicted needing treatment. Discrimination for treatment need was good, with an AUC of 0.81, and a thickness near 8 millimetres marked the practical alert level. The authors propose the simple tape-measure number, taken from routine scans, as a cheap early-warning sign, while asking for outside validation.
pmc-13333760:
Rui Jiang and co-authors tested intermittent theta burst stimulation for leg weakness after stroke in a 2026 randomized study. They tracked recovery with a standard motor scale and with functional near-infrared spectroscopy, which watches cortical activity during tasks.

Sixty-six patients with post-stroke hemiplegia were split evenly between real stimulation plus basic rehabilitation and sham stimulation plus the same rehabilitation. After four weeks the treated group scored better on the Fugl-Meyer lower limb scale. Brain recordings also differed, with stronger task-related activation over the injured side's premotor and primary motor areas and the opposite side's somatosensory area. The combined behavioral and imaging gains suggest this brief magnetic stimulation pattern can aid leg rehabilitation.
pmc-13334060:
Shigeki Tsutsui and colleagues develop a 2026 method to detect Alzheimer-type dementia from bloodstream white blood cells using glow methods and machine learning. Alzheimer-type dementia is the most common cause of dementia, with numbers projected to rise sharply in coming decades. Disease-changing therapies are welcome, yet early treatment maximizes their benefits, so reliable finding from an accessible matrix such as blood matters. The team aimed to detect Alzheimer-type dementia from bloodstream white blood cells using spectral confocal imaging.

Using K114-stained wild type and 5xFAD engineered mouse brain sections as proof-of-principle, spectral imaging of K114 glow was tested. A signal processing and machine learning workflow reliably told apart non-plaque background tissue between strains. The workflow combined spectral wavelet breakdown, dimension cutting, and a support vector machine sorter.  The work points toward a blood-based optical test for early dementia finding.
pmc-13334760:
Yousra Mhande and colleagues report a 2026 case of same-time inside- and outside-abdomen DDLPS. DDLPS tumors are a group of tumors with different types, some more harsh, most often arising in the outside the abdomen, while occurrence within the abdomen cavity is uncommon. Symptoms are usually nonspecific. The case presented major workup and treatment challenges as a combined inside- and outside-abdomen DDLPS.

The patient was a 63-year-old woman with returning outside-abdomen DDLPS who arrived with right upper belly discomfort and progressive belly swelling. Clinical and imaging exams revealed two-sided masses: a left inside-abdomen mass and a right outside-abdomen mass. She underwent debulking surgery involving removal of the inside-abdomen mass, while the outside-abdomen tumor was deemed unremovable due to invasion of the main lower vena cava. Tissue study confirmed DDLPS. Follow-up exams are detailed in the full report.
pmc-13336360:
Benke Huo and co-authors used entropy to decode what makes a metal alloy form glass in a 2026 materials study. The best glass-forming compositions have traditionally been found by the deep eutectic rule of thumb or by trial and error.

Their entropy engineering strategy starts from eutectic or intermetallic phases whose melting entropies can be measured precisely, favoring those with the lowest values. For copper-zirconium-titanium alloys, glass-forming ability ranked in step with the melting entropies of the starting phases. The optimal composition they designed, Cu59.99Zr28.75Ti11.26, landed essentially on the known champion Cu60Zr30Ti10. The authors claim the first quantitative account of the phase competition behind glass formation, giving alloy designers a measurable target instead of lore.
pmc-13338760:
Ki Young Huh, Gaeun Kang, and Kye Hun Kim assess readiness for remote clinical trials across Korea in a 2026 regional study. Trials cluster heavily in Seoul, limiting access elsewhere. Seventeen regions were scored on specialists, nurses, beds, and equipment per patient.

Data covered 1,924 approved trials and 7,760 trial-center pairs as reported. No province outside Seoul reached 80 percent of Seoul's specialist density in the reported comparison, while bed density varied most widely. Combined readiness scores for four disease areas moved together across regions. Gwangju stood out among provinces, showing where remote trial hubs could grow first.
pmc-13341360:
Tomás González-Vidal and colleagues studied low blood sugar after glucose tolerance testing in 2026 in 2,924 adults without known diabetes from the Di@bet.es Study. Participants took a 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test with glucose and insulin measured at 0, 30, and 120 minutes, allowing insulin resistance estimation by HOMA-IR and Matsuda indices. Groups were set by 120 minute glucose: under 70, 70 to under 140, 140 to under 200, and 200 or more milligrams per decilitre.

Clinical features, incident diabetes, and mortality were then compared across groups over follow up, median age 49 with 1,680 women. Post test low sugar may signal distinct metabolic risk rather than reassurance. The study clarifies whether a low result after glucose loading predicts future diabetes or death.
pmc-13343460:
Haruko Tateyama and co-authors synthesize new uranium complexes in 2026, pairing a bulky imidophosphorane ligand with alkyl, benzyl, and hydride groups on tetravalent uranium. Mixed-ligand uranium alkyls are prized but tricky, since uranium-carbon bonds break down easily, so the team built them step by step from a monoiodide starting material.

The route gave benzyl, neopentyl, and methyl versions cleanly, and no fully substituted homoleptic product formed even with excess ligand salt. Chemical oxidation of the neopentyl complex yielded a cationic product holding an ether molecule rather than a uranium(V) alkyl. Hydrogen gas at low temperature produced a terminal hydride, confirmed by NMR and deuterium labeling, which then broke down quickly on warming.
pmc-13344860:
Yuriy Pya and co-authors document a 2026 case replacing two heart valves by catheter in one session. A 68-year-old woman faced severe aortic stenosis plus a mitral valve choked by heavy calcium. She also had severe obesity, diabetes, kidney disease, past chest surgery, and a pacemaker. Open surgery was out of reach.

Planning leaned on a patient-specific 3D-printed heart model, which set implant depth and prompted a fabric skirt addition to the mitral prosthesis. A self-expanding aortic valve went in through the leg first, anchored partly, then a balloon-expandable mitral valve followed through the heart tip. Both seated with no leak around them, though a moderate outflow gradient remained.
pmc-13347360:
Mei Qiu and colleagues grade mine groundwater quality at the Huafeng coal mine with a combined scoring framework, in a study published in 2026. Mine water must be drained to stop roof flooding, yet its reuse needs sound grading. So the team merged game-theory weighting, fuzzy classing, and ideal-point ranking to balance expert and data-driven weights for sandstone aquifer samples.

Quality looked badly degraded, with every sample past Class V limits for dissolved solids and 77.3 percent past that class for total hardness in the reported checks. Sodium and chloride led the pollutants, and rock-water contact inside a folded, confined structure drove the chemistry, with shallow southern water fed sideways and shaped by mineral breakdown.
pmc-13348660:
Sandra C Perez-Hernandez and co-authors told in 2026 of a case of Goltz-Gorlin syndrome, also called focal dermal hypoplasia, in a 49-year-old woman. This rare X-linked dominant illness stems from faulty growth of mesoderm and ectoderm. It hits mainly females. It can touch skin, eyes, teeth, bones, gut, urinary tract, heart, and nervous system.

She came in with many wart-like lumps that began in the mouth and spread elsewhere. Checks found tiny verrucous lumps plus soft yellow oval lumps over a dark patch that followed Blaschko lines. The case plus past work maps the multi-system pattern clinicians should spot. Early spotting matters for joined care across skin, dental, eye, and other fields that these patients often need.
pmc-13349260:
Ruby Kasana and colleagues profiled eating epilepsy in patients from Northeast India, in a 2026 case series from a tertiary hospital in Assam. Eating epilepsy is a rare reflex epilepsy, seen most in South Asian populations, in which eating triggers seizures through insular and perisylvian brain networks. The team reviewed consecutive cases from 2018 to 2025 with clinical, EEG, and imaging records.

Twenty-six patients, mostly young adults with a mean age of 23.9 years, had focal seizures that began in adolescence, and 65.4 percent were male. Rice-related triggers appeared in 30.8 percent, EEG abnormalities in 88.5 percent, and MRI abnormalities in 23.1 percent. The series maps a little-known condition and gives regional clinicians a baseline for diagnosis and treatment.
pmc-13350260:
Liyang Cai and Yuki Nakanishi wrote a 2026 commentary on natural product nanoengineering for gastrointestinal stromal tumours, cancers that resist lasting control despite targeted drugs. Relapse, spread, and resistance to kinase inhibitors still limit treatment.

Zinc oxide nanoparticles draw interest because they generate reactive oxygen, stress cells, and nudge death pathways. Most studies so far use other tumour types, with few examples in tissue like GIST. A recent extension of the approach into GIST is treated as promising but early. The authors balance that promise against the gap between bench results and a therapy patients can actually receive.
pmc-13350360:
Zhenpeng Jiang and co-authors examined how measuring washout timing in contrast ultrasound changes liver cancer diagnosis in a 2026 study. Contrast ultrasound helps classify liver lumps when CT or MRI leave doubt, and when the contrast fades from a lump is a key sign.

For high-risk patients scanned between 2020 and 2021, the team compared washout time read by eye against software-measured values, all against tissue-proven truth. The two readings shifted standard category assignments and accuracy for hepatocellular carcinoma differently, and the authors derived a best software threshold. Precise timing could reduce reader disagreement on a sign that often decides the diagnosis.
pmc-13351960:
Minmin Hu and Chuanfeng Wu write a 2026 letter refining how GLUT1 should be read in non-small cell lung cancer. Their comment responds to work by Hantzsch-Kuhn and co-authors using a large tissue array cohort. High GLUT1 protein linked to worse tumour traits and poorer survival, and staining was stronger in squamous cancer than in glandular cancer.

GLUT1, though, dropped out as an independent survival factor once other traits were counted. Hu and Wu praise the split analysis by subtype but raise biological and method concerns. Immune cells in the tumour setting can also take up much glucose, which clouds a simple tumour-cell reading. They argue more care is needed before GLUT1 guides prognosis or treatment choice.
pmc-13352060:
Stefan Bauer and co-authors wrote in 2026 a letter on wobble risk in cuff-deficient reverse shoulder surgery. The implant angle was 135 degrees. The letter replies to a study that found early X-ray findings were not linked to wobble. The first data came from a highly experienced surgeon. A new metaphyseal-fixated stem system was used. The data deserved praise. Yet the authors argued for an added biomechanical reading.

Drawing on pioneering work by Lippitt and Matsen, the letter explains cup mechanics. A larger glenoid arc steadies a wider range of joint force angles through the humeral head. Liner constraint and cup compression interact with implant angle to set stability. In cuff-deficient shoulders, these mechanics may explain wobble that X-ray findings alone miss.
pmc-13352160:
Mehaboobathunnisa Sahul Hameed leads a 2026 review of AI methods for judging tumour cellularity in digital pathology. How much of a sample is tumour affects gene test quality and treatment choice. Pathologists now estimate the share by eye, and scores vary between readers.

AI systems read digitised slides and return objective cellularity scores that can show whether enough tumour is present for testing. The review gathers public datasets and benchmark tools, compares automated methods, and lists research and commercial options. Barriers to clinic use are covered too, including the need for clear outputs that match how pathologists reason. The authors frame AI as support for, not replacement of, expert review.
pmc-13355260:
Zhaoxia Li and co-authors report a 2026 case of a 73-year-old man with severe gout plus prostate cancer and kidney disease. He had lived with gout for over 20 years, with large lumps of urate crystals, and standard flare drugs were unsafe for him. The team gave a single shot of firsekibart, a drug that blocks a key swelling signal, plus a short steroid course.

Pain and swelling eased within a day, and swelling markers fell sharply over three months. Urate levels reached target on a second drug, kidney function improved, and no tumor growth, bad infections, or heart events appeared. The authors urge larger studies to confirm long-term safety in such high-risk patients.
pmc-13355760:
Tamar Kinaciyan and co-authors report interim results in 2026 from KONFIDENT-S, a long-term study of oral sebetralstat for swelling attacks in hereditary angioedema. Even on preventive therapy, patients still get breakthrough attacks of painful, sometimes dangerous swelling. Thirty-five patients on one of three preventive drugs treated 382 attacks with the study drug and tracked relief times.

Patients took the drug a median of six minutes after spotting an attack. Relief began at a median of about one hour, severity fell by about four hours, and attacks fully ended at about fifteen hours. Results were much like across all three preventive drugs, and no serious treatment-linked harms appeared.
pmc-13356460:
Tingting Xu and Shuhong Li argued in a 2026 letter for risk-stratified care of placenta site nodules with atypical traits. One series found no bad transformation in twenty-two atypical cases, contrasting with eleven to fifteen percent rates of birth trophoblastic neoplasia in earlier series. That discrepancy exposes diagnostic difficulty.

Histologic overlap risks overdiagnosis, and expert agreement was only fair, with consensus often needing three or more worrisome traits such as mitotic action, Ki67 of five percent or more, and necrosis. Lack of look-back review for prior trophoblastic tumours further limits match. The letter urges stratified follow-up based on feature count and harm review, rather than a single rule for all atypical nodules.
pmc-13356760:
Eduardo Solís García and co-authors report a 2026 case of a 75-year-old man with a new squamous cell lung cancer inside his left main airway. He was a former heavy smoker who had lost a right lung lobe to the same cancer type twenty years earlier. The new tumor nearly blocked the airway split, causing severe breathlessness and low oxygen, and surgery was ruled out given his prior operation.

He received focused internal radiation, called brachytherapy, in six weekly doses placed inside the airway. The tumor vanished fully on scope checks and stayed gone at six months. The authors present the method as a strong option for selected airway tumors when surgery or external radiation cannot be used.
pmc-13360760:
The 2026 abstracts of the 7th World Parkinson Congress collect pre-congress course talks and congress presentations on Parkinson's disease research and care. Parkinson's disease is a growing neurodegenerative illness marked by motor symptoms from loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra, with non-motor traits affecting smell, sleep, and autonomic function. Its harm centres on alpha-synuclein aggregates, Lewy bodies, and Lewy neurites.

Course talks cover alpha-synuclein and Lewy harm in brain and periphery, with spread to spinal cord and enteric nervous system. The collection gives doctors and teams a broad snapshot of current Parkinson's science, from tiny harm to medical manifestations, in a single congress volume.
pmc-13361460:
Rubens Camargo Siqueira reviews light therapy for retinal diseases in a 2026 paper. Photobiomodulation uses red and near-infrared light at gentle levels to nudge sick cells toward health. It needs no surgery and no drugs. The review explains the molecular chain the light sets off inside the retina's cells, starting in the power plants called mitochondria.

A cell enzyme, cytochrome c oxidase, absorbs the light at its metal centers. The catch frees a blocking gas, nitric oxide, so energy flow speeds up and the cell makes more ATP fuel. Brief stress signals then switch on defense genes that raise antioxidant shields. Siqueira lays out how these steps could protect the retina, and what proof is still needed before clinics adopt the method.
pmc-13361760:
İzzet Melih Gürkan and co-authors tested a new blood-clot material for gum stem cells in a 2026 lab study. Platelet-rich fibrin is a membrane made from a patient's own blood, widely used to aid dental healing. How the blood tube is coated may change the membrane's structure and power. The team compared fibrin made in plain glass tubes, titanium tubes, and tubes coated with nano-hydroxyapatite, a bone-like mineral.

Gum tissue and blood came from one healthy male volunteer. Stem cells from the gum were grown with each membrane type. A standard test measured how alive and active the cells stayed. If a mineral coating makes the membrane kinder to stem cells, dentists could gain a better healing aid made chairside from the patient's own blood.
pmc-13362360:
Yerkezhan Tolegenova and colleagues published a 2026 study of how much older adults in Astana, Kazakhstan move each day. They surveyed 608 adults aged 60 and older, most of them women, and measured their daily activity with a standard scale made for older people. They also checked body fat, waist size, muscle mass, and hand grip strength.

Most of the group had a moderate activity level, gained mainly from walking and house tasks. Higher activity went with a bit less deep belly fat and a stronger grip, but all of the links were weak. The authors warn that one survey at one time cannot prove cause, yet the work gives Central Asia a first set of local baseline numbers for later studies on aging and health.
pmc-13362760:
Paschalis Karakasis and a large team wrote a 2026 review on atrial fibrillation in people with diabetes. The two conditions often pair up and together mark high risk for stroke, heart failure, and early death. The review spans how common the pairing is, the body changes that drive it, and how care should run from early risk through established disease.

High blood sugar, insulin resistance, swelling, and fat around the heart can scar and rewire the upper heart chambers. As the authors explain, that makes the erratic rhythm easier to start and harder to stop. Care must go beyond rhythm drugs and blood thinners, they argue, to weight, blood pressure, kidney health, and sleep apnea, with checks tuned to each patient's risk.
pmc-13363060:
Laura Grech and Nikolai Paul Pace offer a 2026 perspective on the role of small biobanks in AI-driven genomic medicine. The field often assumes that more data is the main road to trust, yet the authors push back. Small collections, from national and regional banks to hospital and disease-specific sets, reflect local patients closely and carry tight links to clinic records and clear consent rules.

In their view, these banks serve best as proving grounds: models built on huge datasets should be tested, tuned, and checked for fairness on small local sets before real use. Such tests expose weak spots in rare variant calls, privacy care, and fit to local ancestry. Trust, they argue, is earned in these hard local checks, not by scale alone.
pmc-13363160:
Xiaofang Chen presents a 2026 computer modeling study of chabazite, a zeolite sieve, loaded with alkaline-earth metal ions. Zeolites act as molecular sieves in industry, and swapping in different ions tunes what they catch. Chen modeled dried forms holding beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, or barium ions, predicting their crystal shapes, electron traits, and how strongly each ion grips the frame, all by periodic density functional theory.

The five forms kept near-identical frames with slight twists. As the ions grew heavier, each sat closer to the center of the sieve's eight-ring window, and the energy gap and grip strength shifted in clear trends. The beryllium form stood out with the widest gap and strongest grip. The predictions may guide the design of new sieves.
pmc-13364660:
Leqi Xu and others brought in MIXPRS, a plan for multi-people polygenic risk scores using summary statistics, in 2026. Many multi-people risk score ways aim to improve forecast in underrepresented groups, yet no single method wins across all scenarios. Combining ways could help, but usually needs single-level tuning data that are often unavailable.

MIXPRS uses a data fission approach to combine multiple multi-people ways from genome-wide link summary statistics alone, with SNP pruning to reduce linkage disequilibrium mismatch and non-clear least squares for weighting. The plan helps forecast without private tuning cohorts. Genetic teams gain a useful tool for fairer risk forecast across ancestries.
pmc-13365860:
Zhekang Peng and co-workers sum up in 2026 the role of a cell brake gene, NLRC3, in the late immune crash of sepsis. Sepsis first fires the immune guard too hard, then a long calm can leave folks bare to new germs. This brake gene dips in the first hours, then climbs with time.

Its climb can blunt many guard cell types, they note, which feeds the crash phase. Past work ties the gene to that dip and climb in set cell sets. The team frames the gene as a drug aim to right the immune scale and cut late deaths in sepsis care.
pmc-13366360:
Iddi Mapande and co-workers link in 2026 ten years of malaria counts in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, to rain and heat shifts. The coast city grows fast, and its germ risk by month was not well mapped. The team splits trend and season, then fits bend math to the counts.

Case rates fell by more than three fourths in the span, yet a set peak still hits each year just after the rains. Rain one to two months back drives the peak most, and warm nights near a set heat aid it. Warn plans should key on past rain, not just the sky now.
pmc-13367160:
Yuting Feng and Mingqi Zhang sum up in 2026 stem cell shed bits as a care path for dry eye ill, a tear film fault that stings and blurs. The bits calm swell, tune immune acts, and aid heal, with no live cells to seed growths. They can drop on the eye with ease.

Tricks to load the bits, mix them, or set them in gels can lift their stay and aim. Cord stem bits look most ripe for clinic use. Gaps stay: eye walls block uptake, make and store rules lack, and safe proof is thin. The pair map the road to trials.
pmc-13367960:
Mennillo and colleagues apply single-cell spatial transcriptomics, a method mapping which genes are active in individual cells at their exact tissue locations, to archived colon biopsies in 2026 gastroenterology research. The biopsies, preserved in paraffin blocks from healthy controls, ulcerative colitis patients, and patients with checkpoint-inhibitor colitis, were arrayed together for comparison. Three datasets tested different commercial imaging panels, asking which combination best resolves the cell networks that organize inflamed gut tissue.

One platform, MERSCOPE, failed on these samples: only 0.17 percent of its cells passed quality control, so it was dropped from the analysis. Custom Xenium panels of 290 and 480 targeted genes, plus an expanded panel of roughly 5,000 genes, performed the core comparisons. The custom panels gave better sensitivity and cell-type resolution on the old paraffin tissue. Mennillo presents the collection as a practical resource for studying colitis cell networks in routine clinical biopsies.
pmc-13369960:
Ordunez and a large regional panel set priorities for joining up heart, kidney, and metabolic care. Their 2026 paper reports Phase 3 of HEARTS 2.0, the Americas adaptation of the World Health Organization's HEARTS initiative. These conditions overlap heavily yet are usually managed separately, and the panel aimed to pick interventions primary care services can actually deliver together.

A multidisciplinary panel appraised 45 candidate interventions using structured evidence reviews, evidence-to-decision frameworks, and anonymous rating rounds. It prioritised 38 for implementation. Hypertension care remains the entry point. The package adds early diabetes and kidney disease detection, lifestyle support, and risk-based combination drug therapy. It also adds task-sharing with non-physician staff and structured long-term follow-up. The authors present the list as the evidence base for updating the HEARTS clinical pathway at scale.
pmc-13370860:
Rainer Fährrolfes and co-workers give in 2026 PegaPlus, a web tool that lets drug pros sort screen hits by drag on a map while a learn tool learns their hand. First sorts of huge screen pools take long hand work. Their map learns from each drag and re sorts the pool in step.

A learn tool on line takes in pro moves and chem traits, then lifts its own sort calls. Tests show the pair route cuts hand steps by half next to pure hand work on several pools. The tool ships free on the web for drug hunt teams.
pmc-13374360:
Assaeed and colleagues survey the plant life of Rawdhat Khuraym, a depression near Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, now part of a protected reserve system, in 2026 desert ecology research. Rawdah meadows collect rainwater and support rich vegetation for the Arabian desert. The team documented the site's floristic composition across seasons and classified plants by life form and family. They related vegetation patterns to soil properties to inform sustainable management of the protected area and its grazing and recreation pressures.

The survey recorded 89 species from 30 families in the protected depression. Annuals made up 57.3 percent of species, finishing their life cycles in wet spells, while perennials formed 42.4 percent of the flora. Four families, Asteraceae, Poaceae, Fabaceae, and Brassicaceae, supplied 50.6 percent of species found. No species appeared on the international threatened list. Assaeed frames the inventory as the reference against which change in the reserve can be judged.
pmc-13375660:
Kirk E. Evoy and colleagues update the research on gabapentinoid misuse in a 2026 systematic review. A 2017 review and 2021 update had found 114 studies on gabapentin and pregabalin misuse, dependence, or overdose. This update searched PubMed from September 2020 to January 2025 for new data on misuse-related terms, excluding non-English work, reviews, and animal studies.

One hundred studies were included, mostly observational, from North America, Europe, Asia, Australia, and Africa. Sixteen studied gabapentin alone, 20 pregabalin alone, and 51 both drugs. Misuse occurred for therapeutic and non-therapeutic reasons, often with opioids or other substances, and commonly among people with substance use or psychiatric disorders. Newer work strengthens evidence on combined use harms, informing prescribing safeguards.
pmc-13375760:
Justin Joseph Asmus and others test whether direct touch between wine yeast species changes brewing in a 2026 study. Wine fermentations host hostile, neutral, and helpful yeast dealings, driven by nutrient rivalry, metabolite exchange, and killer toxins. Prior work used membrane bioreactors for two-species pairs, leaving three-species contact effects unclear.

The team studied Saccharomyces cerevisiae with Lachancea thermotolerans and Torulaspora delbrueckii, using walls that allow metabolite exchange while blocking touch. Direct contact favoured Saccharomyces growth and shifted amino acid patterns, while indirect contact favoured Torulaspora growth at Saccharomyces expense. The work shows that touch itself, not only shared chemicals, steers wine yeast groups and final wine nature.
pmc-13380260:
Panagiotis Kousidis and colleagues describe a 2026 proof-of-concept study using printed breast models to help pathologists examine tissue removed at mastectomy. Accurate examination depends on matching the removed tissue to earlier scans, which is hard when there are several tumours or treatment has blurred their edges. A physical model could guide where to cut and sample.

The team printed patient-specific models from two breast scan cases, one with a single tumour and one with several. They marked out the breast outline, the tumours, and landmarks for orientation. pmc-13404860:
Keshavaram Pandian and co-authors plan a 2026 scoping review of occupational therapy training for caregivers of neurodivergent children. Parents of autistic children and children with ADHD face lasting strain in daily routines and family life. Therapists train caregivers in practical skills, but reports use mixed terms and varied designs.

The review will map what programmes exist, how they are built and how they are delivered. Details to chart include who teaches, where sessions happen, how long they run and what theory supports them. Secondary aims cover programme structure across settings. The authors aim to give service planners a clear picture of a scattered field rather than a verdict on which programme works best.
pmc-13405060:
Senate Moshoeshoe and colleagues chart a decade of HIV treatment in Lesotho, reporting in 2026. The southern African country carries the world's second highest HIV prevalence, at 25.6 percent in the figures given. Programme data from 2014 to 2024 show how treatment and monitoring expanded.

People on antiretroviral therapy more than doubled, from 111,322 to 242,438 over the decade. Viral load testing coverage climbed from 6 percent to 93 percent, and suppression among those tested rose from 75 percent to 99 percent in the reported years. Average time from sample to result fell from 56 days to 8 days. The authors say Lesotho reached the third UNAIDS 95 target for suppression on treatment.
pmc-13405360:
An Expression of Concern published in 2026 attaches to a 2015 paper by Tao Xue and colleagues on sound stimulation and neural stem cells from hearing centres in the brain. A reader alerted the journal that flow cytometry plots in one figure later appeared in six papers by unrelated teams at other institutes. A western blot band in another figure also seems reused for two different conditions.

The authors replied that the paper's digitised raw data were thrown away under their institute's retention policy after the required period. They maintain full confidence in their findings, the notice states. Editors issued the warning because the integrity questions remain unresolved, with one of the later papers already retracted.
pmc-13406660:
Jingbo Wang and colleagues test a plant compound on burn wounds in mice, in a 2026 study. Piceatannol comes from a traditional Chinese herb used for trauma and inflammation. Deep second-degree burns were treated on the skin surface while several skin cell types were studied in dishes.

Treated wounds closed faster with tidier tissue structure: less inflammatory invasion, better collagen order and more new blood vessels in the reported microscopy. The compound quieted the NF-kappaB alarm pathway and adjusted a redox control system involving KEAP1 and NRF2. Keratinocytes, fibroblasts, vessel cells and macrophages each contributed evidence. The authors frame the benefit as coordination across inflammation, oxidation and rebuilding.
pmc-13407160:
Luigi Ruggiero and co-authors describe, in 2026, microwave resonators built directly on germanium quantum well structures, a pairing hoped to serve future hybrid quantum devices. Earlier versions grown on silicon-based virtual substrates lost too many photons, which blurs quantum signals, so the group tried a different construction.

Their resonators are patterned into the aluminium film of a hybrid stack grown on a commercial germanium wafer. Quality factors passed 1,000 routinely and reached about 49,000 at single-photon levels, roughly ten times better than prior results on comparable structures. The resonance stayed sharp in sideways magnetic fields up to 850 millitesla, a useful trait for spin-based devices. Behaviour in upward fields showed a lag pattern the authors link to competing vortex and particle losses.
pmc-13407460:
Marta C. Bonilla and co-authors, in 2026, tested whether stress hormones change how pig white blood cells fight a lung bacterium that plagues swine herds. Neutrophils are first-responder cells. Cortisol and the adrenaline family can reshape their behaviour. The team exposed pig neutrophils to hormone levels matching those in living animals. Tests ran with and without the pathogen present.

Treated neutrophils produced more reactive oxygen and cast out more web-like traps, especially a vesicle-based form, when bacteria were present. Despite the busier defences, bacterial growth itself was unaffected by the hormones, whether neutrophils were around or not. The authors highlight the vesicle traps as a stress response needing its own follow-up work.
pmc-13407960:
Shana D. Stites and co-authors review, in 2026, the changing place of worry in Alzheimer's disease care. Earlier diagnosis and the first disease-modifying treatments are arriving in primary care. Anxiety was once read mainly as a reaction to noticing one's own decline. The authors, psychologists and psychiatrists among them, argue its role is expanding into the diagnostic process itself.

Focused literature reviews run between January and June 2026 underpin the piece. Anxiety now appears in how clinicians interpret early testing, how patients experience biomarker disclosure, and how the disease course unfolds, making it an informative feature rather than background noise. The summary aims to guide clinicians deciding how to assess and counsel anxious patients at the new diagnostic frontier. It also guides researchers designing studies that should measure anxiety rather than ignore it.
pmc-13408060:
Abel Desalegn Demeke and co-authors pool, in 2026, Ethiopian studies on whether cancer patients actually receive palliative care. Such care eases pain, exhaustion, and despair and supports end-of-life planning, yet Ethiopian evidence was scattered, so the team meta-analysed the literature under standard guidelines, rating study quality and exploring regional differences.

Across the pooled studies, 45.11 percent of adult cancer patients used palliative services, below half, with the Sidama region highest at about 51.5 percent. Higher education stood out as a driver: patients with college or university schooling had roughly two and a half times the odds of using services. The authors call on clinicians and policymakers to widen access deliberately, since utilisation currently follows social advantage rather than need alone.
pmc-13408160:
Ya-Jun Liu and co-authors investigate in 2026 why plant material resists being turned into sugars. Factories use cellulase enzymes to break down tough plant fibres, yet compounds in the biomass quietly switch those enzymes off. The study identifies phenolic compounds, especially phenolic aldehydes, as the culprits behind much of that loss.

Experiments showed the phenolics form permanent chemical bonds with enzyme side chains, a process that needs oxygen and links enzyme molecules together until they stop working. Removing oxygen, or adding competing amino compounds, reduced the damage. The phenolics came both from lignin breakdown and from raw plant extractives. For biofuel and biorefining readers, the work gives practical pretreatment guidance: limit leftover phenolics so enzymes keep working longer.
pmc-13408460:
Kanane Sato, Kyota Suzuki, and a very large team report in 2026 two synthetic compounds that make plants close their leaf pores and survive drought better.
