The compounds block voltage-dependent potassium channels in the pore's guard cells, a route separate from the usual drought hormone.

Treated Arabidopsis plants lost potassium from guard cells, closed their stomata, and resisted drought, while mutant plants lacking the inward potassium channel did not show the accompanying calcium rise. That calcium link ties channel activity to the wider closure machinery. With agriculture absorbing most drought damage worldwide, a chemical switch for stomata offers breeders and growers a concept worth testing beyond the laboratory plant.
pmc-13408660:
Yujian Liu and co-authors present a 2026 tool for drug discovery. It predicts how tightly a candidate molecule will bind its protein target. Most tools demand near-perfect protein shapes, and they falter when a shape is rough or computer-made. Their tool, E-CloudBind, uses electron-density clouds in place of exact atom positions.

Ligand densities come from semi-empirical quantum sums. Protein pockets become soft Gaussian point clouds shaped by atomic size. That keeps the contact geometry while forgiving small errors in position. Encoders read the local non-covalent patterns. A graph network then folds in covalent features for the final affinity call. Across standard tests, and harder tests outside the training set, the tool matched or beat leading rivals. It also held steady when shape quality dropped. Case studies showed atom-level readouts and large-scale screening wins.
pmc-13408860:
Nam Gu Yoon and colleagues show in 2026 that fat cells conscripted by breast tumours depend on a mitochondrial guardian protein to do their damage. Fat beside a tumour morphs into a cancer-associated state, bristling with mitochondria and secreting factors that shield cancer cells from chemotherapy. That factor otherwise activates survival pathways in cancer cells and blunts chemotherapy. Cutting the fat-to-tumour conversation made breast tumours in animals far more sensitive to treatment, nominating TRAP1 as a target on the tumour's support staff rather than the tumour itself.
pmc-13409260:
Viraj Pasindu and Imalka Munaweera review in 2026 how to engineer light-activated particles that kill microbes too tough for ordinary cleaning. Drug-resistant bacteria, biofilms, and viruses shrug off chemical and heat treatments, while plain photocatalysts waste most sunlight and lose their excited charges before chemistry happens. The design problem is aligning a material's energy bands with the exact reactive oxygen species each target requires.

The review explains defect and interface strategies that reshape a semiconductor's energy states, widening the light it can use while keeping its killing potential high enough for safety. Biofilms and viruses get separate treatment, since each demands different oxygen-based ammunition. Applications span water cleaning, self-sterilising surfaces, and wearable devices. The authors write as much for solid-state physicists as for microbiologists, arguing the two fields must design together.
pmc-13409760:
Franziska Zecha, Lena-Marie Hupperich, and Tobias Viere examine in 2026 how life cycle assessment is used across health care. Care services produce large amounts of greenhouse gas, yet studies that count those costs follow very mixed methods. The authors map the rules and guides now on offer and compare them with published work.

Their scan of grey sources and journal studies shows where practice lines up and where it drifts apart. Product-level studies already rest on fairly firm shared ground, which helps buyers choose lower-impact goods. Studies of whole services or hospitals vary far more, since units of comparison differ widely. Clearer rules for wards and care pathways would make results easier to trust and combine.
pmc-13411760:
Jose Ignacio Fernandez-Vigo and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how artificial intelligence can help with central serous chorioretinopathy, a retina condition that blurs vision in working-age adults. Current care leans on eye scans and light therapy. Readings vary between clinicians and treatment choices stay hard to tailor.

Computer models read scan types with high accuracy on test sets, flagged markers of fluid and recurrence, and showed promise for guiding light therapy and follow-up. The review also warns that biased data, weak outside testing, and unclear rules still block routine use, so readers get both the promise and the homework.
pmc-13412060:
Kyowon Gu and colleagues search in 2026 for traits that predict how long liver cancer patients stay free of progression on a first-line drug pair. The pair, atezolizumab plus bevacizumab, is a standard opening treatment for intermediate or advanced hepatocellular carcinoma. Charts and pre-treatment MRI scans covered 47 patients treated between September 2020 and July 2022.

During follow-up, 33 patients saw their tumours progress, and the median progression-free span was 4.3 months in this group. Younger age, tumours spanning ten centimetres or more, and a bright rim pattern around the tumour on MRI each pointed to earlier progression. Patients who also received radiotherapy fared better on this measure, a link the authors say merits closer study.
pmc-13412160:
Amand Floriaan Schmidt and colleagues introduce plot-misc in 2026, a Python package for publication-ready charts in biomedical research. Standard tools such as matplotlib and seaborn leave out chart types that medical papers use constantly. Building those charts from low-level commands takes verbose, fragile code that few teams can reuse.

Plot-misc instead offers ready archetypes, including forest, survival, and volcano plots, plus heatmaps and incidence tables. It stays close to matplotlib, so users keep fine control over every element and can slot the package into existing routines. Tutorials with worked examples help new users start, and the package ships through Conda, PyPI, and GitLab for Python-based research groups.
pmc-13415260:
Sven Jennessen and Tim Krüger reflect on ten years of the ReWiKs project on sexual self-determination for people with disabilities, writing in German in 2026. The project built a media package, trained professional staff, and ran open discussion groups where disabled participants could speak for themselves.

Staff skills grew clearly across the training work. Building sex friendly cultures inside institutions proved harder, blocked by structures and everyday paternalism, meaning well meant control by others. The discussion groups opened room for exchange, recognition, and sexual education. Self-determination in this area stays marginal in participation debates, the authors note, despite clear human rights claims.
pmc-13415660:
Chahrazed Mekadim and co-authors let mice breathe cadmium oxide nanoparticles for nine weeks and watch gut and lung microbes shift, in 2026. Cadmium is a toxic heavy metal, and inhaled particles reach both airways and, after swallowing, the gut. Diversity and makeup of bacteria in colon and lung were profiled, then tracked during a clearance period.

Both communities changed significantly, with gut effects stronger than lung effects. Gut bacteria recovered better after exposure stopped, while lung communities lagged. Three bacterial genera stood out as markers tied to disturbed gut functions. Predicted gene patterns suggested gut microbes may trap cadmium and help push it out in feces.
pmc-13416660:
Benjamin Wick and co-authors compare treated and untreated patients with a blood clot confined to the lower leg veins, in a 2026 report. Their question is whether blood thinners help these patients or mainly add bleeding risk. Records came from the TriNetX network for diagnoses between 2014 and 2024.

Matching produced 4,085 patients in each group with similar starting traits. Lung clots and brain bleeding did not differ clearly at six months. Gut bleeding and death were higher in the treated group at six months, and death stayed higher at one year. The authors argue for selective treatment rather than routine blood thinners for every such clot.
pmc-13416760:
Hawraa Ahmed Ali and colleagues test a gene variant in Iraqi patients with hepatitis B, in a 2026 case control study. The variant sits in STAT3, a gene tied to inflammation and cell growth. They ask whether it tracks with liver cancer that develops in people with chronic hepatitis B infection.

Each group held 80 people: liver cancer cases, chronic hepatitis B patients, and healthy controls. The T form of the variant was more common in the cancer group, and people with two T copies faced higher odds of cancer. The link was clearest with cirrhosis and high virus levels. Findings may aid risk screening in this population.
pmc-13417260:
Xianfeng Hui and co-authors review strategies that attack flu by targeting the host rather than the virus, in a 2026 article. Flu viruses mutate fast and often resist drugs aimed at their own proteins. Host factors, the cell machinery viruses borrow to copy themselves, change far more slowly and could offer steadier targets.

Large scale omics studies, which measure genes, proteins, and metabolites together, now reveal many such host factors. Artificial intelligence helps sift those lists for drug ready candidates. The review gathers known targets and shows how these tools speed discovery. Benefits could span human and animal flu, though safety testing in people remains ahead.
pmc-13417560:

The protein, CagX, spans two rings of the machine's outer core. Mutant bacteria were built making only parts of CagX, or lacking one inner segment.

Every CagX part proved essential for machine activity. One split version still built the lower ring, and one deletion version built partly intact cores. Four partner proteins failed to join the core without whole CagX. The work maps assembly rules for a key stomach cancer risk factor.
pmc-13417660:
Meng Jia and co-authors ask which liver patients regain kidney function soon after a TIPS procedure, in a 2026 single centre study. TIPS is a shunt that eases portal pressure in advanced liver disease, often helping blood flow to the kidneys. Records covered 188 patients, excluding those on dialysis or with very poor kidney function.

About 28 percent improved within a week, judged by a drop in creatinine of over 10 percent. Worse starting kidney function raised the odds of improvement, in a steady linear pattern. Shunt pressures before, after, and the size of the drop did not predict response. Early gains likely reflect reversible strain rather than fixed damage.
pmc-13417860:
Dayuan Wei and colleagues pooled 45 trials with 5317 surgical patients in 2026 to rank warming methods against drops in body temperature during operations. Forced-air warming is the usual standard, yet blankets, suits, warmed fluids, and prewarming vary widely, and the network analysis compared them head to head through shared controls.

Underbody forced-air blankets beat lower-body and surgical-access blankets, and adding prewarming to forced-air warming cut hypothermia significantly. Anesthetists gain a ranked guide for everyday cases, with combined warming favored for older patients and long operations despite wide uncertainty bands.
pmc-13418160:

Fifty competitive players were tested with a handheld force device in both legs during menstruation, the late follicular phase, and the luteal phase. Cycle phase was estimated by calendar or an app, not hormone tests.

Strength differed across phases for most muscle groups. Values peaked in the late follicular phase, with hip abductors strongest, and dipped during menstruation. Phase tracking was imprecise, so the authors urge caution. Still, scheduling strength tests and heavy loads by phase may give fairer readings.
pmc-13418460:

The dataset held 101 player match records from 40 elite players, with thinking tests before and after games. Matches sharply raised perceived effort and mental fatigue, and slowed reaction time, accuracy, and processing speed.

Hard accelerations linked weakly to slower reactions and more variable responses at first pass. Losses hurt thinking scores more than draws in simple comparisons. Careful modelling that accounts for repeated players shrank most load and position effects, leaving a small accuracy effect for outcomes and hard decelerations. Stable player traits explained much of the pattern.
pmc-13420260:

A trifocal lens, a standard monofocal lens, and an enhanced monofocal lens went into staged operations on both eyes. Vision numbers alone miss how patients feel, so a validated survey captured satisfaction at one month.

The study included 242 eyes of 121 patients, with a mean age of 66.8 years in the group reported and ages spanning 31 to 83 years across it. Women made up just over half of the patients. Both eyes of a patient stayed in or out together, keeping the analysis honest at the person level. Results help surgeons match lens promises to the daily reading and driving needs patients describe.
pmc-13420960:

They could also flag early pigment return before relapse shows on the skin, the letter adds.
pmc-13421260:

Most evidence comes from children, so the authors add data from their multi-centre adult registry.

pmc-13421360:

Guidelines clash, so staff fall back on personal judgement, and practice turns uneven. Keen individuals, not set protocols, drive good care. Surgery at a young age tangles the talks, and gaps in the care path put safety at risk. The authors call for standardised routes into surgery.
pmc-13421460:
Muhammad Farhan Jalil and co-workers surveyed 367 eco-smart tourism firms in Malaysia in 2026 to test whether augmented reality drives digital change through visitor engagement. The study framed AR as a spark that builds deep focus, green care, culture richness, trust, green value, and new ideas drive.

pmc-13421660:

pmc-13423060:

pmc-13423160:

pmc-13423360:

pmc-13424060:

pmc-13424260:

pmc-13424360:

pmc-13424560:

pmc-13424660:

pmc-13427060:

Round two used a working draft, with sailors thinking aloud while tapping through. Ratings and talks flagged what felt clear, useful, or clunky to new users. pmc-13427660:

Word-level explanations showed the model keyed on signs of worsening general condition, a known risk factor clinicians recognize. pmc-13427860:

Scores and times from 416 healthy French volunteers were analysed, and 80 of 100 items were kept, split evenly between objects and actions. Surgical teams get a common French tool for comparing language maps across centres.
pmc-13427960:

pmc-13428460:

pmc-13429260:

The training teaches non-judgmental communication, approved medication treatments, and standard screening tools. She argues stigma and knowledge gaps, not lack of empathy, break the clinician-patient relationship on both sides. Because substance use surfaces in primary care and emergency rooms too, she presents the program as a scalable fix beyond addiction specialty settings.
pmc-13429560:
Marisa Valentini and colleagues report function, life quality, and gait after total femur replacement, where the whole thigh bone plus hip and knee joints are rebuilt. The European musculoskeletal oncology group gathered cases from twelve centres for this rare, major operation.

Sixty-five patients, with a median age of 40 years and 60 percent men, had surgery for cancer or other reasons between 1990 and 2024. Patient-reported scores, hip and knee movement, and gait videos were collected. At a median follow-up of 28 months, the median musculoskeletal tumour society score was 63, giving patients a realistic picture of walking after such a rebuild.
pmc-13430160:
Jian Chen and co-authors feed, in a 2026 study, a plant compound plus a probiotic to laying hens with fatty liver disease. Fatty liver hemorrhagic syndrome plagues caged layers, cutting egg output and sometimes killing birds. Ninety-six hens aged 50 weeks were split into four groups. One group ate normal feed. A second ate an energy-rich, protein-poor diet designed to induce fatty liver. Two more groups ate that diet plus the supplement pair, at low and high doses. The pair joined quercetin, a plant antioxidant, with a Lactobacillus strain.

Supplemented hens kept laying at better rates and carried less liver and belly fat than unsupplemented sick hens. Blood fats also ran lower. Gut microbe mixes shifted away from groups tied to the disease diet, while liver gene activity tilted toward fat burning. Benefits grew with dose. Poultry producers get a feed-based candidate against a costly disorder.
pmc-13431460:
Horrmann and a large team report in 2026 a blood test that uses machine learning, a method that learns patterns from data, to detect early-stage breast cancer from plasma proteins. The test was developed with a company collection of biobanked samples.

The classifier was trained on 845 women and then checked on a separate set of 397 women, of whom 202 had breast cancer and 195 were healthy. In that held-out check it correctly flagged about 93 of every 100 cancers while wrongly flagging fewer than 8 of every 100 healthy women. Accuracy stayed high across cancer stages and subtypes. Simulations suggested the test could catch most cancers that mammography misses when used alongside it.
pmc-13432860:
Guo and colleagues show in 2026 how a pig coronavirus hijacks the cell's waste disposal system to copy itself. Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus kills newborn piglets through severe diarrhea. The team ran a genome-wide knockout screen, disabling one gene at a time in monkey kidney cells, to find host factors the virus needs. Two subunits of the HOPS complex, the machinery that fuses waste sacs with the cell's recycling compartments, stood out.

Deleting either subunit, VPS33A or VPS18, sharply cut virus production and froze disposal midway, with waste sacs formed but never fused. Mapping showed specific regions of each protein are required for both fusion and virus growth. Two viral proteins, nsp3 and nsp4, bind both subunits directly. Each alone starts sac formation, but together they push the process to completion through HOPS. The authors name this fusion step a target for antiviral design.
pmc-13434160:
Michał Lis and colleagues compare two ghrelin fractions in unmedicated patients with major depression and obesity against non-depressed controls with obesity. Depression and obesity often co-occur, hinting at shared hormone mechanisms, and ghrelin, which regulates appetite, stress, and reward, is a candidate link.

Earlier work gave mixed results and mostly measured total ghrelin, not its two biologically distinct fractions. Sixty-two adults took part, 31 with depression and 31 controls matched by sex, age, and body mass. All had been unmedicated for at least twelve months. Fasting plasma fractions were measured by ELISA after diagnosis was confirmed by structured interview. The paper reports both acylated and deacylated ghrelin elevated in the depressed group, sharpening a hormone bridge between mood and metabolism.
pmc-13435960:
Aki Gormezano and a large team count new psychosis cases among gay and bisexual men in metro Vancouver in 2026. Health records for 798 men from two cohorts were matched five to one with men from the general pool. Drug use patterns were part of the survey base.

New psychosis ran at 1.74 cases per hundred person years in the cohort. Matched men showed 0.64, so risk sat about 2.7 fold higher. Opioid use, HIV, unstable housing, and anxiety each linked to psychosis within the cohort. The authors point to housing and social support as levers. Care that joins mental health with housing aid may cut new cases.
pmc-13436460:
Aline de Rodrigues de Queiroz and coauthors compare six antioxidants for their grip on a plant heat valve in 2026. The valve, non photochemical quenching, vents excess light as heat to guard photosynthesis. Each antioxidant was dosed across a gradient under matched light and acidity.

Coenzyme M clamped the valve hardest on every gauge. Melatonin and N acetyl cysteine mostly raised its peak or its release. Ascorbate alone sped its opening. Mutant plants show the effects run through the standard valve parts. Two agents push the pigment cycle in opposite directions, which explains their clash. Antioxidant choice in field sprays needs care.
pmc-13436560:
Huo and colleagues compiled a 2026 summary on fall self-awareness in elderly patients after spine fracture surgery. Their fractures came from osteoporosis, a bone-weakening disease, and had been fixed with an operation. Following a ranked evidence model, they searched Chinese and international sources through December 2025 and graded what they found.

Fifteen sources qualified: one clinical decision summary, five guidelines, five expert consensuses, three systematic reviews, and one prior summary. From them the team distilled twenty-eight recommendations in six areas: building a care team from several specialties, fall assessment and screening, health education, osteoporosis self-management, rehabilitation therapy, and follow-up review. They note direct high-quality proof is still thin, and they advise tailoring plans to each patient's fall risk profile and preferences.
pmc-13436660:
Brian Rice and coauthors chart air ambulance care in northwest Alaska from 2020 to 2024 in 2026. Eleven village clinics feed one hub hospital across nearly 36,000 square miles. For many Alaska Native patients the flight is the only link to doctor led emergency care.

The set holds 1,579 flights for 1,119 patients, almost all Alaska Native. Trauma drove about twenty two percent of flights. Median total time ran 262 minutes, far past any golden hour. Decision time, ground wait, and flight time split the total. Each year four to eight percent of the region rides a medevac. Faster decisions may trim total times most.
pmc-13438160:
Sanja Mandaric led a twelve-author summary of immune responses to TAK-003, a live weakened vaccine against all four dengue virus types. Dengue vaccine design is notoriously hard, since partial immunity can worsen a later bout. Across the trial program, volunteers who had never met dengue and those who had were tested in endemic and non-endemic regions. Their 2026 review gathers the size, quality, and power of the antibody and cell responses after each dose.

The vaccine is built on a type 2 backbone dressed with parts of other types, and responses differed by type, age, and region. The review tracks how long protection signals persist, which immune marks predict real protection. No single marker yet certifies protection for dengue, which is why this wide immune map matters. It gives regulators and doctors the fullest available picture of what the vaccine stirs while outcome data keep accumulating.
pmc-13438460: The Frontiers Production Office issued a 2026 correction to a study of hemoglobin and blood movement during dry breath-holding in elite free divers. The notice is a correction only. One percentage in the introduction was printed as twenty percent when it should have read sixty percent. The figure describes the share of a typical man's blood volume held in the muscles and limbs. The corrected passage is reprinted in full, no data or conclusions change, and the original article has been updated.
pmc-13439060:
De Marino Elena's team uncovered a new role in 2026 for p19Arf, a mouse tumor suppressor, in steering stem cells toward pancreatic fate. ARF is famed for tumor surveillance, but its wider jobs were still emerging. Mouse embryonic stem cells with CRISPR mutations in p19Arf were driven toward pancreatic endoderm, with gene networks, cell shape, and architecture tracked.

Mutant cells failed to differentiate efficiently into pancreatic endoderm, gene networks for lineage, skeleton, and shape shifted, and cell architecture broke down, with partial loss leaving pluripotency traits lingering. Developmental biologists get evidence that a cancer guardian also guides early pancreas fate. The work reframes ARF as a differentiation regulator, not only a tumor guard.
pmc-13439260:
Mads Lund Pedersen and co-authors test how a common ADHD medicine changes the way adults weigh costs against gains, in a 2026 trial. Adults with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder often struggle with daily choices that trade effort or loss against reward. The stimulant methylphenidate lifts dopamine and noradrenaline, two brain messengers, and aids choice, but which mental step it changes was unknown. Sixty-one adults with the condition and 63 peers without it played a learned cost and gain choice task.

Participants with the condition gathered evidence poorly and answered too fast, showing blunted feel for both costs and gains. On the medicine, cost sensitivity rose while other steps stayed put. Lower cost sensitivity also tracked with stronger symptoms and higher prescribed doses. The authors conclude that the drug sharpens the cost side of the balance in particular.
pmc-13439860:
Shanquan Chen's team tested language plus risk factors in 2026 to spot mental health difficulties in school children, using a British birth cohort begun in 1958. Observer-based screening is costly and can miss quiet internalizing symptoms, while children's own writing may carry scalable signals. Nearly nine thousand children who wrote an age-eleven essay imagining life at twenty-five were analyzed, with language features joined to perinatal, social, and family predictors.

Combined models were compared against single-source models for predicting teacher-rated difficulties above high cutoffs, with sensitivity checks on parent ratings. The paper asks whether essays add detection value beyond classic risk factors. School mental health teams get a scalable screening lead, with ethics, consent, and false-positive handling as essential guardrails.
pmc-13441260:
Htay Htay and colleagues test whether kidney patients will actually use a phone app for remote monitoring, reporting a 2026 Singapore feasibility study. The Viva Konnect app let patients log vital signs from Bluetooth devices, medicines, symptoms, diet, and dialysis sessions, with a web portal for clinicians. Thirty-five patients joined at Singapore General Hospital, thirteen with chronic kidney disease and twenty-two on home peritoneal dialysis, followed for up to six months.

Eight participants dropped out, leaving twenty-seven finishers. Just over half of finishers met the preset acceptance bar, with kidney disease patients accepting at a higher rate than dialysis patients. Dialysis patients opened the app often but briefly, and device-sent vitals covered only about half their readings. Interviews blamed friction in communication, convenience, and clarity. The authors advise two-way clinician messaging and lighter data entry for the next version.
pmc-13441460:
Fujii reviews preimplantation genomic selection for cattle. Breeding values are estimated from a few cells of an embryo before transfer. So only genetically best animals are produced. Genomic selection after birth already speeds gains by shortening the gap between generations. New DNA methods now work on tiny embryo samples with ease.

The review covers selection systems built on blastocysts, elongating conceptuses, and demi-embryos created by splitting blastomeres. It weighs how each sampling route feeds into estimated breeding values. A second thread tackles embryo quality. Lab-produced embryos implant worse than in-vivo-derived ones, partly through abnormal epigenetic marks and gene expression in culture. Gene expression checks are offered as a hands-on quality check. They could flag weakened embryos before transfer into receiving cows. Fujii argues pairing early genomic prediction with expression-based quality control should lift the yield of in vitro embryo production systems.
pmc-13441860:
Yun-Chung Li and Chia-Hsien Tang ask whether managers who think short term set their firms up for stock crashes, studying Chinese listed firms in a 2026 paper. Crashes often follow long quiet stretches where bad news piles up unseen. The team read short-termism through real earnings management, where managers bend business choices to flatter current figures. Records covered 27,856 firm-years from non-financial A-share companies between 2009 and 2024.

Firms with more earnings management faced higher crash risk the following year on two standard measures, and the pattern survived repeat checks. Longer chief executive equity horizons softened the link, as did stronger analyst coverage. The tie ran stronger in essential-service industries, where failure carries social weight. The authors frame short-termism as a behavioural source of financial instability that pay design and outside scrutiny can damp, while conceding that causation is not proven.
pmc-13442460:
Yuxuan Mo and colleagues report surgery for two groin lumps in one 46-year-old woman in a 2026 case report. One lump was a hernia that could be pushed back, where gut slips through a weak wall spot. The twin lump was a giant fat growth under the skin near the same groin, painless and apart from the hernia path.

Scans and exam split the two lumps before surgery began. The team fixed the hernia through small cuts with a mesh-free inner route, then cut out the fat growth in the same session with scope guidance. Lab checks proved plain mature fat with no signs of fat cancer. The authors call the one-stage plan safe and workable for such paired lumps. They also lay out the body maps and cut steps that made the joint fix possible.
pmc-13442860:
Megan Fowler and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study testing Triumeq, a combination antiretroviral drug, against a form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis driven by TDP-43 protein buildup in nerve cells. The team used mice in which removing doxycycline from the diet triggers TDP-43 buildup, then tracked weight, nerve scores, movement, a urine marker, and inflammation signals during treatment.

Triumeq improved movement early in the disease but did not change other course markers or the final endpoint, a mixed result the authors report plainly. Treatment also broke the link between TDP-43 levels and inflammation genes seen in untreated mice. The findings support further study of the drug for TDP-43 linked disease, with the key open question whether its benefit works through calming that inflammation.
pmc-13443560:
Abu Zafer Mohammed Dayem Ullah and colleagues chart cancer risk in British Bangladeshi and Pakistani people in a 2026 study. South Asian groups sit underread in cancer gene work, despite high marks for some cancers. The Genes & Health pool held 57,416 people, with health records, cancer registry links, and gene reads for 43,462 of them.

Cancer touched 2,782 people, a 4.8 percent share of the pool, with earlier starts than national marks for many types. Wide scans found 132 firm links between cancers and other ills, strongest where the twin ills share a body zone. Gene scans found 39 variant links and 31 gene links, most absent from big gene banks. The authors give the pool as a base for fairer risk tools.
pmc-13445860:
A Lavens and coauthors describe a 2026 project building Belgium's first full diabetes data resource from split lists. The Diabetes Data Cell team listed current data sets, judged quality, and picked core primary-care and hospital-clinic sets for linkage to national coverage and death records.

Cleared linkage for 2017 to 2027 gave a first extract for 2017 to 2024 with 76,964 unique people. It spans findings, length, ages and backgrounds, labs, drugs, treatments, side ills, use, deaths, and costs. The linkage proves feasible within current legal and tech rules, giving policy chiefs a unified view of diabetes care across the country.
pmc-13445960:
Caijian Hua and colleagues build a featherweight brain scan network that runs on a laptop processor, meant for fast first-pass triage of gliomas where no graphics hardware exists, in a 2026 study. Big tumor models need costly processors, which small clinics and field hospitals lack. Their network, GMANet, holds only a fifth of a million settings by design.

Three custom blocks keep the model small while guarding tumor edges and shape across the full scan. On two public brain tumor sets it marked whole tumors with scores in the low nineties, in percent terms, and read a full scan in under ten seconds on a standard laptop. The team trades a slice of fine edge accuracy for speed, pitching the tool as a screen before heavy review.
pmc-13446360:
The India State-Level Disease Burden Initiative Stillbirth Collaborators estimate stillbirth rates for every Indian state under two world definitions, in a 2026 study. India carries the world's largest stillbirth count, and state gaps run wide, so national means hide the local truth. Data came from one hundred twenty-two sources, from surveys to registration systems.

For 2023 the team puts stillbirths near five hundred sixty-six thousand at the earlier cutoff of twenty-two weeks, and near three hundred forty-seven thousand at twenty-eight weeks. Rates swung fourfold across states, lowest in Mizoram and highest in Uttar Pradesh, with that state and Bihar holding near half the national total. The wider cutoff shows how much loss the late-only count misses.
pmc-13447060:
Yajie Fan and colleagues report a fifty-five-year-old man with advanced throat-tube cancer who developed an autoimmune brain disease during treatment with the checkpoint drug sintilimab, published in 2026. A review of like cases joins the report. The disease, GFAP astrocytopathy, attacks a protein in the brain's star-shaped support cells. No past report had tied it in detail to this drug in this cancer.

His care had paired the drug with two standard chemotherapy agents. Early high-dose steroid pulses plus immune globulin by vein brought full remission, which held through a three-month watch window. A side review found seventeen cases of checkpoint-linked brain inflammation with a like face. The authors urge fast drug stopping and strong immune care when nerve signs appear on such therapy.
pmc-13447560:
Viren Sehgal and co-authors report a hybrid fix for a groin artery bulge after a heart valve procedure in a 2026 case study. A pseudoaneurysm, a contained leak forming a pulsating sac, can follow catheter entry through the leg artery. Standard clotting injections through the skin sometimes fail, while open repair and covered stents each carry anatomical or bleeding risks in frail patients.

An eighty-seven-year-old woman, unstable and on blood pressure support plus two anti-clotting drugs, developed a wide-necked sac after her valve replacement. Bedside injection failed, and both surgery and stenting were judged too risky given the sac's spot near a major branch. A balloon inside the artery temporarily blocked the sac's neck while clotting agent was injected under ultrasound guidance. The seal held at one day and one year, with leg flow preserved.
pmc-13447960:
Yanjun Wang and colleagues map a 2026 clinical and genetic portrait of severe combined immune deficiency in Yunnan, China, where data remain limited. The team collected clinical, laboratory, and trio exome details for 11 infants with suspected SCID, reviewing literature for previously reported variants.

Molecular diagnoses reached 10 infants, led by IL2RG, RAG2, LIG4, DCLRE1C, and CD3D genes, including two novel RAG2 variants. Ten of 11 infants died within six months, and one novel-variant case ran milder. The grim toll and diagnostic delays argue urgently for universal newborn screening in China, the authors conclude.
pmc-13448060:
Jung Min Choi and colleagues review imaging of chest wall and diaphragm injuries after trauma in a 2026 article focused on Korean practice. Chest injury is the second most common site in severe trauma and carries a high death rate. Broken ribs and breastbone, plus a torn diaphragm, strongly shape prognosis and feed directly into standard injury severity scores used for triage and payment.

Rib fracture counts and patterns signal how much energy the chest absorbed and hint at hidden lung or vessel injury. Breastbone fractures carry their own associated injury concerns, while diaphragm tears are uncommon yet dangerous when missed, since abdominal organs can slip into the chest. Clear, detailed radiology reporting supports accurate scoring and consistent communication across clinical and administrative teams. The review organises key findings by injury type for everyday reporting.
pmc-13448460:
Sebastian Schröder and co-authors fabricate a skin dermis model with realistic surface topography using two-photon printing in 2026 work. The junction between skin layers carries wavy ridges that house stem cells and anchor the surface, flattening with age and slowing healing. Recreating that wavy architecture in a lab dermis could improve skin models for research and grafting.

Laser printing carved precise templates mimicking the junction, and moulding transferred the micro-features into a gelatin-based gel. Fibroblasts, the dermis builder cells, populated the gel and laid down a rich matrix following the imposed topography. Several ridge geometries were compared through remodelling, and one design performed best in their tests. The resulting model supported surface cell attachment and formation of the basement membrane that glues skin layers together.
pmc-13448660:
Raja Selvaraj and coauthors report a 2026 green making of flower-like zinc oxide nano-bits from rubber fig leaf extract for sunlight-driven cleanup of levofloxacin dirty water. Close looks showed flower shapes, ray patterns showed crystal wurtzite structure at about 45 nm, and light tests proved zinc and surface plant bits.

Under natural sunlight, the flowers broke down the drug with pseudo-first-order pace and great fit, rising with helper dose as surface sites and reactive oxygen species grew. The plant-based route offers a lasting drug dirty water treatment, pending scale-up and reuse trials.
pmc-13449060:
Wojciech Szewczyk and co-authors test in 2026 whether a standardized MRI method for judging knee ligament graft healing gives the same answer when repeated. Twelve adults who had undergone anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction had their grafts scanned. Two radiologists placed five measurement regions along each graft, normalized the signal against the neighboring ligament and background, and repeated the whole process blinded one week later.

Single regions varied in consistency, with reliability coefficients from 0.67 up to 0.90 within a reader and from 0.52 up to 0.83 between readers as a pair. Averaging the signal across all five regions steadied the measure, reaching 0.90 within readers and 0.85 between them on average. The team also reports the smallest change the method can trust, giving clinicians concrete thresholds for telling real graft change from measurement noise in follow-up scans.
pmc-13449460:
Vincent Mayoral and colleagues looked for a way to protect donor organs before they are put in, and their work appeared in 2026. Donor organs often fail over time, in part because blood flow coming back after cold storage injures them. The inner lining of blood vessels is most at risk, and once hurt it is more likely to set off rejection.

The team grew tiny vessel-lining cells in the lab under cold storage like that used for donor organs. They added a drug called MLN4924, which blocks a cell process named neddylation, during that cold phase. Treated cells showed less harm from cold and from the return of blood flow. The results back further tests of this drug as a way to prepare organs and help them last longer.
pmc-13449660:
Mehri Salari and co-authors survey in 2026 how the June 2025 armed conflict between Iran and Israel affected people living with Parkinson disease inside Iran. Chronic stress can worsen this movement disorder, and war piles on drug access problems and fear. An online survey, built on a validated Persian version of the Impact of Event Scale-Revised, went to patients confirmed by movement specialists and to matched healthy controls. It started a week after the twelve-day war and ran over two months.

The headline finding runs against expectation: patients reported lower stress scores than the healthy comparison group. The questionnaire also captured exposure levels, symptom changes such as tremor and slowness, dose adjustments, anxiety medication needs, doctor availability, and interruptions in drug supply. The authors map which symptoms moved with stress in this group, offering rare evidence on how a chronically ill group weathers a national trauma.
pmc-13449860:
Xixi Gao, Jia Huang, and Zhiying Yang document in 2026 a giant liver hemangioma that grew until it consumed platelets and clotting factors in Kasabach-Merritt syndrome. The patient, a 22-year-old man, carried a benign vessel tumor measured at fifteen centimeters in 2020. By May 2024 he arrived with a swelling abdomen; scans showed the mass at 29 by 34.6 centimeters. An embolization meant to shrink it backfired, and by November the tumor neared fifty centimeters, leaving him unable to lie flat or breathe comfortably.

Blood tests confirmed the consumption syndrome: platelets at 92, fibrinogen nearly absent at 0.6 grams per liter, and clotting times stretched. Because the remaining liver lobe still topped thirty percent of standard volume, surgeons removed the right three sections in December 2024. Recovery was smooth, the syndrome resolved completely, and blood values normalized by discharge on day nine. A year later he was asymptomatic, with only small stable hemangiomas left behind.
pmc-13450260:
Ningyun Cai and colleagues engineered a biosensor in 2026 to speed the hunt for microbes that overproduce arginine. Arginine is a valuable amino acid for drugs and supplements, and Corynebacterium glutamicum is a promising production host, but industrial yields remain limited. Fast screening of high producers needs a sensor that responds to arginine alone.

The native LysG sensor also responded to histidine and lysine, so the team reshaped it by semi-rational design and directed evolution. One change, F222I, kept strong arginine response while sharply cutting responses to the other two amino acids. The new sensor then screened a library of enzyme mutants, yielding eighteen improved variants. The best strain, combined with further mutation work, offers a faster route to higher arginine output.
pmc-13450460:
Hala Qasrawi and colleagues reported a 2026 case where benign fatty liver changes mimicked tumors on scans, warning against rushed invasive workups. Fatty liver disease is common and hard to diagnose when focal fat-sparing looks like cancer, causing worry and possibly needless procedures. Careful matching of images with labs and clinical history is the safeguard.

A thirty-four-year-old woman with high lipids and low thyroid function was admitted for acute appendicitis, when scans found multiple liver nodules. Ultrasound showed a fatty liver with dark nodules suspicious for cancer, but contrast CT and MRI reclassified them as multifocal fatty-sparing areas. Labs supported nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, and follow-up scans stayed stable. Radiologists gain a reminder that not every liver nodule in a fatty liver is a tumor.
pmc-13451560:
Avcı and Kaplan Serin review whether the ratio of index finger length to ring finger length relates to breast cancer risk. That ratio, called 2D:4D, is set before birth and is read as an indirect sign of hormone exposure in the womb. Their 2026 systematic review searched three databases under standard reporting rules and kept observational studies that compared women with breast cancer to healthy controls.

Seven studies covering 13,556 women met the criteria. Most case control studies found higher finger ratios in women with breast cancer on one or both hands. But the one study that followed women forward in time found a link for the left hand only, and the largest multi center study found no steady link at all. The authors call the overall signal possible but uneven, and they ask for larger forward looking studies before the ratio earns any role in risk checks.
pmc-13451860:
Matthew Tran and co-authors track in 2026 sex and race gaps in death after a first heart attack, split by time since the hospital stay. Their data held over half a million older United States patients on Medicare, admitted from 2008 to 2018. Death was scored in the hospital, in the first month home, across the rest of year one, and out to three years.

Raw death rates fell for every group across the decade. Once risk was counted, women and Black patients matched peers during the stay and the first month home. Past that point, though, both groups died at higher rates in every year checked. The authors say the late gap, not the hospital phase, is where fair care efforts should aim.
pmc-13452160:
Marianne Elston and co-authors review in 2026 whether bone-sparing drugs help patients whose hormone-gland tumors have spread to bone. Such spread is common and brings breaks and pain, yet the drugs' role here was unmapped. Six databases were searched for studies of these drugs in well-grown tumors of this kind with bone spread.

From over 2,400 finds, only five past studies with 348 patients in all passed the screen, and their designs varied widely. One small study tied monthly drugs of one class to longer survival, three found no gap, and one found fewer bone events. Harm reports were patchy. The authors say proof is too thin and a forward trial is needed.
pmc-13454160:
Safoora Masoumirad and others reframed EEG Higuchi fractal dimension in time units in 2026, to make results comparable across studies. Higuchi fractal dimension is a widely used nonlinear metric for brain signals, but it depends on a free parameter, kmax, the maximum scale in samples. Since EEG signals are not ideally fractal, estimates vary with both kmax and sampling frequency.

The paper argues for reporting results by maximum time interval, tmax equals kmax divided by sampling frequency, rather than kmax alone. That choice determines which frequency range the metric emphasizes, improving interpretation and parameter selection. Researchers gain a simple reporting fix that lets fractal dimension results be compared across labs and recording setups.
pmc-13454460:
Yunjie Jia leads a eighteen-author study, from 2026, of sudden permafrost collapse on the Tibetan Plateau and the carbon it releases. Collapsing slopes, called retrogressive thaw slumps, are the most extreme form of abrupt thaw. The team pooled records of 4,728 slumps with 1,862 field measurements of carbon dioxide and methane from affected ground.

Ground prone to slumps is projected to grow by 17 to 19 percent by 2100, driven mainly by changing rainfall. Collapsed ground breathed out less carbon dioxide than intact ground, by about 14 percent, yet released about 20 percent more methane, a stronger warming gas. Combined releases from slump expansion roughly doubled between 2016 and 2022. Under a middle emissions path, the team projects releases from prone areas to surge about 2.7-fold by 2100. The findings argue for guarding high plateau permafrost.
pmc-13454760: Janine R. Lam, Haeme R. P. Park, and Justine M. Gatt issued a 2026 correction to their study measuring mental wellbeing in teenagers with the COMPAS-W scale. The notice is a correction only, changing the conflict of interest statement and adding no new data. The revised wording notes that, since the study appeared, the senior author founded a wellbeing company that holds the scale's rights. Readers get the corrected disclosure so the scale's ownership and licensing sit plainly on the record.
pmc-13455260:
Özge Aydın Güçlü and others read clinic outcomes and death predictors in blood-cancer patients with probable CMV pneumonia in 2026, in a look-back cohort. Cytomegalovirus infection brings big sickness and death in immune-weak patients. The team read sixty-one patients diagnosed with probable CMV pneumonia from January 2018 to October 2023.

Disease traits, lab scores, CMV DNA levels in blood and lung wash fluid, co-infections, and antiviral care traits were logged. Main outcomes were all-cause death at thirty and ninety days. Death-linked traits were scored by single-factor tests and multivariate Cox models that account for immortal-time bias. Median age was fifty-seven years, with sixty-five point six percent male. The work names death predictors for early and later death in this high-risk group. Blood doctors gain risk sorts for CMV pneumonia care.
pmc-13457160:
Lingfeng Chen and colleagues test whether one gene-sequencing panel can sort endometrial carcinoma into its molecular subtypes as reliably as the standard two-step approach. Molecular subtype now guides prognosis and treatment choices for this cancer of the uterine lining. The 2026 study compares a targeted next-generation sequencing panel covering 116 cancer-related genes against classification built from Sanger sequencing plus immunohistochemistry.

Across 194 classified cases the two routes agreed in 93.8 percent of cases, and agreement rose further once seven disputed POLE mutations were set aside. Sequencing caught 30 POLE mutations where Sanger found 23, missing low-frequency variants. Among 131 tumors the panel also flagged changes in PTEN, PIK3CA, and ARID1A that could point patients toward targeted-therapy trials. The authors conclude that a single sequencing test can match the older workflow while adding sensitivity.
pmc-13457360:
Jian Cao and colleagues used single-cell sequencing to compare penile squamous cell carcinoma tumors from younger and older men, cell by cell. Their 2026 study profiled two tumors from non-old patients and three from older patients, separating tumor cells, T cells, and other immune cells to see how aging reshapes the cancer's surroundings. Penile cancer is rare, and age-related differences inside these tumors had barely been studied before this work.

Tumor cells in older patients showed a stronger senescence pattern, in which aged cells release inflammatory signals, and formed a subcluster with more malignant features. The older tumors also held more exhausted-looking CD24-positive T cells and more blood-vessel-promoting macrophages, which can help cancers grow. Signaling through a molecule called MIF between fibroblasts and other cells was stronger with age, and the team nominates IL1B as a possible marker for predicting patient outcomes.
pmc-13458060:
Kai Li and colleagues uncovered an unexpected partnership between two proteins in pancreatic cancer, a disease with a five-year survival rate near ten percent. Their 2026 study focused on SUFU, a brake on the Hedgehog growth pathway, and asked what controls it inside tumor cells. Database checks showed SUFU and a second protein, JOSD1, rising together in pancreatic tumors. Microscope staining confirmed both were more abundant in cancer tissue than in normal pancreas from the same patients.

The team found that JOSD1 binds SUFU directly and protects it from the cell's protein-disposal system, keeping SUFU levels high. Surprisingly, SUFU helped the cancer here rather than restraining it. pmc-13459960:

pmc-13462560:

pmc-13463860:

pmc-13464260:

pmc-13465560:

pmc-13465760:

pmc-13465960:

pmc-13466960:

pmc-13467060:

pmc-13467360:

pmc-13468060:

pmc-13470260:

pmc-13474860:
