pmc-13478060:
Cheng and Zhang present a forecasting model in 2026 for PM2.5, the fine soot particles that drive air pollution alerts, built to handle the series' wild swings. Their method first splits the pollution record into simpler waves using a technique called variational mode decomposition. Separate deep learning networks then forecast the slow, medium, and fast waves, and an attention step, which learns which parts deserve more weight, blends the three forecasts.

The combined model posted the best scores among the methods tested, with a root mean square error of 16.920 micrograms per cubic meter on the test data. Its mean absolute error was 11.134 micrograms per cubic meter, and its fit score reached 0.960 on the scale where one means perfect prediction. The authors argue that splitting the signal by speed, then letting the blending step learn each band's reliability, is what lifts accuracy over single-network forecasts.
pmc-13479460:
Georgia Fisher and colleagues present a 2026 evaluation of the SAS Mat, a floor mat designed to test and train tandem balance in older adults. Standing heel-to-toe balance predicts fall risk, yet standard tests suffer from ceiling effects and helper bias. Forty-four community-dwelling adults aged 65 and older, averaging about 73 years, took part in two sessions four to seven days apart.

Participants completed the mat-based measure plus the Four Stage Balance Test and the Timed Up and Go in the first session. The mat measure was repeated in session two to check test-retest reliability, and a survey captured how acceptable and feasible the mat felt as both test and training tool. The authors report whether a single device can credibly serve both measurement and practice roles.
pmc-13479660:
Gerda Marčiūtė, Ignas Lapeikis, and Greta Kasputytė published a 2026 review of virtual reality as an add-on for cutting pain and anxiety during care procedures. Forty papers from 2020 to 2025 were read. Deep distraction works by seizing the focus that pain would claim.

Winning uses spanned shots, blood draws, and vein taps in children, plus work in childbirth, bone surgery, vessel surgery, heart care, and dental care. Across age groups, patients felt less pain and fear during sessions with headsets. Side effects were rare, and spirits rose. The authors conclude virtual reality is safe enough and works well enough to join routine practice, while noting studies vary in task type and depth of the virtual world.
pmc-13480260:
Yaxin Zhao and co-authors present a 2026 study of a pay reform for public hospital staff in China, piloted from 2017. Survey panels covered 102 hospitals and more than 111,000 health workers across fifteen provinces in 2016 and 2017. A matched comparison method split reform effects from wider trends in wages and prices.

After the reform, base pay took a larger slice of total pay, rising by over three points, while merit pay edged up by half a point. Total pay rose slightly, with base pay up by a clear margin and merit pay up less. General hospitals led on base share gains, while specialist hospitals led on merit growth. Contract and short-tenure staff gained performance shares without matching total gains, so the equal-pay aim stayed unmet. The authors urge stronger base pay cover for those groups.
pmc-13483560:
Urechescu and co-authors charted how face and jaw fractures in southwestern Romania changed across the COVID-19 years. Their 2026 study covered 914 patients treated at one major center from late 2017 to late 2025. The team split cases into pre-pandemic, pandemic, and recovery periods and compared fracture patterns, causes, and treatments month by month.

Monthly case numbers dipped while pandemic restrictions held, then climbed back afterward toward earlier levels. Yet the recovery was uneven, and the share of patients with documented related injuries stayed lower after the pandemic than before it. The statistical model explained only part of the month-to-month swing, which the authors flag openly. Urechescu cautions that trauma services should plan for rebounds after lockdowns while keeping better injury records than the pandemic years produced.
pmc-13483860:
Wancheng Liao investigates fat droplets as a hiding strategy that lets colorectal cancer cells sleep through chemotherapy and later return. Published in 2026, the work builds dormant, growing, and relapsed cell states from patient-derived grafts and cell lines, then profiles gene activity and droplet contents. Candidate control genes are tested by silencing, boosting, drug blocking, and mutation.

Sleeping cells carried more lipid droplets than growing or relapsed cells. A gene called ACSL5 stood out as switched up in the dormant state, driving droplet buildup that soaked up oxidized fats and lowered damaging reactive oxygen. A partner transcription factor switches ACSL5 on directly. Breaking the chain drained droplets, raised reactive oxygen, and woke the cells, while high ACSL5 in patients tracked with worse outlook. A dormancy maintenance circuit is exposed.
pmc-13486460:
Suwatjanee Naephrai characterizes the venom of a tropical tree ant and finds its main weapon is a doubled peptide with a repeated evolutionary story. Published in 2026, the work on Tetraponera rufonigra isolates Tr1a, a toxin built from two identical chains locked together by three sulfur bridges in a symmetric, two-faced helix pair. The peptide bursts cells, fires mammalian pain neurons, and kills insects.

Similar doubled peptides with similar jobs turn up in other ant lineages that are not close relatives. Independent invention several times over marks the dimer design as a repeatable winning solution rather than a shared inheritance. Ant venoms prove far more inventive at the architecture level than a single-family story would suggest, which matters for anyone mining venoms for drugs or insecticides.
pmc-13486660:
Ruan and team worked out how to calibrate an infrared star-measuring tool whose design defeats ordinary tuning. The device pairs a surveyor's device with an infrared camera sensor, enabling day and night sky angle measurement in a compact package. Its eyepiece is gone, its view is narrow, and its sensor resolution is low. Their 2026 method exploits the device's own angle readings, measuring each target from two faces of the tool to untangle unknowns.

The two-face trick separates the target's true direction from the camera's center-point position, which otherwise trade off against each other hopelessly. With that constraint, the remaining camera settings fall out at the precision sky work demands. Field checks confirmed the tuning held under real watching conditions. Ruan offers the method for other compact infrared tools that share the same tuning headache.
pmc-13487160:
Wenjing Jia and others map gene action cell by cell in colorectal cancer to find what drives harmful change. In 2026, the study looks at single-nucleus data from tumours and matched healthy tissue, looking at programs within each cell type and the signals exchanged between cells. The classic adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence is well known, but cell-specific drivers remain unclear.

Cancerous surface cells switched on two programs tied to stem-like actions and switched off two tied to cell death and chronic swelling. Regulators CEBPB and RUNX1 were activated, while FOXP1 and POU5F1 were repressed. Communication between tumour cells and their surroundings broke down, while fiber cells remodeled surrounding matrix and B-cell immunity weakened. The map points to new healing angles rooted in certain cell states.
pmc-13487960:
Hernan Andres de la Barra Ortiz and colleagues review high-intensity laser therapy for patellofemoral pain in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. This pain sits around the kneecap and is common in active people. They searched many databases for randomized trials and judged study quality with standard tools. Only four small trials qualified, and every one paired the laser treatment with therapeutic exercise such as strengthening or stretching.

Laser plus exercise reduced pain more than control care right after treatment and at follow-up in pooled results. Function scores did not differ clearly between groups. All trials carried high risk of bias, samples were tiny, and results varied, so confidence in the findings is very low. The authors ask for larger, better trials before firm advice is possible.
pmc-13488160:
Yanwei Lv and co-authors design flower-shaped nanoparticles to treat chronic pancreatitis in a 2026 animal and laboratory study. The disease brings lasting pancreas inflammation, scarring, and loss of function, with few effective drugs. The team first tracked pyroptosis during disease development. Pyroptosis is a fiery form of cell death. They then built particles carrying the drug disulfiram inside a coating that responds to gut conditions. The coating lets release happen near the target.

In a mouse model, the particles eased inflammation and scarring, calmed the cell death pathway, and helped restore pancreas structure and digestive output in the reported tests. Gene activity patterns shifted back toward normal, mainly in secretion pathways. The authors present the platform as a delivery strategy needing further safety work.
pmc-13488560:
Hye-Young Yoon and colleagues survey surface disinfection practice among dental hygienists in South Korea in a 2026 questionnaire study. Germs can survive on clinic surfaces, and standard methods exist for each surface type, yet real-world uptake was little studied. Responses from 182 hygienists were analyzed by surface, patient load, and whether the clinic had a named infection control staff member, after incomplete replies were removed.

Full standard practice was rare everywhere, peaking at under a quarter for the bracket table and falling to near zero for drawer handles in the reported rates. Hygienists seeing forty or more patients daily followed standards more often than those seeing few patients. Clinics with a designated infection control person also did better. The authors call for simpler, better-supported routines.
pmc-13491360:
Ramos and colleagues map in 2026 the literature on X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism, a hereditary movement disorder affecting mostly Filipino men with roots on Panay Island. Research had concentrated on genes and movement while neglecting diagnosis, care, and daily life.

The scoping review included 27 studies. The typical course starts with twisting movements in one body part, spreads widely, and adds parkinsonism within a year or two. Most patients tested carried the disease-causing change in the TAF1 gene, yet diagnosis still takes years. Deep brain stimulation reduced the severity of the dystonia, and medicines brought partial benefit. Qualitative studies surfaced stigma, loss of identity, heavy caregiver burden, and financial hardship alongside coping and resilience. The authors call for care models that add psychosocial support to genetic and clinical services.
pmc-13492460:
Meganathan and co-workers in California unveiled in 2026 a chip that can taste potassium at the scale of one heart cell. Potassium flow sets the heart's rhythm, and early faults in that flow warn of rhythm trouble. Older tools read all ions at once or pierce the cell, which harms long term study. Their platform, named KINESIS, grows a forest of tiny pillars tipped with a membrane that picks out potassium alone.

The team grew heart cells made from human stem cells on the pillars. The cells sat on the tips without their skins being pierced. Drug tests gave clear, split readouts: caffeine and ouabain, two drugs that move potassium in known ways, each shifted the signal as the books predict. The authors pitch the chip for drug safety screens and for modeling a single patient's heart faults in a dish.
pmc-13493360:
Xia and colleagues tested in 2026 a modified curcumin compound against glioblastoma, the most aggressive common brain tumour. The compound, called DMC-GF, derives from demethoxycurcumin, a relative of the turmeric pigment. The team ran lab assays on tumour cells and a mouse model with tumours grown in the brain.

DMC-GF significantly suppressed tumour cell growth, triggered programmed cell death, and strongly slowed tumour growth in the mice. It targeted a growth kinase and interacted with a regulator protein, changing the STAT3/AKT signalling axis, a key survival pathway. That shift triggered the mitochondrial route to cell death. Profiling pointed to mitochondrial energy production as a central event in the response. The authors position DMC-GF as a promising candidate drug for glioblastoma. They note such candidates matter because current glioblastoma treatment options remain poor.
pmc-13495160:
Nattanich Intagun, Wannapa Chinadet, and Pinpinut Wanichsaithong survey, in a 2026 study, how ready dentists in Northern Thailand feel to treat patients who have intellectual or learning disabilities. These patients face steep barriers to dental care and suffer worse oral health. The team sent a tested questionnaire to dentists in public hospitals across seventeen provinces and gathered 306 replies.

Most dentists had treated such patients, yet two thirds saw fewer than ten a year. Talking with patients and managing behavior topped the list of hard parts. Over half felt high stress, and some said stress cut the quality of care. Nearly all judged their undergraduate training too thin. Having enough staff and equipment was the one clear driver of confidence, while stress rose with long experience and further degrees. The authors call for stronger training, better-staffed clinics, and firmer referral paths.
pmc-13495260:
Pin Cao, Peng Liu, Lu Ji, and Chong Qiao hunt, in a 2026 study, for warning signs of massive bleeding during cesarean delivery in a high-risk placenta group. Their patients had complete placenta previa, where the placenta covers the cervix, joined with placenta accreta spectrum, where it grows too deeply into the womb wall. Most research covers women with a past cesarean; this group had none.

The team reviewed 109 such patients at one Chinese hospital over five years. About one in five lost at least two liters of blood in surgery, the study's mark for massive bleeding. Three warning signs stood out on their own: older maternal age, a past scope procedure to cut womb adhesions, and a higher pre-surgery ultrasound risk score. The authors urge teams to weigh the woman's history beside the scan score, since scans alone can understate the danger.
pmc-13495360:
Samangan and colleagues showed in 2026 that acute B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia cells remodel their bone marrow home by shedding large oncosomes, oversized parcels budded from cancer cells. Leukemia is known to coach nearby support cells into aiding its growth and drug resistance, but the parcel traffic behind this coaching in this subtype was unclear. The work traces how the large vesicles condition mesenchymal stromal cells, the marrow's support layer.

Conditioned support cells changed the supply of IGF1, a growth factor the leukemia feeds on, in the marrow space. Earlier work from the group ties a clot-dissolving system to freeing this same factor from the surrounding matrix, and the vesicle route now joins that picture. The authors argue that cutting this parcel traffic could starve the leukemia of local support and soften its resistance to chemotherapy, a strategy worth testing in this aggressive childhood cancer.
pmc-13498460:
Shuji Kubo and colleagues test in 2026 whether stem cells can ferry a cancer-killing virus more effectively to tumours spread across the abdomen. The virus copies itself inside cancer cells and carries a gene that makes those cells kill themselves, yet body fluids can inactivate it before arrival. Stem cells that home toward tumours offered a possible shield and transport route, studied here in mesothelioma, a cancer of the lining tissues.

Stem cells from fat, bone marrow, and cord tissue all moved toward tumour cells and produced the virus in the lab. In mouse models mimicking fluid-filled abdominal spread, stem-cell delivery spread the virus through tumours far better than virus alone. Tumour shrinkage was stronger and survival longer with the combined approach under those fluid conditions.
pmc-13498560:
Ningthoujam and a large Indian team spent three years cataloguing fruit flies in Meghalaya, in the country's northeast, where records were scarce despite the insects' power to ruin harvests. From October 2020 to September 2023 they trapped across forest, orchard, and vegetable plots in Ri-Bhoi district. Fruit flies in this family can cause near-total crop losses.

The survey netted 37 species spread across several genera, with Bactrocera the dominant group in the region. Two species were entirely new to science, both in the genus Zeugodacus and found on Khasi mandarin, a local citrus. Community makeup differed clearly between the three ecosystems, with a core of widespread species persisting everywhere and rarer species tied to single habitats. The authors offer the dataset as the reference point for tracking how the region's fruit fly fauna shifts with land use and climate.
pmc-13498960:
Ayesha Almarzooqi and co-authors present in 2026 a rare injury case involving a blood collection under the cartilage at the rim of a child's nostril. Nasal injuries are common because the nose sticks out, yet blood collections usually form in the central septum and count as emergencies. Collections at the outer rim cartilage are far rarer, with only a handful of published cases, mostly in children.

Their patient was a three-year-old girl seen after facial trauma. Untreated collections of this kind can starve cartilage of blood, leading to tissue death, scarring, or infection that spreads deeper. Prompt recognition, surgical drainage, and antibiotic cover are presented as the safeguards against lasting damage. The warning covers both the look and the function of the nose, aimed at clinicians who may never have seen this site involved.
pmc-13499360:
Ahmed Jamal Chaudhary and co-authors test in 2026 whether two cheap admission blood measures can warn early that sepsis patients will develop organ failure. Sepsis, a dangerous response to infection, kills many patients worldwide, and spotting high-risk cases at arrival guides urgent care. Their cross-sectional study ran at a medical college in Turbat, Pakistan, from January to June 2025, enrolling 384 adults with sepsis by consecutive sampling.

Just over one third of patients developed organ dysfunction, and that group arrived with far higher values for a white-cell ratio and for creatinine, a kidney-related waste marker. Both measures predicted dysfunction well in curve analysis and stayed independent predictors after adjustment for other factors. The authors propose the pair as simple, low-cost tools for early risk sorting where advanced tests are scarce, while noting that neither marker is unique to sepsis.
pmc-13499660:
Ronny Vargas and a large co-author team trace in 2026 the path of nanotechnology, engineering at the scale of billionths of a metre. The field has moved from early liposomes in the 1960s toward today's nucleic acid delivery systems. Carriers built from fats, polymers, and inorganic materials can shield drugs and steer them to diseased tissue. The review sorts these carrier families and gives concrete examples of products already approved for sale.

Development energy now concentrates on cancer, infectious disease, brain disorders, and heart and vessel disease, with fat-based nanoparticles gaining ground in pipelines for gene silencing and gene editing therapies. Barriers to clinic remain practical, covering manufacturing scale, long-term stability, regulatory uncertainty, patent issues, and animal models that poorly mirror human disease. No single carrier suits every use, so progress depends on several platforms each proving its own niche.
pmc-13499960:
Ilgın Arı and co-authors test in 2026 an artificial intelligence model that outlines jaw fractures on cone-beam CT scans, a three-dimensional dental imaging method. Accurate fracture mapping guides surgery for lower jaw breaks, a common facial injury. Scan data from 92 patients covering 142 fracture sites were gathered retrospectively, with two maxillofacial surgeons hand-drawing the reference outlines. A standard self-configuring network was trained on most cases and tested on the rest.

Performance was scored two ways, by whole volume and slice by slice, using overlap and distance measures. Volume-based scores beat slice-based scores on every reported metric, with moderate overlap accuracy overall and smaller surface errors in three dimensions. The authors conclude that judging such tools volumetrically gives a fuller and more reliable picture, even though absolute segmentation accuracy remains limited and needs improvement before clinical trust.
pmc-13500560:
Rafal Wolny and others use AI plaque analysis from coronary CT to explain angina in women with non-obstructive coronary disease. In 2026, the WARRIOR trial substudy looks at baseline scans from 117 women with low blood flow and non-obstructive arteries. It quantifies noncalcified, low-attenuation, and calcified plaque across the coronary tree with a machine-learning low blood flow risk score.

Among 109 women with visible plaque, those with more severe angina carried higher total and noncalcified plaque burdens and lower calcified burden. They were younger, had higher blood fat, and less often took statins. Adjusted analysis linked noncalcified burden, low-attenuation burden, and low blood flow risk score to worse angina scores. High-risk plaque phenotypes, not just narrowing, appear to drive symptoms.
pmc-13500660:
Hui Hou and co-authors report in 2026 a treatment that breaks a longstanding trade-off in glow-after-light materials, where plastics that glow longer usually glow dimmer. Their strategy soaks a phosphor-loaded polymer film in an iodine and boric acid treatment. Iodine's heavy atoms help excited molecules cross into the long-lived triplet states that produce afterglow. The treatment simultaneously knits an exceptionally dense cross-linked network that shields those states from being quenched by vibration and air.

The treated film's afterglow lifetime stretched past a full second, a roughly twenty-eight-fold increase in the reported measurements. Its efficiency climbed to about a third of absorbed energy, a similar fold gain. Durability impressed as much as brightness, with bright emission surviving five days underwater and hours in acid, alkali, and hot water. Multicolour security printing, antibacterial surfaces, and water-resistant labels are the suggested destinations.
pmc-13501160:
Aditi Das Shroddha leads a three-author team with a 2026 cardiology case in which a consumer smartwatch first caught a dangerous heart rhythm. A 33-year-old athletic man had recurrent palpitations recorded by his Apple Watch and was treated as though he had a benign form of ventricular tachycardia from the right ventricular outflow tract. An initial catheter ablation, which burns the faulty circuit inside the heart, seemed to settle the problem, yet the arrhythmia returned.

Deeper testing with cardiac MRI and electrical mapping then showed extensive scarring beneath the outer surface of the right ventricle, matching arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. That inherited condition replaces heart muscle with fat and fibrous tissue and can cause sudden death in young athletes. Because the arrhythmias kept recurring and the scar burden was large, doctors implanted a defibrillator under the skin for protection. The case argues for continued doubt when rhythm problems return after ablation.
pmc-13501660:
Christine W St Laurent leads a ten-author team with a 2026 systematic review of how sleep gets measured in studies that use compositional data analysis. That approach treats the day as a fixed budget of sitting, activity, and sleep. Earlier reviews covered activity and sitting reporting but not sleep. The team searched seven databases plus citation chasing and expert input, keeping studies published since 2015 that paired device-measured sleep with the compositional method. Extraction followed sleep medicine guidance for actigraphy practice.

Seventy studies qualified, 60 cross-sectional and 10 longitudinal. Few reported key details of how sleep was measured or processed. Most, 67 studies, included only one sleep component in the daily composition, and fewer than half, 29 studies, noted any sleep-related limitation. Sixty studies rated good quality and ten poor on the assessment tool used. The authors call for standard sleep processing and fuller reporting.
pmc-13501860:
Maryam Edalati Khodabandeh leads a seven-author team publishing a 2026 protocol for a randomized trial of a self-care app for dry eye disease. Stage one built the app, with a Python Flask and SQLite back end and a Flutter front end. Stage two is a blinded trial: both groups receive usual care, and the intervention group adds the app for twelve weeks. The main outcome is tear break-up time, a stability test, with a Persian symptom questionnaire as the secondary measure, checked at six and twelve weeks.

The plan targeted 104 patients, yet COVID-19 disruption changed the course: 181 patients were randomized, 91 to the app and 90 to control, and 104 completed. The dropout rate was 42.5 percent across the arms. The team expects tailored training to reduce severity and strengthen the doctor-patient relationship. The trial sits in the Iranian registry under code IRCT20200721048162N1.
pmc-13502660:
Jurgen Schulz leads an eight-author team reporting a 2026 advance: light-activated labelling reagents fast enough to watch dilute biomolecules in real time. The bioorthogonal reaction, strain-promoted alkyne-azide cycloaddition, crawls at under one unit of rate on the reported scale, and excess dye must be washed away before imaging. The team's two thiophene-based cycloalkynes react with a range of 1,3-dipole tags at rates reaching 1528 on that scale, and they stay dark until they react.

Reaction switches the fluorescence on, brightening up to 150-fold, which removes the washing problem. The probes labelled a glycoprotein under no-wash conditions using as little as five micromolar reagent, finishing in under fifteen minutes while the team watched the signal build. Because the probes are photo-triggered, users also gain timing control over when labelling starts. The authors expect the reagents to open real-time imaging of scarce targets in complex environments.
pmc-13505060:
Neerod Kumar Jha, Abbas Abdul Hassan, and Mohamed Elmahi review what weighs on families through children's heart surgery, from a Middle Eastern view, in a 2026 paper. About one in a hundred babies is born with a heart defect, and half need an operation or catheter procedure at some point. The strain reaches far past the operating room.

Drawing on daily practice and literature from 2013 onward, the review names stress, broken communication, cost coverage, schooling and work loss, and logistics as core burdens. In the region, family cohesion, faith, many languages, and uneven access shape the path to recovery. The authors urge team-based care, counseling, funding support, and wise use of technology, backed by insurers, hospitals, and schools pulling together.
pmc-13505160:
Qiang Huang, Guangjie Wang, Lei Hu, and Jiahui Xie tracked how land use shapes the carbon balance of counties across China's Chengdu Plain. They combined a land-use simulation model with a method that lets driver effects vary across place and time. The plain matters as both a fast-growing economic region and an ecological shield for the upper Yangtze.

From 2000 onward, construction land grew while farmland, forest, and grassland shrank, a pattern projected to continue toward 2030. Net emissions rose first, peaked in 2020, and then eased in the projection. Built land was the main carbon source and forest the main store, together dominating the budget. Spending levels, urban growth, and population pushed emissions up, while investment slightly held them back. The authors propose different carbon plans for city-centre, industrial, and less developed counties rather than one regional rule.
pmc-13506660:
Yohei Iimura, Hitomi Sakai, Isana Nakajima, Seiichiro Kuroda, and Michio Nakamura review, in 2026, eye side effects of cancer drugs in Asian patients. Their search through December 2025 found 70 studies that fit, most of them case reports or reviews of past records. Drug groups ranged from classic chemotherapy to targeted drugs, immune drugs, and antibody-drug pairs.

Harms touched the eye surface, retina, optic nerve, and inner eye, and patterns varied by drug group. Reports on Asian patients were patchy. The authors offer a symptom-based guide for clinics without an eye doctor on site. Steps stress early spotting, simple supportive care, pausing treatment for lasting symptoms, and fast referral when vision falls.
pmc-13506960:
Lucia Yang and colleagues report in 2026 a gene-silencing strategy against diffuse midline glioma, a deadly childhood brain cancer. Most of these tumors carry a mutation in a histone gene, H3-3A, that poisons the cell's gene-control marks and drives growth.

The team designed short synthetic strands, called antisense oligonucleotides, that force the cell to skip the gene segment holding both the mutation and the start signal. Their lead strand skipped that segment precisely, spared a near-identical sister gene, and restored normal chemical marks in tumor cells grown from patients. In mice bearing patient tumors, it slowed growth and extended survival. The authors present exon skipping as a practical way to switch off a harmful gene.
pmc-13507060:
Hoyin Chu leads a 2026 study of angiosarcoma, a rare cancer of blood vessel lining cells, built with direct patient partnership. The cohort held 254 patients who shared samples and records through the Angiosarcoma Project. The team combined gene activity, tumor changes, and inherited variants to compare tumors by body site.

Tumors under the skin often showed growth signals tied to certain driver genes, while skin tumors leaned on MYC programs and sun-linked change patterns. People born with a harmful POT1 variant faced a far higher risk, and those with a second hit in tumors fell ill decades earlier. Site-aware biology could guide drug choices for this hard cancer.
pmc-13507160:
Desta Hailu Aregawi leads a 2026 qualitative study of quality of life among women receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer at Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital in Ethiopia. Eighteen women who had received chemotherapy for at least six months gave in-depth interviews in February and March 2020. Talks in Tigrigna were transcribed, translated, and coded jointly for shared themes.

Women described sharp physical limits, with hard tasks and long walks out of reach, plus common effects such as hair loss, fatigue, and appetite loss. Fear about the future weighed heavily, while counseling eased distress over time. Social isolation and treatment costs added strain. Stronger counseling, mental support, and financial aid are urged.
pmc-13508360:
Tianjiao Zhang leads a twelve-author team presenting SINTER3D, a method that rebuilds full three-dimensional gene activity maps from thin tissue slices, in 2026 work. Spatial transcriptomics reads which genes are active while keeping their place in tissue, yet slices leave large gaps when stacked. Older filling methods treat each gene separately and blur the picture. SINTER3D instead learns gene activity as a smooth function of three-dimensional position using a neural model. That allows it to make virtual slices, mark tissue regions, and estimate cell mixes anywhere in the volume.

The team tested the system on adult mouse brain, human cortex, developing human heart, fruit fly embryo, and breast cancer tissue. Across these sets it beat existing methods and rebuilt structures that made biological sense. The tool could help turn stacks of slices into true three-dimensional atlases of organs and tumors.
pmc-13508460:
Erdem Ozkan and Abdulvahap Kahveci test whether an ultrasound stiffness scan can tell Sjögren disease apart from diabetes in people with dry mouths and eyes, in 2026 work. Both conditions cause dryness, called sicca, yet one is immune attack on glands and the other is metabolic wear. Sorting them matters for treatment. The study enrolled 61 Sjögren patients, 42 diabetes patients with dryness, and 43 healthy controls of similar age. Both major saliva gland pairs were scanned for texture grade and stiffness.

Sjögren glands were stiffer and rougher than both other groups on every measure. Diabetes glands, by contrast, looked and felt much like healthy glands. Stiffness alone sorted the two diseases only moderately well. The authors suggest pairing stiffness with texture grading as a combined scan approach. Such a scan could help clinics triage dryness complaints without jumping straight to invasive gland biopsy, though sharper cutoffs are still needed.
pmc-13512160:
Priyanka Banerjee, Rachel Phillips, Anna G. Holliman, Soren P. Rodning, Wellison J. S. Diniz, and Paul W. Dyce join gene and metabolite data to probe why some beef heifers stay subfertile, in 2026 work. Poor fertility drives early culling and shortens herd life. The team collected egg-support cells and follicle fluid from crossbred heifers classed as fertile or subfertile, then read gene activity and small-molecule profiles in both materials.

Ninety genes differed in activity between the groups, including immune and signaling genes, and nine metabolites differed in the fluid, spanning vitamins, amino acids, and fatty compounds. Network maps in subfertile heifers looked heavily rewired next to fertile ones. Two metabolites, a fatty acid tied to inflammation and a vitamin E form, connected widely to immune genes. Pathway patterns split by group, with sugar and building-block routes marking fertile animals and protein-assembly routes marking subfertile ones.
pmc-13512260:
Aaron Chigona and eight co-authors assess health risks from eating wild foods and soil-like materials gathered along Zimbabwe's Great Dyke, in 2026 work. Communities in this mineral-rich belt rely on wild plants and deliberate soil eating, called geophagy, for nutrition and tradition. Rocks in the area carry toxic elements from the ground itself, and the team measured those contaminants against world health limits.

Half of the wild foods studied crossed the tolerable risk levels set by global food bodies. A wild fig and soil materials from the ultramafic Great Dyke ground carried the highest cancer and non-cancer risks. Taking medicinal plants as hot infusions cut contaminant intake a good deal. The authors urge environmental health policies that raise community awareness of the danger while respecting food traditions, plus safer preparation guidance.
pmc-13513360:
Irina Lyapina and eight co-authors study whether excess fat around the heart predicts how heart muscle remodels after mitral valve surgery, in 2026 work. The prospective study screened 148 patients with acquired, non-infectious mitral valve disease set for surgical repair under a heart-lung machine. Heart scans before surgery measured epicardial fat volume, and ultrasound tracked chamber sizes and strain patterns before surgery and across one year after.

Patients above a fat volume tied to atrial fibrillation showed larger upper chambers on both sides and weaker right heart pumping before surgery. Crossing that fat threshold multiplied the odds of a low right-heart motion score several times over. A second threshold tied to clustering metabolic risk factors framed another comparison. The authors argue that fat around the heart is not inert padding but a marker, and possibly a driver, of worse remodeling around valve surgery.
pmc-13515660:
Sun and colleagues built new drug candidates against tuberculosis by fusing two known weapons into single molecules, work reported in 2026. One half is thiolutin, a natural antibiotic; the other half comes from medicines already used against tuberculosis, including cycloserine and isoniazid. Chemical linkers of seven to ten carbon atoms join the two halves. The hope is that a combined molecule keeps the killing power of thiolutin while softening its harm to human cells.

The team synthesized 15 hybrid molecules and tested them against the tuberculosis bacterium. Cycloserine hybrids worked best, stopping bacterial growth at concentrations as low as 1 microgram per milliliter in the reported assays. Safety tests in mouse immune cells were encouraging: every cycloserine hybrid needed more than 40 micrograms per milliliter to harm half the cells, far gentler than thiolutin alone. Two hybrids, T1-CS and T4-CS, gave the best balance of potency and safety.
pmc-13517660:
Tong Guo and a large team report a mouse study, published in 2026. It asks whether polystyrene microplastics worsen liver harm from cadmium. Cadmium is a toxic metal. Mice received microplastics, cadmium, or both. Exposure lasted six weeks. The team examined liver injury. Gene activity in the liver was examined too.

Mice exposed to both pollutants had the worst liver damage. Their stress and inflammation signals were strongest. Their energy use was most deeply disturbed. The combined exposure disrupted a control pathway. It involves the AMPK and FOXO regulators. The liver cells' mitochondria were impaired. Plastic particles can amplify cadmium's harm in mammals, not just in fish, this suggests.
pmc-13517960:
Ostrovskii and colleagues surveyed in 2026 the genetic diversity of Babesia parasites in cattle across Kazakhstan. Babesia species are tick-borne parasites that invade red blood cells and cause babesiosis, a costly cattle disease. Earlier records for the country were patchy, so the team combined large-scale blood testing with gene sequencing and mapping to show where each species actually circulates.

They tested 6,455 cattle blood samples with nested PCR targeting the cytb gene and identified species using three gene sequences. Overall, 3.87 percent of samples were positive, spread across seventeen administrative regions, and among positives Babesia major made up 31.2 percent, Babesia occultans 29.6 percent, Babesia bigemina 18.0 percent, and the more dangerous Babesia bovis only 7.2 percent of detections. Infection rates varied sharply by region. The authors say molecular monitoring found babesiosis in regions where it had never been recorded.
pmc-13518860:
M T Elling and colleagues traced how distant oceans steer malaria ups and downs in Malawi. Published in 2026, the study joined malaria case records with weather observations, reanalysis data, and climate models to find the physical chain behind year-to-year swings. Earlier work had leaned on local weather links alone, without showing how they arise.

A warm tropical Atlantic brought wet weather to Malawi and more malaria cases, while a warm Indian Ocean brought hot, dry weather and fewer cases. Soil moisture proved the key link, since wet ground shapes the pools where mosquitoes breed and the parasite spreads. Looking ahead, climate change is expected to dry Malawian soils by 2100, though by an uncertain amount, which could redraw transmission maps. The work lays ground for early warning tools built on real climate physics rather than bare correlation.
pmc-13518960:
G Keerthana and R Padmanaban present HOA-OBL in 2026, a hybrid tool for assigning tasks to drone fleets. Drones serve disaster cleanup work, site checks, and watch duties, yet fixed task plans waste energy and overload some aircraft as conditions change. The base method, Hippopotamus Optimization, mimics hippo herd behavior but can settle too early on mediocre plans.

Opposition-based learning was woven in so the search also probes mirror-image plans, widening the hunt. Tests with 20 drones and 100 tasks cut energy use by roughly 17 to 33 percent versus four rival algorithms. Load spread evened out by about 33 to 50 percent. The pair argue the pairing scales better for real missions.
pmc-13520060:
Antreana Hadjipavlou leads a seven-author narrative review in 2026 on artificial intelligence tools for preserving the parathyroid glands during thyroid removal surgery. Missing or damaging these tiny glands causes lasting low calcium, a common and sometimes dangerous complication. Visual spotting by the surgeon remains standard, yet glands are small and wander in location.

Searching three databases for work from 2015 to 2025 surfaced 368 records, of which 11 studies qualified, covering AI or deep learning identification, often paired with near-infrared autofluorescence imaging. Hadjipavlou and colleagues judge the techniques feasible and promising for accuracy and speed. Evidence is still limited, so they call for high-quality prospective studies before clinical benefit can be claimed.
pmc-13520160:
Yu-yang Du leads an eleven-author review in 2026 on lipophagy, the process by which cells digest their own fat droplets through the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment. Stuck fat droplets poison cells and feed metabolic, heart, cancer, and brain diseases. How droplets get selected for digestion, and how to tune the process safely, remained unclear.

Effective digestion needs the droplet coat remodeled, nutrient sensors such as the AMPK-mTORC1-TFEB axis coordinating lysosome supply, and contact points where droplets trade lipids with other organelles. Lipophagy protects when it clears excess fat, yet misfiring can fuel inflammation, scarring, or tumors. The reviewers call for better biomarkers and tissue- and stage-specific interventions.
pmc-13520260:
Haiyue Wu leads a thirteen-author genome survey in 2026 of the myosin gene family in the Chinese mitten crab, a farmed freshwater species whose muscles rebuild in bursts at each molt. Gene activity was tracked across three larval stages, from swimming zoea through megalopa to early juvenile, alongside a full catalog of myosin genes.

The crab genome holds 23 myosin genes in 11 subfamilies, with the muscle-heavy Myo2 group expanded to nine members, likely through tandem copying on one chromosome. Comparisons across 42 animal species showed some myosin classes missing from all arthropods, marking lineage losses. Activity of individual genes rose or fell by stage, matching each phase's muscle demands during metamorphosis.
pmc-13520360:
Natalie B. Lister leads a large team that codes in 2026 what sits inside adult weight loss trials. All trials in the set also tracked eating disorder risk. Trials bundle many parts together. Sorting the parts may show which ones raise risk and which ones lower it.

The search found nearly 15,000 records at first pass. A total of 58 trials fit the coding rules. The trial teams checked coding for 26 of those trials. Checked arms used about 24 methods on average. Methods grouped into clusters such as food teaching. The list gives future trial teams shared words for planning safer weight loss care.
pmc-13521160:
Hosaam Nasr, Faisal A. Almudaiheem and Bader S. Alhamdan describe in 2026 limb-saving hybrid treatment for sudden leg artery blockage appearing shortly after knee replacement surgery. Such blockages are uncommon after joint replacement, yet delayed recognition risks limb loss because pain mimics normal post-surgery soreness.

Care combined open surgery to clear the artery behind the knee with catheter-based methods to restore flow down the leg. Trial evidence cited suggests hybrid routes can match limb salvage of either approach alone. The case walks through diagnostic pitfalls and staged revascularisation choices, offering a template for orthopaedic and vascular teams facing the same emergency.
pmc-13522060:
Mike P Wattjes and colleagues set consensus guidance for using MRI in multiple sclerosis diagnosis and monitoring in Germany. Published in 2026, the panel paper from the German Society of Neuroradiology, endorsed by the German Society of Neurology, responds to the 2024 McDonald criteria revisions. Those revisions added optic nerve imaging as a fifth site for spread, plus the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as markers for earlier diagnosis.

Guidance also covers MRI tracking of treatment, including progressive disease. New markers such as slowly expanding lesions and rim lesions are moving from trials toward routine care. Readers get a practical update that ties global criteria to German clinical routines.
pmc-13522360:
Xiaoxuan Zhu and colleagues published a 2026 community study from the Jidong area of China that sets reference ranges for blood vessel density in the macula, the central part of the retina. Healthy adults provided the reference group, while a separate group was used to test links with body-wide illness. Diabetes stood out in the second group, where people with diabetes tended to have lower density in the deeper layer and more often fell below low percentile cutoffs. Clinicians could use the ranges to judge an individual scan, although testing in other populations and on other devices is still needed.
pmc-13524160:
Pi-Yi Lin, Yu-Tong Yen, Ming-Jen Lu, and Han-Shui Hsu study, in a 2026 cohort, whether meeting early calorie targets helps septic patients in intensive care, grouped by nutritional risk score. Malnutrition is common in critical illness, yet benefit from early feeding was uncertain. The analysis used the modified Nutrition Risk in the Critically Ill score.

The cohort held 258 ventilated adults with sepsis in a surgical intensive care unit during 2021 and 2022. About 63 percent received under half of estimated calorie needs in the first five days, and the rest received at least half. Twenty-eight-day intensive care mortality did not differ significantly between groups. Kidney replacement therapy and longer ventilation predicted death in adjusted analysis. The authors conclude early calorie adequacy alone did not improve survival here.
pmc-13525960:
Cigdem Soydal leads a very large multicenter team in a 2026 study of dose and survival after transarterial radioembolization for a bile duct cancer arising inside the liver. The treatment delivers radioactive yttrium-90 microspheres through liver arteries. Which dose measures predict response and survival, for glass versus resin spheres, was the central question.

The retrospective cohort gathered patients treated between January 2014 and December 2024 across thirteen centers with lobar or segmental approaches. Post-treatment imaging, either SPECT or PET based, was reviewed centrally, and absorbed doses were computed for perfused liver, tumor, and whole liver with specialist software. Response was judged by comparing scans before treatment with scans two to four months later, grouping complete and partial responses together. Liver toxicity was graded on a standard scale.
pmc-13526460:
Bong and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 41-year-old woman who developed a painful left buttock mass years after gluteal fat grafting, known as a Brazilian butt lift. Her swelling appeared five years after a revision surgery, far later than most complications of the procedure.

Surgeons removed a mass measuring about five centimeters across and sent it for testing. The tissue showed fat death, hardening deposits, and a pocket of inflammation, but tests found no bacteria and no cancer. The authors note that such delayed sterile reactions can look like infection or tumors. They urge long-term follow-up after buttock fat grafting so late problems are caught and treated correctly.
pmc-13528060:
Mengjie Chen and three colleagues profile how lupus patients respond to the drug telitacicept in a 2026 exploratory study. The drug blocks two signals that drive antibody-making cells. Ten patients were sampled before and after treatment. Ten healthy controls joined for comparison. The team sequenced gene activity and B-cell receptor repertoires. The authors urge bigger studies to test that signal.
pmc-13529860:
Yoshinobu Kanda and six colleagues report a phase three trial of maribavir for cytomegalovirus in Japanese transplant patients in a 2026 study. The virus threatens people whose immunity is suppressed after grafts. Sixty-one patients enrolled at twenty-two sites. Forty-one received the oral drug, twice daily for eight weeks. Most were stem cell transplant recipients.

By week eight about sixty-eight percent had cleared the virus from blood, confirmed by repeat tests. About eighty-eight percent reported some side effect. Nausea led at about twenty-four percent, then anemia, fever, and headache. Two deaths occurred and were judged unrelated to the drug. The authors call the balance of benefit and tolerability acceptable. The group included patients whose infections resisted standard drugs. Maribavir thus fills a real gap in post-transplant care.
pmc-13530160:
Chih-Ping Hu and co-authors simulate in 2026 how chip panels warp and peel during fan-out panel-level packaging. Two build orders receive comparison: wiring first versus molding first. Carrier plates of steel, glass, and ceramic support the work, and two large panel sizes enter the models.

Heat, material shrinkage, and stepwise adding or removing of layers all shape the predicted bending. The wiring-first route matched real results best at an average reference temperature. Stress peaked in the same layers across cases, while the molding-first route warped sharply when panels were released. Close agreement with experiments backed the design guidance.
pmc-13531060:
Ajay P Kerai and co-authors detail a 2026 combined heart-lung transplant for a giant pulmonary artery aneurysm driven by high lung pressure. The 58-year-old woman had longstanding pressure disease of unknown cause, heart strain, and a leaking pulmonic valve. Her aneurysm had grown close to nine centimeters across.

Transplant replaced both organs at once, and graft function stayed excellent afterward. A stroke during recovery caused major lasting harm despite the sound grafts. The authors note aneurysms can keep growing even when pressure readings look stable, so waiting too long can close the transplant window.
pmc-13531760:
Priyadarshini Dutta and co-authors test in 2026 whether vaped cannabidiol relieves nerve pain in rats without harming lungs. CBD vapor did ease pain measurably. Lung tissue showed shifts in inflammatory signals and in a danger-sensing pathway that may explain harm. pmc-13531960:
O Trent Hall and colleagues survey in 2026 whether pain erodes safer injection habits among people who inject opioids. A total of 130 people recruited at a syringe service program compared their own practices during best and worst pain over the prior week. Everyone had training and free sterile equipment, which isolates pain as the variable.

At worst pain, participants washed hands less, cleaned the injection site less, and waited less often for a clean safe place. Equipment reuse rose, as did injecting faster or at a higher dose. Pain itself emerges as a harm-reduction target beside equipment supply.
pmc-13532760:
Chen and Martinez-Cardoso studied job lock in 2026, the bind of older workers who keep working out of need even though they want to retire. Using a long-running national survey of Americans aged 50 and over, they tracked 5,217 workers for more than six years to see whether feeling locked in predicted later health problems.

Job lock was common, reported by more than three in four workers at the start. Those workers later had higher odds of rating their health as fair or poor, of depressive symptoms, of other psychiatric problems. Of being overweight or obese, even after pay, background, and habits were taken into account. Links grew stronger for people who stayed employed the whole period, and for workers aged 62 and over heart disease joined the list. The authors urge steps that lower the money and insurance barriers to retiring.
pmc-13534660:
Matej Martinc and colleagues benchmark in 2026 machine learning models that map electric polarisation in ferroelectric materials from advanced electron microscope data. Such maps reveal function, yet reading them from four-dimensional diffraction data is hard by hand. Four model types were trained and compared on a niobate material.

Models trained on synthetic patterns scored high on matching synthetic tests, yet the gap to real experiments stayed a major barrier. A prototype training scheme plus classic dimension methods with augmentation looked most promising for closing that gap. Error patterns also matched crystal defects, hinting at defect detection uses.
pmc-13536760:
Clement Munguiko leads a 2026 scoping review mapping models for teaching health trainees at the bedside. Training now demands shared skills worldwide, yet guidance on teaching models stays scattered. Searches in early January 2026 across five databases plus grey sources covered work from 2000 to 2025. From thousands of records, 26 studies qualified and eight distinct teaching models were mapped.

Two models appeared most often, one built around brief focused coaching and one built around learner-led case reasoning. Most studies came from the United States and involved medical students, with none from Africa. No single model fit every setting. Clear structure, active learner roles, reflection, feedback, and role modeling recurred across models. The authors urge faculty training and research in low-resource settings.
pmc-13536860:
Alemayehu Abate and Melkamnesh Azage study bloodstream infections in young children in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, in a 2026 clinic survey from late 2025. Blood infections with drug-resistant germs threaten children under five years most. About one in five children had a bloodstream infection, most often from Klebsiella pneumoniae, with gut and related germs making up most isolates. Resistance ran high against many common antibiotics and lowest against two reserve options. Infants, fever lasting over a week, and partial or missing immunization each raised infection odds. The authors urge stronger drug oversight, fuller immunization, and faster diagnosis.
pmc-13536960:

Published in 2026, the study ran two rounds of talks with 20 adults who had doctor-confirmed severe hypertriglyceridemia and recent symptoms. The scale, built for familial chylomicronemia syndrome, asks about that condition's symptoms and daily impacts.

All 20 adults named trouble thinking and tiredness, 19 named diarrhea, and 18 named belly pain, matching the scale's four items. All 20 found the items easy to grasp, and most said a one- to two-point gain would count as real progress. The authors conclude the four items fairly capture symptoms in this group. Readers get a tested scale for trials and care in severe high blood fats.
pmc-13538060:
Saadia N. Mirza and colleagues report new enzyme routes to improved polyene antifungals in a 2026 study. Polyenes kill fungi broadly yet harm patients through toxicity and dissolve poorly, while chemical rebuilding is costly and wasteful. The team uncovered pathways to previously unknown polyenes, including unusual enzymes that attach sugars to the core structure. A second enzyme family was also retuned to swap a harmful chemical group for friendlier options.

Adding a second sugar plus swapping the harmful group produced polyenes with stronger fungal killing and lower toxicity in tests. Clean fermentation and enzyme routes reached the new compounds without heavy chemical synthesis. The authors present enzyme tailoring as a practical path to safer, more affordable antifungal drugs as resistance rises.
pmc-13538460:
Hirotake Ishida and colleagues track sensory nerve activity after burn injury in mice in a 2026 study of lingering pain and itch. Burns often leave weeks of itch during healing, yet nerve workings behind the timeline stay unclear. Pain behavior peaked on the first day and faded within five days, while itch behavior peaked at one week and lasted up to four weeks. Numbers of spontaneously active nerve cells rose on both checked recovery days. Heat-sensing cell shares held steady, while itch-probe cell shares dipped early and partly recovered. The authors link heightened spontaneous nerve firing to both post-burn pain and itch.
pmc-13538560:
Fangyuan Zheng and colleagues compare light-activated particles for destroying a stubborn drug pollutant in varied waters in a 2026 study. Chloroquine phosphate survives standard wastewater treatment and threatens aquatic life. Five metal oxide particles were tested under ultraviolet light in pure water, drinking water, and synthetic seawater. Particle traits were measured alongside the aggressive oxygen species each produced.

Titanium dioxide performed best, clearing most of the drug in drinking water in line with its top oxygen species output. Zinc and cerium oxides worked moderately, swayed by acidity and salt content. Bismuth and tungsten oxides lagged, especially in complex waters. The authors stress testing cleaners in realistic waters and back titanium dioxide as the sturdiest option.
pmc-13540260:
Zhenrong Zhang and seven colleagues ask, in a 2026 modelling study, whether resting pulse rate helps predict falls among older people with glaucoma. Glaucoma steals side vision, and falls in this group can mean fractures and long hospital stays.

From a national Chinese ageing survey, 249 people with glaucoma who had not fallen at the 2015 baseline were followed to 2018, with a much larger non-glaucoma group for comparison. Several prediction methods, including an XGBoost model, combined health, medicine, vision, and laboratory measures. Interpretable machine learning was used to weigh what the pulse reading added. The authors stress that pulse is a supporting feature, not a stand-alone eye measure.
pmc-13540460:

Mitochondria then take up copper and trigger a copper-driven death called cuproptosis, followed by iron release and a second death mode, ferroptosis. The team packaged the compound in membrane-coated nanoparticles aimed at these cells and saw matching effects in rodents.
pmc-13542160:

The method first scores how strongly variables interact. It phrases the cutting task as a maximum-cut problem. An Ising-model solver then makes the cut. Delivery routing tests showed clear gains. Feasible answers came far more often than before. The method reached in one minute what the naive method needed thirty minutes for. It also cut most variables out of the main problem.
pmc-13542760:

pmc-13543360:

pmc-13543760:

pmc-13547360:

The combination shifted the markers more than either drug alone. The authors call for further study of a supportive role in lung cancer settings.
pmc-13547560:

pmc-13548560:

pmc-13548660:

pmc-13549760:

pmc-13549960:

pmc-13551760:

Average stereotype scores sat near the middle of the reported scale. Regression linked stronger stereotypes to first-time surgery and higher illness burden scores, while patients who preferred active decision-making scored lower in the reported model. The authors aim the findings at spotting high-risk patients early so perioperative support can protect recovery and quality of life.
pmc-13551860:

pmc-13551960:

pmc-13554160:

pmc-13554360:

pmc-13558560:

Calm, controlled inflammation at the meeting point of mother and fetus is essential, yet how this alarm is tuned across gestation was murky. The team compared tissue from early pregnancies, preterm births, and full-term births, measuring gene activity, protein amounts, enzyme processing, and cytokine levels side by side.

Early placentas carried the highest cytokine levels and the most inflammasome protein despite quiet gene readings. Preterm placentas grouped apart in gene activity and stockpiled alarm parts without switching the key enzyme on. Term placentas raised gene activity while protein and one signature cytokine fell. The authors describe later pregnancy as a primed yet restrained state, loaded but held back, with preterm tissue caught in its own distinct configuration.
pmc-13558760:
Claire Huchthausen and six colleagues showed in 2026 that teaching a lung nodule model with more mature cases only helps when the image statistics are corrected with biology in mind. Radiomic models promise earlier cancer calls on CT scans, yet early nodules in their set numbered barely a hundred and scanners vary. Classifiers trained on those alone performed near chance, so the team added more than two hundred later-stage benign and malignant nodules and tried three ways of harmonising the four acquisition protocols.

Plain harmonisation that ignored biology failed to improve the models consistently. Correcting with a covariate that knows which dataset each nodule came from, or harmonising each dataset separately, lifted test accuracy significantly on both standard measures. The authors call the study a proof of principle on a small single-centre set, with a clear methodological moral for radiomics.
pmc-13559460:
Jingyao Hui and colleagues built a machine learning model to predict bone marrow suppression in lung cancer patients receiving PD-1 inhibitors plus platinum doublet chemotherapy. Their 2026 study drew retrospectively on patients treated at the First Hospital of Lanzhou University between July 2018 and March 2026. Marrow suppression is a serious complication of this common regimen for non-small cell lung cancer.

Three feature-selection methods converged on eight predictors, including age, body mass index, tumor size, and several blood counts. Several learning models were trained and compared, with light gradient boosting performing best. Its accuracy held up reasonably in a held-out test set and in a later, separate patient cohort used for external validation. Explanation analysis showed which factors pushed individual predictions up or down. The authors offer the model as decision support for anticipating marrow toxicity, while noting its roots in a single center's records.
pmc-13562460:
Denise Aparecida Passarelli, Táhcita Medrado Mizael, and Júlio C. de Rose surveyed a thin research field: studies of anti-Black bias inside behavior analysis, a branch of psychology built on observable behaviour. Following standard review methods, they gathered 23 empirical studies published across 27 specialist journals between 1964 and 2026. Their 2026 review sorts the studies into surveys, measurement tests, and interventions.

Surveys linked values, mental flexibility, and racial attitudes, while measurement tools based on relational frame theory caught hidden biases that questionnaires missed. Training programs, especially with children, showed early promise in loosening biased associations, but many studies lacked control groups or follow-up. The authors call for a more careful, cumulative research agenda to support antiracist work in the field.
pmc-13563860:
Bakhtiyar Islamzade and two colleagues measure stress, anxiety, and depression among postgraduate dental students, a group carrying patient responsibility on top of study demands. Undergraduate distress is well documented; the postgraduate years are not. Their 2026 study surveyed 192 trainees with a demographic form and the DASS-21 questionnaire, a 21-item distress scale. Scores were doubled to match the severity bands, then related to training factors with correlation and regression models.

The three states moved together tightly, every pairing significant. Stress and anxiety together explained a share of depression scores, with a model value of 0.696 for variance explained. Most trainees landed in the normal band on each subscale. Feeling financially middling, rather than comfortable, hinted at higher distress without holding up in the full model. Year of training, specialty, housing, and smoking showed no differences. The authors advise reading the web of distress as one problem, not three.
pmc-13563960:
Madeline Pan and co-authors examine, in a 2026 retrospective study, vision in 450 patients with intermediate dry age-related macular degeneration at one academic center over a decade. Care records for 759 eyes were split by smoking history and by whether patients took AREDS vitamin supplements, a standard aid for this stage of disease.

Patients taking the supplements started with better vision than those who did not, in both smokers and non-smokers. Vision changes through follow-up were tracked with standard eye-chart measures converted for analysis. The work highlights a baseline gap that can shape how later results are read, and it gives eye clinics a reason to record supplement use and smoking carefully.
pmc-13566460:
Julia A. Ford and Ora Gewurz-Singer write, in a 2026 review for rheumatologists, about kidney disease driven by the antibody IgA, and whether progress in one condition can help another. IgA nephropathy harms only the kidneys, while IgA vasculitis also causes skin, joint, and gut symptoms, yet evidence increasingly links their causes.

Drug trials in nephropathy have recently produced several targeted approvals, while vasculitis still lacks strong randomized trials. The authors compare how the two illnesses appear, explain the shared multi-step disease model, and ask which new drugs might suit vasculitis patients with kidney involvement. Rheumatologists get a bridge between a fast-moving field and their own slower one.
pmc-13569260:
Roberto Busi's team identified the mutation behind herbicide-resistant brome grass in southern Australia, in a 2026 study. Brome grass ranks among growers' most troublesome weeds, costing tens of millions in lost yield, and two groups collected before the 2023 harvest survived several ALS-blocking herbicides. The team characterised the level and mechanism of resistance in both groups.

All thirty plants examined carried the same point mutation, swapping tryptophan for leucine at position 574 of the ALS enzyme, and blocking detox enzymes did not change survival. The finding marks the first report of this mutation driving cross-resistance to three ALS herbicide classes in Australian brome grass. Growers will need pre-emergence herbicides, tolerant crops, and harvest weed-seed control to manage these groups.
pmc-13570360:
Guanglong Liu and colleagues feed, in a 2026 trial, plant flavonoids from Silphium perfoliatum to 250 young broiler chickens challenged with a bacterial toxin that injures the gut. Five groups compared no treatment, toxin alone, and toxin plus three flavonoid doses in feed, with growth, gut shape, antioxidant enzymes, immune signals, and gut microbes all measured.

Flavonoid-fed birds regained growth, grew taller gut villi, and carried stronger antioxidant defenses with calmer inflammatory signals. Gut barrier genes switched on more strongly, and the cecal microbe mix recovered diversity and helpful species. Poultry producers get a feed additive candidate that protects the gut during inflammatory stress.
pmc-13571260:
Danii L. S. Suijk and colleagues write, in a 2026 letter, about testing losartan, empagliflozin, and both together for lowering blood uric acid in people with type 2 diabetes. High uric acid tracks with heart and kidney disease in this group. Twenty-four participants aged from twenty-five upward entered the comparison of the two familiar drugs.

Each drug is thought to raise uric acid loss in urine through the same kidney transporter. One is a proven diabetes and kidney protector. The other is a blood pressure drug with a known uric acid benefit in a landmark trial. Because the pair is often prescribed together, the study separates their individual and combined effects on uric acid levels and urine clearance. The design answers a practical question for combination prescribing.
pmc-13572360:
Meng Zhang and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how the fuel choices of macrophages, the immune cells that crowd ovarian tumors, decide whether those cells attack the cancer or shelter it. Sugar burning, oxygen-based energy, and glutamine use each push macrophages toward one of two broad states, inflammatory or suppressive.

Tumor-associated macrophages mostly settle in the suppressive state, helping the cancer escape immunity and resist treatment. The review connects each metabolic pathway to that balance and surveys nanoscale delivery strategies that aim to reprogram macrophage fuel use precisely inside tumors. Ovarian cancer remains highly lethal, and retraining its resident immune cells offers a route that direct tumor drugs have not delivered.
pmc-13572460:
Marianna Piras, with 15 colleagues, reports a 2026 study of blood chemistry shifts tied to weight gain from mental health drugs. Many such drugs add weight and raise heart risk, but the body changes behind the gain are not well mapped. The team used a broad scan of small molecules in blood plasma, not just a few set markers.

The study drew on a cohort of patients who started a weight-linked drug, with 151 follow-up visits from 135 patients. Blood was drawn at the start and again later, and a strict selection method picked 56 features tied to weight change per month. Ten were named, and six were confirmed against standards. Gains in fat-like molecules and in breakdown products of tryptophan tracked with more weight gain. Two compounds tracked the other way. The named set may seed early warning tests.
pmc-13572560:
Lucie Frejlichová, with five colleagues, details a 2026 study of a fungus that may threaten oak seedlings in nurseries. Pedunculate oak anchors European forests, and nursery stock can carry hidden trunk pathogens. The fungus Cadophora luteo-olivacea is known from grapevine disease, but its power to harm oak was unproven.

Inoculated seedlings grew stem lesions that averaged 11.9 centimetres, while controls showed just 0.9 centimetres of wound response. That gap met the classic test for proving a pathogen. In paired dishes, a second fungus, Trichoderma atroviride, cut the pathogen's spread. Protein and chemical scans of the contact zone at days four and eight found 257 shifted proteins by day eight, among them wall-cutting enzymes. Ergosterol, a fungal membrane part, fell. The work feeds nursery risk checks and biocontrol trials.
pmc-13573360:
Yang and colleagues built in 2026 a prediction chart, called a nomogram, for deep vein thrombosis before surgery in patients with broken lower leg bones from injury. Such clots in deep veins are a common and dangerous complication. The team studied 950 surgical patients at their hospital, split into a training group of 665 and a checking group of 285. They tested a blood score called the systemic immune-inflammation index, which blends immune cell counts.

Yang found five independent predictors of clots before surgery: age, fracture site, the inflammation index, a clot breakdown marker called D-dimer, and a clotting time measure. The nomogram built from these factors matched observed outcomes well in both the training and checking groups. The authors say the chart helps clinicians flag high-risk fracture patients early, before surgery, so preventive steps can start in time.
pmc-13573460:
Xiang-yu Zhang, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 study of blood sugar swings in intensive care patients with severe pneumonia. Sugar control often slips in critical illness, and swings, not just high levels, may harm. The team asked whether the path of those swings over the first days splits patients into risk groups.

The study followed 315 patients at one Chinese hospital from 2021 to 2024. A trajectory model found two paths: a small group whose swings started high and stayed high, and a large group with low, steady swings. Early outcomes matched, but after day 14 the high-swing group died more often. On arrival, that group also showed higher infection and long-term sugar markers. Those two markers together flagged the high-swing path well. The authors urge early checks to catch the risky path.
pmc-13574160:
S. Marina Casalino-Matsuda and a large team report a 2026 study of a channel blocker drug in severe viral pneumonia. In bad COVID-19 lung disease, T cells and lung macrophages feed each other's inflammation in a loop. Both cell types use CRAC channels to take in calcium, and the blocker Auxora closes those channels. A prior trial had linked it to far lower 30-day death.

This side study followed a small group of ventilated patients with lab-confirmed disease. Blood levels of two signals, one that calls in fresh immune cells and one growth factor, fell after the drug but not after placebo. Lung wash cell mixes did not shift clearly, and gene changes stayed below firm proof. In lab tests with healthy donor cells, the drug blocked calcium entry in a dose-linked way. The authors frame the work as exploratory mechanism hunting.
pmc-13574760:
Serena Basta, with two colleagues, presents a 2026 proof-of-concept measure for body schema, the brain's working map of the body in action. Few tools can put a number on that map, and lifestyle may shape it over a life. The team used the disorder, or entropy, in the strokes of a self-drawing as the number.

Forty-four adults drew themselves, then a flower as a control, and filled in an activity survey. Body drawings carried lower local entropy than flower drawings once stroke length was counted, which hints the score taps body-specific structure. Leftover entropy fell with age, as if the map settles over time. Activity showed no clear main effect, yet active older adults held their entropy steady. The authors call for balanced follow-up studies to firm the method up.
pmc-13575260:
Hojun Yu leads a 2026 study building a machine learning model that predicts worsening chronic kidney disease in Korean patients. The standard risk equation was built abroad and performs unevenly across ethnic groups. It also misses how a patient's readings change over time.

Records from a Seoul hospital covered 28,209 patients for model building, with a national cohort of 3,960 used for outside checking. Four learning methods were blended into one voting model. Inside the hospital data it scored 0.939 on the standard discrimination measure, clearly above the standard equation. Outside performance was closer to the equation's score. Starting kidney function, its rate of change, albumin, and haemoglobin mattered most. The authors propose the equation for community screening and their model for hospital care.
pmc-13576260:
Weipeng Li and six colleagues study whether the change in a clotting marker around surgery predicts dangerous blood clots in womb cancer patients, in a 2026 cohort study. D-dimer is a protein fragment that rises when clots form and break down. Vein clots after surgery are a severe risk in this cancer.

The study followed 307 surgical patients in Fujian from 2022 to 2024. Each unit rise in D-dimer change lifted clot odds by about 20 percent after wide adjustment. The link was not a straight line: below a change value of 3.78 the risk climbed steeply, while above it the risk eased. Blood thinners, infection, and one lab value explained almost none of the pattern. The authors call the findings early signals that tracking the marker's path, not single values, may sharpen risk checks.
pmc-13578260:
Weiting Shi, Wenkai Shi, Ye He, and Yuwei Wang chart how well art and cultural tourism fit together across China in a 2026 study. They built yearly scores for 31 provinces from 2014 to 2023. The scores ask how smoothly the art side and the travel side adapt to each other. That question grows sharper as the field shifts from growth in size toward growth in quality.

Fit rose over the decade in a wavy climb. Most provinces still sat at low or middle levels, with wide gaps between regions. A machine learning model with an explainer tool ranked what drives the fit. Clean surroundings and public services set the floor. Roads and data links carried the system. Spending on culture and new ideas drove lasting gains. Each driver helped most at certain stages, not in a straight line.
pmc-13578860:
Ingmar Visser leads a thirty laboratory team that retested a famous claim about how babies learn sound rules, in a registered report study. A 1999 study reported that seven month olds learned abstract patterns in syllable strings and applied them to new sounds. The new effort ran a close copy across many labs, testing 839 babies aged five to twelve months, with 650 kept after exclusions.

Babies heard pattern strings, then new strings that matched or broke the pattern, while looking times were timed. Longer looking at the odd ones out would signal learning. No such gap appeared in the pooled results, and a second analysis leaned strongly toward no effect at all. Language mix, age, and test variant changed nothing. Thirty of thirty one lab samples matched the null result, raising hard questions for the field.
pmc-13579760:
Maria Castronuovo and colleagues trace a two way partnership between two proteins that drive chronic lymphocytic leukemia, in a 2026 study. The proteins, called FAK and ROR1, sit in the signal webs that help these white blood cells survive, move, and hide in tissues. Patient cells were prodded with a signal molecule, dosed with a FAK blocker, and sorted into dividing and resting fractions by surface markers.

Triggering ROR1 switched FAK on, while blocking FAK lowered ROR1 in return, proving the loop runs both ways. Dividing cells fresh out of lymph nodes carried the most of both proteins. The FAK blocker teamed with standard targeted drugs to kill far more leukemia cells, even when support cells tried to shield them. The authors pitch the drug pair for hard to treat cases, citing the blocker's clean safety record in solid tumor trials.
pmc-13580060:
Nima Khodakarami and colleagues trace which children keep returning to emergency rooms for asthma, in a 2026 study built on emergency records from three U.S. states. The data hold over four hundred fifty seven thousand asthma visits for children aged two to eighteen. Office care and drug plans often fail these families, pushing them back to hospital doors.

Visit rates ran more than two times higher for children under eleven than for teenagers. Black and Hispanic children and those on public insurance carried heavier burdens, as did children in poorer or non metro areas. Good prior office care cut the return odds by about a fifth, a protective lever the authors highlight. They close with calls for drug access fixes and smarter discharge planning.
pmc-13582060:
Kazuki Aihara and colleagues compared three drug-coated balloons in rabbits, asking which delivers drug to the artery with the least downstream harm. Coated balloons help leg arteries, but drug particles washing downstream can injure distant muscle, a worry in severe limb disease. Their 2026 study gave 18 rabbits aorta balloon treatment with Ranger, IN.PACT Admiral, or Luminor devices, then checked treated arteries and downstream leg muscle at 28 days.

Drug levels at the target and muscle-cell loss there were similar across devices. Downstream, however, Luminor left far more drug in muscle and the worst particle embolisation, followed by IN.PACT, with Ranger lowest. The authors conclude that the low-dose Ranger device pairs strong local delivery with lower downstream risk, while clinical studies must confirm limb outcomes.
pmc-13582360:
Konstantinos Prokopidis and colleagues test how hospital stay length and muscle loss feed each other in older patients, in a 2026 study from Copenhagen. Just over one thousand inpatients aged sixty five and up had muscle mass, grip strength, walking speed, and chair rise power measured within a day of arrival. Sarcopenia, the named syndrome of weak, thin muscle, was scored by European rules.
